PREFACE 

The purpose of these volumes is to supply adequate text material, and questions and problems for courses in intermediate and advanced accounting. Each of the two volumes is self-contained. Either volume may be used independently, or both may be used, or certain sections of each volume may be selected to fit the demands and requirements of the accounting curricula of any college or university. 

The fundamental prerequisites for a full comprehension of the more complicated and intricate phases of intermediate and advanced accounting lie in the first year course. Volume I of Advanced Accounting opens with a short review of first year general principles, and then develops the problems of advanced working sheet and financial statement preparation. The following series of chapters is devoted to a full development of corporation accounting. The problems of income determination and the valuation of assets and liabilities are then considered; the material for asset and liability valuation is divided into a chapter for each asset and each liability, or into chapters for each class of asset and liability. Comparative statements, the statement of application of funds, and financial statement analysis conclude 

Volume I. 

Volume II is more specialized in nature, opening with a consideration of agencies and branches, followed by chapters dealing with consolidated balance sheets and consolidated statements of profit and loss. 

Advanced accounting problems of partnerships are treated next, followed by a section on receiverships, the statement of affairs, and the statement of realization and liquidation. The section pertaining to the accounting for estates and trusts is followed by chapters concerning insurance accounting, managerial accounting, bank accounting, stock brokerage accounting, foreign exchange, budgets, and governmental accounting.

Modern practice is emphasized throughout both volumes. The effect of the decisions of regulatory bodies on accounting is developed. 

Each chapter contains questions and problems adequate to fulfill the requirements of any course in intermediate and advanced accounting. The problem material, which appears in a separate section at the back of this book, is sufficient to enable the instructor to alternate the problems over a two or three year period, depending upon the number of hours devoted to the course.

Chapter I  

Introduction. Introductory courses in accounting emphasize the principles which govern the construction and operation of accounts. 

This is proper, because analysis, interpretation, valuation, and income determination are impossible unless accounts have been properly constructed and accurately kept. The mere compilation of data is ineffective; at frequent intervals the data must be subjected to analysis. The beginner studies the recording aspects of accounting. The more advanced student pursues accounting into its more intricate phases, relates the accounts to management, and thereby interests himself in whatever conclusions may be drawn from the analytical study of the accounting data.

To render all processes of analysis, interpretation, valuation, and income determination effective, adequate personnel and appropriate methods must be employed, and the routine procedures should be such as to reduce the possibility of error to a minimum. 

Transactions. Strictly from the point of view of account recording, a transaction is an occurrence which necessitates an accounting entry. 

The transaction may be the result of an exchange or contract between the business and an outside party, or it may be the result of operations or occurrences exclusively within the organization. In either case, the transaction must result in a monetary consideration affecting values and income in order to qualify for account entry. When a transaction occurs, it is analyzed in terms of its effect upon the accounts of the business, and then is recorded. 

Journalizing. After proper analysis, the transaction is entered in a journal, which is the book of original accounting entry. The journal may vary from the two-column general journal to special multi-column journals designed to meet the requirements of any individual organization. When special journals are used, the general journal is restricted to opening entries, adjusting entries, closing entries, correcting entries, and unusual or non-recurring entries which cannot be placed 1

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

in a special journal. Journal vouchers frequently are used in place of a general journal; each journal voucher carries a complete transaction analysis, and a complete file of these journal vouchers constitutes the general journal.

Under modern accounting machine practices, routine entries are entered directly into the accounts from the original evidence of the transaction (sales slip, cash register tape, customer invoice, creditor invoice, etc.); these business papers are then filed and become substitutes for the various journals. 

Posting to the Accounts.-After transactions are entered in the journals they are posted to the ledger accounts. Ledgers may be classified as general ledgers and subsidiary ledgers. A controlling account is one in the general ledger, the balance of which equals the sum of the balances of a group of accounts in a subsidiary ledger. Subsidiary accounts are kept constantly up-to-date by daily posting from the journals. Controlling accounts and other general ledger accounts usually receive their postings (1) from special columns at the end of the month, (2) from the general journal, and (3) from the miscellaneous or "sundry" columns of special journals at the time the entry is journalized or at the convenience of the bookkeeper. 

Because special column journal postings are deferred to the end of a month or other time interval, the general ledger is not "in balance" until all postings are completed at the end of a period. 

The Trial Balance.-At the end of the period, or more frequently if desired, the equality of debits and credits in the general ledger is tested by the preparation of a trial balance. The balance of each 

General Ledger account is extracted and listed in either the Debit or the Credit column of the trial balance. If the trial balance of the accounts does not balance, the errors must be located before progressing with additional work. Periodically, it is necessary also to prove the balance of each controlling account against the sum of the subsidiary accounts controlled, to determine that neither the controlling account nor the subsidiary accounts are incorrect.

The Work Sheet.-Trial balances commonly are entered directly on the work sheet, which, when completed, contains the adjusting entries and all data necessary for the preparation of the statements and for the closing journal entries. The work sheet is a convenience tool, and is not a part of the formal accounts and records. The reader

is familiar with at least the simple eight-column working sheet; advanced work sheets are presented in chapter III. 

Adjustments. A thorough knowledge and understanding of endof-the-period adjustments is necessary before one is adequately equipped to prepare work sheets and accounting statements. 

When properly kept, double entry books provide an accurate record of details covering all transactions. These details are arranged in accordance with the classification of accounts used, so that a trial balance taken at the end of an accounting period provides the basis for the orderly preparation of statements and their interpretation. 

The Importance of Adjustments.-The trial balance of the accounts is normally taken before the accounts are adjusted at the end of the accounting period. As a result, the trial balance does not contain all of the data necessary for the preparation of an accurate statement of profit and loss, a balance sheet and a Statement of Surplus. Therefore, after determining the accuracy of the equality of account debits and credits as expressed in the trial balance, it is necessary to correct or adjust certain of the accounts (1) so that they may lead to correct statement preparation and (2) so that they may lend themselves to proper and accurate analyses. 

The trial balance is taken and a work sheet prepared for the following reasons: 

1. A company may wish to prepare statements once a month and at the same time may wish to close its books only once a year. By taking a trial balance each month, and by preparing an interim work sheet, accurate monthly statements may be prepared without disturbing or adjusting the ledger accounts. An untold amount of work would be required if it were necessary each month to prepare the adjusting journal entries, post them, and then prepare the statements. 

2. Trial balance figures are necessary for the preparation of certain adjusting entries. 

3. The trial balance may be extracted immediately following the posting of all routine transactions. 

4. If frequent trial balances are prepared, errors are segregated to a relatively short period. 

5. By recording the adjustments first on the work sheet, all of them are scientifically organized in one place, to be copied into the journal and posted when time permits. 

6. By taking a trial balance first and then by recording the adjust-

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

ments in the work sheet, statements may be prepared in a shorter time from an organized source, and they are available at an earlier date than they would be if their preparation awaited the formal closing of the books.

Classes of Adjustments.-There are six natural classes of adjusting entries: (1) for inventory, (2) for depreciation and bad debts, (3) for accrued expenses, (4) for accrued incomes, (5) for deferred charges, (6) for deferred credits to income. Adjusting entries are the same in nature as any entry, representing transactions which have occurred, but which were not entered during the accounting period simply because it was more convenient to record them at the close of the period.

The third method of adjusting inventories is the same as the second, 'but the adjusting entries are entered directly in the Profit-and-Loss accounts, thus eliminating the Cost of Goods Sold clearing account. 

Depreciation and Bad Debts.-Depreciation is a decline in value due to wear, tear, the natural action of the elements, inadequacy, obsolescence, and the passage of time. Bad debts is an expense arising from the uncollectibility of sales made on account or for notes. 

Depreciation is a continuous expense which does not stop for one instant of time; however, it is the customary and simpler procedure to wait until the close of an accounting period to record the depreciation instead of recording it more frequently. 

Depreciation expense accounts should be maintained so that depreciation may be divided between manufacturing, selling, and administrative expenses when a statement of profit and loss is prepared. If only one Reserve for Depreciation account (known as a "blanket" reserve) is maintained, no indication is given of the amount of the reserve for each depreciable asset or group. If a blanket Reserve for 

Depreciation account is maintained on the general ledger, subsidiary ledgers should also be maintained for depreciation réserves for each asset, or for each asset group, such as Buildings, Machinery, and others. 

In computing the periodic depreciation expense of an asset, three factors must be known or estimated: 

1. The cost or other basis of valuing the asset 

2. The estimated life of the asset 

3. The estimated scrap value of the asset 

Assume that a building cost $54,000.00, and had an estimated life of 25 years and an estimated scrap value of $4,000.00. The annual depreciation rate is 4 per cent of depreciable value and the amount is $2,000.00. The rate of depreciation based on cost is 3.7037 per cent. 

The annual adjustment to record the depreciation is: 

Depreciation Expense on Building.... 

Reserve for Depreciation of Building..

To record the annual depreciation expense on building for the year 1942. .2,000.00 2,000.00

If the company closed its books once a month instead of annually, the amount in the foregoing entry would be reduced to one-twelfth of the annual amount or $166.67.

The debit to Depreciation Expense on Building appears as an annually recurring expense on the statement of profit and loss. The Reserve for Depreciation of Building account is shown in the balance sheet as a deduction from the cost or other basis of valuing the asset. The 

Reserve for Depreciation account, through the annual credits to it, increases until its balance is $50,000.00 (25 years X $2,000.00 per year), at which time depreciation adjustments stop.

The Depreciation Expense account is, as its name indicates, an expense account which is closed to the Profit-and-Loss account at the end of the period. The Reserve for Depreciation account is an asset valuation account, representing a suspended credit to the asset. By permitting the asset to remain in its account at cost, and by permitting the reserve to accumulate, the original valuation and the total expired portion of the value are both shown. On the balance sheet, the accumulated total of the reserve is shown as a deduction from the asset; thus at the end of ten years: Building

Less: Reserve for Depreciation of Building. 

$54,000.00 

20,000.00 $34,000.00 

To summarize the adjustments for depreciation: 

Depreciation Expense on (name of asset). 

Reserve for Depreciation of (name of asset) .XXX

XXX The debit is always an expense. The credit is to the asset valuation account, which has the effect of reducing the carrying or book value of the asset.

The adjustment for bad debts is similar to that for depreciation. 

The entry is as follows: 

Bad Debts Expense. 

Reserve for Bad Debts.. 

.XXX

XXX The Bad Debts Expense debit is shown in the statement of profit and loss and the account is closed to the Profit-and-Loss account. The 

Reserve for Bad Debts is shown in the balance sheet as a deduction from the Accounts Receivable balance. It is a suspended credit to 

Accounts Receivable; that is, it is suspended until the identity of the bad accounts is determined, at which time the transfer entry is made. 

When the reserve is set up at the end of each period the amount charged to Bad Debts Expense and credited to the Reserve does not

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

represent the accounts that actually have proved to be uncollectible; if this were the situation the entry would be a charge to Bad Debts Expense and credit to the Accounts Receivable control account and to the proper subsidiary accounts. The adjusting entry rather is the estimate of the amount that is uncollectible now, but not possible of allocation to specific accounts until a future date. When that future date arrives and an account does prove to be uncollectible, the entry is: 

Reserve for Bad Debts.. 

Accounts Receivable 

To charge off the account of James James as uncollectible. .XXX

XXX Thus it is seen that no expense is incurred when the account receivable is charged off. The expense is incurred in the period in which the sale is made, by the end-of-the-period adjustment. 

Some companies do not use the reservè method, but charge off each account directly as it proves to be uncollectible by a charge to the Bad Debts Expense account and a credit to the Accounts Receivable account. 

In such situations no reserve appears on the balance sheet, and bad debts expenses normally are recognized in some accounting period other than the period in which the sale is made which is responsible for the bad account.

When the reserve method is used, the reserve must be large enough to cover uncollectible notes receivable and acceptances receivable in addition to accounts receivable. The reserve is not for a specific period in the future, but should continue to have a credit balance so long as any present accounts receivable are on the books and doubtful of collection.

Accrued Expenses.—An accrued expense is one that has been incurred but is not payable at the closing date. The accrued expenses necessitate adjusting entries because they do not appear in the trial balance; they accrue in proportion to time or in proportion to services rendered, or at the end of the period invoices have not been received for certain expenses; therefore they have not been recorded as expenses prior to taking the trial balance. An accrued expense is at the same time a liability of the concern incurring the expense; the liability will be liquidated at some date beyond the close of the fiscal period, and under the accrual method of accounting the expense must be recorded as such for the period in which it is incurred, not in the period in which it is paid. Whenever an accounting period ends on a date which is not the same date as the payment of expenses that accrue, adjust-

ments must be made so that expenses and liabilities are correctly shown on both the accounts and the statements. Among the expenses which commonly accrue are: taxes, wages, salaries, rent, commissions, interest. 

To illustrate accrued expense, assume that an accounting period ends on Saturday, December 31, and that wages are always paid on Wednesday for all services rendered through Tuesday. Therefore, on 

Saturday, December 31, wages have accrued for Wednesday, Thursday,

Friday, and Saturday. If the wages for these four days total $4,000.00, the adjustment is:

Wages Expense 

Accrued Wages..

To set up the accrual of wages for the last four days of the period. .4,000.00 4,000.00

All accrued expenses are handled in a similar manner. The debit is always to an expense account which is closed to the Profit-and-Loss account and is shown on the statement of profit and loss as an expense, or as a portion of the total similar expense. Accruals of expenses are not segregated from the same paid expense on the statement of profit and loss. The credit to the Liability account is a current liability on the balance sheet and in the ledger. 

Accrued Incomes.-An accrued income is an income which, at the end of the accounting period, has been earned but not received. 

Ordinarily the accrual of income is not recorded daily and the trial balance will not show either the income or the accrued receivable: therefore, at the end of the period the income must be accrued on the books, regardless of which period will record its receipt in cash. The accrued income is a receivable which will be collected subsequent to the date of the balance sheet.

As an illustration of an accrued income, assume that Jones loaned 

Smith $10,000.00 at 6 per cent interest on October 1, 1942, the interest to be paid each six months. Jones closes his books on December 31, three months after the loan and three months before he will receive the first interest from Smith. Jones has been earning interest during 

October, November, and December and on December 31 will have earned three months' interest, which amount has accrued to his credit. 

The adjustment at December 31, on the books of Jones is: 

Accrued Interest on Notes Receivable. 

Interest Income.... 

To record interest earned for October, November, and December. .150.00 150.00

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

The student should note that if Smith also closed his books at this same date, Smith will have an accrued interest expense of $150.00. 

The accrued interest receivable is a current asset on the balance sheet of Jones and the $150.00 interest income is shown in his statement of profit and loss along with whatever other interest income he has earned during the year. All accrued incomes are handled in a similar manner. The debit is always to a current asset account and the credit is always to an income account. When the income is received in a subsequent period, it will be credited to the Accrued Income Receivable account and will not then again be taken up as income. 

Deferred Charges and Prepaid Expenses.-From an accounting point of view, an expense, if paid in advance of the current accounting period, is deferred as an expense until some future accounting period. 

A prepaid expense or a deferred charge is an expense, service, or supply that has been purchased but which is not totally consumed at the close of the period, thus leaving an unexpired asset value. The unconsumed portion of the future expense is an asset at the balance sheet date; when consumed in a future accounting period, the asset becomes an expense.

Prepaid expense is the term usually applied to short-time prepaid expenses; deferred charges usually represent long-time prepaid items, such as bond discount. In a balance sheet, it is advisable to distinguish between short-term prepaid expenses and long-term deferred charges.

Other common names for deferred charges and prepaid expenses are: deferred charges to operations, deferred assets, deferred expenses, prepaid assets, prepaid charges, prepayments, deferred debits. 

A service or supply may be purchased during the accounting period. 

When it is purchased it may be (1) charged to an asset account or (2) charged to an expense account. At the trial balance date, if the service or supply has not been entirely consumed by the purchaser, either (1) an asset or (2) an expense is overstated. If the original charge was to an asset account, an asset is overstated and an expense is understated. If the original charge was to an expense account, an expense is overstated and an asset is understated. If permitted to remain unadjusted, the trial balance figures would result in incorrect balance sheets and incorrect statements of profit and loss. 

Common examples of prepaid expenses and deferred charges are: prepaid interest, prepaid rent, prepaid salaries, unexpired insurance,

stamps on hand, prepaid supplies, prepaid interest, unamortized bond discount, and many others.

To illustrate the adjusting entry treatment for deferred charges and prepaid expenses, assume that a five-year fire insurance policy was purchased on January 1, 1942; the cost is $1,000.00..

Illustration I.-Assume that when the policy was purchased the premium was charged to an asset account:

To summarize the procedure for prepaid expenses and deferred charges at the close of the accounting period: 

1. If the original charge was to an asset account, the adjustment is a debit to an expense account and a credit to an asset account for the amount of the prepaid expense consumed. 

2. If the original charge was to an expense account, the adjustment is a debit to a prepaid expense or a deferred charge account and a credit to an expense account for the amount of the expense prepaid. 

Deferred Credits to Income.-A deferred credit to income, also called unearned income, is an income that has been received but has not yet been earned at the end of the accounting period. It represents payment received preceding the rendition of services or the delivery of merchandise. The income received but unearned at the end of the period represents the amount to be deferred as income to some future period. When an income is received before it is earned, the recipient is liable for merchandise or services. At the closing date, the liability for future services or merchandise deliveries must be recognized as such in the balance sheet. If income has been received in advance, and if only a portion of it has been earned at the closing date, either an

income account or a liability account is overstated if the accounts are not adjusted.

When income is received in advance, the credit may be (1) to a liability account or (2) to an income account. At the trial balance date, if services or merchandise must still be rendered or delivered, either (1) a liability or (2) an income is overstated. If the original credit was to a liability account, a liability is overstated and an income is understated. If the original credit was to an income account, an income is overstated and a liability is understated. 

Common examples of unearned income are: rent received in advance, subscriptions received in advance, merchandise orders, advance ticket sales, deferred interest income. 

To illustrate the adjusting entry treatment for deferred credits to income, assume that rent was received on May 1, 1942, $4,800.00, for one year in advance.

Illustration I.-Assume that when the rent was received it was credited to a liability account: Cash

To summarize the procedure for deferred credits to income at the close of the accounting period: 

1. If the original credit is to a liability account, the adjustment is a charge to the liability account and a credit to an income account for the amount of the income earned during the period. 

2. If the original credit is to an income account, the adjustment is a charge to the income account and a credit to a liability account for the amount of the income unearned.

Reversing Entries.-When adjustments have been made which create prepaid expenses and prepaid incomes, a reversing entry is required in order to restore the prepaid item to an expense or an income account. Reversing entries are optional for adjustments which have created accrued expenses and accrued incomes. The reversal, made on the first day of the new accounting period, has the effect of returning all prepaid expenses, accrued expenses, unearned incomes, and accrued incomes to expense or income accounts, thereby closing out the balance sheet account created by the adjustment. Thus in the new accounting period, all accrued and deferred balance sheet items created by prior adjustment are re-established in expense and income accounts, thus simplifying the accounting of the succeeding period; a few illustrations are presented.

Chapter II FACTORY COSTS 

General.-In order to understand fully the manufacturing work sheets presented in chapter III and the financial statements for manufacturing concerns presented in chapter IV, it is necessary at this point to present a brief discussion of factory costs. Up to this stage, the student has dealt primarily with work sheets and statements for mercantile concerns where the merchandise bought for sale undergoes no physical changes or transformations before it is offered for sale. 

In a mercantile concern there is only one type of inventory; in a manufacturing company, this inventory is replaced by three classes of inventory: (1) raw materials inventory, (2) work-in-process inventory, and (3) finished goods inventory. 

In a manufacturing company, raw materials are purchased for fabrication or assembly; the raw materials are placed in a storeroom and issued to the factory as required for use in operations; while being processed they are known as work-in-process; upon the completion of the manufacturing operations, the finished product emerges in condition for sale.

In a mercantile concern operating expenses were divided into two classes: (1) selling expense and (2) administrative expense. In a manufacturing concern, these two classes are retained, but a third class of expense, called manufacturing overhead, is added. Manufacturing overhead enters into the cost of the product, while selling and administrative expenses are absorbed as operating expenses in the period in which they occur. Other names for manufacturing overhead are: manufacturing expense, factory expense, factory burden, burden, overhead expense, factory overhead, overhead, overburden. 

The Elements of Cost.-In the manufacture of any product, there are three elements of factory cost: 

1. Direct material cost. 

2. Direct labor cost. 

3. Manufacturing overhead cost. 21

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Direct Material Cost.-Direct materials are those directly entering and becoming a part of the finished manufactured product. Direct material cost, then, is the cost of the materials which enter the manufacturing processes and emerge as finished goods. Materials which are used in the manufacturing process, but which do not become a portion of the finished product do not constitute direct materials, but are treated as indirect materials, a part of manufacturing overhead. (This topic is discussed later in this chapter.) 

Direct Labor Cost.-Direct labor cost is the expense of the labor employed directly upon the manufacture of the product. Direct labor alters the shape, size, form, or color of the materials. Labor which augments or services the manufacture of the product, but which is not used directly in the fabrication is known as indirect labor (considered below in the discussion of manufacturing overhead). Another name for direct labor is productive labor. 

Manufacturing Overhead.-Manufacturing overhead includes all factory costs other than direct material and direct labor. Factory costs do not include selling and administrative expenses. 

Examples of commonly found items of manufacturing overhead include: (a) factory supervision, or the cost of managing the factory; (b) foremanship, or the costs of the departmental or subdepartmental foremen not engaged in productive operations; (c) indirect labor, such as repairmen, janitors, factory office help, storeroom employees, power plant employees, cost department employees, planning and routing department employees, and others; (d) indirect materials, such as lubricants, fuel, and general factory supplies which are necessary to the manufacture of the products but which do not become a direct part of the finished product; (e) taxes on factory land, buildings, machinery, and equipment; (f) insurance on factory buildings, machinery, and equipment; (g) employers' liability insurance; (b) depreciation on factory buildings, equipment, patents, patterns, dies, jigs, machinery, and tools; (i) heat, light, and power costs; (j) cost department expenses; (k) factory rent if the quarters are not owned; (1) factory welfare and recreation expenses; (m) factory repair and maintenance expenses; (n) freight and cartage inward (if this item is not included in raw materials cost); (o) royalties paid on the use of patented machinery; (p) packing supplies; (q) receiving department costs; (r) any other costs incurred for the factory and not directly chargeable to the product being manufactured.

FACTORY COSTS 

23. 

Several of the expenses listed above must be prorated between selling, administrative, and manufacturing expense. For example, the administrative offices and sales offices may be in the same building as the factory; when a property tax bill is received, it will be in one lump sum for the whole building. It is necessary to prorate the tax bill over the selling, administrative, and factory divisions on some equitable basis such as floor space or cubic contents used by each division. 

Development of Formulas.-At this point several formulas are developed, leading to the cost of goods manufactured and sold. 

1. Cost of raw materials used the opening inventory of raw material, plus purchases (minus purchase returns and allowances), plus freight and cartage inward, minus the closing inventory of raw materials. (The reader should note that this formula is the same as the cost of goods sold section of a statement of profit and loss for a mercantile concern, with the substitution of the term "raw materials" for "merchandise inventory.") 

2. Prime cost = cost of raw materials used plus direct labor cost. 3. Cost to manufacture prime cost plus manufacturing overhead. Stated another way, the cost to manufacture direct material cost plus direct labor cost plus manufacturing overhead costs. 

4. Cost of goods manufactured cost to manufacture plus the opening inventory of work in process, minus the closing inventory of work in process. 

5. Cost of goods manufactured and sold cost of goods manufactured plus the opening inventory of finished goods, minus the closing inventory of finished goods.

These five formulas are of importance from the point of view of understanding financial factory operations and of developing an understanding of the manufacturing work sheet of chapter III and the manu facturing statements of chapter IV. 

Earlier in this chapter the three elements of cost for a manufacturing organization were given as direct material cost, direct labor cost, and manufacturing overhead cost. The sum of these three elements of cost incurred for any one period then equals the cost of goods manufactured, formula 4 above. In connection with the three elements of cost, for any one accounting period, it must be remembered that: a) Direct material cost equals (1) the opening inventory of raw materials, plus purchases (net), plus freight and cartage inward, minus the closing inventory of raw material, plus (2) the opening inventory of materials in process, plus materials placed in process during the period, minus materials in process at the close of the period.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

1 b) Direct labor cost equals any labor in process at the opening of the period, plus labor placed in process during the period, minus the labor in process at the close of the period. c) Manufacturing overhead cost equals any manufacturing overhead in process at the opening of the period, plus manufacturing overhead placed in process during the period, minus the manufacturing overhead in process at the close of the period. 

Treatment of Factory Costs.-The field of cost accounting is outside the range of this book; therefore, no attempt is made to describe even briefly cost accounting procedure. However, a few fundamental cost principles are indicated, together with a brief presentation of the cost systems in use. The student must realize that for many reasons a good cost accounting system is essential in any factory; without it unit costs of manufacturing could not be determined and correct valuations could not be assigned to the inventories of work in process and to furnish goods. The correct determination of unit costs is necessary so that sales prices may be properly established and the relative profitableness of each product may be determined. Correct valuations must be assigned to work in process and finished goods inventories so that balance sheets and statements of profit and loss do not present misstatements of values and profits. 

Cost systems are of three general types: (1) the job order cost system, (2) the process cost system, (3) the standard cost system. Some accountants use only the first two classifications, and interpret standard costs as a special method of costing applying to either of the first two systems.

Job Order. When a job order cost system is in operation, each order manufactured is costed as such, regardless of whether the order is manufactured for a specific customer or for finished stock, and regardless of whether the order be for few or many units. In any case the costs of each production order are determined, and are accumulated on a cost card especially prepared for each order. From day to day the raw materials requisitioned for the order are tabulated in the material cost columns on the cost card for the order; direct labor costs expended upon the order are recorded in the labor cost columns on the card and each department where the labor was applied is also noted. Thus, two of the elements of cost are quite simply determined for each job order. 

Each job order must also be charged with its proportionate share of the manufacturing overhead. The total manufacturing overhead for,

FACTORY COSTS 

25 say, each department may be estimated for the year in advance, the advance estimate being based on past actual performance and future expected conditions; thus a total estimated departmental manufacturing overhead is determined. The total direct labor cost for each department may likewise be estimated. If the estimated departmental manufacturing overhead is divided by the estimated departmental direct labor cost, a manufacturing overhead rate per dollar of direct labor cost is established. Then for every dollar of direct labor expended on an order, a certain amount of manufacturing overhead is added to the cost of the order. In this manner, the manufacturing overhead is applied to the cost of each order, and costs are determined immediately upon the completion of each order. If manufacturing overhead rates were not predetermined, costs could not be ascertained until the end of the accounting period when all actual manufacturing overhead was recorded. It frequently happens that the manufacturing overhead rate is too high or too low; in such cases cost adjustments must be effected. 

To illustrate the job order procedure, assume: Estimated normal manufacturing overhead for Department A, for 1942 = $500,000.00. 

Estimated direct labor cost for Department A, for 1942 $200,- 000.00. The normal manufacturing overhead rate for Department A 500,000.00 =250% of direct labor cost. Now assume that an 200,000.00 order enters the factory, to be manufactured in Department A. For this order, $3,000.00 of materials are used, and the total direct labor expended on it equals $5,000.00. The cost of the order is summarized: 

Material Cost Direct Labor Cost...

In the foregoing illustration, the manufacturing overhead cost applied to a production order was computed as a percentage of the direct labor cost of each separate department. It may be also based upon the direct labor cost for the entire factory or the direct labor cost for each machine; or it may be based on the direct labor hours for the factory, department, or machine, or on prime cost, or any combination of the above bases. 

Process Costs.-A process cost system is one in which production is

not costed on an order basis. Production is continuous, and the same products are continuously manufactured; each unit of the same product is similar to each other unit. Costs are accumulated by departments, and after the product has been processed through each department, the total costs divided by the number of units processed equals the unit cost for the product in the department and cumulatively. Some companies using the process cost system manufacture similar products in which certain relatively slight differences are apparent, as exemplified by the varying body styles available for any named automobile. In such cases, one style may be selected as a base, and a certain amount added to or deducted from the base figure for other styles. 

Standard Costs-Standard or predetermined cost systems are operated by estimating each element of expense in advance and then accumulating actual cost figures as production progresses. Periodically, actual figures are compared with the estimates, the deviations from standard noted, and the standards are changed or operations are controlled in order to bring actuals into closer conformity with standards.

FACTORY COSTS 

27 The standard figures may or may not be recorded in the accounts, together with the actual figures. When a standard cost system is in operation and properly controlled, a factory budgetary control plan is in operation. Standard cost systems may be used for either job order industries or process industries.

Chapter III  

This chapter is divided into two sections: Section I, the work sheet for a mercantile concern; Section II, the work sheet for a manufacturing company.

SECTION I: The MercantILE WORK SHEET 

This section is a review, together with advanced material, for the work sheet of a mercantile concern. The simplest manner in which to summarize all of the accounting data for a fiscal period is to prepare a work sheet. From the work sheet statements are prepared, and adjusting journal entries and closing journal entries are copied into the journal and posted to the accounts. 

Thus the work sheet is a tool or intermediary step in the accounting process which serves as the basis for all work after the completion of the trial balance. The work sheet is not a substitute for any of the accounting work; it is merely an aid. To summarize the accounting cycle: 

1. Transactions are journalized during the period. 

2. The journal entries are posted to the proper ledger accounts. 

3. A trial balance is taken. 

4. A work sheet is prepared. 

5. The financial statements are prepared. 

6. The financial statements are interpreted. 

7. The adjusting entries are journalized. 

8. The adjusting entries are posted. 

9. The closing entries are journalized. 

10. The closing entries are posted. 

11. The closed ledger accounts are ruled. 

12. The open ledger accounts are balanced and the balances are brought forward for the new accounting period. 

13. A post-closing trial balance is taken. 28

By preparing and interpreting the statements at steps 5 and 6, statement preparation and use is speeded, and steps 7 through 13 can be performed when time is available. 

In the preparation of the physical form of the work sheet, the accountant is guided by: 

1. His individual preference as to form. 

2. The data to be shown in the work sheet. 

3. The accounting statements to be prepared from the work sheet. 

4. The methods used to close the books. 

The work sheet as an instrument for statement preparation, analysis and interpretation of accounting data is of such universal application that the experienced accountant is constantly changing it and fitting it to his needs for each particular job. When a work sheet is prepared in practice, it is advisable to copy all ledger accounts, whether or not the account has a balance when the first trial balance is taken; the accounts with no balances before adjustment may be used when the adjustments are made. If the accounts with no balances are not copied from the ledger into the work sheet, it is usually necessary to add accounts at the bottom of the trial balance where they are not in proper order for statement preparation. The columns of a work sheet may be altered and shifted at will in order to satisfy each requirement. 

For example, a work sheet set up to prepare an analysis of administrative expenses should contain columns to correspond with the headings under which the analysis is to be made. 

In the case of a manufacturing concern it is desirable to show data for the cost of goods manufactured and sold in separate columns. 

Work sheets for manufacturing concerns are shown later in this chapter.

In the preceding illustration, the purchases are carried directly to the Profit-and-Loss Debit columns; the opening inventory is carried directly to the Profit-and-Loss Debit column and the closing inventory is carried directly to the Profit-and-Loss Credit column and the Balance Sheet Debit column. Thus the profit-and-loss columns of the work sheet present all data for the preparation of the cost of sales section of the statement of profit and loss. In closing, Purchases and Opening 

Inventory are closed directly to Profit-and-Loss and the new inventory is set up out of Profit-and-Loss.

6. The work sheet might be subdivided into sections, so that one sheet of paper would be used for each of the following: Assets, Liabilities, Net Worth, Incomes, Expenses. If such an arrangement is used, each sheet is closed individually. Such an arrangement is advantageous in large audits and in order to segregate each general class of accounts. An alternate arrangement is to place all Balance 

Sheet accounts on one sheet and all Profit-and-Loss accounts on another sheet.

A work sheet may be arranged in cumulative form, so that statements may be prepared each month which reflect (1) the operations for the month and (2) the cumulative operations for the year to date. 

In this manner, (1) comparisons between months of the same year can be made, (2) comparisons can be made between the same months of different years, (3) comparisons can be made for any given number of months of one year with the same number of months of some other year.

SECTION II: THE MANUFACTURING WORK SHEET 

In a manufacturing concern there are three classes of inventory instead of one; consequently, it is necessary and desirable to expand still further the work sheet and to rearrange it so that it is adequate for its desired purposes. In any work sheet for a manufacturing concern, a debit and a credit column should be included for "Cost of Goods Manufactured and Sold," or the work sheet must in some manner be arranged so that the cost of goods manufactured and sold is distinctly recognized in the working papers. 

Illustrations.-Several illustrative manufacturing work sheets are presented for study. The data for all illustrations are from one original

VANCE 

35 source, the December 31, 1942, trial balance of the Fireside Manufacturing Company, together with the supplementary data given below the trial balance.

Work Sheet I.-The columns are self-explanatory. Credit columns for selling expenses and for administrative expenses are not used because they are not necessary. 

The final inventories are placed in both Adjustments columns and each inventory item, initial and final, is carried out to its proper statement column.

If desired, the inventories may be omitted from the Adjustments columns, and entered directly into Cost of Goods Manufactured and Sold and to the Balance Sheet columns. 

The Profit-and-Loss columns are used for sales, sales returns and allowances, financial expenses and financial incomes, non-operating expenses and non-operating incomes, and for the clearing of all preceding column balances.

By the addition of more columns, this work sheet can be expanded for departments, factories, or products.

Work Sheet II.-In work sheet II, the final inventories are entered without adjustment in the Adjustments columns, which method differs from work sheet I. The change in the method of handling the inventories is purely optional and either method may be used in any manufacturing work sheet. 

The changes in form are relatively few in number but they are important because they reflect the methods used to close the books. 

The Manufacturing columns show only the cost of goods manufactured, not the cost of goods manufactured and sold. The finished goods inventories are adjusted through the Selling columns; sales and sales returns are also carried to the Selling columns rather than to the 

Profit-and-Loss columns.

The addition of a credit side to the Selling and Administrative columns should be noted, as should the change in name to the Manufacturing columns. The assumption is that the ledger carries a Manufacturing account, a Selling account, and an Administrative account, through which the manufacturing, selling, and administrative expenses are cleared on the way to the Profit-and-Loss account.

Chapter IV FINANCIAL STATEMENTS Uses of Financial Statements.--Financial statements are numerous in kind and varied in use. Perhaps the most significant classification of such statements is into: (a) those used internally and (b) those used externally. By internal use is meant managerial use for purposes of the direction of activities in an intelligent manner. By external use is meant the conveying of information to creditors and to investors in such a manner that they will obtain a satisfactory understanding of the status of the enterprise in question, and also learn something of its historical development and future prospects. The form of a financial statement is determined by the uses to be made of it. 

Many agencies have become interested in the improvement of financial statements, among which are the American Institute of Accountants, the National Association of Credit Men, and the Investment 

Bankers Association. The Securities and Exchange Commission requires that submitted statements conform to certain minimum standards. The 

Securities and Exchange Commission administers the Securities Act and the Securities Exchange Act; the effect of this administration toward better statements has been tremendous, and probably will be still more effective in the future. This is a benefit to the accounting profession, unless regimentation results.

In the preparation of all financial statements the following rules must be meticulously observed: 

1. The statements must be correct mathematically. 

2. They must reflect correct principles of income determination and valuation, so that profit-and-loss statement figures and balance sheet figures are correctly determined. 

3. They must not be misleading. 

4. They must be as concise as possible at no sacrifice of necessary detail. 

5. Detail not essential to the statement proper must be placed in supporting schedules. 47

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 6. Headings must be correct. 

7. Classifications must be clear and must not overlap, and must be effective for their purposes.

Basic Financial Statements.-The financial statements regarded as basic are: 

1. The balance sheet. 

2. The statement of surplus. 

3. The statement of profit and loss. 

4. The statement of cost of goods manufactured and sold (for a manufacturing concern). 

5. Schedules in support of the statements. 

Any of the foregoing statements may be presented in comparative form in order to show increases and decreases, and to show financial trends. The student must understand that in a statement there is no universally accepted standard form. The form of statement varies according to (1) the nature and type of the business, (2) the information to be shown, (3) the wishes and preferences of the accountant preparing the statements, and (4) the uses to which the information will be placed. Uniformity and standardization of statements is not necessarily a benefit to statement preparation if salient features and data are buried by the adherence to standard forms. Standard forms of statements are useful as guides in proper statement preparation, but adequate information must not be sacrificed simply to follow a prescribed standard statement form. The "standard" statement should mean the minimum amount of financial information to be shown in any given case. 

The Balance Sheet. The Special Purpose Versus the General 

Purpose Balance Sheet.-A balance sheet designed to meet a specific requirement and arranged accordingly is a special purpose balance sheet. One arranged to meet any one of a variety of requirements is a general purpose balance sheet. Some examples of specific uses of balance sheets are: 

1. Presentation to a bank when requesting a short-term or longterm loan. 

2. Presentation to the manager to enable him to formulate and execute policies. 

3. Presentation to the board of directors to assist in the formulation of policies regarding dividends, expansion, and other major problems of administration.

FINANCIAL STATEMENTS 

49 4. Presentation to stockholders to enable them to ascertain how well their investment is being managed and preserved. 

5. Presentation to the Securities and Exchange Commission to obtain authority to issue securities. 

6. Presentation to tax authorities as a basis of valuation or revaluation, or in connection with the payment of income, capital stock, and other taxes.

Evidently, balance sheets must be devised to fulfill either general or specific requirements. The requirements of commercial banks contemplating short-term credit extension may be set forth on their own forms. The requirements of the Bureau of Internal Revenue for corporations submitting income tax returns are set forth on the forms. used for such reporting and are explained in the detailed regulations issued by the Treasury Department.

A short summary and review of balance sheet principles, rules, and content are presented at this point. 

1. A balance sheet is a statement of assets, liabilities, and proprietorship at a definite date. 

2. The balance sheet is used to some extent for purposes of managerial control and policy direction. 

3. The balance sheet should be prepared on the same consistent basis, so that the comparative balance sheet will show accurately the changes from date to date. 

4. The net worth section must be explicit because net worth changes are of vital importance. 

5. The balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss constitute the sources of information used by banks and others for credit purposes. 

6. Current assets are cash or those assets that will be converted to cash in the normal operations of the business. 

7. Investment assets represent interests in other companies and may be classified either as current or as permanent investments, depending upon the purpose of the investment, as well as the marketability of the security. 

8. Fixed assets are tangible assets that will remain in the business. for a relatively long period of time and (with the exception of land) are turned into cash by the recovery of depreciation expense. 

9. Prepaid expenses (or deferred charges) are services and supplies bought in advance and not consumed at the balance sheet date.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

1 10. Intangible assets have no material existence and usually represent exclusive privileges. 

11. Current liabilities are legally enforceable debts, payable within one year. 

12. Deferred credits to income represent income received but unearned at the date of the balance sheet. 

13. Fixed liabilities are legally enforceable debts, maturing after one year.

Balance sheets are of two general types: (1) the report form and (2) the account form. The report form is classified in accordance with sound accounting standards. The assets, grouped according to their classifications, are presented first, followed by the liabilities and net worth. The account form of balance sheet is the same as the report form, the only difference being that the account form presents assets on the left side of the statement and liabilities and net worth on the right side of the same statement. 

An "unclassified" balance sheet simply lists assets on the left and liabilities and net worth on the right, without classification. The balance sheets illustrated later in this chapter are report forms. 

In any classified balance sheet, asset and liability classifications must be clearly indicated. One suggested asset classification is: (1) current assets, (2) prepaid expenses, (3) investment assets, (4) fixed assets, (5) intangible assets, (6) deferred charges. Liabilities may be classified as: (1) current liabilities, (2) deferred credits to income, (3) fixed liabilities. It must be clearly understood that this order is merely suggestive; this suggested order may be interchanged to suit individual preferences and needs. Regardless of arrangement, classification must always be correct, as serious consequences result from shifting an asset or a liability from one class to another. 

Dissimilar items must not be combined in a balance sheet. For example, a balance sheet may show "Cash, Accounts and Notes Receivable, $2,468,987.00," "Land and Buildings, Less Reserves, $7,673,- 

746.00." Such combinations are definitely meaningless; it is impossible to ascertain any information from such a statement. In the foregoing illustration it would be perfectly possible that a bank overdraft exists, being hidden in the cash, accounts receivable, and notes receivable combination. Cash free and available for general commercial purposes must be shown separately from restricted funds; accounts receivable must be broken into trade, nontrade, officers, and employees; notes

FINANCIAL STATEMENTS 

51 receivable should be divided into trade notes not due, trade notes overdue, nontrade notes; inventories should be divided into raw materials, work-in-process, and finished goods; investments should be divided first into temporary and permanent, and then into investments in stocks, bonds, and notes; fixed assets should be shown as machinery, building, land, etc., with each depreciation reserve shown and subtracted from the asset to which it applies. Similar procedure must be followed for all asset and liability classification. The net worth section of the balance sheet must be fully shown so that each class of capital stock is set forth together with its par value, the amount of the authorization, the unissued stock, the issued stock, and any treasury stock. Surplus must be divided between earned, capital, paid-in, donated, and reappraisal or unearned. 

The valuation methods employed for the assets must be indicated on the balance sheet whenever it is necessary to do so. The balance sheet must indicate, for example, whether investments are valued at cost, market, or the lower of cost or market; fixed assets should be indicated as valued at cost or appraisal; the same holds true for each class of asset. When nothing is mentioned in the balance sheet as to the method of valuation used, the inference should be that valuation is at cost.

A liability never should be subtracted from an asset and only the net value of the asset shown. Each asset and each liability should be shown separately, even though liens exist against the asset, and even though title to the asset has not passed. In other words, throughout the balance sheet, each item should be separately and fully shown; the "offset habit" must not be acquired; the balance sheet must never be condensed at the sacrifice of necessary detail. 

Footnotes should be appended to the balance sheet explaining fully any items which cannot be explained adequately in the balance sheet proper. Naturally, the fuller the content of the balance sheet proper, the fewer the footnotes; if a balance sheet can be prepared without footnotes, that is advisable; however, footnotes should never be omitted at the sacrifice of the clarity of the statement.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING The Statement of Profit and Loss.-Other names for the statement of profit and loss are "the statement of income and expense," "the statement of income" and "the statement of operations." "The statement of income and expense" is the most truly descriptive title, but it has not come into general usage. When statements of profit and loss are prepared in comparative form they are valuable for purposes of trend studies of incomes and expenses. 

The statement of profit and loss should not be condensed at the sacrifice of detail. If it is desirable to omit details in a statement of profit and loss, supporting schedules must be prepared, or two statements of profit and loss must be prepared, one carrying the expense and income details and the other presented in summary form. Statements of profit and loss are rather definitely standardized into the following sections: 

1. The income or sales section. 

2. The cost of sales section. 

3. The operating expense section. 

4. The financial income and expense section. 

5. The extraneous (non-operating) gain or loss section. 

The student is familiar with the statement of profit and loss used for a mercantile concern. For a manufacturing concern, it is desirable to expand and elaborate the cost of goods sold section, because of the three types of inventories and the addition of factory costs, discussed in chapter II. Consequently, the cost of goods sold section of a statement of profit and loss, for a manufacturing concern, expands to a section for the cost of goods manufactured and sold; it may be shown in the statement of profit and loss proper, or it may be shown by means of a supporting schedule. 

In the following statement of profit and loss, supporting schedules are shown for the cost of goods manufactured and sold, selling expense, administrative expense, financial expenses and financial incomes. If separate schedules are not desired for any or all of these expense groups, they must be included in detail in the statement of profit and loss proper.

Variations in the Form of the Statement of Cost of Goods Manu factured and Sold. If desired, a separate schedule of manufacturing overhead items may be submitted, instead of placing the manufacturing expenses in the statement of cost of goods manufactured and sold; such procedure simply shortens the manufacturing statement and adds one more schedule. In the statement of cost of goods manufactured and sold, or in the cost of sales section of the statement of profit and loss if a separate manufacturing statement is not prepared, practices differ with respect to the treatment of finished goods. 

Some accountants prefer not to show the beginning and ending inventories of finished goods as a part of the cost of goods manufactured and sold. If these inventories are not included here the statement of cost of goods manufactured and sold becomes the statement of cost of goods manufactured. The items pertaining to finished goods inventory omitted from the statement of cost of goods manufactured will be shown in the statement of profit and loss. In such cases the work sheet should be changed accordingly, as shown in the Manufacturing column of work sheet II, chapter III. If a statement of cost of goods manufactured is prepared, the statement of profit and loss must take care of the variations for finished goods inventories, as demonstrated below for the Fireside Manufacturing Company.

Controversial Points.-There are several controversial points involving classification of certain items appearing in the statement of cost of goods manufactured and sold and in the statement of profit and loss. The reader must understand the controversies and be guided by sound judgment as to proper classification. Several items upon which uniformity of opinion does not exist are discussed below. 

Scrap Sales and By-Product Sales.-Sales of scrap and sales of by products may be considered as (1) sales, (2) a reduction of the cost

FINANCIAL STATEMENTS 

65 of the principal products manufactured, or (3) as non-operating income. Arguments can be supported for any position taken. After the accountant is firmly convinced of the soundness of the method of treatment he desires, he should follow it consistently. If the scrap or by-product sales are considered as sales, it may be desirable to show them as "Scrap Sales" in the statement of profit and loss, showing regular sales separately. If the scrap or by-product sales are considered as a reduction of the cost to manufacture the principal product, the scrap sales should be deducted from the cost of goods manufactured figure. If they are considered as non-operating income, the scrap sales should appear in the non-operating (extraneous) income section of the statement of profit and loss. To the author, it seems as though scrap and by-product sales are not extraneous incomes as the results are too closely connected with the manufacturing and sales functions of a business. Whether scrap and by-product sales should be treated as sales or as cost reductions depends upon the circumstances in each case. If the material sold is truly scrap, a cost reduction should be effected. If the material sold is a naturally evolved by-product resulting from the breakdown of the original raw material, and if costs may be charged to it, the sales should be treated as such, since gross income is thus realized.

Sales Discounts and Purchase Discounts.-Sales discounts and pur chase discounts are known as cash discounts. Sales discounts may be shown as financial expenses or as deductions from sales. Purchase discounts may be shown as financial incomes or as a reduction of the cost of the raw material or merchandise purchased. 

Cash discounts are offered for the prompt payment of an invoice. 

The discount is offered by the seller so that he may rapidly liquidate his receivables, thus supplying himself with cash, and so that he may eliminate certain possible bad debt losses. A buyer may borrow from his bank in order to take advantage of the discounts offered. In the case of either the buyer or the seller, cash discounts are closely connected with the payment of interest; therefore they are usually considered as financial items. Cash discount rates are normally established so that it is cheaper to borrow and pay a bill promptly than it is to not borrow and await the final day of settlement; in other words, if a 2 per cent discount is offered for payment within ten days for an amount due net at the end of thirty days, the equivalent interest rate is 36 per cent per year. If money can be borrowed at 6 per cent,

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

the savings effected by borrowing (if funds are not otherwise available) are obvious. The financial operations of a business are separate from the normal buying and selling functions; therefore, the author favors treating purchase and sales discounts as financial items in the period in which the discount is taken. The theoretically sound method of treating purchase discounts is to show purchases net, and to treat the purchase discounts not taken as a financial expense. 

Discounts in excess of reasonable interest are not true cash discounts; for example, 2/10, n/30 is farther away from a true cash discount than is 2/10, n/60; also, for a sound credit risk, 2 per cent may be less of a true cash discount than 5 per cent for a poor credit risk. Normally, however, discounts in excess of 2 per cent, regardless of the net date, are viewed as trade discounts offered as an inducement to purchase or offered for large quantity purchases. When such discounts are granted, the purchases should be recorded in a manner to ignore the trade discount. 

Bad Debts Expense.-Some accountants consider bad debt expenses as selling expenses, some as financial expenses, and others as administrative expenses. Losses from uncollectible accounts are too closely connected with normal business operations to be considered as financial. 

The sales division of a business should not be responsible for the granting of credit or the collection of accounts; therefore bad debt losses should not be treated as selling expenses. The duty of credit extension and collection logically belongs to the administrative division of a well-organized business. Consequently, losses from bad accounts should be considered as administrative expenses. 

Freight-Out on Sales.-Freight on sales is considered as (1) a selling expense or as (2) a deduction from gross sales. The author prefers to view freight-outward as a selling expense, because if the freight is paid by the seller, it is one of the costs of distributing the goods. 

It sometimes happens that a seller will prepay the freight for some customers and will not prepay it for others; in such cases where uniformity of policy is lacking, it should definitely be treated as a selling expense. Also, if merchandise is shipped f.o.b. destination, and if customers are at varying distances from the point of sale, the costs of shipment 'should be treated as a selling expense and not as a sales deduction, or it will be impossible to obtain comparative sales figures. 

Freight-In on Purchases.-Freight-in is a part of the cost of the goods purchased and logically should be added to that cost in the

FINANCIAL STATEMENTS 

67 statement of cost of goods manufactured and sold. However, from a practical point of view, it may involve a tremendous amount of work to apportion freight on all of the various items bought in any one shipment of materials; therefore, the practice of keeping the freight-in in a Freight-In account may be the more reasonable in certain instances. 

Freight-in may be shown as an addition to purchases in the cost of goods manufactured and sold section if the freight is considered as a part of the cost of the materials purchased; if proper apportionment cannot be made, it may be shown as a manufacturing expense. 

Advances to Salesmen.-Some accountants believe that advances of money to salesmen, buyers, etc., should be treated as current assets; others believe that they should be treated as prepaid expenses. The purpose of its advance should govern its classification. In all probability the purpose of the advance is to enable some one to pay his expenses while traveling or while engaged in sales promotion work; the intention is not a conversion directly back to cash. Therefore, the most logical conclusion is the inclusion of such prepayments as prepaid expenses. 

Supplies. The question frequently arises as to the correct classification of factory supplies. Some contend that they should be classified along with inventories, as current assets. Others contend that they should be classified as prepaid expenses or deferred charges to operations. The purpose of the supply is in some way to augment production; the supply as such will not be turned into cash in the normal operations of the business but in effect is converted into cash when the products are sold and the accounts collected. Consequently, the supplies could be classified as current assets but are frequently listed separately as prepaid expenses or deferred charges.
