Chapter V CORPORATIONS 

Definition and Organization. The corporation is an artificial entity, separate from its owners. The corporation owes its existence to the state, as it is created by statutory law. Corporations are established in accordance with either (a) special acts of the legislature, or (b) general incorporation acts. Formerly all business corporations were established under special legislation, but the increase in the number of corporations and the spread of industrialism made it necessary for the states to enact general legislation for incorporation. In accordance with state laws, application for incorporation is made to the secretary of state. After investigation of the proposed incorporation, if the office of the secretary is satisfied that all requirements have been met, a charter, or certificate of incorporation, is issued. Thus authorized, the newly formed corporation may engage in business within the limits of its authorized powers.

Although a corporation exists upon the filing and acceptance of the articles of incorporation, it cannot begin business until a minimum amount of capital specified by the state law has been paid in. The procedure for organizing a corporation is practically the same in all states, any variation between states being minor in nature. Most states specify that there must be at least three (some states five) incorporators, that the incorporators must be natural persons of full age, and that a majority of them must be citizens. Thus minors, other corporations, partnerships, and fiduciaries are barred from organizing a corporation. 

Each incorporator must sign the articles of incorporation and the signatures must be notarized. The articles of incorporation are filed and recorded with the proper state officials, and the corporate filing fees are paid. Usually the filing fee is based upon the number of authorized shares of capital stock, with a minimum fee applicable to all cases.

The articles of incorporation, which constitute the charter application, ordinarily must include the information given below. It must be 69

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

understood that the information must be in conformity with the laws of the state of incorporation. 

1. The specific name of the corporation, which may begin with the word "the,” and shall end with or include "Company," "Co.," "Corporation," "Incorporated," or "Inc." The corporate name must. not be misleading to the public, nor may it be similar to the name of another corporation of the same state, unless the written consent of the other corporation is obtained and the consent filed with the articles. 

2. The place in the state where the principal office of the corporation is to be located. 

3. The purpose or purposes for which the corporation is organized. 

4. The classes of capital stock. 

5. The maximum number of shares of each class which the corporation is authorized to have outstanding, and the par value of the shares. 

Stated value may be assigned to no-par stock in those states not requiring a minimum issuing price. 

6. The express terms and provisions of the shares of each class of stock, such as dividend rates, preferences, conversion rights, voting rights, pre-emptive rights, rights in stated capital, option rights, participation rights, redemption rights, amounts payable on redemption, amounts payable on shares of any class upon dissolution, liquidation, consolidation, merger, or sale of the entire assets of the corporation. 

7. The amount of capital with which the corporation shall begin business. (Most states have a minimum amount; in Ohio it is $500.00.) 

8. The name of the agent of the corporation upon whom tax notices and demands may be served. 

9. The duration of the corporation if a limited existence is desired. 

Most state laws grant a perpetual existence. 

When issued, the corporate charter is a contract between the sovereign power granting it and the incorporators and their successors. The charter grants certain powers, privileges, rights, and immunities to the corporation. Being a contract, the charter may not be rescinded by one party without the consent of the other, unless the corporation abuses its powers, in which case the courts may declare the charter forfeited.

Amendments to Articles of Incorporation.-A corporation, once organized, may desire to amend its articles of incorporation. The legally required percentage of outstanding shares of stock must be

CORPORATIONS 

71 voted affirmatively in a stockholders' meeting legally called for the purpose of amending the articles. Corporate charters may be amended in any way desired, so long as the general powers conferred upon such corporations are not exceeded. A corporation may, by properly executed amendment: (a) change its name; (b) change the place in the state where the principal office is located; (c) change the purpose or purposes for which it was organized; (d) increase or reduce the par value of issued or unissued shares having a par value; (e) increase or reduce the authorized number of shares of any class; (f) change par shares to no-par shares, and vice versa; (g) create a new class or classes of stock; (b) authorize the board of directors to alter dividend rates, redemption prices, and liquidation prices on treasury stocks; (i) change the terms and provisions of any class of stock. 

Stockholders. The stockholders are the owners of the corporation. 

As such, they usually are not actively engaged in the management of the business, but they may be active as officers or directors, or both. 

Immediately after obtaining the charter, and upon obtaining capital stock subscriptions equal to the minimum paid-in capital, the first meeting of the stockholders is called by the incorporators or a majority of them. The purpose of the meeting is to elect the board of directors and to prepare the by-laws. Unless waived, the notice for the first meeting shall be by mail.

A stockholder of a corporation has certain rights and privileges, individual and collective. The individual rights of a stockholder are: 

1. To buy or otherwise acquire shares of stock 

2. To sell or otherwise dispose of his shares 

3. To share in the management by: a) Attending stockholders' meetings b) Voting on those questions which must be presented for the consideration. of the stockholders 

4. To share in the profits by: a) receiving dividends as a result of profitable operations, if dividends are declared b) receiving undistributed assets which are in excess of the claims of creditors at the time of the liquidation of the corporation 5. To inspect the books of the corporation 

6. To sue the corporation

The collective rights of shareholders are: 

1. To change the charter 

2. To change the by-laws

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

3. To elect directors 

4. To dismiss directors 

5. To pass upon the disposition of assets 

6. To dissolve the corporation 

7. To approve or disapprove all acts of the board of directors 

Board of Directors.-The stockholders elect the board of directors, which constitutes the body exercising directional management of the affairs of the company. The directors are trustees of both the stockholders and the creditors of the corporation, but the relationship of directors and corporation creditors is limited to the non-disposition of corporate assets if creditors are thereby deprived of their rights to property. The directors elect the administrative officers of the organization and thus delegate their management through the chosen company officials. The stockholders must act through the elected board of directors as that body is selected by the stockholders to represent them. It is the duty of the directors to act at all times in a manner beneficial to the stockholders. A vacancy occurs on a board of directors when one of them dies or resigns, or when his term expires. A board may declare the office of any one director vacant if he is of unsound mind, or a bankrupt, or if he does not qualify for the directorship within a stated period of time. In the event of a vacancy, the remaining directors may select a director for the unexpired term of office. There is no limitation on the maximum number of directors, but most states stipulate a mînimum number; for example, in Ohio, the minimum number is three. 

The number of directors can be increased or decreased only at the regular meeting of the stockholders called for the purpose of choosing the board, and no such action can have the effect of removing a director before the expiration of his term of office. 

The directors may not act as individuals, but only as a board, the powers of the board being joint. Individual acts of directors make them personally liable for their individual acts. Directors are individually and collectively liable to both the corporation and the creditors of the corporation for the performance of an illegal act, such, for example, as paying dividends out of capital. If a director does not acquiesce to an illegal act, he is not personally liable if he has his vote recorded in the minutes, or if he was not present at the meeting during which the illegal act was adopted. The managerial powers of the board, as a body, are supreme at all times. 

The directors may meet whenever they desire, either in regular or

CORPORATIONS 

73 special session. The only limitations on the powers of the board of directors are found in the corporate by-laws, the charter, court decisions, and in the laws of the states. 

Directors may delegate certain officials to execute their powers. In general, the duties and powers of directors are as follows (these duties are generally delegated): 

1. To formulate and supervise the execution of the general business policies of the corporation 2. To make contracts for the purchase and construction of new company assets 3. To make contracts for sales and purchases 

4. To borrow money for short terms, or, if the by-laws do not limit the approval of bond issues to the stockholders, to issue bonds 

5. To prepare and transfer negotiable paper 

6. To appoint and remove major executives 

7. To establish executive salaries 

8. To establish dividend policies 

9. To authorize the payment of dividends 

10. To authorize corporate litigation In general, the following list indicates acts from which directors are restricted and for which they are liable. 

1. Withholding full disclosure of all personal business dealings with the company 2. Voting on measures in which they hold a personal interest, aside from their corporation interest 

3. Violating the powers of the stockholders 

4. Personally using the money of the corporation 

5. Performing acts contradictory to the charter 

6. Increasing or decreasing the capital stock, if the consent of the stockholders is required 7. Removing or appointing a director in violation of the state law 8. Amending the by-laws of the corporation 

9. Cancelling capital stock or capital stock subscriptions 

10. Declaring illegal dividends 

11. Making false reports 

12. Issuing stock at a discount if state law does not permit 

13. Issuing stock as fully paid unless it is fully paid 

14. Issuing stock in excess of the authorized amount

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

15. Transferring corporate property to any one, in the event of insolvency 

16. Voting by proxy 

17. Advancing money to officers or directors 

18. Issuing false statements knowingly

By-Laws of a Corporation.-The first meeting of the board of directors takes place immediately following the first meeting of the stockholders, at which time the directors are elected. The stockholders draft the by-laws (or code of regulations) of the corporation, unless they authorize the board to draft them. The board adopts the by-laws at its first meeting.

The corporate charter contains only the skeleton information necessary to the organization and formation of a corporation. The charter does not contain definite regulations and instructions defining the major policies of the company, except those implied by state and court law pertaining to the authority and liability of directors and officers. Specific instructions, information, and duties of an internal nature are incorporated in the by-laws, or code of regulations, which are the internal governing rules of the corporation. The by-laws may not, of course, be in violation of law regulating the corporation and its directors. Corporate by-laws may contain many items, or they may contain only a few. Essential to the by-laws of any corporation are: 

1. The place, date, and manner of calling the regular annual stockholders' meeting 2. Requirements for special meetings of the stockholders 

3. The date of closing the capital stock records, which date must precede the meeting of the stockholders 4. The requirements for a quorum for a stockholders' meeting 

5. The method of voting, and the manner of execution, revocation, and the use of proxies 6. The order of business at stockholders' meetings 

7. The method of electing corporate directors 

8. The term of office of directors 

9. The number of directors 

10. The meeting place of the directors 

11. The requirements of a quorum of directors 

12. The duties and powers of the directors 

13. The appointment of an executive committee (and any other committees)

CORPORATIONS 

75 14. The method of choosing the officers of the corporation 

15. The duties and authority of the officers 

16. The corporate policy with respect to dividends 

17. The corporate policies with respect to the incurrence of indebtedness 18. The method of transferring capital stock from one owner to another 19. The method of amending the charter 

20. The method of altering the by-laws 

Classes of Corporations. Corporations may be classified as: 

I. a) Public. Governmental units and governmentally owned operating units. b) Private. Owned by individuals, partnerships, and other private companies.

II. a) Stock (or corporations organized for profit), wherein capital stock is issued. b) Non-stock (or no-profit corporations), wherein capital stock is not issued.

Corporations in II (b) may be public or private. 

III. a) Domestic. A corporation is domestic to its state of incorporation. b) Foreign. A corporation is foreign to all states other than that of incorporation. 

IV. a) Open. Wherein the capital stock is easily and freely transferable. b) Closed. Wherein the stock ownership is restricted to a few persons.

Corporations in IV (a) and (b) are always private. 

Advantages and Disadvantages of Incorporation.-When beginning a business the decision must be made as to the form of business organization to be adopted, that is, whether the business shall be organized as a single proprietorship, a partnership, or a corporation. 

The corporate form of organization presents special problems to those who thus organize a business. These special problems are (a) legal, (b) financial, and (c) accounting.

The corporate form of organization offers certain advantages and certain disadvantages, from the standpoint of the legal, financial, and accounting problems involved.

The advantages of the corporate form of organization are: 

1. Limited Liability of Stockholders.-A corporation is a legal entity, separate from the body of stockholders owning the organization. Under normal conditions the claims of the creditors of a corporation, while they may exceed the assets owned by the corporation,

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

cannot be paid in excess of the corporate assets; that is, the personal wealth of a stockholder, aside from the amount spent in obtaining his stock, cannot be forfeited to a corporation's creditors. Thus the liability of the stockholder is limited to the amount invested in the capital stock of the corporation. Partnerships must have at least one partner whose liability is unlimited, thus making the unlimited partner personally liable for all debts which cannot be liquidated by the partnership. In other words, a partnership is not a legal entity, separate from the owners.

If capital stock of the corporation is originally sold by the corporation at a discount, the owner of the stock may be held liable to the corporate creditors for the amount of the discount. The stockholder will be held for the discount liability only if the corporation is unable to pay its debts and if legal action for payment is taken by the creditors. 

In many cases, stock is issued at a discount, and later the discount is written off against surplus, the stock then ostensibly being issued as fully paid. The write-off of the discount to surplus does not cancel the liability of the stockholder. 

2. Unlimited Life.—Another advantage of the corporation is the perpetuity of its existence. A corporation may be chartered for a limited period of time, but normally the charter will confer perpetual existence. The transfer of stock, the death or insanity of a stockholder, the admission of a new stockholder, do not terminate the life of the corporation. The life of a corporation may be terminated by: a) Insolvency (if liquidation is decided upon in conformity with the bankruptcy laws) b) Expiration of the charter c) Forfeiture of the charter (for violation of law) d) Voluntary dissolution e) Court dissolution

In the case of a partnership, dissolution is effected by any of the following: a) Death of a partner b) Insanity of a partner c) Bankruptcy of a partner or the partnership d) Retirement of a partner e) Termination of the partnership agreement f) Expulsion of a partner in accordance with the partnership agreement g) Court decree

CORPORATIONS 

77 it 3. Legal Entity. Because the corporation is a separate legal entity, may sue or be sued by any one or several stockholders. A partnership cannot sue or be sued as a unit by a partner, as the suing partner would then be bringing suit against himself. A plaintiff partner may, of course, bring suit against the remaining partners as individuals. 

A corporation may also contract and be contracted with; purchase, acquire, lease, convey, mortgage, or dispose of real or personal property; it may borrow money; it may dispose of capital stock; and it may do any other act requisite to the proper conduct of the business.

Because the partnership does not exist as a legal unit, the business acts of an individual partner are binding upon the remaining partners, even though the remaining partners were innocent of a knowledge of the act, and even though they had not consented to the act. In a corporation, on the other hand, the individual acts of a shareholder in no way affect the corporate entity. A corporation is bound by the acts of the stockholders only when they are in authorized assembled meetings. 

4. System of Management.--The system of management in a corporation is flexible. The stockholders vote for a board of directors in proportion to their stockholdings and thereby delegate the management to the chosen board, which in turn elects the major administrative and other officers. The officers chosen by the board are free to direct actively the affairs of the company, working within the limits of authority delegated to them by the board. This method eliminates top-heavy management, thus avoiding conflicting ideas and the slowness certain to result if all owners were to be consulted before action could be taken on any point. If the stockholders are dissatisfied with the management of a corporation, they may elect a new board of directors at the annual meeting. This narrowing of responsibility and authority is best demonstrated by comparison with a partnership. In the latter, regardless of the respective capital investments of partners, each partner has an equal voice in the management of the partnership, and equal ability to bind the partnership by his individual acts. Of course, it is possible to limit the authority of a partner by stating specifically the restrictive conditions in the articles of co-partnership: 

But this agreement among partners does not eliminate partnership liability for unauthorized contracts of a partner if the other party to the contract is not informed of the agreement. In a corporation, acts bind-

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

ing the company are limited to those of the board acting jointly, the designated officers and the designated agents; the acts of any ownerstockholder, as such, are not binding upon the corporate entity. 

5. Large Capital.—Still another advantage of the corporate form of organization lies in its ability to secure large amounts of capital. 

This advantage is due to the large number of owners, which in turn is possible because of (1) limited liability, (2) centralized management, (3) the ease of transfer of ownership. By selling shares of capital stock which carry limited liability, many thousands of investors are easily reached; this makes the possible aggregate capital practically unlimited without interfering with a centralized system of management. 

In a partnership, the capital is limited to the sum of the amounts obtainable from the partners, and if large amounts are obtained by bringing in a large number of partners, the management of the partnership is made difficult, cumbersome, and inefficient. 

6. The Capital Stock System.-Corporate capital is divided into equal shares represented by easily transferable stock certificates. If the capital stock of a corporation is listed on an organized stock exchange, a shareholder may buy additional stock or dispose of all or a part of his stock holdings in a few moments of time. If the stock is unlisted, the stock may be acquired or disposed of almost as quickly in over-the-counter sales, or otherwise. In the event of either listed. or unlisted stocks, the owner may dispose of or acquire his shares without the consent of other shareholders. In a partnership, acquisition or disposition of partnership capital can be effected without the consent of the remaining partners, but a new partner has no management rights without the consent of the other partners. 

Capital stock certificates may be easily pledged as loan collateral. 

A partnership interest is difficult to pledge. 

The disadvantages of the corporate form of organization are: 

1. Legislative Limitations.-The federal government and the state governments frequently enact laws which may hamper a corporation in its operations. Most regulatory legislation of this nature applies to corporations and not to partnerships or single proprietorships. Corporations are subject to the laws of the state of incorporation and to the laws of the states in which they operate. In addition, certain corporations must comply with the requirements of the Securities and Exchange Commission, some with the requirements of the Federal Communications Commission, some with the Interstate Commerce

CORPORATIONS 

79 Commissions rulings, some with the rulings of various public utilities commissions, and so on. 

2. Reports to States.-Corporations must file numerous reports with the proper authorities of the state of incorporation and the states in which they are operating. In addition, each corporation must file a tremendous volume of reports with federal agencies; this is particularly true for corporations engaged in interstate commerce. 

3. Taxes, Fees.-The total tax burden of corporations is ordinarily much greater than for other forms of organizations. They are subjected to a greater number and variety of taxes and fees; consequently more legal and accounting work is required as well as larger tax payments. 

Taxes and fees required only of corporations include: organization fees; foreign corporation fees; annual franchise taxes, both domestic and foreign; capital stock transfer taxes; excess profits taxes; capital stock tax. 

4. Formalities.-The formal business procedure of a corporation must be conducted through meetings of the board of directors. Minutes must be kept of board actions. Directors may incur personal liability if legal stipulations for corporate indebtedness is exceeded. Profits can be divided as dividends only after being formally declared and passed by the board. Dividends must be proportionate to stockholdings. Dividends must not impair corporate capital. While all the formal restrictions are disadvantages as far as ease of operation is concerned, most of them are really advantages as far as the upholding of good business practice is concerned. 

5. Manipulation.-Through unscrupulous action by a board of directors, or by a majority of the stockholders, the affairs of a corporation may be fraudulently manipulated to the personal enrichment of the directors or the majority holders. Of course, fraud has been known to exist in partnerships. 

6. Type of Business.-A corporation is generally limited to the purpose clause of its charter. This disadvantage is not serious, as the charter is easily amended for purposes of expansion or contraction of purposes. The present tendency is to include a "blanket” clause covering everything not actually prohibited, such as the practice of medicine for all corporations. 

Classes of Capital Stock.-Capital stock, whether of a par value or of no-par value, may be of one or more classes. There are many classes of capital stock, but they are usually variations of (1) common

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

or (2) preferred. In any one corporate organization there may exist more than one class of either common or preferred, with each issue having rights or restrictions different from other issues of the same class. For example, there may be a Common "A" stock and a Common "B" stock, the "B" stock carrying exclusive voting privileges. Any issue of capital stock may be made redeemable or convertible. Any share of stock confers on its owner (1) a right in the management (unless the stock is non-voting), (2) a right in the profits, and (3) a right to the assets in the event of dissolution. 

Common Stock.—If a corporation issues only one class of stock, each share being identical with all other shares as to powers and privileges, it is automatically common stock. If a corporation issues more than one class of stock, each class must be clearly designated. Common stock is subordinate in some respects to the other classes. The claims of the common stockholders follow, or are subordinate to, the claims. of other classes of stockholders; as a result, greater risk is attached to the ownership of common stock, but this is compensated for by the possibility of larger profits; these profits may come from larger dividends or from increased market value of the stock. All common stock, or at least one class of common if more than one class of common is outstanding, carries the voting privilege, on the basis of one vote for each share owned.

Preferred Stock.-If, in addition to common stock, preferred stock is issued, the preferred stock may be: 

1. Preferred as to assets in dissolution. 

2. Preferred as to dividends. If the stock is preferred as to dividends, it may be: (a) cumulative or non-cumulative, (b) participating or non-participating. 

3. (a) voting, (b) non-voting, (c) or it may have contingent voting powers.

Preferred stock always has some or all of the foregoing preferences over the common. The purpose of the preference is to make the stock attractive to the investor.

Stock Preferred as to Assets in Dissolution.—If stock is preferred. as to assets on dissolution, the preference must be specifically stated; in no case is such preference implied. When stock is preferred as to assets, the preferred stockholder, in the event of liquidation, will receive a minimum of the par or stated value of his investment before the common stockholder receives anything. If preferred dividends are in

CORPORATIONS 

81 arrears, they are not payable in liquidation unless (1) the stock is cumulative, and (2) the surplus is large enough to cover the cumulative dividends which are in arrears. 

When a deficit exists in a corporation which has an issue of stock preferred as to assets in liquidation, the deficit should be shown on the balance sheet as a deduction from the common stock only, thus: Preferred Stock Common Stock Deficit

Total Net Worth. 

$500,000.00 .$500,000.00 100,000.00 400,000.00 $900,000.00

The deficit does not impair the preferred stock, unless the deficit is larger than the common stock. If the deficit is larger than the common stock, the excess should be shown on the balance sheet as a deduction from the preferred stock, in order to show the encroachment upon the equity of the preferred stockholders. 

Stock Preferred as to Dividends.-For any class of stock, the payment of dividends depends upon the earnings, the condition of the surplus, the cash position, and the discretion exercised by the board of directors. When stock is preferred as to dividends, it will receive its dividends before the common stock receives any dividends. Stock preferred as to dividends may be cumulative or non-cumulative, participating or non-participating. A discussion of these features follows. 

Cumulative and Non-Cumulative Preferred Stock.-Dividend rates are definite for preferred stock. When preferred stock possesses the cumulative feature, a dividend passed by the board of directors in any one dividend period becomes a lien against the profits of future periods. All unpaid cumulative dividends must be paid before current dividends are paid on either the preferred or the common stock. Cumulative preferred stockholders are thus assured that the common stock, normally the voting stock, will not receive dividends until all formerly passed and current dividends are paid on the cumulative preferred stock. Preferred stock is always cumulative, unless the stock is specifically designated to be non-cumulative. 

If a dividend is declared on cumulative preferred, or any other stock, the dividend payable must be set up as a liability. If a dividend on cumulative preferred stock is not declared, that is, if the dividend is passed, no liability exists and none should be shown; the failure to declare a dividend does not create a liability, but does give rise to a

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

prior lien on future profits and dividends. When dividends on cumulative preferred stock have been passed, a footnote should be attached to the balance sheet setting forth the total unpaid cumulative dividends. 

If preferred stock is non-cumulative, a dividend once passed is not paid in the future, as the unpaid dividends do not accumulate to the benefit of the stockholder. Consequently, if preferred stock is non-cumulative, it is a doubtful investment and even a doubtful speculation, because if the voting control is exercised by the common stockholders, or if the common stock vote exceeds the non-cumulative preferred vote, the non-cumulative preferred stockholders are unable to obtain remedial measures. Consider the following illustration of the undesirability of non-cumulative preferred stock: Assume that the common stock carries the voting rights. The board of directors may vote to pay no dividends on the non-cumulative preferred or on the common for the current year, (1) because the money is needed in the business, or (2) because they may wish to pay extra dividends on the common in the next year. The non-cumulative preferred stockholders thus have forever lost their current dividend, unless they can show to the satisfaction of a court that dividends were unreasonably withheld. In the subsequent year, the board may declare the regular dividend on the non-cumulative preferred, and also abnormally large dividends on the common, a portion of which rightfully should have gone to the non-cumulative preferred holders in the preceding year.

Participating and Non-Participating Preferred Stock.-Preferred stock is participating unless it is specifically designated as non-participating. This is true because all stockholders have the right to share ratably in any profit distribution. When preferred stock is participating, it shares in all extra dividends along with the common stock, after the common stock has received dividends equal to the preferred rate. 

For example, if the preferred stock is fully participating, the regular dividend (say 6 per cent) is declared on the preferred, and a 6 per cent dividend is declared on the common. After this declaration, the board of directors may desire to declare extra dividends to the common stockholders of 2 per cent. They must also declare a 2 per cent dividend to the participating preferred shareholders. If the preferred stock is non-participating, the holders thereof will receive 6 per cent and no more. Participation may be (1) full, or (2) limited; normally the participation is stated; if nothing is stipulated, the participation is full.

CORPORATIONS 

83 By granting participation to all preferred stock, the voting common stock is prevented from receiving all extra dividends. 

Preferred stock may thus give the stockholders: 

1. A right to receive dividends before the common 

2. The accumulation of unpaid dividends, unless it is noncumulative 3. Participation in extra dividends to the extent commensurate with dividends paid on the common, if it is participating. 

4. Preference as to assets in the event of dissolution, if the preference is stated 5. The privilege to vote, unless specifically denied 

Most preferred stock is cumulative, non-participating, and nonvoting. 

Miscellaneous Features of Preferred Stock.-Voting.—Preferred stock has the privilege of voting unless the right is specifically withheld. A few state laws prohibit the withholding of the vote from the preferred stockholder by the corporation. In most cases, also, specific provision is made that if the preferred dividends are passed for a given number of periods, the preferred stockholders may elect the board of directors, and thus take over the management of the corporation to the exclusion of the common stockholders. Voting is on a ratable basis, each share carrying one vote.

Classes of Preferred.-One corporation may issue many classes of preferred stock, as (1) first preferred, (2) second preferred, (3) third preferred. Regardless of the number of classes of preferred stock, all preferred rights are prior to those of the common stock, unless the preferred contract specifically withholds any privilege. The rights of the first preferred are senior to the rights of the second preferred and so on. Regardless of name, the conditions and preferences surrounding each issue must be fully stated and understood. 

Redeemable and Non-Redeemable Preferred.-Preferred stock may be made redeemable, at the option of the corporation, after a certain or determinable date, at a definite or determinable price. The redemption price usually is a few points above par. If it is redeemable, it must be issued with redemption features set forth at the time of issuance. 

When the stock is called for redemption, any dividends in arrears must be paid. Most state laws provide that a corporation can redeem its stock only "out of surplus"; therefore at the time of redemption surplus must equal the price paid for the stock. The preferences surrounding

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

the preferred make it a somewhat less speculative investment. Redeemable preferred stock must be issued so that the option of redemption rests with the corporation. 

Conversion Rights.-Convertible preferred stock may be exchanged for common stock at the option of the stockholders, before a definite date and at a specified ratio of exchange. The conversion privilege must be stated in the preferred stock. It is attached to make the preferred attractive to investors. 

Guaranteed Stock-Guaranteed stock has its dividends guaranteed by another company, commonly a parent company, or a lessor of the corporation's property. No company can guarantee its own dividend. The guaranty applies only to the dividend and not to the par or stated value of the stock. The guaranty is a legally enforceable liability against the guarantor. The earnings of the guarantor and the actions of the guarantor's board of directors have no bearing on claim for the dividends, for they are not contingent upon either of these factors.

Founders' Stock.-Founders' stock entitles its owners to a disproportionately large share of the dividends. The dividend provisions must be specifically stated in the founders' stock contract. For example, a corporation may organize with 100,000 shares of common stock, of which 10,000 shares is designated as founders' stock, which will go to the organizers. The founders' stock may carry a dividend rate of 12 per cent while the remaining stock may carry a dividend rate of 6 per cent. Instances of founders' stock exist wherein the dividend on the founders' stock will at all times equal the total amount of the dividends on all other classes of stock. Naturally, the existence of founders' stock serves as a detriment to the sale of other shares. It is not common in the United States, but it is rather common in Great Britain. 

Par and No-Par Stock.-As compared with other forms of business organizations, the two distinguishing features of the corporation are (1) the general treatment of corporate net worth, and (2) the characteristics of capital stock. 

Up to this point, this chapter has not distinguished between capital stock carrying a par value and capital stock of no-par value. If stock has a par value, there attaches to each share an arbitrary valuation fixed by the charter. If the stock is of no-par value, no such arbitrary value appears, although a stated minimum value may be used, or a minimum issuing price may be required by state law. All states now

CORPORATIONS 

85 permit the issuance of common stock without par value; some states permit the issuance of preferred stock without par value. Some states require the establishment of a minimum issuing price for no-par stock (the New York law places the minimum issuing price at $5.00 per share); others do not.

Par Value Stock. In any individual case, the articles of incorporation will specify whether the stock is of a par value or is of no-par value. If the stock is of par value, the amount of the par of each share is printed on the stock certificate. Par value is simply a nominal and arbitrary figure and is arrived at by common usage, individual preference, the financial condition of the country or community at the time of stock issuance, and the class of investors to which the selling appeal is directed. The par value of a share of stock is no indication of the real value of the stock, its earning capacity, its market value, or its book value. The par is simply the amount at which it is recorded in the capital stock accounts of the issuing corporation. Stock of a par value originally may be sold at: (1) par, (2) a price above par, (3) at a price below par, if the state law does not prohibit. 

When stock of a par value is originally sold for a price below par, the purchaser is liable to the creditors of the corporation for the discount. If the corporation is successful the creditors will not be forced to enforce the collection of the discount, with the result that it never will be collected. Discount and premium on sales of capital stock are treated in chapter VI. 

No-Par Stock.-No-par value stock has no given nominal amount attaching to each share, and the stock is carried on the books at (1) the amounts for which it is sold, even though the shares do not all sell at the same price, or (2) the minimum issuing price, if one is required, or (3) a stated value, if one is assigned to the stock. If no-par stock has a stated value or a minimum issuing price of, say, $5.00 per share and is sold for $7.50 per share, at least $5.00 is credited to the No-Par 

Stock account and the balance is credited to the Paid-In Surplus account. 

In the last illustration, there is nothing to prevent the corporation from crediting the No-Par Stock account for $7.50, as the entire receipt represents permanent capital. As far as control and privilege are concerned, there is no difference to the stockholders between par and nopar stock.

The accounting for stocks of a par value and of no-par value is considered in chapter VI.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING The Characteristics of Par and No-Par Stock.—The characteristics of par value stock are: 

1. The rigid requirements surrounding original issuance at a price at least equal to the par value. 

2. The purchaser's liability for the discount in the event of corporate insolvency. 

3. The par value printed on the stock certificate is not a reflection of the real value of the stock, which value is constantly. changing. 

4. The prohibition of the sale at a price below par. This leads to various subterfuges, such as the issuance of stock in exchange for assets at inflated values. 

5. The confusion in the minds of investors resulting from the use of a par and their inability to reconcile the par value with fluctuating market values.

The characteristics of no-par stock are: 

1. It can be sold at any price, or, if it carries a minimum issuing price, at any price above that figure. 

2. There is no reason to inflate the value of the property received in payment, since there is no arbitrary capital stock figure which must be maintained. 

3. As there is no par, there can be no discount, and therefore, there is no liability to corporate creditors in the event of insolvency, unless fraud is practiced. 

4. Investors are not misled by the establishment of an arbitrary par value. 

5. Treasury stock transactions are greatly reduced, as there is no value figure which must be maintained during the period of original stock issue. par 

6. "Bargains" cannot be offered in items of "sale far below par value." 

7. For stock transfer tax purposes and for organization fees, nopar stock is often treated as though it had a $100.00 par; changes in laws are being effected to relieve this situation. In order to avoid various taxes on no-par stock, when the tax is levied on the basis of a $100.00 par, no-par shares are sometimes changed to a low par value. 

8. Its use may mislead an investor when a corporation in poor financial condition desires more capital. The embarrassed corporation may be able to sell its no-par stock very cheaply, whereas it might not be permitted to sell par value stock at less than par.

CORPORATIONS 

87 9. If the state of incorporation has no requirements for stated value, the corporation may sell its no-par stock at say $4.00 per share, credit $1.00 to capital stock and credit $3.00 to surplus, thus misleading the student of the balance sheet. The better state laws require the segregation of paid-in surplus. 

10. In paragraph. nine, above, early years' losses will not be shown as a deficit (but they should be so shown), but will be charged off to surplus created by capital contribution, thus presenting an untrue financial condition. The better state laws prohibit this practice. 

Stock Certificate.-A stock certificate is the evidence of ownership issued to the purchasing stockholder. Each certificate is issued for the number of shares of corporate capital purchased by the stockholder. A certificate may be issued for any number of shares. Each certificate is serially numbered. For example, a stockholder may have one certificate, No. 891 for one share, and another certificate, No. 899 for one thousand shares. If he desires one certificate for the 1,001 shares, he may obtain it by surrendering the two he holds. The owner of a certificate may sell the entire number of shares specified in it, or only a part of his total shares to another, or he may assign his entire share holding or a part of it to the other person by indorsement, or by indorsing the certificate in blank. In the event of assignment or sale, the transfer from one person to another must be recorded on the books of the corporation if the buyer is to receive dividends or is to vote his stock. 

The new stockholder sends his newly acquired certificate to the corporation (or its transfer agent, described below) and receives in exchange a certificate made out in his own name. The newly acquired certificate bears a new serial number, and the old certificate is cancelled; transfer tax stamps are attached to the cancelled certificate or to its stub in the certificate book. If stockholder A sells only a portion of the shares called for in his certificate to B, he indorses the number sold to B, and A's certificate is sent to the corporation. The corporation cancels A's certificate, and issues two in its place, one to A for his retained shares, and one to B for his acquired shares. Stock frequently goes through several hands without recording the transfer on the books of the corporation; also, many shares are carried in a "street name" consistently, for ease of trading.

If a stock certificate is lost, a new certificate will be given, but usually bond must be posted so that the corporation is protected against loss. The issuance of new certificates in place of those lost, stolen, or

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

destroyed, is in conformity with a court order issued in the county in which the principal office of the corporation is located; the court must investigate the loss, theft, or destruction, to be certain that no harm will come to the corporation as a result of the issuance of the new certificate.

Records Peculiar to a Corporation.-The differences in general and subsidiary ledger records for a corporation arises because of the more complicated nature of the net worth of a corporation as compared with other types of organizations, particularly that section of the net worth pertaining to capital stock issues. General ledger accounts commonly found on the books of a corporation not found on the books of other businesses include: Subscription, Calls, Preferred Stock, Com mon Stock, Authorized Preferred Stock, Authorized Common Stock, Unissued Preferred Stock, Unissued Common Stock, Common Treasury Stock, and Preferred Treasury Stock. Because of the issuance of capital stock certificates, it is necessary that a corporation maintain highly specialized records dealing with the capital stock so that information is at all times available for all transactions surrounding the status of each individual stockholder. 

The normal transactions pertaining to capital stock are: a) The receipt of stock subscriptions b) The payment for the subscriptions, either in full or on the installment plan

The issuance of the stock certificate d) The transfer of stock from one owner to another e) The payment of dividends f) The purchase and sale of treasury stock

Subscriptions Journal and Subscriptions Ledger.-When subscrip tions are received from interested parties, the subscriptions are entered in the subscriptions journal, as a debit to Subscriptions. A subsidiary ledger account is kept with each subscriber to which the subscription journal entry is posted. The controlling account, Subscriptions, is charged with the periodic total subscriptions. When cash is received from the subscribers, the subscription accounts, both controlling and subsidiary, are credited. Each subsidiary account shows the condition of one subscriber, and the control shows the summarized total condition. A subscription ledger should always be used if the subscription is payable on the installment plan; it may or may not be used if payment in full accompanies the subscription or if full payment is made

CORPORATIONS 

89 after receiving the subscription contract. Also, when subscriptions are payable in installments, an installment journal may be used, in which 

Installment No...... is charged and Subscriptions are credited.

The Stock Certificate Book.-After the subscriptions are fully paid, a stock certificate is issued to the stockholder. The certificate constitutes the evidence of ownership of a designated number of corporate capital shares; it is made out in the name of the stockholder and signed by the proper corporation officials. Usually the blank certificates are in a book detachable from a certificate stub. The stub of the certificate contains space for the name of the stockholder, the number of shares represented by the certificate, the serial number corresponding to the certificate, the date, the name of the seller, and the name of the assigner. When certificates are cancelled, that fact is recorded on the stub, and the cancelled certificate is attached to the stub. The sum of the shares listed on the uncancelled stubs constitutes the total number of shares outstanding. Information contained on the certificate stub is posted to the subsidiary stockholders' ledger. 

The Stockholders' Ledger.-The stockholders' ledger is subsidiary to the proper Preferred or Common Stock account, kept in the general ledger. A stockholders' ledger card is kept for each stockholder for each class of stock. Normally, the stockholders' ledger is kept in terms of the number of shares involved, and not in terms of par or the stated value of the stock; it is never kept in terms of market price paid by holders when buying or selling shares. The back of each stock certificate contains space for the assignment of interest in the shares owned. If the assignment is indorsed in blank, the certificate may continue to circulate until a new certificate is issued to a stockholder, at his request. The total of the number of shares indicated in the stockholders' ledger will agree with the total according to the stock certificate book, and will also agree with the total as shown in a capital stock account. Each stockholder's ledger account is charged with cancellations and transfers, and is credited for new and additional shares issued.

The Stock Transfer Book.-In order to know the names of its stockholders so that dividends may be paid them and notices of meetings and annual reports may be sent to them, corporations must keep a record of transfers between holders. Stock normally is transferred from holder to holder by sale. Transfers between stockholders are recorded in a stock transfer book, which is a journal, and from which

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

postings are made directly to the stockholders' ledger. Transfers have no effect upon the controlling capital stock accounts. 

Minute Book. The minute book of a board of directors, kept by the secretary to the board, serves as the evidence of authority for all major actions taken by the properly delegated officers of the corporation. All corporate actions must be in accordance with the charter and the by-laws. Any action subject to recording which is not recorded constitutes unauthorized procedure. The minute book contains such data as: a) A copy of the corporate charter b) A copy of the by-laws of the corporation c) A record of the proceedings of stockholders' meetings d) A record of the proceedings of directors' meetings e) Authorization for the acquisition of new assets and plant construction f) Authorization for the flotation of bond issues g) Dividend actions b) Authorizations for increases or decreases of capital stock i) Authorization for surplus reserve creations

The Registrar and the Transfer Agent.-Large corporations, with active stock, appoint one trust company to act as registrar and another trust company as transfer agent. If the stock is listed, the appointment of a registrar is compulsory. Some corporations serve as their own transfer agents and appoint only registrars. The registrar is appointed so that (1) an outside party may certify to the propriety of a newly issued stock certificate and so that (2) there will be no overissuance of the total authorized stock issue and consequently no fraud. The transfer agent keeps a record of all transfers between holders. When a transfer agent is employed, the corporation does not keep the stock transfer book or the subsidiary stockholders' ledger. Upon the transfer of a certificate from one owner to another, it is routed to the transfer agent, who approves the transfer, cancels the old certificate and attaches the stock transfer tax stamps to it, makes the entries in the transfer journal, posts them to the stockholders' ledger; he then prepares the new certificate and sends it, together with all pertinent data, to the registrar who determines that there is no overissue, and who registers the stock in the name of the new owner. Both the transfer agent and the registrar have duplicate records of the authorization, the unissued stock, and the number of shares outstanding.

Consideration for Capital Stock.-Capital stock may be paid for in cash, property, or services. Most states prohibit the payment for capital stock in promissory notes. Statutory provisions differ in the various states, but the usual requirement for par value stock is that it must be fully paid for in order to release the subscriber from further liability thereon.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

When payment for par value stock is not made in cash, but in property or services, the question immediately arises as to the proper valuation of the assets, other than cash, taken over by the corporation in exchange for its capital stock. Courts hesitate to question the valuation placed on corporate assets by the board of directors except when gross inflation is evident. Consequently, the way is left open for material misstatement of facts, and the consequent inequitable treatment of the stockholders who pay cash for their stock. The Securities and 

Exchange Commission is being quite consistent in ruling against gross overvaluations in the statements of registrants. 

This problem of valuation is a most important one, and one that will carry through all of the valuation work in this book. When capital stock is overvalued, it normally is the result of overvaluation of some asset. To illustrate, assume that the Georgian Corporation is to be organized and that interested persons are willing to contribute $150,- 000.00 in cash, services, and property. To anticipate future requirements for capital, as well as to meet present requirements, the application for a charter specifies that the authorized common stock is to be $200,000.00, each share having à par value of $100.00. 

The names of the three incorporators are listed below, together with the allotment of stock and the amount and character of the assets which each contributes.

NAME 

James Seeds 

Albert Bochache 

George Kramer

AMOUNT OF STOCK SUBSCRIBED 

.$ 25,000.00 90,000.00

How PAID FOR 

Promotion services 

Property 

Cash 35,000.00 $150,000.00

The valuation problem attaches to both Seeds' and Bochache's contributions. If Bochache's property, at reasonable valuation, is worth only $70,000.00, and if Seeds' promotion services are in reality worth but $10,000.00, it is obvious that the value attached to the capital stock of $100.00 per share is fictitious. It is also obvious that Kramer is paying an excessive price for his stock.

The precise accounts to carry in any one specific instance depends upon the method of accounting employed; variations depend upon whether the stock is sold outright for cash or on the installment plan, and whether, if it has a par value, it is sold at par, at a premium, or at a discount. The accounting procedure in every case is demonstrated in the next chapter.

Authorized Capital Stock.-The charter of a corporation confers the power to issue a specified amount of each class of capital stock. The number of shares called for by the charter, and approved by the state, constitutes the total shares the corporation is authorized or permitted to issue. It is never necessary that the corporation actually issue the entire amount of its authorized stock at any one time. After the entire authorized amount of any class of stock is issued, additional amounts may be authorized by the amendment of the corporate charter. The amount of the originally authorized capital stock called for in a corporation's charter is regulated by the amount of original capital the corporation desires and by the amount of incorporation fees the company is willing to pay. Most states base their incorporation fees for private profit organizations on the basis of a charge per authorized share of each class. The fees are on a sliding scale, as for example, those of Ohio: 

1-1,000 shares authorized.. 

1,001-10,000 shares authorized. 

10,001-50,000 shares authorized. 

50,001-100,000 shares authorized. 

100,001-500,000 shares authorized. $0.10 per share .05 per share .02 per share .01 per share 

500,001-infinity shares authorized.

Many states have a minimum fee of $25.00. .005 per share .0025 per share

Issued Capital Stock.-Authorized capital stock may be sold for cash, property, or services. When the authorized stock or any part of it is sold, and the stock certificates are issued, the stock becomes issued or outstanding stock. The unsold portion of the authorized capital stock may also be used to pay stock dividends, in which case it also becomes outstanding.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING Unissued Capital Stock.—The authorized portion of the stock which remains unissued constitutes the unissued portion, and is available for issuance at any time.. 

Treasury Stock.—Treasury stock is capital stock that has been issued and later reacquired by the corporation. It may be reacquired either by purchase by the corporation or by donation to the corporation by holders of the stock. Treasury stock is different from unissued stock in that it has been issued; the liability arising from sale at a discount does not apply to treasury stock. It is similar to unissued stock in that both are eligible for sale by the corporation. Treasury stock is treated fully in chapter VII. 

Watered Stock.-Watered stock exists when the value of the assets taken in exchange for the stock is less than the recorded value of the stock. Water may be eliminated by: 

1. Directly writing down the value of the assets with a contra charge to a surplus account 2. Reducing the par of each share of stock, accompanied by a reduction in the value of the assets 3. Reducing the number of shares outstanding, accompanied by a reduction in the value of the assets 4. Obtaining donated stock, selling it, and crediting the proceeds to the overvalued asset 5. Retaining profits in the business and crediting the overvalued asset accounts 6. Purposely ignoring bona fide increases in asset values 

7. Charging capital asset purchases to expense.

Owing to the requirements of state laws it is usually necessary that there be at least three incorporators; consequently, a single proprietor, when incorporating, must interest at least two other persons, each of whom must subscribe for at least one share of stock. Relatives or associates may be asked to do this. Two illustrations are presented: Case 1, the incorporation of a single proprietorship; Case 2, the incorporation of a partnership.

Chapter VI CORPORATIONS-Continued CAPITAL CONTRIBUTIONS 

Issuance of Stock.-As pointed out in chapter V, capital stock is issued at the time of incorporation, and additional amounts may be issued at later dates. The steps in recording capital stock transactions are: (1) authorization, (2) subscription, (3) payment, (4) issuance.

If the stock is issued at the time of subscription, steps (2) and (4) are combined. There are two possible legal situations at the time of subscription: (1) the subscriber receives immediately all the rights and privileges of a stockholder; that is, the stock is issued, although the certificates may not be released until later, or (2) the subscriber has no rights as a stockholder until the stock is fully paid and issued. The law of the state of incorporation and the form of the subscription agreement determines the status of the subscriber. 

Stock may be exchanged for (1) cash, (2) property, or (3) services.

The opening entries on the books of the corporation, for recording the disposition of the capital stock, vary with the following conditions: 

1. (a) The entry may be made only for the amount of stock issued, or (b) The entry may be made for the entire amount of authorized stock. 

2. (a) Full payment in cash may be made at the time of subscription, or payment may be due at a date after subscription, or (b) Payment may be partly in cash and partly in property and services, or (c) Payment may be by installments. 

3. If the stock, of par value, is issued at a premium or at a discount. 

4. If the stock, of no-par value, is issued at varying prices. 

PAR VALUE STOCK 

Opening Entries for Stock of a Par Value.-As pointed out in chapter V, the records of the issuing company must be complete with respect to the authorized stock, the issued and the unissued stock, and discounts and premiums on the sale of the stock. 99

Method I. By this method, capital stock is recorded in the Preferred Stock or the Common Stock account at its par value only when the stock is sold; a memorandum entry is placed in the stock accounts for the full amount of the authorization. Method II.-This method is simply a variation of Method I. 

Instead of receiving cash immediately, subscriptions are received for the stock, payment to follow later. Capital stock is recorded in the accounts when the stock is subscribed. This is legally proper in those states in which a subscriber enjoys the rights of a fully-paid stockholder. At the time of incorporation, a memorandum entry is placed in the capital stock accounts for the amount of the authorization. The Capital Stock accounts will show only the amounts subscribed. 

When all of the stock is sold, the Capital Stock accounts will show the full amounts of the authorizations as credits. The debit balances in the Subscription accounts show the unpaid subscriptions. Where subscriptions and payments are simultaneous, it is not necessary to open the Subscriptions accounts. Usually, however, it is preferable to open these accounts, because the procedure then conforms more closely to the legal point of view. First, subscriptions are secured; these are obligations of the subscribers. Second, payment is received, and the subscribers' obligations are thus liquidated.

Stock Issued on the Installment Plan.-In the preceding illustrations the assumption was that the subscriptions from each subscriber were paid in one lump sum. However, it frequently happens that capital stock is sold by a corporation under a plan whereby the entire amount of each individual's subscription will not be paid at one time; it will be paid in installments, each installment falling due either on specified dates or dates to be determined by the corporation. 

When an installment is due for payment, the corporation will mail the subscriber a "call," which is notification of the next installment due, giving the date when the installment is to be paid. Usually the

CORPORATIONS 

105 dates and the amounts of each installment are determined at the time of obtaining the subscriptions. The subscriber is delinquent if he does not respond to a call by paying for the subscription due at that time. 

In some states a subscriber is considered to be a stockholder as soon as a legal subscription contract is brought into existence, even though he has paid nothing and has not received his certificate. In some states the subscriber has no rights as a stockholder until his subscriptions are fully paid.

Assume (using the Belmont Company) that G. H. Haven subscribes for 100 shares of preferred, at par, on February 20. Payment is to be made: 50 per cent at the time of subscription; 25 per cent on 

March 20; 25 per cent on April 20. The transactions are recorded as follows (NOTE: The Belmont Company set up the unissued and the authorized accounts on January 28):

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

When subscriptions are received, payable on the installment plan, any of the four methods for recording capital stock issues may be used. 

The only additional step in the installment plan is to set up the Call or Installment accounts, which are intermediary between the Subscriptions account and the Cash account. Some companies set up subsidiary installment ledgers for stock sold under this plan; others record the calls in the subscribers' subsidiary and controlling accounts. 

Treatment of the Subscriptions Account and the Installment 

Accounts in the Balance Sheet.-There are differences of opinion among accountants as to whether unpaid balances in the Subscriptions account and the Installment accounts should be shown in (1) the asset section of a balance sheet, or (2) in the net worth section. The question and its consequent decision will arise only if a balance sheet is prepared before all outstanding subscriptions and calls are collected. 

From the point of view of balance sheet presentation: 

1. The subscriptions may be shown as current assets: a) If the subscriptions normally will be collected in the near future, or b) If the subscriptions are payable on the installment plan. 

If they are shown among the current assets of the balance sheet, they must be titled "Subscriptions Due from Capital Stock," or otherwise clearly labelled so that none will believe that they are trade accounts or trade notes receivable. 

2. The subscriptions may be shown as assets (not current assets) if there is no intention to call the subscription in the near future. The better practice in such a case is to show the subscriptions as net worth valuation items, deducted from the capital stock, so that paid capital stock may not be overstated. See form below. 

3. The subscriptions must be deducted from the capital stock if there is no intention of ever calling for the unpaid subscriptions, so that paid-in capital may not be overstated. See form below. 

4. The subscriptions must be shown as a net worth valuation account if there is a contingency with respect to payment, such as, for example, if the subscriptions are payable only out of dividends. earned on the stock. 

If the intentions are as indicated in (2), (3), or (4) above, the net worth section of a balance sheet will be as follows: 744

It may be necessary to write off the Subscriptions account or the Call account because the subscriber does not complete his payments; this is treated in chapter VII, under "Forfeited Stock." Or it may be that the corporation wishes to write off the subscription in accordance with an understanding with the subscriber; such an agreement is illegal unless it is approved by all stockholders. In this case, the Subscriptions account is written off to Surplus. This, of course, affects the net worth of the stockholders who paid par for their stock, as the subscribers who had their subscriptions written off really received their stock at a discount.

Capital Stock Sold at a Discount.-If capital stock is originally sold for less than its par value it is said to be issued at a discount. 

The discount measures the difference between the par value of the stock and the value of the cash, services, or property received for it. 

Some states permit a corporation to sell its capital stock at a discount, and other states make the practice illegal when applied to original issues. Some states require that a corporation be in business for a required number of years, before it can sell stock at a discount. Only stock of a par value can be sold at a discount, as the discount constitutes a reduction from a basic figure, par. Statutory requirements in most states stipulate that par value stock must be carried in the proper capital stock accounts at par. 

The occasion for the issuance of stock at a discount arises when funds are needed and the stock cannot be sold at its par value. The

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

legal prohibition of original issues of "stock at a discount has led (a) to the subterfuge of excessive valuations where property and services are used to pay subscriptions to stock, (b) to treasury stock transactions, (c) to the use of no-par value stock, (d) to the failure to call for the last installment due, by prior secret agreement, (e) to account manipulation, such as charging a discount to an expense or an asset.

Where a corporation may legally issue stock at a discount, the purchaser has no liability to the corporation for the discount or for additional assessments. The certificates will contain a statement that the stock "is fully paid and non-assessable." The purchaser's stock is, in effect, fully paid so far as the corporation is concerned; however, it is not fully paid so far as the creditors of the corporation are concerned. 

In the event that the corporation becomes insolvent, the creditors may compel the stockholders to pay the amount of the discount. 

To illustrate the treatment of discount, assume that 50 shares of the preferred stock of the Belmont Company are subscribed and paid for at a discount of 7 per cent, or $93.00 per share. Using Method III:

Subscriptions, Preferred Stock.. 

Discount on Preferred Stock. 

Unissued Preferred Stock.

To record the subscription of C. L. Long for 50 shares of preferred stock at a 7 per cent discount. .4,650.00 350.00 5,000.00 Cash

May 7, 1942 

Subscriptions, Preferred Stock. 

Payment in full received from C. L. Long for subscriptions of May 1. 4,650.00 4,650.00 

The Subscriptions account is always charged with the amount to be received from the subscriber; the Discount account is charged with the amount of the discount, and the proper capital stock account is credited at par.

Disposition of the Discount Account.-A discount on stock account may be: (a) left on the books permanently, (b) written off to earned surplus, (c) written off to capital surplus. 

The best practice is to allow the Discount on Capital Stock account to remain open on the books, as a true picture is then presented of the amounts received from capital stock sales; in most cases, however, the discount is written off. When the account is permitted to remain, the 179

CORPORATIONS 

109 discount is shown in the net worth section of the balance sheet, as follows: 

Common Stock Surplus Less Discount on Common Stock.. 

Total Net Worth.. 

$ 75,000.00 40,000.00 $115,000.00 5,000.00 $110,000.00

Some accountants prefer to write the discount off to a surplus account over a period of years rather than in one lump sum. If the discount has been written off to surplus, the assumption is that the capital stock has been issued as fully paid by the elimination of the discount as a reduction of the net worth available to the stockholders. 

The write-off to a surplus account does not eliminate the stockholder's liability to the creditors of the corporation. The legality of such writeoffs should always be checked from the angle of the state law involved. 

Discounts on capital stock issues should never be written off to profit and loss, either over a period of time or in one sum. The discount is purely a capital transaction and has no relationship to current profit-and-loss operations.

Capital Stock Sold at a Premium.-If capital stock is sold at a price above par, it is said to be sold at a premium. A Premium account should be set up to take care of the premium. Assume that 75 shares of the common stock of the Belmont Company are subscribed and paid for at a 5 per cent premium.

Subscriptions, Common Stock..

7,875.00 

M. J. Carcourt pays his subscription of May 15 in full.

As in the case of discounts, when stock is sold at a premium, the Subscriptions account is charged at the full subscription price. 

Disposition of the Premium Account.-The sale of capital stock at a premium results in paid-in surplus to the amount of the premium.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Such premium represents a part of the stockholders' investment and any treatment accorded the premium must take this fact into consideration. A Premium on Stock account may be: (a) left on the books permanently, (b) closed to paid-in surplus, (c) closed to earned surplus, (d) closed to capital surplus. 

The best practice is to permit the Premium on Stock account to remain permanently, so that the capital contributions may be distinctly shown.

If a distinction is to be made between paid-in surplus and earned surplus (and such distinction should be made) and if at the same time it is desired to close the Premium on Stock account, the account may be closed to the Paid-In Surplus account, or to the Capital Surplus account if the former is not used. 

The premium, if legally available for dividends, may be closed to Earned Surplus, and then distributed as dividends; this is not good practice, although most states do not prohibit dividends from premiums. 

In any event the origin of the premium should be clearly set out and its treatment determined accordingly. In no case should the premium be written into income.

NO-PAR VALUE STOCK Capital Stock of No-Par Value.-Capital stock of no-par value has no nominal value. Therefore, there are no arbitrary values to be maintained in the no-par stock accounts. No-par stock may be sold (1) at whatever price it will bring, or (2) at or above a certain mini-

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

mum price per share, the minimum price being established either by (a) the board of directors, or (b) the corporation law of the state. 

When stock is of no-par value there can be no premium and no discount, because there is no base upon which to compute the premium or discount. The stock may, of course, be sold at varying prices. Regardless of its sale price, there is no liability for discount attaching to any share.

All states permit the issuance of no-par common stock, and some states permit the issuance of no-par preferred stock. All states require that each stock certificate show the number of shares represented by the certificate. Some states require that each certificate show the total authorized number of no-par shares so that the percentage of ownership represented by any one certificate can be determined. Some states require a minimum issuing price, below which the stock cannot be marketed. Some states set up no requirements as to minimum issuing price. Some states permit the directors to divide the issuing price into (a) an amount for credit to the no-par stock account, and (b) an amount for credit to paid-in surplus. Some states make no stipulations concerning the division of the selling price between stated capital and paid-in surplus, but do not deny the directors the privilege of dividing it. Some few states require that all amounts received from no-par stock, regardless of minimum issuing price, be credited to the no-par stock account. Certain states with lax laws exercise no jurisdiction over the allocation of the assets received for the capital stock, even to the extent of permitting dividends from capital contributions. 

To summarize the possibilities, we have: 

1. No minimum issuing price requirements, in which case the corporation may a) Credit the No-Par Capital Stock account with the entire receipts from the sale of the stock, or b) Credit the No-Par Capital Stock account with a stated amount and credit Paid-In Surplus or Capital Surplus (or even Earned 

Surplus) for the remainder. 

2. A minimum issuing price established by state law, in which case the corporation: 

a) Must credit the No-Par Capital Stock account with at least the minimum issuing price, and may credit Paid-In Surplus or Capital Surplus (or Earned Surplus) for all or part of the amounts received in excess of that price, or

CORPORATIONS 

115 

b) May credit the No-Par Capital Stock account for the entire amount received. 

3. No minimum issuing price, but the establishment of a stated value the board of directors, in which case the corporation: 

a) May credit the No-Par Capital Stock account with the stated value and credit Paid-In Surplus or Capital Surplus (or Earned 

Surplus) for all or a part of the excess amounts, or b) May credit the No-Par Capital Stock account for the entire proceeds of the sale. (This probably will not be done, as there would be no point in deciding upon a stated value, if the entire credit were to go to the No-Par Capital Stock account.) 

In accounting for no-par stock, care must be exercised so that correct procedure is followed for the three possible conditions pointed out above. In the case of stock of a par value, it was pointed out that all shares sold were to be credited to the proper capital stock account at par. From an accounting point of view, the accountant would be materially aided in recording sales of no-par value stock if there were some semblance of uniformity in the state laws. The advantages and disadvantages of no-par stock were discussed in chapter V. 

Accounting for No-Par Stock with a Minimum Issuing Price or with a Stated Value.-When a minimum issuing price is required or when a stated value is assigned, the excess amounts received over the minimum or stated figure, may be (1) credited to the No-Par Stock account, or (2) credited to a surplus account, preferably Paid-In Surplus or Capital Surplus depending upon the requirements of the state law or upon the lack of requirements. Assume that the Mers Company is organized with 10,000 shares of no-par common stock as its authorized capital. The requirements of the state of incorporation are that each share must be sold for at least $5.00. Assume also that the state requires that the No-Par Common Stock account be credited with the minimum issuing price, or that the board of directors wishes to show the credit to the No-Par Common Stock account at that figure if the state does not require it. 

Assume that the stock is subscribed for $55,000.00: Subscriptions 

No-Par Common Stock.

The remaining transactions are the same as those shown for stock of a par value. The credit to Paid-In Surplus should be noted particularly. A Premium account should not be used, as there is no par value. 

A credit to Earned Surplus or to Capital Surplus is misleading as it does not indicate the source of the surplus. The credit to Paid-In Surplus definitely labels the source. While it is true that the corporation starts business with a surplus, the surplus is not earned and should never be made available for dividends; Paid-In Surplus is as much a part of the fixed permanent capital of the corporation as is the amount appearing in the capital stock-accounts.
