Stock Discount as Organization Expense.-Discounts on original stock issues and discounts taken on the sale of treasury stock frequently are charged to the Organization Expense account. Such use of the 

Organization Expense account is very bad practice. The only charges which should be placed in the account are those items, truly expenses, and not capital items, incurred for the purpose of and during corporate organization.

Stock Assessments.-Most state laws require that stock be issued as non-assessable. However, some states permit the board of directors or the stockholders to levy assessments. Assessments usually are on a proportionate basis on the outstanding shares, and assessments normally take place when a reorganization is contemplated or when working capital is necessary in order to avoid bankruptcy. The stock assessment is recorded on the books of the corporation as follows: Cash

Deficit (or Paid-In Surplus) 

XX XX If desired, a Stock Assessments account may be set up at the time the assessments are levied. If this is done the entries are: 

Stock Assessments Deficit (or Paid-In Surplus) 

When the assessments are collected:

XX XX Cash

Stock Assessments 

XX XX Uncollected assessments are closed to the account which was set up when the stock assessments were made. If the state law so provides, stock may be forfeited if assessments are not paid when due. 

Bonus Stock. As an inducement to buyers of stocks or bonds, stock of another class may be given as a bonus. Common stock may be given to the purchaser of preferred stock or bonds; preferred stock may be given to the purchaser of bonds. If the bonus stock is from an original issue, and if original issues cannot be sold below par under the laws of the state of incorporation, then bonus stock can only be given in connection with the sale of a bond. Of course, if stock were sold at a premium, or if either the stock sold or the bonus stock were of no-par value, a bonus is possible. A bond may be legally sold at any price; consequently if the bond is sold for at least the par value

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

of the bonus stock, the transaction should be recorded as though the bonus stock is fully paid and the bond sold at a discount. 

If par value common stock were given as a bonus in connection with the sale of preferred shares at par then the par value common stock is issued at a 100 per cent discount, thus making the purchasers of the stock liable for the entire par value. As a result of the attachment of the discount liability, bonus stock of a par value usually is treasury stock, because the discount liability does not attach to treasury shares.

Bonus stock is a concession made by a corporation. Consequently, it should be shown as such, so that the accounts do not present a misleading condition. It should also be borne in mind that there is no distinction between a bonus and a stock discount. If a discount is granted, it is openly recognized; if a bonus is given, a discount is granted, but it is covered by a gift. 

Assume that one share of $100.00 par value common stock is given as a bonus with the purchase at par of ten shares of $100.00 par value preferred stock, which is selling at $94.00 per share without the bonus. 

The correct entry is: a) Cash

Discount on Preferred Stock.. 

Bonus (or Discount on Common Treasury Stock, if it is treasury stock) or (Discount on Common Stock).

Preferred Stock Common Stock 

. 1,000.00 60.00 40.00 1,000.00 100.00 

This entry shows the true discount on the preferred and also shows the true discount on the common. 

The incorrect entry is: b) Cash

Bonus Preferred Stock Common Stock 1,000.00 100.00 1,000.00 100.00 Of course, if the market price of the preferred stock cannot be determined, or if it is selling at par, the method shown as (b) is the only one to be used, but the discount is definitely hidden, and the vague and undesirable "Bonus" account appears. It must be pointed out in passing, though, that method (b) probably will be used, as it is the desire to hide the discounts.

When no-par common stock is given as a bonus in connection with the sale of preferred stock at par no formal entries can be made in the No-Par Capital Stock account. The only memorandum is a notation in the account of the number of shares given as a bonus. If state law establishes a minimum issuing price and at the same time prohibits sale of stock at a discount, then the gift of bonus stock hints of an extra-legal transaction. The fact of the bonus may be dishonestly concealed, but there appears to be no honest entry. 

Change from Par Value to No-Par Value Stock. The laws of all states permit corporations with par value stock to change the stock to no-par value.

If a corporation with 1,000 outstanding shares of stock with a par value of $100.00 each, replaces the par value stock with no-par value stock, the entry is:

Common (or Preferred) Stock.. 

No-Par Common (or Preferred) Stock. 

.100,000.00 100,000.00

The dollar amount credited to the No-Par Stock account is the same as the former credit in the account with the par value stock. Whether the number of shares of no-par stock is the same, or is greater or less than the former number of shares of par value stock, the number of new shares authorized and issued are recorded in the No-Par Stock account. 

If the directors desire, they may transfer a portion or all of the surplus account to the capital stock account at the time of changing from par to no-par value stock. Of course, the directors must take proper action to do this, and they may or may not declare a stock dividend in order to accomplish their purpose. If the directors take no action, the Surplus account should remain as it was before the change from par value to no-par value stock. Assume that a company has outstanding 1,000 shares of common stock with a par value of $100.00 each, and a surplus of $200,000.00. The company decides to call in the 1,000 shares of par value stock and to issue in its place

The entire new stated capital will be $250,000.00; therefore, $150,- 

000.00 must be taken from the Surplus account. The entry is:

Common Stock No-Par Common Stock. 

Surplus 

100,000.00 150,000.00 250,000.00

If a corporation has a deficit, instead of a surplus, and changes from stock of a par value to no-par stock, the deficit may (1) remain, or (2) be eliminated if the state law does not prohibit. If the deficit is eliminated, (a) no stated value is assigned the new no-par stock, or (b) a stated value is placed at a figure which is less than the par value of the old stock. Assume a corporation with 1,000 shares of common stock of $100.00 par per share outstanding, and a deficit of $50,000.00.

In the event that the par value capital stock originally was sold at a premium, and in any other event that gave rise to capital surplus of a permanent character, such accounts may or may not be closed to the No-Par Capital Stock account. At the time of change from par to no-par stock, if it is desired to transfer such accounts as Premium on 

Capital Stock, Capital Surplus, Donated Surplus, Paid-In Surplus, to the No-Par Capital Stock account, the board should pass the resolution authorizing the transfer. 

Reduction of Capital Stock.—A corporation may wish to reduce its outstanding capital stock issues because (1) the outstanding capital is larger than necessary, (2) fixed assets may have declined in value, when compared to cost, to such an extent that the entire capital structure is greatly overstated, (3) a profit cannot be earned on the basis of the inflated asset values, and consequently dividends cannot be paid; therefore, book losses may be prevented by scaling down the capital structure. 

Capital stock may be reduced by: 

1. Retiring part of the outstanding stock

CORPORATIONS 

121 2. Exchanging the new stock for a smaller number of shares of the old stock 3. Changing from par value stock to stock of no-par value with a lower stated value 4. Reducing the par per share 

5. Reducing the stated value per share 

The provisions of the General Corporation Act of Ohio are typical of requirements for reduction of capital stock. Of course, all laws are not precisely the same as that quoted. 

The stated capital of a corporation may be reduced only as provided in this section. 

1. Shares which by the express terms and provisions of the articles are subject to redemption may be redeemed or paid off at not to exceed the price, including premium, if any, specified in the articles, at the times, in the manner and when authorized by such resolution or action as is provided in the articles, or, if the articles do not otherwise provide, by resolution of the board of directors.

When any such shares are so redeemed or paid off, a reduction of stated capital shall be effected and shall be entered on the books of the corporation, and it shall not be necessary to file a certificate of such reduction, but if the articles provide that shares so redeemed shall be cancelled, a certificate signed by the president or a vice-president and the secretary or an assistant secretary of the corporation shall be filed in the office of the secretary of state, setting forth the number and class of shares so redeemed and a statement that by the terms and provisions of the articles such shares are to be cancelled. Such certificate shall operate as an amendment of the articles and shall reduce the number of shares of the class so redeemed which the corporation is authorized to issue by the number so redeemed and cancelled. 

2. Unless otherwise provided in the articles, treasury shares (not including shares subject to redemption) may be retired and the stated capital of the corporation may be reduced, by the adoption of a resolution of the board of directors authorizing such retirement of shares and reduction of stated capital. 

Treasury shares may also be retired and stated capital may be reduced by such action as may be prescribed in the articles. 

3. The stated capital of a corporation may also be reduced by and pursuant to a resolution adopted by the vote of the holders of two-thirds of the shares of each class of shares outstanding, regardless of limitations or restrictions on the voting power of any such class, or by such other vote as may be prescribed in the articles.

Unless otherwise provided in the articles, the method and manner of adjusting or changing shares, the entries to be made on the books of account to conform to the stated capital as reduced, the price to be paid to acquire shares for retirement, the method of selecting and acquiring shares for retirement, the amount to be withdrawn from or written off from stated capital and/or surplus,

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

the distribution or disposition of any excess of assets resulting from reduction of stated capital, and all matters and details connected with or arising from the reduction of stated capital shall be determined and provided for in the resolution authorizing the reduction of stated capital, and shares and books of account may be changed to conform to stated capital as reduced (a) by retiring all the outstanding shares of any class, (b) by selecting by lot the shares of any class for retirement and retiring the shares so selected, (c) by the exchange or substitution of shares of any class for a different number of shares of the same class or for the same or a different number of shares of another class, (d) by the exchange or substitution of shares having par value for shares without par value or shares without par value for shares of par value, (e) by the purchase of shares for retirement pro rata from all holders of the class to be retired, (f) by the purchase of shares for retirement in the open market or at private sale at such price or prices as may be fixed or authorized in the resolution, (g) by the retirement of treasury shares, (b) by reducing and writing down the stated capital represented by shares without par value, or (i) or in any way not unfair, inequitable, or repugnant to law. Any reduction of stated capital and any adjustment or change so authorized shall be presumed to be fair and equitable to all shareholders. 

4. The amount of stated capital which may be withdrawn and applied to the redemption or retirement of shares shall be determined as follows: (a) When the par value of the outstanding shares is to be reduced, the amount shall be equal to the amount of the reduction of par value. (b) When shares having par value are to be redeemed or retired, the amount shall be equal to the par value of such shares. (c) When shares without par value are to be redeemed or retired, the amount shall not exceed that stated in the articles or determined in the manner provided in the articles to be withdrawn or applied to the redemption or retirement of such shares. (d) In all other cases, the amount shall be determined in the resolution of shareholders, except that in case the shareholders do not determine such amount, and in cases in which the board of directors may authorize a reduction of stated capital, and when the articles grant the authority to the board of directors, the amount shall be determined by the board of directors. 

When the articles so provide, and premium (not in excess of the amount specified in the articles) paid on the redemption of shares having par value, may be withdrawn and applied from stated capital represented by shares without par value. 

5. Whenever a reduction of stated capital is to be effected in a manner' requiring an amendment of the articles, it shall be necessary to adopt an amendment and file a certificate of amendment. An amendment of the articles and a reduction of stated capital may be included in one certificate filed in the office of the secretary of state. 

6. In no case shall the stated capital of a corporation be reduced contrary to the restrictions or limitations, if any, in the articles or in any contract or obligation.

CORPORATIONS 

123 7. Unless the articles otherwise provide, no action taken by a corporation under the provisions of this section shall operate as a reduction of the number of shares which such corporation is authorized to have outstanding, and whenever shares are redeemed or retired, such shares shall have the status of authorized but unissued shares. 

When capital stock is reduced by purchase, the proper capital stock account is charged for the amount of the reduction at par or at stated value or at carrying value if there is no stated value, Surplus is debited for any amounts paid over and above the par or stated value, and Cash is credited for the sum of the two.

Redemption of Capital Stock.-Capital stock occasionally is issued with the provision that it shall be, or may be, redeemed in accordance with certain specified redemption features. This is frequently the case with preferred stock. As soon as financial conditions warrant it, the company may decide to exercise its right to redeem the stock. 

When no provision has been made for the redemption of capital stock, it may be redeemed in accordance with whatever agreement the corporation is able to make with the stockholders; state laws must be observed at all times. State laws normally provide that when capital stock is purchased for retirement, surplus must exist which is at least equal to the amount paid for the stock. Consequently, the retirement of capital stock, even at a premium, must not reduce net worth below the paid-in capital; that is, after retirement, the same net worth will exist as if no stock had been retired and the surplus had been paid as a dividend.

The following case involves the redemption of an issue of preferred stock in accordance with a contract entered into at the time of issuance. 

The Denover Corporation has an outstanding issue of $100,000.00 of 

6 per cent preferred stock, sold originally with the provision that, after three years, the company may redeem the stock on any dividend date by paying all accumulated dividends, and a premium of $3.00 above the par value of the stock. Dividends are payable semi-annually, March 1 and September 1. The company, having paid all dividends up to and including September 1, 1942, notifies its preferred stockholders that on March 1, 1943, it will redeem the entire issue at $103.00 plus accrued dividends. Redemption of Capital Stock in Liquidation.-By redemption of capital stock in liquidation is meant its repurchase by the corporation with funds secured through the disposition of the assets of the company. The amount received by the stockholders in such a case depends on the amount available after the disposition of prior claims. There may be departures from this procedure to meet individual requirements. Thus, the bondholders may first be charged as subscribers, their Subscription accounts being credited when they deposit their bonds in exchange. Again, there may be made allowance for accrued interest on bonds, in which case the bond holders may receive preferred stock to the amount of the bonds plus accrued unpaid interest. The purpose of an exchange of bonds for stock is to avoid the fixed interest charge on the bonds. 

Stock Issued in Units of Preferred and Common.-Occasionally, capital stock is sold and issued in units, at one price for the unit. Thus: 

1. One share of preferred and one share of par value common may be sold as a unit. 

2. One share of preferred and one share of no-par value common may be sold as a unit. 

3. One share of par value common and one share of no-par value common may be sold as a unit. 

4. One share of no-par value common of one class and one share of no-par value common of another class may be sold as a unit. 

If the directors do not designate the values to be assigned to each section of a unit, both sections of the unit must be booked in one capital stock account at the time of issuance, and must remain in the one account until values are established for each section in the open market. 

If both shares of the unit are of no-par value, and if one share has a stated value, that value is credited to a capital stock account for that stock and the remainder allocated to the other no-par value no-statedvalue stock account.

If both shares of the unit are of no-par value and no stated value, the directors must assign capital divisions, or wait until the stock is separately purchased and sold by subsequent holders, in order to obtain amounts for the respective capital stock accounts. 

Assume that a company issued 500 shares of par value preferred, par $100.00 each, and 5,000 shares of no-par value common, stated

Stock Split-Ups.-Capital stock is frequently split into a greater number of shares, because of the desire for a wider market or because the price of the stock in the market before the split-up is too high to obtain the greatest marketability for the stock. Such problems and their solutions are largely those of corporation finance. The accounting problems involved are quite simple. Assume that a company splits its stock on the basis of two new shares for each one share now outstanding. If the stock is of par value, the par may be reduced by half. If the par is reduced by one-half, each share retains its original proportionate part of the corporate net worth. Only a memorandum entry is necessary in the proper capital stock account.

Chapter VII CORPORATIONS-Continued TREASURY STOCK 

Treasury stock is capital stock, either preferred or common, that has been issued and later reacquired by the issuing corporation. The treasury stock is acquired either by (1) purchase by the issuing corporation, or (2) donation to the corporation by a stockholder, or (3) by forfeiture. When treasury stock is acquired by donation it is commonly known as donated stock; when acquired by forfeiture it is commonly known as forfeited stock. The distinction between treasury stock and unissued stock lies in the fact that treasury stock has been issued, whereas the unissued stock has never been originally issued by the corporation.

In some cases the difficulty in selling par value capital stock for cash at its par value has given rise to certain undesirable treasury stock practices. The property or services, or both, contributed by one or more stockholders, in exchange for their stock, may purposely be set up at values in excess of the real values of the properties or services contributed. These stockholders may then donate some of the stock thus acquired to the corporation's treasury. This stock is, in form at least, fully paid stock. By law, stock once fully paid, if reacquired by the issuing corporation, may be reissued at a discount without subjecting the buyer thereof to any liability. By selling treasury stock for whatever it will bring, the corporation secures the necessary cash with which to carry on operations. This procedure is mere subterfuge; the law is observed in form, but violated in spirit. Some states do not permit their corporations to reacquire capital stock as treasury stock. The abuse of par value treasury stock as a means of securing funds has been an important consideration. on the part of the advocates of no-par value stock.

Balance Sheet Treatment of Treasury Stock.-A company's pur chase of its own stock may be made with a view to: (1) its resale, or (2) its cancellation. 128

CORPORATIONS 

129 If the treasury stock is purchased with the intention of reselling it, it is commonly shown as an asset. This practice is based on the somewhat questionable belief that the corporation had the choice of purchasing its own stock or the stock of some other company, and if it had purchased the latter, an asset would have been acquired. Furthermore, the intention might be to resell the treasury stock, and the position of an item in the balance sheet frequently is affected by the intention of management. However, from the point of view of good accounting theory, the better practice is to consider all treasury stock transactions as capital items, and to show the treasury stock as a deduction from the proper capital stock item in the balance sheet. 

When treasury stock is purchased with the intention of cancelling it, net worth definitely is reduced. The treasury stock in this case is always shown as a deduction from the proper capital stock item in the balance sheet.

In those few cases where treasury stock is properly viewed as an asset, it should be entered in the Treasury Stock account at cost, and shown at cost on the balance sheet. 

Par Value Treasury Stock.-Par value stock may be reacquired as treasury stock (1) at par, (2) at a discount, or (3) at a premium.

If par value stock is purchased for cancellation it must be cancelled at par. Hence, if the stock is bought at a price below or above par value, some account must be charged or credited with the difference. 

This account may be called Premium (or Discount) on Treasury Stock, which ultimately should be closed to Capital Surplus, or if that account does not exist, then to the Earned Surplus account. It is perfectly proper to make all charges and credits directly to the Capital Surplus account, instead of using the Premium (or Discount) on Treasury 

Stock account.

In the following par value illustrations, treasury stock is viewed as being acquired for cancellation, and is therefore taken up at par in all instances. If it is viewed as an asset for resale, the purchases are all recorded at cost and the sales at sales price, and any difference between the sales and the purchase price is charged or credited to the Capital Surplus account, or to the Earned Surplus account if a Capital Surplus account does not exist. A less desirable treatment is to consider the difference between sales price and purchase price as an extraneous profit or loss, to be credited or charged to an Extraneous Profit and 

Loss account.

(b) If the book value was less than par, the acquisition of one share at par decreases the book value of the remaining shares. (c) If the book value of the acquired share was more than par, the acquisition of one share at par increases the book value of the remaining outstanding shares.

Special Considerations for Treasury Stock Purchased at Less Than Book Value.-The foregoing treatment of treasury stock transactions is the usual one regardless of the relation between the book value of the stock purchased and the price paid for it. However, there is a good argument for a more exact treatment when the stock is acquired at less than its book value.

Assume that Corporation A has outstanding 5,000 shares of common stock of a par value of $100.00 each, and has a surplus of $100,000.00. 

The book value per share is therefore $120.00. If one share is repurchased as treasury stock at $110.00, what is the correct entry?

The answer depends upon the interpretation placed upon the difference of $10.00 between book value and purchase price. If it represents a discounting of the value of some asset, it is evident that the stockholder is of the belief that surplus is overstated and is willing to accept what he believes should be correct book value, that is, $110.00. Charging Earned Surplus only with the difference between par and the price paid ($10.00) would result in an increase in the book value of the remaining shares, which is contrary to the desired result. 1

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Therefore, the difference between par and book value ($20.00) should be charged to Earned Surplus and the difference between book value and purchase price ($10.00) should be credited to Capital Surplus. The analysis is as follows: 

Surplus charge, applicable to one share.. 

Excess of book value over purchase price: 

Book value of one share. 

Purchase price

Credit to capital surplus.. 

The journal entry is as follows:

Capital Surplus.

No-Par Value Treasury Stock.-As previously stated, no-par stock may be sold (1) with a stated value or minimum issuing price, or (2) without a stated value or minimum issuing price. It also may be sold (a) all at one price per share, or (b) at varying prices per share. 

Therefore, upon the acquisition of no-par value stock as treasury stock, the proper value to assign to the no-par treasury stock immediately arises. If a stated value is used, the procedure for no-par value treasury stock is the same as though the stock were of a par value. of There are three possible methods of accounting for the purchase no-par stock of no stated value. 

1. The No-Par Treasury Stock account is charged with the issuance price of the treasury shares acquired. Theoretically, this procedure is perfect, but practical considerations may render its application a virtual impossibility. For example, if 100 shares of stock were issued at $5.00 per share, and later were reacquired at $7.00 per share, the entry is:

No-Par Treasury Stock... 

Capital Surplus (or Paid-in Surplus) 

Cash.. .500.00 200.00 700.00 

The No-Par Treasury Stock account is a valuation account to the 

No-Par Stock account, and thus the difference between the two shows the correct carrying value of the remaining outstanding shares. Howif the stock of the company is actively traded in the market, and ever,

CORPORATIONS 

135 if the company buys its treasury shares in the market, it is almost impossible to apply this method because the amount paid for each share must be traced to the original transaction, and the company may have issued stock dividends and sold additional shares from time to time. 

Assume, for example, that Mr. Smith purchased 100 shares at $5.00; later he purchased another 100 shares at $6.50; still later he purchased another 100 shares at $8.00; then he turned in this three certificates and obtained one for 300 shares. After a lapse of time, the company bought 200 shares from Mr. Smith as treasury stock. Using this method, which shares of the original three purchases did the company buy? It is impossible to answer the question.

When treasury stock is sold under this method, the Treasury Stock account is credited for the amount paid, and any difference is charged or credited to Capital Surplus or Paid-In Surplus. 

2. Under the second method, the No-Par Treasury Stock account is charged for the average price at which the stock was sold. For example, Company A issued 5,000 shares of stock at varying prices, and received in total therefor, $60,000.00. The average issuance price, therefore, is $12.00 per share. Later, the company buys 100 shares at $14.00 per share.

No-Par Treasury Stock.

Cash. 1,200.00 200.00 1,400.00 

This method permits an allocation to surplus, but the allocation may be theoretically incorrect. For example, in the foregoing illustration, perhaps the 100 shares acquired were issued at exactly $12.00, or perhaps $5.00 or perhaps $15.00. When treasury stock is sold, under this method, the Treasury Stock account is credited at the average cost of acquisition, and all differences between this figure and the sales price are charged or credited to the Capital Surplus or the Paid-In 

Surplus account. 

3. The third method is the most practical and results in an accurate picture of the capital structure. Under this method the No-Par Treasury 

Stock account is charged with the price paid upon acquisition. For example, a company issues its no-par stock at prices ranging from $5.00 to $8.00 per share. Later, it purchases 100 shares of the stock at $9.00.

The entire situation is shown on the balance sheet by deducting the Treasury Stock from the Capital Stock, and thereby arriving at a balance which is the net amount received for the stock outstanding. Most state laws stipulate that treasury stock must be "purchased out of surplus," which means that an amount of surplus equal to the cost of the treasury stock is not available for dividends.

Donated Stock.-Treasury stock given to the corporation by the stockholders may be called donated stock to distinguish it from treasury stock acquired by purchase. Stock may be donated to a corporation in order to: (1) provide a surplus to absorb early years' losses; (2) provide working capital by resale of the donated stock.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Par Value Donated Stock.—When par value stock is donated, it should be charged to the Treasury Stock account or to the Donated Stock account at par. The credit should not be passed to the Earned or Capital Surplus account but to a Donated Surplus account. This account is desirable in order that surplus from this source be segregated from all other surplus. In any case Earned Surplus should not be credited for transactions in the treasury stock of the company.

70,000.00 .30,000.00 100,000.00

The debit to Donated Surplus may be made first to Discount on Donated Stock, which is then closed to Donated Surplus. 

The $70,000.00 balance in the Donated Surplus account may be: 

1. Transferred to Capital Surplus to show the transaction as a capital transaction and to maintain a proper separation from normally accumulated operating surplus. 

2. Credited to an overstated asset. Frequently the facts of the case are such that theoretically this would be correct procedure, but it probably would not be practical; the books then show a truer value of the asset, which is not equal to the par value of the stock originally exchanged for it. Consequently the donated stock would not be true treasury stock, and the purchasers thereof may be held liable for the discount. Furthermore, by law, a board of directors has the absolute power to assign values to property taken in exchange for stock subject only to the existence of fraud. Anyway, highly inflated asset values probably will be recognized by alert prospective investors. 

No-Par Value Donated Stock.-Aside from the possibility of a shortage of unissued stock, no particular reason exists for donated stock of no-par value, because no-par stock can be sold at any price without the incurrence of a discount liability. It may be donated to be sold to obtain working capital, or it may be donated to cancel an operating deficit.

Donation for Specific Object.-When stock is donated with the understanding that proceeds from its sale are to be used for a specific purpose, the entries should reflect the condition. Thus if a deficit exists which is to be removed, the Donated Surplus account balance, or as much thereof as is required, should be closed to the Deficit account. 

Thus if a corporation has outstanding common stock of $50,000.00, and through losses incurs a deficit of $10,000.00, and the stockholders agree to contribute $15,000.00 stock on a pro-rata basis, the entry is: 

Donated Common Stock. 

Donated Surplus... 

.15,000.00 15,000.00

The company may or may not plan to dispose of the stock thus donated. In either case it is safe to carry $10,000.00 from the Donated 

Surplus account to the Deficit account, thus eliminating the deficit. 

There now exists a donated surplus of $5,000.00. Should the company decide to sell the donated stock to obtain additional working capital, the Donated Surplus account should be adjusted for the difference between the par (or stated) value of the stock and the amount for which it is sold.

If stockholders contribute proportionately, they are in the same relative position after making the stock donation as before and have neither increased nor diminished their wealth. If contributions are not proportionate to stock holdings, those making the relatively larger gift sustain book losses. Those who make no contributions, or whose contributions are proportionately less than their holdings of stock, gain in proportionate interest.

Treasury Stock Pledged as Loan Collateral.-Occasionally, treasury stock is pledged as collateral for a loan. It is not necessary to provide a journal entry for the transaction, but if one is made, the procedure is as follows: 

If 100 shares of $100.00 par stock are pledged, the entry, if made, is as given below.

If a balance sheet is prepared while the stock is out as loan collateral and if no journal entry for the pledged stock has been made, a footnote to the balance sheet should state the facts; the treasury stock item in the balance sheet will appear as it did before the stock was pledged.

Treasury Stock Issued for Property. Sometimes treasury stock is given in exchange for property or services acquired by the corporation. 

In such cases the property or other accounts should be charged with the cash-sale value of the treasury stock and not with the par value of the stock. The difference between the par value of the treasury stock and the value of the property acquired should be charged or credited to the Earned or Capital Surplus account, or to the Discount or Premium on Treasury Stock account, depending on which is used. 

Forfeited Stock, Par and No-Par.—If a subscriber to capital stock fails to meet his subscriptions or installments as they fall due, the stock subscriptions may be declared forfeited to the corporation. The accounting procedure after forfeiture depends upon the laws of the state of incorporation. There is much diversity between state law in this respect, but one of the two following conditions generally holds. 

1. In some states, the entire amounts paid in by the defaulting subscriber can be retained by the corporation. 

2. In some states, the' forfeited stock may be offered for public sale, or it may be privately sold, and in either event all proceeds remaining after deducting the amount due, discounts allowed the new purchaser, and the expenses of the resale, must be given to the defaulting subscriber. 

The law of Ohio, for example, follows (2) above and reads:

In the case of default in the payment of any contract of subscription or purchase the corporation may collect the amount unpaid, and in addition to other remedies, unless the contract of subscription shall otherwise provide, the corporation, thirty days after notice setting forth such default and the time and place of the proposed sale of his shares shall have been given the subscriber or purchaser by registered mail, may sell his shares at public auction. Notice of the time and place of sale shall be published once at least fifteen days prior thereto in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the principal office of the corporation is located. Any proceeds remaining after paying the amount due on the shares and the cost of sale shall be paid to the subscriber or purchaser. 

Sec. 8623-27.

Chapter VIII CORPORATIONS-Continued SURPLUS 

Definition. Surplus is the equity of the owners in the assets in excess of liabilities plus capital stock. Surplus is frequently expressed in a balance sheet in one item-Surplus. 

This one item leaves unexplained the origins, uses, and divisions of the surplus. A balance sheet which shows one account for "surplus," regardless of its source, is as unsatisfactory and as meaningless as a balance sheet that simply shows all assets under one caption "assets," with no indication of the kind of assets. As will be shown later, a completely analyzed statement of surplus sets forth not only the divisions of surplus by origin, but also divisions by application. 

A generally accepted principle is that surplus retained is distributed throughout all the assets; it is impossible to allocate surplus specifically to definite assets or asset groups. Much has been done, and much more is being done at the present time toward the correct and proper classification of surplus, in the face of great diversity of opinion among accountants concerning its concepts. Legal definitions, coupled with a popular misunderstanding of the entire concept of surplus, have tended to discourage and retard the speed of the development of surplus definitions and concepts which are adequate to the requirements of finance and business management.

Classification of Surplus. In order properly to determine and to show the origin and uses of surplus, it should be divided into its natural classifications. For accounting purposes, and for statement purposes surplus may be divided into the classes listed below. 

1. Earned Surplus (or Free Surplus) (or Deficit) 

a) Earned Surplus reserves (appropriations of earned surplus) 

2. Capital Surplus 3. Paid-In Surplus 4. Donated Surplus 

146

CORPORATIONS 

147 5.

Unearned Surplus (or Surplus Arising from the Revaluation of Fixed or 

Current Assets) (or Reappraisal Surplus) 

Another way to classify surplus is as follows: 

1. Earned 

2. Capital 

If this classification is used, Paid-In, Donated, and Unearned Surplus are subdivisions of Capital Surplus, and usually appear as parts of that account.

Origins of Surplus in General.-In corporation accounting, the original net worth is measured by the amount of capital stock, stated in dollars, plus any additional amounts originally contributed and credited to Capital Surplus and Paid-In Surplus. As soon as profits are realized, they are segregated in a separate account called "Earned Surplus," and to this account losses are charged and profits credited at the close of the fiscal periods. The accounting for surplus would be relatively simple were all changes in proprietorship due to operating profits and losses, because the uses of surplus arising from profits and losses are fairly well standardized.

In addition to profit accumulation and segregation, "surplus" also arises from the following sources: (a) treasury stock purchased below issuance price; (b) treasury stock sales above the issuance price; (c) premiums on sale of par value capital stock; (d) sale of no-par value stock at prices in excess of the minimum or stated value; (e) donations; (f) stock assessments; (g) the reduction of capital stock in reorganization; (b) the revalution of fixed assets. As pointed out before, and re-emphasized again, where "surplus" has arisen from one or more of these sources, in addition to profits, it is not proper to label the total simply "surplus," thus failing to indicate the origin and nature of the component parts. The classifications shown on the preceding page may be used as a guide to the proper type of surplus involved in any transaction.

The following table shows, in summary form, the sources and uses of the various classes of surplus. The origin of the items that comprise any surplus account is ascertained by a study of the credits to that account. The uses made of any surplus account is only partly divulged by a study of the debits, because the surplus retained is in the asset accounts and so is not expressed as a debit to the account. In the

following table, the asterisk (*) marks such uses of surplus. It must be understood that the sources and uses do not match in accordance with the cross-line of the table.

Earned Surplus.-Earned surplus is the accumulated normal net operating and non-operating profits which are retained in the business. 

Out of this surplus dividends are declared, operating losses absorbed,

CORPORATIONS 

149 and reservations of the surplus effected. If the Earned Surplus account is to be correctly shown, assets, liabilities, expenses, and incomes must be correctly valued, and correct allocation of expense and income between accounting periods must be made. Also, the correctness of valuation, liability and surplus reserves must be ascertained before the correctness of the Earned Surplus account is established. 

State laws are lax in specifying the composition of Earned Surplus, and the accountant will discover many cases wherein credits to Earned Surplus actually belong in some other surplus account. Credits to the 

Earned Surplus account are normally made at the closing date, directly from the profit and loss accounts. Debits to the account may arise at any time during the fiscal period, except that an operating or a nonoperating loss will usually be closed at the end of the period. The attempt should always be made to keep the Earned Surplus account and all other surplus accounts free from current entries. 

Earned Surplus may be: (1) free and available for dividends, or (2) appropriated for certain specific purposes, thereby making this appropriated portion unavailable for dividends. Surplus reserves are treated later in this chapter. 

The existence of a debit balance in the Earned Surplus account arises from accumulated operating losses in excess of accumulated operating profits, or from dividend payments in excess of such accumulated profits. When Earned Surplus has a debit balance, it is customary to call it a "deficit" instead of a "surplus" on the balance sheet, although the account in the ledger probably will still be titled "Surplus." 

Capital Surplus.—As stated, the sources of capital surplus include: profits on the acquisition and disposition of treasury stock; amounts received from stockholders when capital stock assessments are levied if the assessments are not on stock sold at a discount and therefore to be credited to a discount account; increases brought about by the conversion of capital stock from one class to another; and the amount realized upon subscription forfeiture (if the forfeiture is not returned to the defaultor). It must be emphatically noted that all of these sources are directly connected with capital (net worth) transactions, as opposed to normal operating transactions. As capital surplus usually arises at a time subsequent to incorporation and the disposition of capital stock, the Capital Surplus account need not be interpreted as being one representing paid-in or permanent légal capital which cannot and should not be returned to the stockholder as a dividend. If capital

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

surplus is interpreted as including all surplus other than earned, then at least a portion of the capital surplus represents permanent capital; subsequent discussion of other types of surplus will make this last point clear.

Paid-In Surplus.—Paid-in surplus should result only from transactions connected with the capital stock of the issuing corporation. 

Paid-in surplus arises from the sale of par value stock at a premium, and the sale of no-par stock above stated value. As its name indicates, paid-in surplus is paid in to the corporation by the stockholders, at the time of issuing capital stock, and in return for capital stock. Therefore, it should constitute permanent capital in the same sense and to the same extent as do the amounts credited to the capital stock accounts.

Poor accounting practices are frequently encountered in connection with paid-in surplus. For example, one reason sometimes advanced for the creation of paid-in surplus is to give the corporation a "surplus" account for the absorption of early years' losses. This definitely is not the proper function of the Paid-In Surplus account, and any tendency to use it as a hiding place for a deficit should be discouraged. Neither should dividends be declared from paid-in surplus, as this simply constitutes a return of capital to the stockholders. Paid-in surplus, once created, should remain permanently on the books. However, as a matter of practice dividends frequently are paid from paid-in surplus, except in those states where the law specifically prohibits dividends from this source.

Donated Surplus.-Donated surplus arises from gifts of treasury stock, from capital stock assessments, and from gifts of assets. The donated surplus should be treated as invested capital, to be maintained permanently on the books, unless the specific purpose of the donation requires its disposition; for example, the common stockholders may donate common stock to be sold in order to raise funds to pay dividends on preferred stock.

The ownership of donated assets frequently is contingent upon some specific performance; for example, a municipal promotion organization may give to a manufacturing corporation a land site, if the corporation will build a factory and employ, say, 500 men for a period of five years. In such a case, the donated surplus is not actually realized until the requirements attaching to the donation are fulfilled. Again, capital stock of a corporation may be contributed by the stockholders, to be

CORPORATIONS 

151 sold by the corporation so that working capital may be raised; in such a case, the actual amount of the donated surplus cannot be determined until the donated stock is resold. This has been demonstrated in chapter VII. 

Unearned Surplus.-Unearned surplus, or surplus arising from the revaluation of fixed or current assets, is the result of a write-up of some asset. This account is also variously called Appreciation Surplus or 

Revaluation Surplus, or Reappraisal Surplus, or Reserve for Unrealized 

Appraisal Increment. When prices are rising over a long period of time, a company may desire to revalue its properties upward in accordance with the new and higher price level. When these increased valuations are reflected on the books, no profit or gain is actually realized. 

Consequently, the write-up should be credited to an account which clearly shows the true nature of the increase in net worth; the use of the term "Unearned Surplus" or "Revaluation Surplus" gives immediate notice that the "surplus" is merely a book figure, and is not the result of an actual profit. A good balance sheet must definitely segregate under a proper title surplus which was created by revaluation. 

Such unearned amounts should never be made available for cash dividends, even though state laws may not prohibit dividends from these sources, because no liquid assets result for the payment of a dividend and because the increased value is in the fixed assets. The payment of stock dividends from unearned surplus is permissible, because the payment of such a dividend has no effect on current assets. 

Unearned surplus may be created for several reasons, legitimate or otherwise. (1) It may be created in order to write off a deficit, so that a more satisfactory balance sheet is presented. (2) It may be created in order to declare and pay stock dividends, thereby increasing the capital stock accounts. (3) It may be created in order to equalize depreciation expenses between assets purchased at different price levels, so that production costs may be equalized, and so that comparisons can be made with competitors entering the field under high-cost conditions. (4) It may be created in order to reflect current higher actual production costs and thereby segregate "price" profits from other operating profits. (5) It may be created as the result of a reorganization. (6) It may be created for a better determination of (a) tax values, (b) sales values, (c) credit bases, (d) insurance values. (7) It may be created in order to effect new financing of bond or stock issues, or

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

notes. Regardless of the reason for its creation, no gain is realized, and none can be realized until the asset is actually sold or written off into depreciation expense; the reappraisal reflects a remeasurement of the purchasing power of the dollar, made necessary by changing price levels, or by a change in a specific price or value. 

Accounting for the Appraisal.—When reappraisals are made, the accounts involved must be adjusted to the new figures applicable. 

Appraisals, to receive legitimate standing, should be made by wellqualified and competent appraisers. When an appraisal is made, it normally is made on the basis of the present reproduction cost of the old assets which are being appraised. Reproduction cost new, minus the accumulated depreciation to the present time, on the replacement basis, equals present sound value. This concept of present sound value is important. The accounting procedure to follow in connection with the reappraisal must cover two parts: 

1. The entry to record the result of the appraisal. 

2. The depreciation policy to be followed subsequent to the reappraisal; that is, will depreciation be (a) based on original cost or, (b) based on the reappraisal figure. 

Assume that the Centerville Corporation has fixed assets which cost $1,000,000.00 five years ago (estimated total life 25 years), and against which a depreciation reserve of $200,000.00 has been set up ($40,- 

000.00 per year). As of January 1, of the current year, an appraisal is made which shows: reproduction cost new, $1,500,000.00; accrued depreciation based on reproduction cost, $300,000.00; present sound value, $1,200,000.00.

There are two entries possible at the time of reappraisal: 

(1) Plant Appreciation Reserve for Depreciation of Plant Appreciation Reappraisal Surplus 

To record the appraisal made by the U. S. 

Appraisal Company. .500,000.00 100,000.00 400,000.00

Under this method a new asset account, Plant Appreciation, is set up so that the original cost may be carried in a separate account; a new reserve for depreciation is set up to take care of the depreciation on the appreciation to date; and Reappraisal Surplus is credited with the excess. Thus, both cost and the amount of the appraisal are distinctly shown. This is the best method to use, but in all probability it will not be used, because (a) of the additional work involved, and (b) the

CORPORATIONS 

153 amount of the increase is shown. Therefore, the following method is commonly employed: (2) Plant

Reappraisal Surplus 

500,000.00 100,000.00 400,000.00

This method merges the reappraisal and the accumulated depreciation thereon with the old accounts, and effectively hides the true picture so far as the cost of the asset is concerned. 

Two theories have been advanced relative to the subsequent treatment of depreciation on assets which have been written up following an appraisal. The first theory is that the cost of the assets continues to be the correct basis upon which to compute depreciation expense. Assuming, in the foregoing illustration, that the assets which cost $1,000,000.00 have a life of 25 years, then the annual depreciation expense, on a cost basis is $40,000.00 per year. Since the asset account has been written up $500,000.00, the depreciation reserve at the end of the life of the assets, if based on cost, will fall short of the required amount by $400,000.00, the amount of the write-up, less the credit to the reserve at the time of the write-up. As the remaining life of the assets is 20 years, it is necessary to make an adjustment each year for 1/20 part of the $400,000.00 by transferring it to the reserve for depreciation, thus: 

If method 1 is used:

If this method is followed, no provision is made for financing the replacement of the asset. The only thing accomplished is that the balance sheet carries plant values up to current market prices.

The second theory holds that depreciation expense should be computed, not as a percentage of cost, but as a percentage of the appraised value. Under this plan the company owning the assets realizes or

This theory is sometimes subjected to the objection that it inflates operating expense by basing depreciation on a figure which exceeds cost. This subject of revaluation is treated more fully in chapters XVIII

Reappraisal Downward, or Devaluation, and the Surplus Problems Involved. Because devaluation affects corporate net worth, it is considered briefly at this point. The reasons for asset revaluation upward have been given, together with the methods of handling the reappraisal and the depreciation problems involved after reappraisal. The effects upon the surplus accounts involved have also been outlined and demonstrated.

Assets frequently are revalued downward during periods of falling prices, particularly when business is inactive, so that depreciation charges may be reduced in order to show a more satisfactory statement of profit and loss. When considered from the point of the security behind a bond issue or a stock issue, a balance sheet showing assets acquired at high prices is misleading in a period of low prices, for it might lead to the belief that the margin of safety for bondholders is much greater than is actually the case. High book values in low cost

CORPORATIONS 

155 periods might also mean that the proprietary interests of a stockholder would be wiped out if current reproduction costs were used. 

In any case of reappraisal upward or downward, there should be good evidence of the permanency of the change. Revaluations should not be made at every change in the current price level; a revaluation of fixed assets should be made only after the evidence is clear that price levels have changed for a reasonable period of time. Also, in every balance sheet, the basis used for asset valuation should be clearly reflected, so that the auditor's certificate attached to the balance sheet in no way misleads the reader of that statement. 

When devaluation is decided upon, the decision must be made as to whether depreciation will be based (a) on cost, or (b) on the new appraisal. If depreciation is to be based on cost, about the only reason for the devaluation is the presentation of a more conservative balance sheet. Too much conservatism in this direction means that a secret reserve is created. If depreciation is to be based on the newly appraise! value, the devaluation serves to relieve expenses of high depreciation. charges, so that larger profits are shown. 

Devaluation may be recorded in one of several ways. a) Capital Surplus or Earned Surplus may be charged and the asset credited. b) A temporary adjustment account, called Asset Devaluation may be charged and the asset credited for the amount of the write-down. 

In this case, depreciation will be based on the appraisal value and the 

Asset Devaluation account will be closed to Surplus. c) If the devaluation follows an appraisal upward, the Reappraisal Surplus account must be reduced by the amount of the devaluation. 

It occasionally happens, at times of devaluation, that the Capital Surplus or the Earned Surplus account (or the Reappraisal Surplus account if one is on the books) is of insufficient size to absorb the reduction in the value of the assets. For example, a company may have on its books an asset costing $1,000,000.00; the par value capital stock stands at $2,000,000.00; the Earned Surplus (the only surplus account) stands at $300,000.00. The company wishes to write the value of the asset down to $500,000.00. It can be seen that if this were done, a deficit of $200,000.00 would be created; the creation of such a deficit probably will not be desired. Therefore, the solution lies in (1) reducing the par or stated value of the stock, thus creating a capital surplus; or (2) calling in the outstanding shares and issuing, say, one share

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

for each two shares outstanding, thus creating a capital surplus; or (3) changing from stock of a par value to stock of no-par value, with a lower stated value than the par of the former shares and thus creating a capital surplus; or (4) obtaining stock donations in order to create a 

Donated Surplus account. Assume that the company decided to adopt the first method, that is, reduce the par of the stock, and that it was reduced from a par of $100.00 to a par of $50.00. 

Capital Stock Capital Surplus. 

. 1,000,000.00 1,000,000.00

The $500,000.00 devaluation is then recorded: 

Capital Surplus 

Asset or 500,000.00 500,000.00

If the Earned Surplus must be exhausted before write-offs are permitted to Capital Surplus, the entry is: 

Earned Surplus

Capital Surplus 

Asset 300,000.00 200,000.00 500,000.00

In any case of asset devaluation, it must be remembered that the position of the creditors is not affected at the moment if the write-off is to Earned Surplus, or to Capital Surplus, or to any other permanent net worth account. However, if the write-off is to Capital Surplus, and if an Earned Surplus account exists, the creditor's margin of safety may be reduced by dividends paid from the remaining Earned Surplus. Of course, if devaluations are actual, and if at the same time there is no Earned Surplus, or if it is too small to cover the devaluation, the creditors' margin of safety is impaired, regardless of whether or not a devaluation is booked. In such a case, the write-off to a Capital 

Surplus account simply acknowledges the capital impairment. 

If a devaluation is charged to a Capital Surplus account, and if at the same time an Earned Surplus account exists, the latter should be set aside by board action, as not available for dividend distributions. 

Discovery Surplus. In the extractive industries, a price may be paid for land or for a lease, which, after operations have started, proves to be a price too low when considered from the point of view of the real value of the mineral. For example, a mining company might 4974

CORPORATIONS 

157 pay $10,000,000.00 for a tract of ore land; subsequent mining operations, backed by geological surveys, indicates that the ore probably has a value of $50,000,000.00. Such a discovery results in an increase in net worth, which is booked by a charge to the Mining Properties account and a credit to the Discovery Value Surplus account. The 

Discovery Value Surplus account is in the nature of a Reappraisal Surplus account, and must be treated accordingly. 

Surplus Reserves.-A surplus reserve is a segregation of surplus' established to prevent the distribution of earned surplus through the declaration and payment of dividends; such a reserve affords protection to creditors who may be interested in the maintenance of a certain amount of net worth; or it may afford protection to the corporation by insuring against excessive dividends. The procedure to establish a reserve of surplus is to debit the Earned Surplus account and credit a Surplus Reserve account. Such reservations of surplus, if optional, are matters for the board of directors to determine, for it alone possesses the power to create them for suitable purposes. Contractual reserves as, for example, reserves for the retirement of bonded indebtedness are based on compulsory provisions in the deed of trust, and their establishment is not at the discretion of the board of directors. Contractual reserves are established (a) by contract with creditors or (b) by contract with stockholders. 

Common examples of surplus reserves are: a) Reserve for contingencies b) Reserve for future anticipated declines in inventories c) Reserve for loss on purchase commitments d) Reserve for plant extension e) Sinking fund reserve f) Reserve for capital stock redemption 

Reserve for fire loss* b) Reserve for flood loss* i) Reserve for lawsuits*

In the case of all surplus reserves, the amount reserved is ultimately returned to Surplus; this is done at the expiration of the purpose for which the reserve was created. 

Reserves Are Not Funds.—A surplus reserve is not a fund. Funds are assets and appear on the asset side of the balance sheet, whereas It is debatable whether these are surplus or liability reserves.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

surplus reserves are a part of General Surplus, and appear in the net worth section of the balance sheet. All surplus is really a general purpose reserve, and all cash is a general purpose fund. It is necessary to label part of surplus as a special reserve or a part of cash (or some other asset) as a special fund, only for special purposes, that is, because of a contract, or to give investors more complete information. Funds are usually kept in the form of cash or in securities which are readily convertible into cash, so that cash will be available to meet the requirements for which the fund was established. The presence of such funds, as, for example, funds intended for future plant improvement, may lead to a demand by stockholders that they be used to pay dividends. 

To a degree, the directors may forestall such demands by reserving corresponding amounts of surplus, properly designating the reserve. 

Such reserves, being voluntarily created, may likewise, at the board's option, be transferred back to free surplus. Consequently, the protection of the fund may be more apparent than real. 

In certain cases, there may be danger inherent in appropriating surplus. The credit standing of a corporation is peculiarly related to its treatment of surplus. Creditors know that free surplus is always available for dividends. Consequently, one who extends credit on the strength of such surplus may shortly thereafter find the credit standing of the corporation materially weakened as the result of dividend distributions. To remedy this situation the board of directors might segregate a part of surplus, thus rendering it unavailable for distribution. However, this procedure may lead to difficulties later on when free surplus is really urgently needed to pay dividends, unless, when the reserve is created by the board of directors, stipulations for its return to free surplus are included. 

Reserve for Contingencies.—A Reserve for Contingencies is set up out of Surplus, as a matter of conservative practice, to provide for some possible future contingency. A contingency reserve is established in order to prevent the distribution of assets that will be needed if the contingency develops. The creation of such a reserve without some real expectation that a use for it will actually develop constitutes a fraud toward the stockholders for it creates a secret reserve. When a contingency reserve appears on the balance sheet, it is impossible to determine in advance the exact charges which will be made against it.` 

Because the reserve is a segregation of surplus, the charges made against it are made, in effect, against Surplus. Reserves for Contin-

CORPORATIONS 

159 gencies are closed to Surplus, (a) when the contingency develops and results in a reduction of assets or the creation of a liability, or (b) when the contingency fails to develop and it is no longer considered necessary to appropriate part of the surplus. 

Assume that the X Corporation decides to set up a Reserve for 

Contingencies of $50,000.00. The entry is:

Surplus Reserve for Contingencies 

50,000.00 50,000.00

The creation of this reserve withdraws $50,000.00 of Surplus from availability for dividends or any other distribution, and thus protects both the assets of the company and its net worth position. Some time after the reserve is created, assume that the company loses a $40,000.00 lawsuit. The $40,000.00 cost of the lawsuit, if considered as a current expense, must be shown as such. 

Legal Expense 

Cash... .40,000.00 40,000.00

The Legal Expense account is closed to Profit and Loss and thence to Surplus. The effect is a surplus reduction, which can be restored by transferring $40,000.00 from the Reserve for Contingencies.

Reserve for Contingencies. 

Surplus. 

.40,000.00 40,000.00

The reader can see that, if a contingency reserve is thus established, there is no possibility of creating a debit balance in the Surplus account as a result of the maturing of the contingency unless the loss is greater than expected.

Reserve for Future Anticipated Declines in Inventories.-The ac counting treatment of this reserve is discussed fully in chapter XIII, Inventories. When this reserve is created it is set up out of Earned 

Surplus for an amount equal to the anticipated future inventory decline, thus protecting the assets and the capital of the corporation by earmarking a portion of Earned Surplus. If the future anticipated decline becomes a reality, the inventory loss is charged as an expense; the reserve is then closed to Earned Surplus, as the reserve has accomplished its purpose by preventing the distribution of surplus to the extent of the decline.

Reserve for Purchase Commitments.-The accounting treatment of

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

this reserve is discussed in chapter XIII, Inventories. The reserve is created out of Earned Surplus; if a loss on purchase commitments develops, it is charged to expense, and the reserve is then closed back to Surplus, having accomplished its purpose of protecting corporate capital and assets during the period when the loss on purchase commitments was in development. 

Reserve for Plant Expansion.—If a company decided that it wanted to increase its current assets in order to expand its plant in the future, it might limit the availability of Earned Surplus for dividends by creating a Reserve for Plant Expansion. The entry to set up the reserve would be as follows: 

Earned Surplus

Reserve for Plant Expansion. 

.XX 

XX The reserve could be set up in one lump sum or by periodic entries. 

This would restrict dividends to an amount equal to the Earned Surplus remaining after the creation of the reserve. When the plant was expanded it would be paid for and recorded in the usual manner: Plant Cash

XX XX The assets to pay for the plant would be built up by the restrictions previously placed on the use of the surplus. After the plant is built, the Reserve for Plant Expansion, having accomplished its purpose of asset protection may be closed back to Earned Surplus. However, the cash invested in the plant is not available for dividends; this may be indicated by closing the reserve to Capital Surplus. 

Reserve for Sinking Fund.—The Reserve for Sinking Fund is treated in chapter XXII, Funds and Reserves; Sinking Funds. After the accomplishment of the purpose for which the Reserve for Sinking Fund was created, the reserve is closed to Earned Surplus from which it was created, or to Capital Surplus. 

Reserves for Fire Loss, Flood Loss, and Lawsuits.-If the view is taken that these reserves are surplus reserves, they are created out of Earned Surplus. The actual fire, flood, or lawsuit loss should be charged as a non-operating expense which in turn is closed to Earned Surplus. After the fire, flood, or lawsuit loss has occurred the balance in the reserve may be closed to Surplus unless another such loss is anticipated.

CORPORATIONS 

161 If the view is taken that these reserves are liability reserves, they are created by charges to expense accounts at dates preceding the event. 

At the actual occurrence of the event the losses suffered thereby should be charged to the reserve, as the expense already has been recognized. 

Secret Reserves.-When the net worth of a corporation is understated, a secret reserve exists. The secret reserve results from: a) An undervaluation of assets. (1) Complete omission of an asset (2) Excessive depreciation of assets (3) Charging capital expenditures to income (4) Crediting income to a liability account b) Overstatement of a liability One motive behind the creation of secret reserves is conservatism and a desire to have resources in addition to those expressed on the balance sheet. Another motive for the secret reserve is to equalize profits between good and bad years. In years of large profits, directors might resort to a procedure resulting in a secret reserve; this would result in a lower profit, and stockholders would be stopped from suggesting additional dividends. In a poor year, the reserves secretly created before are eliminated by profit and loss credits, thereby resulting in a favorable profit position and a net worth condition which is the same as though the secret reserve had not been created; thus the credit standing of the company is maintained. The net effect for the whole period is the same as though a secret reserve had not been created.

The secret reserve may be intentional or unintentional. If a corporation understates the value of an asset by writing the asset off to Surplus, the procedure is intentional; if, on the other hand, a corporation over-depreciates an asset, honestly believing the rate of depreciation it is using to be correct, the creation of a secret reserve is unintentional. Regardless of whether or not the understatement of an asset or the overstatement of a liability is intentional or unintentional, the result is always an understatement of net worth. 

Naturally, if net worth is incorrectly stated, expense and income likewise have been incorrect, unless the reserve has been created by direct surplus charges. From an income tax liability standpoint, it is important that incomes, expenses, and the resultant net profit be correctly shown. Therefore, secret reserves are not as commonly found

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

as before federal tax legislation became effective. From the point of view of the stockholders, secret reserves are undesirable, as the reports to the stockholders are falsified by the amount of the secret reserve; such a condition might cause an unsuspecting shareholder to dispose of a profitable investment at a loss. The wisdom of carrying secret reserves is extremely doubtful, because it is not good practice to show any condition in other than a truthful manner. Deliberate misstatements of profit-and-loss items and deliberate misstatements of assets and liabilities, where both misstatements create secret reserves, is just as deplorable as overvaluation; both should be avoided. 

An Introduction to Guides to the Proper Determination of 

Surplus. Accounting is not exact. It is an art in the proper execution of which the judgment of the accountant plays an important part, and the judgment of all accountants is not equally sound. Also, there are many phases of accounting upon which opinions vary between equally competent men. Thus, the inexactness of some phases of accounting, and the judgment and the opinion of the accountant are all reflected in the final statement of the net worth of any company. There are, however, certain guides or rules or principles which are rather universally accepted as criteria for the proper determination of income and net worth. These are fully discussed in chapter X, Income Determination. A few of these guides are briefly considered at this point, because their proper interpretation results in a correct or an incorrect net worth statement for the corporation. 

At the present time, it is accepted as good practice to close both operating profits and losses and non-operating profits and losses to Earned Surplus. On the statement of profit and loss, these two classes of profits and losses should be shown separately and distinctly, so that there can be no confusion as to the source of a profit or loss. Operating profits and losses result from the sale of the products regularly manufactured and sold. Non-operating profits and losses result from the disposition, at a profit or a loss, of such assets as securities held as temporary or permanent investments, land, buildings, and machinery, interest expense and income, and purchase and sales discounts. 

Some companies do not show all non-operating profits and losses on the statement of profit and loss, but rather close certain items directly to Surplus. In such instances, the statement of surplus (considered in chapter IX) must clearly indicate the source of the surplus adjustment. The better practice is to show all non-operating profit and

CORPORATIONS 

163 loss transactions in the profit-and-loss statement, as these items must be taken into consideration for the proper determination of the federal income tax liability; furthermore, non-operating transactions result in profits and losses as readily as do operating transactions.
