Chapter IX CORPORATIONS-Concluded SURPLUS; DIVIDENDS Analyses of Accounts and Adjustments of Surplus. During a fiscal period, and at the end of a fiscal period, it is often found that adjustments to a surplus account are necessary. The adjustments may be the result of: 

1. Normally recurring charges and credits to a surplus account 

2. Mistakes in the operating accounts of prior periods, discovered during the current period, which, if taken to current Profit-and-Loss, will result in an error in the current Profit-and-Loss, unless the corrections are shown separately as non-operating items 3. An auditor's analysis of the asset, liability, expense, and income accounts for the preceding period, after the client has closed the books 4. Incorrect charges or credits to one surplus account, when another surplus account should have been charged or credited. 

Normally, most surplus adjustments affect the Earned Surplus account. When surplus adjustments are to be made, they may be carried directly to the proper surplus account, or, if they are numerous, it may be preferable to open a Surplus Adjustment account. All adjustments are made directly to this account, its balance in turn being carried to the proper surplus account at the close of the accounting period. A 

Surplus Adjustment account usually will be necessary only for the adjustments to be made to the Earned Surplus account. 

If possible, the Earned Surplus account should be kept free of entries during the current period; all earned surplus charges and credits should be collected and summarized in separate accounts and then closed to Earned Surplus in summary form at the end of the period. For example, some companies, in following this policy, set up a Dividends account, charging thereto all dividend declarations made during a fiscal period. The Dividends account is closed to Earned Surplus at the erd 166

CORPORATIONS 

167 of the year.

This procedure eliminates many entries in the Earned 

Surplus account. 

There are two schools of thought with respect to adjustments of preceding periods. One school holds to the theory that errors of preceding periods, discovered in the current period, should be adjusted to Surplus, so that the statement of profit and loss for the current period does not contain items which pertain to some past period. The second school holds to the theory that errors of preceding periods, discovered in the current period, should be shown as extraneous or non-operating items in the current statement of profit and loss, although they are not necessarily in the correct period. Thus all expenses and incomes appear on some statement of profit and loss, and the totals of a number of successive statements are correct. 

The modern tendency in accounting practice is to show profit-andloss errors of preceding periods in the current statement of profit and loss as extraneous expenses or incomes, thus following the second of the two views set forth in the preceding paragraph. But if the statement of surplus is shown immediately following the profit-and-loss statement, or as a part of the statement of profit and loss, the adjustments of both the current period and preceding periods are shown in one of the two related statements. 

Charges and Credits Which Normally Are Made to a Surplus 

Account. For any given company, the charges and credits normally appearing in a surplus account will depend upon the practices followed by the organization. The following charges and credits to the surplus accounts normally are correct; the alternative of a charge or credit to 

Profit-and-Loss is noted in those instances where a difference of opinion may exist.

The Earned Surplus account should be credited with (1) operating and non-operating profits, through the closing of the Profit-and-Loss account; (2) unamortized bond premium remaining after the bond issue is retired, unless the preferable practice of a credit to non-operating income is followed; (3) surplus reserves credited back to Surplus after their purpose has been fulfilled; (4) devaluation of capital stock, unless credited to Capital Surplus; (5) prior years' errors in profit and loss, if the preferable practice of using non-operating income accounts is not followed. The Earned Surplus account should be charged with (1) operating and non-operating losses, through the closing of the Profit-and-Loss account; (2) dividends declared; (3) federal income

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

taxes, if the preferable view that income taxes should be charged to Profit-and-Loss is not followed; (4) unamortized bond discount remaining after the retirement of a bond issue, unless a charge is made to a non-operating expense account; (5) the creation of surplus reserves; (6) mistakes of preceding years which were not charged to expense in the period of occurrence, if the preferable practice of a charge to expense in the period of discovery is not followed; (7) direct charge-off of assets, unless a prior write-up of these assets has been credited to some other surplus account. 

The Capital Surplus account should be credited with (1) profits on treasury stock purchases and sales; (2) capital stock assessments; (3) capital stock conversions if the conversion results in capital surplus; (4) gain on the forfeiture of stock subscriptions; (5) devaluations of capital stock, unless credited to Earned Surplus; (6) change from par value to no-par value stock if the stated value of the new stock is lower than the par value of the old. The Capital Surplus account should be charged with (1) losses on treasury stock transactions; (2) write-down of assets where a prior write-up has been credited to Capital Surplus; (3) cash or stock dividends, or surplus reserve creations specifically designated to be from Capital Surplus. 

The Paid-In Surplus account should be credited with (1) premiums on the sale of par value capital stock; (2) amounts realized on the sale of no-par value stock at a price above stated value. The Paid-In 

Surplus account should be charged with (1) capital stock discounts; (2) adjustments resulting in a reduction in paid-in surplus. 

The Donated Surplus account should be credited with (1) donations of capital stock; (2) donation of assets; (3) capital stock assessments. The Donated Surplus account should be charged with (1) losses realized upon the disposition of donated capital stock or donated assets; (2) dividends specifically declared from this source.

The Reappraisal Surplus account should be credited with (1) the amount of asset revaluation upward. It should be charged with (1) devaluation of assets formerly written up; (2) stock dividends specifically declared from this source. 

Mistakes in Prior Years' Operating Accounts.-As pointed out earlier in this chapter, mistakes in prior years' operating accounts, discovered during the current period, may be adjusted either to a surplus account (usually Earned Surplus), so that the normal operations of the current year are not distorted, or they may be adjusted to Profit-and-

CORPORATIONS 

169 Loss as extraneous items. For example, a company has $100,000.00 of 

6 per cent bonds outstanding; the interest is payable March 1 and

September 1; the company neglected to accrue interest on the bonds at the end of the fiscal period, December 31, 1942, and interest expense is therefore understated. In the next period, when the interest is paid on March 1, 1943, the total interest expense is overstated by the amount of the interest for the last four months of 1942, which should have been charged to expense for 1942. If the view is taken that the adjustment should be to Surplus, the following adjustment is necessary: 

Earned Surplus

Interest Expense on Bonds 

.2,000.00 2,000.00

The debit to Earned Surplus corrects the 1942 profits which have been closed to Surplus; the credit reduces the overstated expense for 1943. 

If the view is taken that the adjustment should be made through Profit-and-Loss, the statement of profit and loss should separate the 1943 normal expense from the expense applicable to 1942. 

As another example, assume that a deferred charge of $6,000.00 which should have been written off in former years is still carried on the books. Since the expense and income accounts of former years cannot be reopened and the Profit-and-Loss for the proper period adjusted, the Earned Surplus account may be charged $6,000.00, thereby reducing its balance to the amount which would have existed had the item been treated correctly in the first instance. If the adjustment is made to current Profit-and-Loss, the $6,000.00 charge should be set forth separately in the statement of profit and loss, with the statement that it is applicable to a past period. 

It must be remembered that neither procedure corrects, the statement of profit and loss for the year in which the errors were made; hence, successive comparative statements of profit and loss are not correct unless they are recast for comparative purposes. 

But there is one difference which is significant enough to be repeated. If these corrections are made through Profit-and-Loss and appear as extraneous expenses or incomes on some statement of profit and loss, then the totals of a series of comparative statements of profit and loss are correct; readers of these statements are much less likely to be misled.

An Auditor's Analysis of an Account.-The analysis of an account by an auditor may lead to the discovery of (1) mistakes made in pre-

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

ceding years, or (2) incorrect charges and credits to the various surplus accounts employed, or (3) overstatement or understatement of current expense charges or income credits. The entries made by an auditor are not "different"; they are simply based on errors discovered by an "outside" party. If the mistakes are those arising in prior years, adjustments are made in the manner illustrated above; in any event, the auditor will reflect in his corrected statement of profit and loss any adjustments that affect the current period. 

If the analysis shows that certain expenses or incomes are understated or overstated, the adjustments may be (a) made to Surplus if the client's books have been closed for the current period, or (b) made to current Profit-and-Loss if the books have not been closed. In either case, a correct statement of profit and loss and a correct balance sheet can be presented for the current period, as the auditor is analyzing the accounts for this very purpose. 

If the books have not been closed, adjustments for the current year are made to the proper income or expense accounts; therefore, no surplus adjustments are made. To demonstrate a few adjustments that might arise as the result of an auditor's analysis, a few illustrations are submitted. Assume that the analysis of an asset account and its related depreciation reserve account led to the discovery that the asset had been overdepreciated to the extent of $10,000.00 over the past ten years. 

This means that Depreciation Expense has been overstated by $1,000.00 in each of the past ten years and Earned Surplus understated. The adjustment is:

Entries to Wrong Surplus Account. If the mistakes consist of in correct charges or credits to one surplus account when another surplus account should have been charged or credited, the total net worth is not changed, but simply incorrectly classified. The mistake may be discovered accidentally or by an auditor's analysis. The amount in error should be transferred to the proper surplus account. 

Miscellaneous Items Concerning Which There Is Lack of Uni formity of Opinion Does Not Exist.-Accountants are not in complete agreement with respect to the treatment of certain transactions of a non-operating or extraordinary nature. Some think they should be treated as surplus adjustments and some consider them as extraneous expenses and incomes. A few instances wherein differences of opinion are prevalent are cited here. When opinions differ as to the correct disposition of an item, full explanation of the item is of vital importance..

Profit and Loss on Disposition of Fixed Assets.-The first case deals with the profit and loss on the disposition of fixed assets. Some accountants advocate carrying such profits and losses direct to Surplus, since their entry in the Profit-and-Loss account renders the statement of profit and loss more or less useless for comparative purposes. This practice is not approved by the best authorities. It makes the Surplus account a dumping ground and a hiding place for miscellaneous items which, in reality, affect current profit and loss, and which, being carefully distinguished as non-operating items, should be shown therein. because a profit is realized or a loss incurred. It is true that the profit or loss may not be directly attributable to the current period, but allocation between accounting periods is an impossibility in such cases, and, in addition, profits and losses are taken up when they are realized. 

Therefore, logically they should not be buried in Surplus. Also, the corporation federal income tax return requires a reconciliation of surplus as at the close of the preceding year with surplus as at the close of the current year. As a consequence, making adjustments of current items directly against surplus may necessitate clumsy adjustments in the income tax returns. 

Since it is desirable to show extraordinary items of profit and loss in the profit-and-loss statement, it may be desirable to open an account entitled Extraordinary Profit-and-Loss, or some similar title, to which such extraordinary items of expense and income are carried. At the close of the accounting period, the balance of this account is closed

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING OUNTING 

into the Profit-and-Loss account and shown as a separate item on the statement of profit and loss. A more detailed and better procedure is to set up as many extraordinary expense and income accounts as necessary, closing each to the Profit-and-Loss account, and thus showing proper detail in the statement of profit and loss. 

Bad Debt Losses.-The next case arises when, during periods of depression, large losses result from uncollectible accounts. Should such losses, in excess of normal, be charged to surplus? The procedure is highly questionable, even if the losses are the result of sales of prior periods, because the losses are actually realized in the current period. 

During prosperous years reserves for bad debts should be strengthened to meet the increased burden arising from depressions that may follow. 

Provisions for bad debts, and bad debts in excess of the provisions, should all be currently absorbed in Profit-and-Loss. 

Inventory Losses.-Inventory losses are incurred because of the shrinkage in value of the inventory. Such losses should be taken up as such when they are encountered by: 

Loss on Inventory Decline..

Inventory 

XXXX XXXX and should not be charged to Surplus. If a company consistently carries its inventories at cost, the losses are realized in the period in which the inventory is sold, through reduced sales prices resulting in a lowered profit; by this procedure the losses are not specifically shown as such. See chapter XIII for a full discussion of inventories.

Statements of Surplus.-When adjustments to surplus are few in number either during the fiscal period or at the termination of the fiscal period, it is possible to show the analysis of surplus in the proprietorship section of the balance sheet. The better practice, however, is to show each class of surplus, such as earned surplus, capital surplus, and so on, individually as one amount in the balance sheet, and to prepare a schedule supporting each of the balance sheet surplus figures; these schedules should present a detailed analysis of the surplus charges and credits during the period and at the end of the period, together with the initial and closing balances. This statement of surplus enables the accountant or other interested person to visualize significant changes in the surplus accounts and in the asset and liability sections of the balance sheet.

Accountants usually include a statement of surplus in their reports

CORPORATIONS 

173 on audits or other investigations. As a rule, such a statement is a reconciliation of each of the surplus accounts, beginning with the balance on the opening day of the accounting period, followed by an itemized list of debits and credits, and closing with the balance at the end of the accounting period. When the auditor returns the next year to audit the books, he finds the statement of surplus for the previous year helpful in taking up the analysis of surplus at the proper point. 

Prior years' statements of surplus may eventually prove to be incorrect, because of belated adjustments necessitated by discoveries in subsequent periods.

ADVANCED. ACCOUNTING 

This procedure conforms to accepted practice in the preparation of the net worth section of a balance sheet, as shown below under "Surplus and Reserves in the Balance Sheet." The student should study published statements of surplus to become acquainted with the great variety of forms in existence, all commonly used in the preparation of surplus statements.

Restatement of Surplus.-Reference to Illustrations II and III 

above suggests the desirability of recasting the surplus account over a period of years, so that it will be in the same form as if no errors had been made. If this is done, comparative statements of profit and loss also should be recast, to support the corrected net profit figures in the surplus statements. Errors which affect profit and loss in a given period are of two classes: (1) counterbalancing errors, (2) non-counterbalancing errors. 

Counterbalancing errors are automatically adjusted in the following period, so that if a profit is overstated or understated in one period, it is understated or overstated by the same amount in the following period, and surplus at the end of the second period is correctly stated. 

Thus if the closing inventory is overstated by $2,000.00 at December 

31, 1942, this results in the overstatement of profits by $2,000.00 in 

1942, and the understatement of profits by $2,000.00 in 1943. The balance of surplus. is correctly stated at December 31, 1943. Of course, if the December 31, 1942, error is corrected before December 31, 1943, the profit for the latter year is correctly stated. 

Non-counterbalancing errors are not automatically adjusted in the next period; hence surplus remains incorrectly stated until adjusted. 

Assume that the allowance for depreciation in 1941 should be $3,000.00 but is not entered. Consequently, profit is overstated by $3,000.00; also, surplus is similarly overstated and remains so until corrected by an adjusting entry, or until the asset is disposed of. 

Although both counterbalancing and non-counterbalancing errors affect profit and loss for one period, all errors affecting expenses and incomes are finally counterbalanced as follows: (1) automatically in the next period, (2) automatically or consciously over several periods, (3) by counter charges or credits to surplus.

Dividends.-A dividend is the distribution of the accumulated earnings of a corporation among the stockholders. The dividend may be distributed in: (a) the assets of the corporation (normally cash), or (b) the capital stock of the corporation (a stock dividend), or (c) obligations of the corporation. 

Dividends from accumulated earnings may: (a) decrease the corporate net worth, or (b) not decrease the corporate net worth. 

Dividends decrease the corporate net worth when they are paid in: (a) the assets of the corporation, or (b) the liabilities of the corporation.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

When assets are used for dividend payment, cash is the commonly used asset, but any asset may be employed. 

When liabilities are used for dividend payment, they will take the form of (1) scrip, (2) notes payable, or (3) bonds payable. When corporate liabilities are used for dividend payment, the corporation eventually must liquidate the liabilities in cash. 

Dividends do not decrease the corporate net worth when they are paid in the form of the capital stock of the corporation. 

When dividends are paid in the capital stock of the corporation, the amount of the dividend is transferred from Surplus to the proper capital stock account. This, of course, has no effect upon the total net worth of (1) the corporation, or (2) the stockholder; the equity of the latter is simply represented by more shares, instead of a larger value per share for a smaller number of shares. 

Corporation Profits and the Stockholders' Rights to Dividends. 

-The profits of a corporation, both past profits closed to Surplus, and currently earned profits, "belong" to the stockholders of the corporation for they are the owners of the corporation. At the same time, no stockholder has the right to receive a dividend at his own discretion, because the stockholder has delegated his managerial powers to the board of directors of the corporation. Therefore, in the absence of fraud toward stockholders, the right to declare or not declare a dividend rests exclusively with the board of directors. 

Several determining factors must be considered in connection with the declaration and payment of a dividend: 

1. The condition of the Surplus account(s) 

2. The condition of the Cash account 

3. The necessity for funds for maturing obligations 

4. The need for working or fixed capital 

5. Probable future business conditions 

6. The amount of treasury and unissued stock available for dividends Dividends are declared from surplus, but actual payment is made in the form of cash or other assets, scrip, notes or other liabilities, or capital stock.

Rescission of Dividends.-The power of the board to rescind a dividend depends upon whether the dividend is payable in cash or in the capital stock of the corporation. If a cash dividend is legally declared, it cannot be rescinded by the board if notice of the dividend

CORPORATIONS 

181 declaration has been given to the stockholders; notice is interpreted to mean a general announcement of the dividend which will appear in newspapers of general circulation; notice does not mean that each stockholder must be individually advised of the dividend action. Upon declaration and notice the power of the board ceases with respect to the dividend, and the declared dividend becomes a legally enforceable debt of the corporation. The only condition under which a legally declared cash dividend may be rescinded is that all of the stockholders agree to the revocation. The declaration of a dividend or the failure to declare a dividend should be announced by the board as soon as the dividend action is taken, so that (1) stockholders may use their judgment with respect to disposing of stock or acquiring more stock, and (2) directors may not be placed in a personally advantageous position because of their knowledge of the board action. 

If a stock dividend is declared, it may be rescinded by the declaring board at any time preceding the distribution of the certificates. This is permissible on the basis that the stockholders' equity in the corporation is not increased or in any way affected by the receipt of a stock dividend; if the stockholder does not receive a stock dividend his interest per share is greater than if a stock dividend were given, but his total interest remains the same in both cases. A stock dividend is not considered to be income to the stockholder, but simply a division of his part of the net worth into a greater number of shares. 

If a dividend, either cash or stock, is illegally declared, (1) it may be rescinded at any time before payment, (2) it may be restrained by enjoining action, (3) it must be returned to the corporation, if it has been paid or issued.

In the event of corporate dissolution, declared dividends rank with the liabilities of other unsecured creditors.

Legality of Dividends and Liability of Directors. In general dividends are illegal: a) When they reduce net worth below the amount of the contributed corporate capital (unless they are liquidating dividends). b) When they are in violation of the charter or by-laws of the corporation. c) When a declaration on one class of stock violates the rights of other classes of stock. act. d) When they violate a specific provision of the state corporation

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Dividends may be declared (1) from profits currently earned if a deficit does not exist, or (2) from past accumulated profits, that is, from surplus. Thus, from a legal point of view, the ability of the corporation to pay dividends depends upon the condition of the surplus, not upon the profits from any one period, and not upon the amount of cash on hand. From the point of view of the discretion of the directors, however, current profits and cash are important considerations. Legally, a dividend may be declared in a period when a loss is incurred, providing the condition of the surplus justifies the dividend. 

Thus it is clear that in the United States, the balance sheet is the guide for the legality of dividends. In Great Britain, this is not the case; there dividends depend upon the current profits of the corporation. 

The statement of profit and loss is the legal guide. 

State laws vary widely with respect to their requirements for the legality of a dividend. The usual provisions covering illegal dividends are pointed out above, but the following situations also exist: a) Some states require provisions for depletion of wasting assets before the surplus is determined; other states do not make such requirements. b) Some states prohibit dividends from unrealized surplus; others permit stock dividends, but prohibit cash dividends; others permit both stock and cash dividends from such surplus. c) Some states prohibit dividends from capital surplus; other states require that the capital surplus be definitely earned before being used for dividends. d) Some states prohibit dividends from paid-in surplus; others permit them; others limit such dividends to specific classes of stock. e) Some states permit dividends from surplus arising from any source. f) Some states permit dividends from surplus created by the reduction of capital stock provided creditors are not thereby harmed; others prohibit it. g) Some states prohibit dividends before discounts granted on capital stock have been written off to surplus; others permit dividends before the write-off. h) Most states (47) prohibit dividends when a deficit is on the books.

CORPORATIONS 

183 The dividend provisions of the General Corporation Act of Ohio (Sec. 8623-38) are quoted below. It is suggested that the law of your state be compared with it. (a) A corporation may declare dividends payable in cash, shares, or other property out of the excess of the aggregate of its assets less the deductions hereinafter required over the aggregate of its liabilities plus stated capital. (b) In computing the excess of the assets, deduction shall be made for depletion, depreciation, losses, and bad debts. In computing the excess of assets for the purpose of determining the fund available for a dividend payable otherwise than in shares of a corporation deduction shall also be made for the unrealized appreciation, if any, appearing on its books unless the amount thereof shall have been transferred to or included in stated capital. If the articles so provide, a corporation whose business consists substantially of the exploitation of wasting assets, may pay dividends without making deduction for the depletion of such assets resulting from lapse of time or from the consumption or sale of such assets incidental to their exploitation. (c) No corporation shall declare or pay a dividend in cash or other property when there is reasonable ground for believing that it is unable or, by the payment of the dividend, may be rendered unable to satisfy its obligations and liabilities. (d) Whenever a dividend is paid, in whole or in part, out of other than earned excess of assets appearing on the books of the corporation at the time of the declaration of such dividend, the shareholders receiving such dividend shall be notified as to its source. (e) Whenever two or more corporations have heretofore been or shall hereafter be consolidated or merged (pursuant to section 8623-67 of the General Code or by purchase) or whenever a corporation has heretofore been or shall hereafter be reorganized, the earned excess of assets appearing on the books of the constituent or merged corporations or on the books of a corporation prior to reorganization, may, to the extent that it is not capitalized, be entered as earned excess on the books of the consolidated corporation or on the books of the corporation into which the other or others are merged, or on the books of the reorganized corporation, and thereafter may be treated as earned excess.

A corporation may, by action of its board of directors, apply any part or all of any paid in surplus or any excess of assets however created or arising excepting only surplus arising from revaluation of assets, to the reduction or writing off of any deficit in the account of earned surplus or to the writing off of any particular loss or expense or to the creation of a reserve or reserves for any proper purpose and thereby make available for dividends without notice to the shareholders as to the source of such dividends any earned excess of assets remaining or resulting therefrom or thereafter arising, but in case such action is taken a disclosure thereof shall be made in the next annual statement of the corporation.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Any excess of assets hereafter arising otherwise than from the earnings of a corporation shall be classified according to its derivation and so shown in separate accounts. (f) Nothing contained in this section shall prevent the directors of a corporation from setting apart out of the excess of assets available for dividends a reserve or reserves for any proper purpose or from abolishing any such reserve.

Whenever the board of directors of a corporation shall be of the opinion that its assets, including patents or good will, have a fair value to the corporation in excess of the amount at which they are carried on its books, and shall determine the amount of such fair value, it may order all or a part of the fair value, so determined to be entered on its books and thereby create an excess of assets, which the board of directors may apply to a dividend in shares of the corporation and transfer to stated capital or apply to an increase of stated capital represented by shares without par value. 

Any transfer of excess of assets to stated capital shall be deemed to have been made from that part of the excess, if any, which resulted from unrealized appreciation. A dividend payable in shares without par value may be declared and paid upon the transfer of stated capital of any amount that may be ordered by the board of directors, or, without any change of stated capital, as the board of directors may determine.

No dividend shall be paid to the holders of any class of shares in violation of the rights of the holders of any other class of shares. 

The liability for illegal dividends is established for the protection of the creditors of a corporation. Of course, if an illegal dividend is declared and paid, and if the creditors actually do not suffer, nothing will result from the illegal actions. All state corporation laws set up liabilities for illegal dividends, and here, again, state laws vary widely with respect to penalties. In most states the directors who affirm the illegal dividends are liable to the creditors of the corporation for the amount of the dividend, and the stockholders are liable for the return of the illegal dividend to the corporation. If a director dissents to the dividend, he is not liable. Some states make the illegally declared 'dividend a misdemeanor for the assenting directors. Some states make the directors liable not only for return of the dividend but also liable for all corporate debts incurred during the directors' term of office. 

Some states limit the liability for the return of the illegal dividend to those stockholders who knowingly accepted it. The unlawful dividends section of the Ohio General Corporation Act (Sec. 8623-1236) is as follows: 

The directors of a corporation shall not declare or pay dividends or authorize the withdrawal or distribution of any part of its assets except as provided in this act.

CORPORATIONS 

185 Any shareholder, who shall knowingly accept or receive any dividend or distribution not authorized by this act to be made, shall be liable to the corporation in the amount accepted or received by him with interest at the rate of six per centum per annum until the same shall be repaid. 

In case of any wilful or negligent violations of the provisions of this section, the directors, under whose administration the same shall have happened (except those who shall dissent as hereinafter provided), shall be jointly and severally liable to the corporation for the full amount of any such unauthorized dividend or distribution with interest at the rate of six per centum per annum until the same shall be paid.

A director shall not be held to have been negligent within the meaning of this section if he relied and acted in good faith upon the books of a corporation, or upon a balance sheet and profit and loss statement of the corporation and a statement of the assets available for a dividend or distribution represented to him to be correct by the president or the officer of the corporation having charge of or supervision of its accounts, or certified to be correct by a public accountant or firm of public accountants of good reputation, nor shall he be held to have been negligent if in good faith he considered assets at their book values, nor if in any case he followed what he believed in good faith to be sound accounting and business practice.

Any director against whom a claim shall be asserted by or on behalf of a corporation under or pursuant to this section, or who shall be held liable under or pursuant to this section, shall be entitled to contribution from other directors who are liable, according to the number of such directors, and any and all directors against whom a claim shall be asserted under or pursuant to this section or who shall be held liable, shall have a right of contribution against the shareholders who knowingly accepted or received any dividend or distribution not authorized to be made, and such shareholders shall contribute in proportion to the amounts received by them respectively. 

Stockholders' Rights in the Event of No Dividends. Because the discretion for the declaration or passing of a dividend rests with the board of directors, stockholders disgruntled because of the lack of dividends may: (a) dispose of their holdings, (b) elect a new board of directors, or (c) resort to the courts.

The action of a board of directors is final with respect to the legal declaration or passing of a dividend, and courts usually will not interfere with the actions of directors unless fraud is present, or unless the directors have abused their discretionary powers to the detriment of the stockholders. Stockholders have the privilege of resorting to a court of equity at any time, but the courts normally will not interfere unless fraud exists: The courts operate on the basis that the directors are more intimately acquainted with the financial requirements of the

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

corporation than any other body. If the court is convinced that fraud is present, or that earnings are being accumulated unnecessarily, or that minority interests are being discriminated against, it may order a dividend.

Declaration and Payment of Dividends.-Dividends must be de clared by the board of directors, and the dividend action recorded in the minute book. Some companies, knowing that their dividends will be regular throughout the year, formally declare the dividends once a year, noting in the motion the payment dates throughout the year; other companies declare each dividend separately. A dividend declaration may be recorded in the minute book somewhat as follows: "Dividend 

No. 246, for the quarter ending October 1, 1941, of 112% of the outstanding preferred stock, has been declared by the board of directors out of earned surplus, payable November 1 to stockholders of record as of the close of business October 13." There are three dates in connection with a dividend: (1) the date of declaration, (2) the date of closing the stockholders ledger, so that the corporation may determine precisely what stockholders should receive dividends, and (3) the date of payment of the dividend. When dividends are declared the entry is: 

Earned Surplus 

Dividends Payable

To record the liability for the quarterly dividend of 12 per cent of the preferred stock, in accordance with the declaration of the board of March 1, the dividend to be paid April 1 to stockholders of record of 

March 15. 

When the dividend is paid: 

Dividends Payable Cash.. 

To pay the dividend of March 1. 10,000.00 10,000.00 . 10,000.00 10,000.00

When a stock dividend is declared instead of a cash dividend the first entry is the same, except that the title of the credit becomes "Stock Dividends Payable," to show that it is not a liability. The second entry, assuming that the dividend is in common stock, becomes: 

Stock Dividends Payable. 

Common Stock . 

. 10,000.00 10,000.00

When dividends are paid in par value stock the entries are for an amount equal to the par value of the stock to be issued. If no-par

CORPORATIONS 

187 stock is issued as dividends, and if the state law establishes a minimum issuing price the entries should be for an amount at least the minimum value. If there are no minimum value or stated value requirements, the No-Par Capital Stock account should be credited with at least the book value of the shares issued. However, where there are no minimum or stated value requirements, it is possible to pay the stock dividend and make no transfer from Surplus to the No-Par Stock account. 

In this case, the number of no-par shares issued is noted in the No-Par Stock account. Usually, the action of the board of directors specifies the amount of surplus to be transferred to the No-Par Stock account. 

As pointed out earlier in this chapter, some companies have several dividend declarations each year and prefer to use a Dividends account; this avoids more than one entry per year in the Surplus account. The 

Dividends account is charged with each dividend declaration, and is closed to Surplus at the end of the fiscal period. 

Most dividends are paid in cash and unless another form of property is designated at the time the dividend is declared, are held to be payable in cash. A declared dividend is a debt and may be settled as any debt. For example, if a stockholder is indebted to the corporation, the corporation may use the principle of offset. Most cash dividends are paid by check, and the indorsement of the stockholder on the paid check is considered to be a satisfactory receipt for the dividend paid. 

Dividend rates on stock of a par value may be stated either as a percentage of the par value or in dollars and cents per share. Dividends on stock of a no-par value can be stated only in terms of dollars or cents per share, for there is no base figure upon which to compute a percentage dividend.

At the time of the dividend payment, it is entirely possible that the cash of the corporation may be low, thus making borrowing necessary. 

Corporations may borrow in order to pay dividends, if the declaration of the dividend is legal and if the borrowing will not impair the rights of creditors. If the borrowing impairs the rights of creditors they may enjoin the payment of the dividend on the basis of indiscretion or fraud in the declaration of the dividend, but not in the payment of the dividend. A well-managed concern normally will be able to guide its finances so that cash is available for dividend payments at the dividend date. 

At the date upon which the stockholders' ledger is closed, in accordance with the dividend action of the board, the transfer agent

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

sends to the corporation a list of the stockholders as of that date, indicating thereon the number of shares of each class of stock held by each stockholder. (If the corporation keeps the stockholders' ledger, the transfer agent sends only a list of the transfers.). With this list before him the treasurer of the corporation determines the amount of dividends due each stockholder, and prepares the checks for mailing. 

Stock sells "ex-dividend" after the date of closing the stockholders' ledger.

Summary of the Classes of Surplus Available for Dividends.- 

There is presented below a summary of the classes of surplus available for dividends, from the standpoint of acceptable accounting practice, regardless of state law. A full discussion of the details summarized here appears throughout the preceding four chapters. 

1. Cash dividends may be declared from: a) Earned surplus b) Capital surplus, unless frozen by law or by board action c) Donated surplus, if the donation is for that purpose 

2. Stock dividends may be declared from: a) Earned surplus b) Capital surplus, unless restricted by law or by action of the board of directors c) Donated surplus, unless restricted by law or by action of the board of directors d) Paid-in surplus, unless restricted by law or by action of the board of directors e) Reappraisal surplus It must be realized that, in some states, any class of surplus is available for dividends, while in other states only specifically named classes are legally available. 

Stock Dividends.-A stock dividend is declared when: 

1. The payment of a cash dividend is considered inadvisable, but when a dividend in some form is deemed advisable. 

2. The corporation desires a wider distribution of its capital stock. 

3. The corporation desires a larger permanent capitalization. 

The effect of a stock dividend is to convert some of the surplus into capital stock and thereby convert mobile capital into fixed capital. 

Stock dividends of the same class of stock "dilute" the stock, resulting in a lower book value and market value per share. The lower market

CORPORATIONS 189 value usually makes the stock a more marketable security; this is particularly true of large stock dividends. Either unissued stock or treasury stock may be used to pay stock dividends. 

A stock dividend removes the surplus used for the dividend from the control of the board of directors, and subjects it to state corporation law by transferring the amount of the dividend from surplus to capital stock. When par value stock is used for a stock dividend, it is immediately considered as fully paid, provided, of course, that the surplus is at least equal to the par of the stock used as the dividend. 

When no-par value stock is used for a stock dividend, it is fully paid, but the directors must designate the amount of surplus to be transferred to the Capital Stock account; if the no-par stock has a stated value, this figure is normally used. 

Stock dividends are not considered to be income, but are viewed simply as a further division of the evidence of ownership. Under the provisions of the federal income tax law, stock dividends do not constitute taxable income to the stockholder if the stock dividend is of the same class as that held. Any profit realized on the sale of purchased capital stock or upon that received as a stock dividend is subject to income taxation.

Property Dividends.-Dividends may be paid in the form of assets other than cash. Dividends payable in non-cash corporate property are not common. When dividends of this nature are encountered, they usually consist of securities which are owned by the declaring company. 

Scrip, Note, and Bond Dividends.—Scrip dividends are sometimes issued when a dividend is desired, and when cash is not now available but soon will be; this frequently happens in seasonal industries. The scrip normally is a promise to pay at a determined or determinable future time; frequently the scrip is issued on a serially maturing basis. 

The scrip may or may not bear interest. If the scrip is issued on an unconditional basis, the scrip is negotiable. 

Liquidating Dividends.-The dividend ordinarily declared and paid is a distribution of earnings. A dividend which represents a return of part or all of the permanent capital of the corporation is known as a liquidating dividend. When liquidating dividends are paid, the stockholder should be so advised. Other than in cases of complete liquidation, liquidating dividends are not usually paid except by corporations engaged in the extractive industries, where wasting assets are

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

involved. Frequently in these industries depletion is not charged to profits, and dividends ostensibly from profits actually are liquidating dividends. The point is that depletion charges are available for liquidating dividends because wasting assets are not currently replaced. It would appear that this should be equally true for the depreciation charges of a corporation owning, say, a single office building or other asset which is not to be replaced; in such cases, however, both legal requirements and accepted accounting practice provide that depreciation be deducted in determining profits available for dividends. Strictly speaking, dividends out of profits before allowance for depletion should be charged to the proper capital stock account; usually they are charged to a "Liquidating Dividends" account, which will be closed to the Capital Stock account at the termination of operations or will be shown as a negative net worth account. The dividend checks should clearly distinguish between liquidating dividends and dividends paid. from profits. If the Liquidating Dividends account is held open, the net worth side of a balance sheet should appear as below: 

Capital Stock Liquidating Dividends Returned to Stockholders. 

Total Net Worth. 

. $5,000,000.00 3,000,000.00 $2,000,000.00 

Dividends in the Balance Sheet.-Dividends declared and paid do not show on the balance sheet, but are shown on the statement of surplus. Dividends declared but unpaid constitute a current liability of the declaring corporation. Past cumulative dividends are shown as a balance sheet footnote; there is no liability until declaration. Past non-cumulative dividends, being lost forever to the stockholders, are not shown.

Dividends and Capital Losses. In a preceding paragraph, the statement was made that dividends should not, and legally could not, be paid if the payment would have the effect of reducing corporate capital below the originally contributed amount. This must not be interpreted to mean that, in the case of extractive industries corporations, dividends representing a return of capital cannot be paid; the payment of dividends from capital in the case of wasting asset corporations is regarded favorably both from an accounting point of view and also from a legal point of view; the only requirement is that the corporation inform the stockholders what dividends represent a return of capital. Creditors of a wasting assets business are protected to a

CORPORATIONS 

191 smaller degree as capital is reduced. Naturally, if an extractive industries corporation plans to continue operations after its present mine, quarry, oil well, or timber tract is exhausted, it must make allowance for depletion and not return paid-in capital to its stockholders; this is simply the exercise of good business judgment. 

During periods of declining prices many mercantile and manufacturing companies suffer large declines in the values of fixed properties. 

If the new, lower price levels were to be reflected on the books, the capital would be materially reduced. The question arises as to whether unrealized losses of this nature are to be taken into consideration before the payment of dividends. The answer to this question is that most state laws simply stipulate that "all losses be made good" before dividends. The interpretation is that capital encroachments must be taken into consideration in the payment of a dividend. The law does not stipulate that current profits must be used to make good past asset value declines. At least one state law provides that dividends can be paid from current profits regardless of past encroachments on capital. 

Therefore, the consideration of whether a decline in value of fixed assets constitutes "loss" rests largely with the judgment of the corporation. Of course, if a corporation charges such declines to surplus and thereby depletes this surplus, dividends cannot be paid. However, it is possible to reduce the par or stated value of the capital stock, thereby creating a surplus against which the assets may be written off and leaving any subsequently earned surplus available for dividends. 

If this last procedure is followed, no question of the legality of a dividend can possibly arise.

Book Value of Capital Stock.-There are several types of value in connection with capital stock, among which are: (1) par value, (2) market value, (3) liquidating value, (4) book value.

There is no necessary connection between any of these values, although any two or more of them may accidentally be about the same amount; one is not dependent upon the others. For corporations whose stock is listed on exchanges, the only point accomplished by book value computations lies in showing the relationship existing between book value and market price. Book value computations are important, however, in determining values in close corporations, or in corporations whose stock is unlisted.

Book value is the total net worth of a corporation, as shown by the books. If only one class of stock is outstanding, book value per share

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

is determined by dividing the total corporate net worth by the number of shares outstanding. Thus:
