Chapter X PRINCIPLES AND OBJECTIVES OF VALUATION AND THE  

The Meaning of Accounting Valuations.-Up to this point in the study of accounting, the amounts involved in accounting transactions and entries have in most cases been taken for granted. The emphasis of the study has been placed upon the analysis of the transactions and the determination of the accounts affected. Little attention has been given to valuation, the problem of determining the monetary amount to be recorded for business transactions. The term "business transaction" is used here to include sales, purchases, receipts, expenditures, etc., and also the adjustment of the book values of assets, liabilities, and capital. The increase or decrease of an asset due to revaluation, the establishment of reserves, the recording of accruals and all other adjustments—all of which might not be thought of as transactions in the strict sense are included in this general statement. 

The term "valuation" has many interpretations and valuations are made for many purposes. The valuation of assets for taxation purposes presents problems different from those involved in the determination of the amount at which the assets are to be recorded and readjusted on the books of a going concern. 

The valuation problems of the accountant are dual in nature: first, there is valuation for balance sheet purposes and, second, there is valuation for purposes of a statement of profit and loss. As a result of the proper valuation of all transactions, it should be possible to present both a correct balance sheet and a correct statement of profit and loss. 

The decision with respect to the valuation of assets and liabilities for the balance sheet determines to a large extent the results to be reflected in the operating statements. The converse is equally true, that is, decisions with respect to the determination of the amount of income and expense to be allocated to a given accounting period are immediately reflected on both the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss. 

For example, in the determination of the value of accounts receivable 197

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

for balance sheet purposes, there is automatically determined the amount of bad debts to be shown on the statement of profit and loss." 

Conversely, the decision with respect to the amount of depreciation to be charged to a given period and to be reflected in the statement of profit and loss determines also the proper balance sheet valuation of the corresponding assets. The only exception to this general rule arises from the fact that a revaluation of assets or liabilities may be reflected directly in a surplus or other permanent proprietorship account and therefore may not be reflected in the profit or loss for the current period. For example, a decision to write up the value of a fixed asset may be effected by a charge to the asset account and a credit to a proprietorship account, such as Capital Surplus or, better, Surplus Arising from the Revaluation of Fixed Assets. A transaction of this nature is not reflected in the statement of profit and loss. 

As a result of the foregoing discussion, it is seen that the determination of correct income is equally as important as correct balance sheet amounts. The application of proper valuations to balance sheet accounts is directly reflected in the income; indeed the primary purpose of the proper valuation of assets, liabilities, and capital is to determine correctly the income and expenses. Considerable attention has always been given to the proper valuation of assets for balance sheet purposes but too little emphasis has been placed on the problem of income and expense determination. For example, the most important factor in depreciation problems should be the determination of the amount properly chargeable to the current period. If depreciation for a given accounting period is understated $10,000.00, the financial condition is overstated $10,000.00. If the profits were to be capitalized in order to estimate the value of the business as a going concern, the $10,000.00 error in profits would result in an overvaluation of many times that amount.

The Allocation of Income between Accounting Periods.-As pointed out in the preceding sections of this chapter, the problem of valuation is twofold, affecting both financial condition and income. 

The problem of income and expense determination is almost wholly a matter of "timing," that is, of determining the accounting period or periods in which the various items of income and expense should be recognized. The problem is one of determining when income is earned, and when expense is incurred. For example, a fixed asset subject to depreciation will inevitably become an expense as it wears out; the

problem is to determine how much of the total depreciation expense shall be allocated to each accounting period within the life of the asset. 

In the case of merchandise sales, the exact amount of the final net income will not be known until the last account receivable is collected or is written off as a bad debt, but it is necessary before that time to allocate to one or more accounting periods the portion of that sales income properly attributable to that period. Similar problems of allocation between periods arise in connection with most of the items of income and expense appearing on the statement of profit and loss. 

One general method of "timing" used is the so-called cash basis; the general principles are easily understood: cash received is income; cash disbursed is expense; the net increase in cash during a given period is profit, or the net decrease in cash is loss. The cash basis is a simple one, but it is appropriate only if one of two conditions is true: either the amount of all assets and liabilities, except cash, must be negligible, or their values must be constant from period to period. 

If either of these conditions exists, cash receipts furnish a good measure of income and cash disbursements a good measure of expense. 

Another general method of "timing" is the so-called accrual basis: income is recognized as such when it is earned, whether that be indicated by a cash receipt, by the increase of a receivable, or by the decrease of a liability. Expense is recognized as such when it is incurred, whether indicated by a decrease in cash or any other asset, or by the increase in a liability. The accrual method is the one most generally used in accounting for business concerns. 

Objective of Valuation.-Accounting statements represent expressions of opinion, and not statements of fact. Not only must the content of the balance sheet be correct and explicit, but the values used must be accurate and well founded, so that the business as an entity may be measured in terms of value and the adequacy of the earnings be appraised. Improper valuation may result in gross and even fraudulent misstatement of balance sheet items and of incomes, expenses and profits. The objectives of valuation are to determine the quality of the content of the balance sheet and the correctness of the incomes and expenses. If the methods of accounting achieve the objectives of valuation, then the methods of valuation lead to (a) a correct expression of expenses and incomes, and (b) the proper statement of the values of assets, liabilities, and net worth.

Formerly, the balance sheet was the all-important statement of a

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

business. It is now realized that the net result shown on a statement of profit and loss determines to no small extent the significance of the valuations applied to balance sheet items; consequently, today the statement of profit and loss has attained some of the importance it so richly deserves. As a statement giving rise to a reasonable judgment of the condition, position, progress, or regress of a business, the profit-and-loss statement is at least equal in importance to the balance sheet. 

Because they are primarily statements of opinion and not statements of fact, both the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss make necessary the formulation of sound and adequate guiding rules to apply to the values attaching to assets, liabilities, expenses, incomes, and net worth.

This and the following chapters will deal with the principles involved in the valuation of balance sheet accounts and expense and income accounts; as stated, the objectives of valuation are the correct expression of balance sheet values and the proper determination of income. Income represents an increase in net worth, and if the income is incorrect as a result of improper application of valuation principles, the net assets are incorrectly stated. 

Chapter IV stressed the importance of the form of the balance sheet and the manner of presentation of items within the statement. We are now interested in these same matters of form plus the even more important consideration of deciding upon the values to attach to the items in the balance sheet (1) at acquisition, and (2) subsequent to acquisition, particularly when reappraisals, additions, deductions, improvements, and changes in value take place. As balance sheet values change, incomes and expenses change; incomes and expenses and balance sheet values are mutually dependent, each upon the other. As changes occur in incomes and expenses, the effect of the changes on the balance sheet must be recognized and studied; as balance sheet values change, the effect of the changes on incomes and expenses must be considered.

In many instances, the assignment of values to balance sheet accounts is to a large extent a matter of opinion based upon sound judgment, which, in turn, must depend upon sound valuation principles. 

Valuation is not simple of solution, because it is so frequently not based on a statement of fact; correct statements of financial condition and operating results cannot be prepared, unless proper methods of valuation are followed.

General Principles of Valuation.-At this point it is necessary to mention that there is no universal principle of income determination or of valuation applicable to all incomes and expenses and to all balance sheet accounts. Different principles govern different items and different principles are required for various purposes of the valuations. 

For instance, it will be shown that entirely different principles govern the valuations of inventory and land, and yet both valuations are made for the purpose of properly determining income. Different principles govern valuation for purposes of taxation as opposed to the valuation applied for purposes of obtaining fire insurance. 

However, certain general principles of valuation may be formulated to serve as guides in the correct presentation of values and in the proper determination of income. 

Proper distinction must be made between capital and revenue expenditures; otherwise a balance sheet item will be understated or overstated, and a profit-and-loss item will be understated or overstated. The term "expenditure" must not cause confusion. An expenditure does not necessarily involve a cash disbursement; an expenditure is made (1) when cash is paid, or (2) when an obligation is incurred which later will be liquidated in cash. Thus an expenditure is made when an asset is acquired or when an expense is incurred; the expenditure may be accompanied by a cash disbursement, or the cash disbursement may follow at a later time.

Capital expenditures result in the acquisition of fixed tangible assets, fixed intangible assets, or permanent investments. The asset acquired is one that will last for a considerable period of time; that is, it will not be consumed in the current period. A revenue expenditure may be defined in two ways (1) it is an expenditure which increases an expense or (2) it is an expenditure which decreases income or revenue. 

Capital expenditures are capitalized; that is, they are added to asset accounts. Revenue expenditures are charged to expense. 

The distinction between a capital expenditure and a revenue expenditure is often difficult to make, and the accountant must frequently call upon all of his ingenuity in order properly to distinguish them. 

If proper distinction is not made, income, assets, and net worth may be overstated or understated. For example, if an asset is purchased and charged to expense, assets are understated and profits and net worth are understated. If ordinary repairs to the asset are charged to the asset account, assets, profits, and net worth are overstated. The

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

purchase of the asset should be treated as a capital expenditure and the repair costs as revenue expenditures. In chapter XVI the distinction between capital and revenue expenditures is discussed at some length. 

Another valuation principle is that all losses should be provided for and no profit should be anticipated. If consistently followed, this rule should avoid overstatement of profit; however, should a too rigid application of this rule produce an understatement of profit in one period, it results in an overstatement of profit in a subsequent period. 

The rule simply means that, for the correct determination of profits, and consequently of assets and net worth, probable and possible losses should be taken up in the accounts, and no expected or possible profits should be booked at any time preceding the actual realization of the profits. In this connection, it must be remembered that a profit is not possible unless accompanied by a sale of either goods or services; a profit is made by selling, not by purchasing or holding. As applied to losses, the rule is sometimes difficult of application if overcharges to current profits are to be avoided; this phase of the problem is developed later in this chapter. 

The "anticipation of no profit" rule is less difficult to interpret. 

Profits should not be anticipated (a) by valuing ending inventories at a price in excess of cost, thereby reducing the cost of the goods sold for the current period; (b) by taking a factory profit on work in process or on finished goods; (c) by adding a profit on merchandise shipped to branches or sales agencies, when the merchandise is still unsold; (d) by considering consignments-out as sales at the time of consignment; (e) by failing to defer income to its proper period; (f) by crediting profit and loss for increases in the value of fixed or other assets due to appraisal. 

It should be emphasized that the allocation of expenses and incomes to their proper periods is a primary principle of valuation. If a statement of profit and loss is to be correct, the expenses and incomes must be properly allocated to the periods to which the expenses are chargeable and the incomes applicable. There must be no confusion between the cash basis and the accrual basis of accounting. For expenses: (a) accrue and include those that should be taken up in the current period but which have not been so recorded; (b) defer and exclude expenses which are applicable to future periods; (c) exclude expenses which are applicable to prior periods; if errors of preceding periods are corrected through profit and loss, separate the expenses of the current

period from those applicable to prior periods, so that the profit for the current period is shown separately; (d) exclude purchased assets from expenses if the life of the asset extends beyond the current accounting period. For incomes: (a) accrue and include those incomes that should be taken up in the current period but which have not been so recorded; (b) include all sales for which the goods have been shipped or delivered; (c) if a sale has been made ad if cancellation is probable, exclude the sale from revenue; (d) include profit on installment sales in accordance with the method used to account for such sales; (e) defer and exclude all incomes received in advance which are applicable to future periods; (f) exclude from the results of the current period all income applicable to preceding periods; if errors of preceding periods are corrected through profit and loss, the incomes applicable to the preceding periods should be separately set forth. 

Another principle of valuation is that operating economies should not be considered as profits even though they may result in greater future profits. A company may rearrange its departments or its production line and thereby reduce the number of employees and increase the volume of production; the action is an economy which may result in greater future profits, but the elimination of employees does not constitute a present profit. As another example, a company may construct a fixed asset for its own use, thereby saving $5,000.00 as compared with the lowest outside bid received. The $5,000.00 saved is not a profit, and the asset should be recorded at its actual cost. 

Another principle of valuation is that incomes and assets should never be misstated. Overstatements result in an overstatement of net worth. Understatements of the values of assets and incomes are equally incorrect for they result in hidden or secret reserves. Neither understatement nor overstatement of values can be defended; values should be expressed so that the result is a correct presentation of incomes and assets. Likewise expenses and liabilities should be correctly expressed, as their understatement results in an overstatement of profits and net worth, and their overstatement results in an understatement of profits and net worth.

Purposes of Valuations.-Valuations may be made for many different purposes. The purpose of the valuation of a balance sheet account depends upon the disposition to be made of the item as a result of the valuation. Several purposes of valuations are as follows:

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 1. Valuation for Purchase and Sale.-When a valuation is being made for purposes of either a purchase or a sale, cost figures are of slight significance. Present values, based either on market values, on reproduction cost, or on income-producing ability, are the primary considerations. Such valuations are important from the standpoint of the going concern. 

2. Valuation for Liquidation.-Liquidation may be voluntary or involuntary, but in either instance valuation is made for the purpose of determining the probable price to be realized under conditions of forced sale. Again, cost is of no significance; whatever can be secured in the cash market is "value" for this purpose. 

3. Valuation for Fire Loss Adjustments.-Valuations are necessary for assets destroyed by fire. In general, valuations applicable to fire losses are the sound cash values at the time of the fire. Any difference between carrying value and the value for fire loss settlement purposes must be adjusted on the books. 

4. Valuation for Taxation.-Properties must be valued by taxing authorities for purposes of establishing a basis for a tax levy. Valuation figures for taxation purposes bear no necessary relationship to the carrying values as expessed on the books of the owners, but rather reflect the political and financial policy of a governing body. 

5. Going-Concern Valuation. This is the type of valuation in which the accountant is primarily interested. It means the valuation of balance sheet items for a concern in business, operating and expecting to continue to operate in a normal fashion. Going-concern valuation does not apply to a concern anticipating dissolution and liquidation. 

Going-concern valuation is in answer to the question: "What values shall be attached to the assets, liabilities, and net worth of an operating company, so that the values may be correctly expressed and so that the income may be properly determined?" All valuation discussion in succeeding chapters will be from the point of view of the going concern unless otherwise noted.

Divisions or Kinds of Value.-In dealing with a business organization, there are several kinds or types of value applicable under differing circumstances and at different times. These types of value are not necessarily separate from the purposes of valuation presented above, but at some time or other are applicable to every business organization. Certain types of value apply to the going concern, and therefore are going-concern values; other types do not apply to going

205concerns. For example, taxation values are necessary to a going concern although the taxation values are not reflected on the concern's books.. 

As another example, a going concern may contemplate the retirement of certain assets; in such a case liquidation values would be estimated for these assets but might not be reflected on the books until the assets are actually liquidated. The various kinds of value are: 

1. Cost value 

2. Market value 

3. Sales value 

4. Book value or carrying value, that is, cost minus depreciation 

5. Scrap value or salvage value 

6. Liquidation or forced sale value 

7. Taxable value 

8. Sound value 

9. Insurance value 

10. Earnings value, that is, earnings-capitalized value

Cost Value.-Cost value is commonly thought of as the purchase price. However, cost value includes not only the invoice price, but also all costs necessary to place the asset in condition for sale or use. 

To a mercantile concern, the cost of inventory is the purchase price plus transportation charges, insurance in transit, storage costs, and all other handling charges necessary to place the inventory in salable condition. 

For a manufacturing concern, the cost of manufacturing the finished product includes the costs mentioned above, plus all direct labor and manufacturing overhead costs. Further consideration is given to these problems in chapter XIII, Inventories.

The cost value of fixed assets includes the purchase price, transportation, installation, and any other charges necessary to place the fixed asset in condition for use. When fixed assets are constructed, certain other items may be included in or excluded from their cost. 

These problems are discussed fully in chapters XVI and XVII, Fixed 

Tangible Assets.

Cost will vary from time to time; a company may purchase a machine at one cost one year, and in the following year purchase an identical machine at a cost lower or higher than that of the first machine. The two costs are different; they need not be brought into agreement. Also, the cost of similar assets may be different for two companies, because one obtains a more favorable price than the other, or because transportation, installation, or other costs are different for

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

the two companies. As a result of varying costs under differing conditions, income may vary. 

Market Value.-Market value is the present cost price in the market normally pertaining to the item in question. Every asset has a market value but in accounting market value pertains particularly to inventories. Cost and market coincide at the time of purchase; if the market price of a purchased item rises or falls, its cost, of course, remains the same.

Sales Value.-Sales value is the amount obtainable under conditions of normal, as opposed to forced, sale. 

Book Value, Carrying Value, or Cost Minus Depreciation.—For depreciable assets, this value is cost minus the depreciation accumulated since the date of acquisition. For non-depreciable assets, it is the values at which the assets are carried on the books, usually cost. 

Scrap Value, Salvage Value.-Scrap value or salvage value is the realizable value at the expiration of the useful life of a fixed asset, and it is the value obtainable for waste and scrap arising from the manufacturing process.

Liquidation or Forced Sale Value.-Liquidation value is the amount obtainable under conditions of compulsory selling, or voluntary selling when rapid liquidation is desired. Liquidation values ordinarily have no effect upon the determination of income of a going concern.

Taxable Value.-Taxable value is that value assigned by taxing authorities for purposes of levying taxes. The primary basis of taxable values is reproduction cost, or market; however, many extraneous factors are likely to be injected into the situation, including, strangely enough, the income required to operate a governmental unit for a period of time.

Sound Value.-Sound value is the reproduction cost new minus the accumulated depreciation on the basis of the reproduction figure for the length of time the old asset has been owned. For example, a building cost $100,000.00 five years ago; the rate of depreciation is 

5 per cent per year. Today, the balance of the reserve is $25,000.00 (5 per cent of cost for five years). The present reproduction cost new of the same building is estimated at $150,000.00. On this basis, the reserve for depreciation would be $37,500.00 (5 per cent of $150,- 

000.00 for five years). The present sound value is $150,000.00 minus $37,500.00 or $112,500.00.

Insurance Value.-This is the value placed upon an asset for insurance purposes. The insurance value may or may not be related to cost. 

Reappraisals of assets and the computations of their sound values are often considered in order to obtain insurance commensurate with market conditions, particularly when assets have been purchased at favorable prices.

Earnings Value, or Earnings-Capitalized Value.-In order to place a value on a business based on its earning capacity, the profits may be capitalized at a given rate. For example, if profits average $10,000.00 per year, and if it is desired to capitalize this average profit at, say 121/2 per cent, the resulting capitalized value of the earnings would be $80,000.00.

The General Underlying Basis of the Valuation of Assets for a Going Concern.-When placing values on any asset, some base must serve as the starting-point of the valuation procedure. The cost of the asset is in general the underlying basis of valuation used for a going concern; this is true because the cost figure is the only estimate of value at the time of acquisition; furthermore, it is normally ascertainable and is definite. Where valuations are made at a figure either above or below cost, the deviations usually are measured from the underlying cost basis. 

Cost is a reasonable basis of valuation procedure because the return on an investment is generally measured in terms of the cost involved. 

Furthermore, in the absence of other evidence, it is assumed that the business man obtains a fair value when he purchases an asset, and for the purpose of initial entry the cost is used. It must be remembered that deviations from cost may be properly made at dates subsequent to acquisition, providing that the reasons for the revaluation and the basis of the revaluation are well founded. 

Certain people advocate valuing all assets at market, claiming that such practice maintains all records in an up-to-date, current condition. 

But if inventories, for example, are valued at a market price in excess of cost an anticipated profit is brought into the books, predicated upon the future sale of the inventories. If fixed assets are periodically valued at market, a tremendous amount of work is involved in obtaining the market figures, and in the case of highly specialized industrial equipment, a market price might be impossible of determination if a sale is not contemplated. There is ordinarily no great advantage in valuing fixed assets at market value; there would be no permanent basis for

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

measuring income, and the assignment of market values to old assets would be an impossibility in many instances. 

Sales value is generally objectionable as an underlying basis of valuation for a going concern. There is no intention of selling the fixed assets of a going concern, and they would have to be offered for sale in order to determine adequately their sales prices. If current assets, particularly inventories, are valued at sales price, a profit is anticipated and would be taken up in a period other than the period of sale. 

Furthermore the establishment of a sales price for inventories does not result in assurance that all the inventory will be sold at the established price. Certain other assets, such a good will, may have no sales value apart from the business as an entirety; to value legitimate good will of a going concern at zero would be to underestimate the value of that asset.

Consideration is now given to a very brief survey of the valuation of the various classes of assets, liabilities, and net worth, and the effect of the valuations on income. Since only brief and necessarily incomplete statements can be made at this point, the general principles suggested may appear to be arbitrary. A more complete discussion of the valuation of each individual item is deferred to the chapters which follow.

Current Asset Valuation.-Current assets normally should be valued at not more than minimum expected realization figures; that is, they should be valued and shown in the balance sheet at figures which are not in excess of going concern realizable values. With respect to inventories and marketable securities, the method can be stated as valuing these two items at the lower of cost or market, the lower figure being a measure of the minimum realizable cost. Current assets should be valued at not more than cash realizable values in order that cost of sales, expenses, and incomes may be conservatively stated. If overstatement of current assets does exist, creditors may be misled as to the debt-paying abilities of the debtor and as to the income-producing ability of the business. Thus, it can be seen that current assets are assigned a cost value at the time of acquisition; under normal conditions of bad debt losses and market fluctuations, however, another and lower valuation after acquisition may be proper; at the time of revaluation, cost serves as the basis of the computations. Valuation problems pertaining to each current asset are treated in chapters XI, XII, XIII, and XIV.

Investment Asset Valuation.-Investments may be either temporary or permanent. If they are temporary, representing investment of temporarily unneeded funds, they are current assets and are so valued. If the investments are permanent in nature, they are valued at cost at the time of acquisition. If they consist of stock of subsidiary companies, the valuation after acquisition depends upon the method of taking up profits and losses on the investments. The investments may be carried at cost and no entries for income be made until dividends on the investments are received. Or such investments may be recorded at original cost, their values increased as the subsidiary companies report their profits, and their values decreased as the subsidiary companies report losses or pay dividends. By this latter method the income from investments is not based on dividends from the subsidiary companies but on the reported profits and losses of these companies.

If the permanent investments are in bonds, they are carried at cost, plus amortization of discount, or minus amortization of premium. 

In general, losses and gains on permanent investments are not recognized until disposition, unless the decline in the market value of the investment is so drastic that no ultimate recovery to a figure approximating cost is anticipated. In such cases, the long-term decline in the value of the investment may be charged to an extraneous Profit and 

Loss or to Surplus.

Investment asset valuation is treated fully in chapter XV. 

Fixed Asset Valuation.-The valuation of fixed assets represents a matter of utmost importance to industrial and utility corporations. 

When fixed assets are purchased or constructed, they ordinarily are valued at cost; as the assets depreciate, they ordinarily are valued at cost less accumulated depreciation. Scrap value and market value are of no consequence for valuation of fixed assets for a going concern, as there are no intentions of liquidation. Some exceptions may be made to the rule that valuation of fixed assets is ordinarily net cost less depreciation. Prices may radically and permanently change, advantageous locations may shift, assets may have been acquired at unusually low or high prices, insurance values may change, or a bond issue may be contemplated. For one reason or another it may be considered wise to revalue the fixed properties for the correct determination of the values of the assets and for the correct determination of depreciation expense. 

The revaluations, based upon cost, are in all probability made in terms

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

of present sound values, because such values result in figures by which current income may be measured. Full consideration is given these problems in chapters XVI, XVII, XVIII, and XIX. 

Intangible Asset Valuation.-Intangible assets, while commonly valued at cost minus proper amortization, are valued in many different ways. For example, various methods of valuation are applicable to good-will. The values applied to intangible assets may have some effect on the determination of the income of an organization. These valuation problems are treated in chapter XX. 

Deferred Charge Valuation.-Deferred charges to operations should be so valued that the cost of the unconsumed portion of the charge is shown as an asset and the expired portion is charged to expense. In any event, care should be exercised that in no case is a doubtful deferred charge omitted from the expenses and shown as an asset on the balance sheet; when in doubt as to the legitimacy of deferring an expense, it should be charged to the expenses of the current period.

Liability Valuation.—In general, liability valuation is not so difficult nor so controversial as the valuation of assets. About the only principle of valuation applicable to liabilities is that all known or probable liabilities should be set up at their full amounts, so that expenses will be properly charged and incomes will not be overstated by the failure to set up as liabilities incomes received but not yet earned. In the balance sheet, the liabilities must be correctly classified as to current, fixed, and deferred credits to income. Therefore, full inclusion and correct amounts are of predominant importance. If liabilities are included at improper figures, not only is the balance sheet incorrect, but the statement of profit and loss is also incorrect if the incorrectly stated liability relates to an expense or an income. In general, the values of liabilities are ascertainable from the contracts and invoices in evidence of debt. In certain instances, however, liabilities cannot be ascertained on this basis; this is particularly true of liabilities arising from such transactions as selling under a product guaranty, selling on a coupon redemption basis, long-term construction contracts with a guaranteed completion date, and the final disposition of pending and contemplated lawsuits. In such cases, judgment must prevail as to the value to be attached to such liabilities. In connection with long-term bond issues, where the bonds are sold at a discount or at a premium, valuation accounts for the discount or the premium

must be set up and properly amortized over the life of the bonds, the bonds payable being shown at par in the balance sheet. Chapter XXI is devoted to liabilities.

Net Worth Valuation. The proper valuation of capital stock, surplus, and surplus reserves is of utmost importance, because the net worth section of a balance sheet shows the interests of the owners in the business. The proper valuation of assets, liabilities, expenses, and incomes results in the proper valuation of the corporate net worth. 

The reader must remember that the net worth section of a balance sheet does not show the current value of a share of stock; this value is reflected through market prices. The proper charges and credits to the various surplus accounts have been developed in chapter IX. The proper methods to be followed for the correct valuation of net worth items per se were discussed in chapters V, VI, VII, and VIII. 

In summary, we see that valuation and the determination of income is to a great extent a matter of the exercise of good judgment, guided by the light of sound principles. These principles, as applied in the chapters following, have varying applications, dependent upon whether the incidence of application is at acquisition or subsequent thereto, and depending upon the purposes of applying the principles. Also, the principles vary in interpretation between accountants; this simply means that opinions as to proper valuations are subject to variance, and that there are few, if any, "standard" principles, susceptible of universal application.

The Securities and Exchange Commission is exerting and will continue to exert a beneficial influence on the preparation of truthful accounting statements. The methods of valuations adopted by registrants are critically surveyed by the Commission.

Chapter XI 

CASH Valuation problems seldom arise in connection with cash, because of the definite value of the medium of exchange at any given moment. 

The principal problem is to account properly for the cash during the accounting period, to count it correctly at the end of the accounting period, and to show it in proper technical manner on the balance sheet. 

Special problems of income determination in connection with cash. arise when cash is in closed banks, and when cash is in foreign branches or foreign banks. 

Items Considered.-Cash includes (1) all money on hand, (2) money on deposit in banks, (3) undeposited money on hand, (4) undeposited checks, (5) undeposited bank drafts, (6) undeposited express money orders, (7) undeposited postal money orders. 

In some instances, stamps, IOU's, readily marketable bonds, and stocks are considered as cash; this is incorrect and the inclusion of such items in cash constitutes poor practice. Stamps are not commonly accepted as a medium of exchange and should be classified as deferred. charges or prepaid expenses. If stamps are accepted by the seller in lieu of cash, the stamps received may be charged to a Postage (or some other deferred charge) account; another method is to charge all postage stamps received from sales to a special account, so that the Cash account is separated from the postage receipts. IOU's are simply promises to pay a certain sum of money; they are not money. Frequently, employees and officers borrow from petty cash or other funds, and give their IOU's for the money thus obtained; IOU's should be shown as "Accounts or Notes Due from Officers and/or Employees," and should not be shown as cash, either free or restricted. Readily marketable temporary securities are not commonly accepted as a medium of exchange; regardless of their ease of convertability, they should not be shown as cash.

The question occasionally arises as to whether paper given a bank for collection should be considered as a receivable or as cash. The 213

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

answer depends upon the conditions under which the bank accepted the paper. If the bank credited the depositor's account at the time of receipt, the depositor may consider the item as cash; if the bank merely accepted the paper for collection, the depositor should treat the paper as a receivable. 

Frequently, a portion of the cash is restricted for a special purpose. 

In such instances, the balance sheet, and also the accounts, should show the amounts restricted separate from the amounts. free and available for general business purposes. When cash is restricted, as in special funds, it should not appear in the current asset section of the balance sheet, but should be shown in the permanent investment section, clearly titled to indicate its purpose and nature. 

Holding the Cash Books Open.-In order to present a more favorable balance sheet, the practice of holding the cash books open for a few days after the close of the period is sometimes encountered. Such practices are to be deprecated, and an auditor should always reverse the entries so as to show a true condition. 

If the cash receipts book is held open for payments on accounts receivable, the current section of the balance sheet as an entirety is not altered; however, cash is increased above its correct figure as of the end of the period. If the receipts book is held open to receive cash sales rightfully belonging to the new period, then cash, total current assets, sales, and net income are all overstated. 

When the cash disbursements book is not promptly closed, the purpose ordinarily is to show a better than actual current ratio position, by paying liabilities that actually are not liquidated until the new period. Of course the cash is reduced, but the current ratio is misstated. As an extreme example, consider the following illustration: 

CURRENT ASSETS CURRENT LIABILITIES 

Cash $200,000.00

Accounts Payable 

.$200,000.00

Accounts Receivable 

50,000.00

Inventory 50,000.00 $300,000.00 $200,000.00

Current ratio is 1.5 to 1. 

If the cash disbursements book is held open, and if $100,000.00 of the accounts payable are paid early in the new period, the picture becomes:

CASH 

CURRENT ASSETS 

Cash

Accounts Receivable 

Inventory 

CURRENT LIABILITIES 

. $100,000.00

Accounts Payable 

.$100,000.00 50,000.00 50,000.00 $200,000.00 $100,000.00

This results in an apparent current ratio of 2 to 1, a much better ratio than obtainable by following accepted, honest practices. 

If both the cash receipts and the cash disbursements books are held open, the current position can be manipulated at will. For example, if in the preceding illustration, only $50,000.00 of cash was on hand, and if the accounts receivable balance was $250,000.00, the collection of cash after the close of the period and the payment of liabilities with the cash collected could have resulted in any desired current position. 

The accountant should insist upon the prompt closing of all records at the end of a fiscal period, and should prepare his statements on that basis, regardless of the practices of his client. 

A variation of holding the cash disbursements records open is to prepare checks, enter them as charges to Payables and credits to Cash, but not mail them until sometime after the close of the period; this too overstates the current ratio. When the auditor reconciles the cash shortly after the close of the period, these unmailed checks appear to be outstanding; if he calls for another bank statement within a few days, the checks will still appear as outstanding, whereas under normal conditions they should have cleared through the bank. If the auditor reconciles the cash several days or weeks after the close of the period, the perforation dates of the checks serve as an excellent clue as to what actually happened, because checks normally clear in a few days. 

Forms of Fraud in Cash Receipts and Disbursements.-Fraud in cash receipts and cash disbursements takes many forms. The auditor has many devices at his command which enable him to detect fraudulent practices. The forms of fraud are only mentioned here and are not discussed fully, for such discussions belong in a text on auditing. 

Fraud in Cash Receipts.-Some, but not all, of the fraudulent practices in cash receipts are: 

1. The theft of all or a part of a cash sale, before the sale is entered on a sales invoice or entered in a cash register. 

2. The theft of cash, its entry at the correct amount, followed by underfooting a cash debit and some other credit column.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

3. Debiting an expense account when cash is received. 

4. Overstating sales discounts. 

5. By lapping. This involves the receipt of money from a customer, its theft, and the failure to credit the customer's account. Later, when another customer remits, part or all of the remittance is credited to the first customer's account and charged to Cash, but the account of the second customer is not credited. This procedure is continued indefinitely. The embezzler must always be certain that a customer who has remitted does not receive a second statement. 

6. By stealing the money when a customer remits, and then writing off the accounts receivable as uncollectible. 

7. By undercharging customers on the books, charging them fully on their bills, and keeping the difference between the correct remittances and the amounts according to the ledger records. 

8. By creating a fictitious customer on the books, charging the sales made to a legitimate customer to this account, stealing the remittance from the legitimate customer, and later writing off the fictitious account.

Fraud in Cash Disbursements.--Some, but not all, of the fraudulent practices in cash disbursements are: 

1. The theft of money from petty cash, covered by fictitious receipts or petty cash vouchers. 

2. The forging of checks, covered by fictitious charges. 

3. Raising of a paid check, and stealing the amount of the raise from cash receipts. 

4. Submitting false vouchers for approval, and forging an indorsement on the check in payment thereof. 

5. Presenting a voucher a second time for approval, and abstracting the check in support thereof, forging an indorsement. 

6. Understating purchase discounts. 

7. Understating or omitting purchase returns and allowances. 

8. Kiting of checks. This occurs when cash is stolen and the bank balance is below the ledger account balance for cash. Kiting is practiced by drawing a check on bank X and depositing it in bank Y, and at the same time not showing the check on bank X as a cash credit; thus the theft is temporarily hidden. 

9. By payroll manipulation. 

Systems of Internal Check for Cash Receipts and Disbursements. -From the point of view of the individual and from the standpoint 4444

CASH 

217 of the good of society, it is much better to prevent fraud than it is to be forced to detect it after occurrence. Cash must be adequately safeguarded as to its receipt and its disbursement. 

In order that cash receipts may be properly controlled: 

1. One person should open all mail and list all cash and check remittances. One copy of the remittance list is turned over to the cashier; another copy to the bookkeeper; and a third copy to the treasurer. 

2. After making the deposit of the cash in the bank, the cashier should show the duplicate deposit slip, initialed by the bank, to the employee making up the cash remittance list, who compares it with his list, and signs it if it is in agreement. 

3. At the end of each month, the bank statement should be checked by both the cashier and by the person preparing the remittance list. 

The latter must check against his daily lists. 

4. All cash must be deposited intact daily, preferably by someone other than the cashier or the bookkeeper. 

5. Cash sales must be checked against register readings or sales slips and deposited intact daily. The system of inventory control must be satisfactory. 

6. The bookkeeper and the cashier must not have access to each others' records.

In order that cash disbursements may be properly controlled: 

1. All payments should be made by check, except authorized petty cash disbursements. 

2. Checks should be supported by invoices and vouchers before being signed; the invoices and vouchers are then indelibly stamped "Paid." 

3. At least two signatures should be on the checks. 

4. The cashier should not have unwitnessed access to the paid checks. 

5. Purchase returns, allowances, and discounts must be verified. 

6. Purchasing procedure must be properly controlled. 

7. Payroll computation and payment must be properly controlled and checked.

The cash receipts functions and the cash disbursements functions must be separated as widely as possible. Accounts receivable must be reconciled to the controling accounts at least once a month. The cashier must have no contact with the bookkeeping. Jobs should be

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

rotated, if possible. Vacations should be given all employees handling cash. Bank reconciliations must be prepared at least once a month. 

Cash must be deposited daily, intact. 

If the foregoing suggestions are enforced, collusion between two or more persons is necessary before fraud can be perpetrated. 

Petty Cash. In the majority of business organizations it is impossible to make all payments by check; small bills may be payable at incurrence, articles may be hurriedly purchased through sources where credit is not established, employees may be given transportation money, customers may be entertained, accommodation checks may be cashed, and a daily variety of other occurrences are constantly taking place which necessitate a fund for cash disbursements. When such a petty cash fund is operated, it should be operated on the imprest system, with proper protection for the fund, and proper authorization for disbursements from the fund. 

When a petty cash fund is established, the decision as to its amount is made, and a check for this amount drawn to Petty Cash; the check is cashed and the money turned over to the petty cashier; the entry is a debit to Petty Cash and a credit to Cash. When money is expended from the petty cash fund, one person (not the petty cashier) should approve the expenditure by signing a petty cash voucher, the petty cashier should sign it, and the person receiving the money should sign it. If it is possible to obtain an independent receipt from the recipient, this too, should be done. The petty cash voucher should be indelibly dated so that it cannot be used again, and it should contain notations of the purposes of the expenditure. The petty cash vouchers plus the cash on hand will always equal the total of the fund. Some companies also maintain a petty cash book, in which the expenditures are classified and recorded.

At the close of the accounting period, or when the fund is nearing depletion, the vouchers are classified according to expense classifications (or the petty cash book columns are added if such a record is kept). A list is prepared showing the total amount for each expense or other classification. This list, together with the petty cash vouchers is sent to the cashier. A check is prepared for the total of all the vouchers; an entry is made in the cash disbursements journal charging the expenses or other accounts on the list and crediting Cash. The check is cashed and deposited in the petty cash; the fund now is reimbursed back to its original amount, and operations continued. The

CASH petty cash vouchers should be mutilated in such fashion that they cannot possibly be used again.

The purpose of reimbursing the petty cash at the end of the accounting period, even if only a small amount has been paid from the fund, is to charge the disbursements to the proper accounting period. 

Entries are made in the Petty Cash account (1) at the time of creation, (2) when the fund is increased or decreased permanently, (3) when the fund is banished; it should be noted that entries are not made to this account at reimbursement. 

Cash Reconciliation.-Periodically, at least at the end of each month, the bank statement and the Cash account ledger balance should be reconciled. When commercial accounts are active, the balance according to the bank and the balance according to the books are seldom in agreement. This condition is caused by charges and credits made by the bank during the period (notification of which is not given the depositor until he obtains the bank statement), checks issued by the depositor which have not yet cleared through the bank, and deposits made on the last day of the period after the bank has closed its records. 

It is therefore necessary to reconcile the bank's and the depositor's records, so that the cash records of the depositor may be shown accurately in the ledger and in the balance sheet and so that proof of agreement between the bank and the depositor is obtained. The type of cash reconciliation statement to use depends upon (1) the simplicity or complexity of the reconciliation, (2) the number of bank accounts, (3) the individual preferences of the accountant. Examples are presented of three types of reconciliation statements. 

The Simple Reconciliation.-If numerous charges and credits are not made by the bank, and if only deposits and checks constitute the transactions during the period, then in all probability book adjustments will not be required. In such cases, the cash reconciliation can be simple in form. For example, assume that the Cash account in the ledger shows a balance of $6,239.38, as of April 30, 1942. When the bank closes its books for that day the bank statement shows a balance of $6,421.18, but after the bank's closing hours, a deposit of $954.20 is made. After matching the checks returned by the bank with the check record, it is discovered that the following checks are outstanding: 

No. 142 for $162.00; No. 144 for $24.00; No. 147 for $329.00; No.

When the depositor reconciles his Cash account, the checks are listed among those outstanding. After the depositor has waited for a reasonable length of time for the checks to clear, he should stop payment on the checks at the bank; he is also justified in returning the cash to his

XX XX Bank Overdrafts.—When cash records are incorrectly maintained, or when an inadvertent error is made, more money may be spent by the depositor than exists to his credit at the bank. The depositor

CASH should always exercise care to avoid bank overdrafts. Frequently overdrafts in the Cash account are intentional, for subsequent deposits can "cover" the checks issued before they reach the bank. If the clearing time is long, due to the distance between bank and payees, the depositor's books may show an overdraft much of the time and the bank's records may never show one. Usually an attempt is made to avoid overdrafts at the end of the accounting period; when such overdrafts do exist, the question arises as to their proper treatment in the balance sheet. If only one bank account is maintained, the amount of the overdraft should be shown as a current liability, titled "Bank Overdraft." On the ledger, a new account is not opened; the Cash account merely shows a credit balance. If two or more bank accounts are used, and if an overdraft exists in one, the correct procedure is to show the amount on deposit as cash and to show the overdraft as a current liability. The principle of offset should not be used, for accounting statements, if correctly formulated, do not offset liabilities against assets. If the principle of offset is used, the balance sheet is distorted, and various balance sheet ratios are falsely presented. 

Cash in Foreign Branches.-When cash is held in foreign branches, it must be converted to United States dollars at the balance sheet date. 

The question is "What conversion rates shall be used?" The better practice is to convert to United States dollars at the rate of exchange existing at the balance sheet date. The second plan is to use a standard conversion rate; this should be permitted only if the rates of fluctuation are small. If foreign situations are uncertain and if the withdrawal of funds is restricted, a reserve for possible loss should be established or the foreign balance should be carried at an arbitrarily small figure, say $1.00.

Either a loss is incurred or a profit is earned upon the conversion to United States dollars. This profit or loss may be credited or debited to current non-operating Profit-and-Loss, or a reserve for fluctuations may be established in order to remove conversion fluctuations from current Profit-and-Loss.

Cash on the Balance Sheet.-Cash should be shown as a current asset if it is unrestricted and therefore available for general spending. 

Restricted cash must be shown in some other section of the balance sheet. If money to be disbursed as dividends is in the hands of a fiscal agent, cash held by the agent should be shown as a fund. Sinking fund cash should be shown in the investment section of the statement.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Overdrafts should be shown as current liabilities. Cash in closed banks is not a current asset, and should be shown under "other assets, or under "items in suspense." If cash is in a closed bank, and if a loan is payable to the same bank, the principle of offset usually applies; in such cases the two items on the balance sheet offset against one another; however, if the principle of offset does not apply, the cash on deposit and the loan due the bank should be shown separately on the balance sheet, for if the bank should liquidate at a figure below the amount of the loan, an enforceable liability would exist which was not otherwise shown.

Chapter XII  The Problem of Valuation. The valuation of receivables has a pronounced effect upon the balance sheet and upon the proper determination of income. If receivables are understated or overstated in amount, balance sheet values are too small or too great; because a misstatement of receivables usually arises from an incorrect estimate of their collectibility, bad debts expense and therefore net income is affected in those periods at the end of which the receivables are valued. 

When the Reserve for Bad Debts is adjusted at the close of a period, and if possible bad debt losses are computed at amounts that are too high or too low, income for that period is understated or overstated. 

There will be considered in this chapter the valuation of all types of receivables for balance sheet presentation and the proper determination of periodic income.

ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE 

Classification of Accounts Receivable.-In order to show correctly the current position of a company, extreme care must be exercised in the classification of receivables in general; at this point interest is centered in the correct classification of accounts receivable. Frequently the caption "accounts receivable" appearing in a balance sheet includes many items that are not currently receivable, or which do not originate in the normal operations of the business. 

Accounts receivable should be classified as follows for balance sheet purposes: 

1. Trade accounts receivable 2. Non-trade accounts receivable: 

a) Amounts receivable from officers, employees, directors, and stockholders, for other than current sales to them b) Amounts receivable from subsidiary companies (not advances) c) Agency receivables 226

d) Branch receivables e) Stock subscriptions receivable f) Deposits on bids 

8) Receivables on uncompleted contracts b) Future delivery contracts i) Amounts receivable from sales of fixed assets or other non-merchandise assets Consideration is now given to each class and type of account receivable. The term "account receivable" has the natural connotation of a value arising from a sale of the commodity or service in which a business regularly deals; such an implication is most misleading, if the item "accounts receivable" contains amounts which did not arise from sales and are not currently receivable. If the term "accounts receivable" is used without qualification, it should be understood to mean only amounts due from trade debtors. If the use of the term "trade debtors" or "customers accounts" could be promoted generally, non-trade and non-current accounts would be forced from their present hiding places, and statements involving more accuracy would be forthcoming. There have been sporadic attempts to eliminate the ambiguous accounts receivable terminology, but no great results have been achieved in this direction.

Trade Accounts Receivable.-Trade Accounts Receivable arise from sales of merchandise or services regularly offered. The trade receivables should be shown in the balance sheet as: 

Trade Accounts Receivable, Current Trade Accounts Receivable, Past Due 

XX 

Many companies sell on the installment plan. In such instances, Installment Accounts Receivable accounts should be carried in the ledgers. On the balance sheet, the installment receivables should be shown as:

Installment Accounts Receivable, Current Installment Accounts Receivable, Non-Current 

.XX .XX 

Non-Trade Accounts Receivable.-Amounts due from officers, em ployees, directors, and stockholders, arising from commodity sales made to them under the same conditions as sales made to an outsider, may be carried as Trade Accounts Receivable. Frequently, however, investigation proves that amounts due from these sources are the result of

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

advances or loans, with constant renewal of the loan or advance, and with no evident intention of payment in the near future. Such amounts should not be shown as current assets, but should be placed in "other assets" or possibly in "permanent investments." Such advances and loans are possible of recovery by creditors, in the event of the insolvency of the company. In some cases, sales made to employees and others connected with the company are made with the understanding that payment terms may be shorter or longer than those applicable to regular customers; in cases where the terms are longer, such accounts receivable should not be classified as current; in many instances, employees leave the organization without liquidating their indebtedness for purchases or advances.

Amounts due from subsidiary companies may be the result of merchandise sales to the subsidiary companies or may be the result of advances of money to the subsidiaries. If the amount due is from a sale in the regular course of business, it is classified as a current asset, but it should be shown separately from regular trade receivables. If the subsidiary receivable is the result of an advance, the amount should be shown as a permanent investment, because, in all probability, the advance is not currently payable; furthermore if the advance is shown as a current receivable, the reader of the balance sheet is led to believe that collections of regular trade receivables are slower than they are. 

Agency receivables and branch receivables, like amounts due from subsidiaries, may be the result of merchandise sales made by the agency or branch, or may be the result of advances. If the receivables are from agency or branch sales, they should be shown as current assets, specifically labeled as arising from the branch or agency. If the receivables are the result of advances of money, merchandise, of any other item, from the home office the branch or agency account and the home office account are eliminated against each other when a balance sheet is prepared, and only the consolidated condition is shown. 

Stock subscriptions receivable may be shown as a current asset on the balance sheet, specifically titled to avoid confusion and indefiniteness; they should be shown as current assets only if the intention is to collect the subscriptions within a reasonable time. If there is no intention to collect, or if there is any doubt about the collection, the stock subscriptions should be shown as a deduction from the proper proprietorship account. Stock subscriptions are sometimes evidenced by notes; in such cases, a definite clew is given as to their collectibility.

Deposits on bids represent advances of cash, normally for short periods of time. Regardless of the time element, such items should be shown in some classification other than current while the bidding is pending; this is true because the cash deposits are restricted. After the bids are awarded, the money will be returned to cash. 

Amounts receivable on uncompleted contracts should not be shown as current assets until the contract is completed and payment is due. 

Such amounts, and amounts from future delivery contracts, may be shown as "other assets."

Accounts receivable from the sale of fixed or other assets may be shown as current assets, clearly titled, if the amounts are currently due; otherwise the amounts should be shown in the permanent investment section of the balance sheet. 

Valuation of Trade Accounts Receivable.-Trade accounts receiv able should be valued at their cash realízable value. The object of valuation is to charge against the period of the sale all expenses allocable to the final realization of the proceeds of the sale, and to show the amount of cash which will be available for the payment of debts and other current purposes. The basis of valuation is the face value of the accounts minus certain reserves. The reserves are: (1) reserve for bad debts, (2) reserve for discounts, (3) reserve for allowances, (4) reserve for freight. In practice, the reserve for bad debts is almost universally used; the last three reserves are seldom employed.

Reserve for Bad Debts.-Regardless of the degree of efficiency of the credit department and the collection division, losses will arise from sales made on open account. Periodic provision consequently must be made for the estimated amount of these losses. The objectives of creating a Reserve for Bad Debts are (1) to value properly the accounts receivable at their cash liquidation value, (2) to charge bad debt expense to the accounting period in which the sales were made. 

Methods of Creating the Reserve.-There are five possible methods of creating a reserve for bad debts: 

1. On the basis of a percentage of total sales for the period 

2. On the basis of a percentage of charge sales for the period 

3. On the basis of a percentage of open receivables at the end of the period 4. By aging the accounts receivable 

5. By deciding upon an arbitrary amount, guided by past experience

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Regardless of the method used by any particular business, experience in collection is the guiding factor in determining the estimated bad debt losses. Thus, standard percentage figures do not exist for sales or receivables; consequently, a new concern will experience considerable difficulty in estimating its bad debt losses during the first few years of operation.

Reserves Based upon Total Sales or Charge Sales.-Naturally, bad debt losses cannot arise from cash sales. However, it is immaterial whether total sales or only credit sales are used as a base, unless there are wide variations in cash sales relative to credit sales from year to year.

If total sales are used as the base, the percentage figure applicable in order to determine the reserve will be smaller than would be the case if credit sales only were used.

Creating the reserve on the basis of sales has the effect of charging the loss to the period in which the sale was made and from that point of view is extremely desirable. 

Reserves Based upon the Balance of Receivables.-Under this method the balance of the receivables is multiplied by a percentage figure. It is necessary to include notes receivable with the accounts receivable, as losses occur on both, and the reserve for bad debts must be great enough, under this or any other method, to cover both, unless a separate reserve for doubtful notes is created. One advantage of this method is that the accounts may be more accurately valued than they are by a percentage of sales method if general business conditions and therefore the prospect for collections have changed sharply. One disadvantage is that bad debt losses are not necessarily charged to the period in which the sale is made but to a later period when prospects for collections have changed; some of the losses may be charged off in the period of discovery rather than in the period of sale. 

Reserves Based upon Aging the Accounts.—By aging the accounts receivable is meant the classification of the accounts on the basis of their age. Credit terms vary widely between industries and between individual organizations within an industry. For purposes of illustrating the procedure of aging, let it be assumed that all accounts are payable within thirty days from the date of sale; in such a situation, a class interval of thirty days is practical. If credit terms exceed thirty days, larger intervals should be used in the schedule.

ANALYSIS OF ACCOUNTS Receivable 

In the foregoing aging schedule, only the accounts receivable with balances over 30 days due are listed. If desired, all accounts may be listed, but no particular advantage is gained by copying good, current accounts. The 1-30 day column is provided so that accounts with both current and overdue balances may be listed. 

The use of the "Reserve for Bad Debts" column deserves comment.

This is the amount to be charged to Bad Debts Expense and to be credited to the Reserve for Bad Debts. The amounts appearing therein. are the result of decisions based upon account examination. An alternate procedure is to eliminate this column, and to apply a percentage figure to each "age" column in order to determine the reserve credit. 

The percentage figures thus adopted are based upon experience. 

By aging the accounts, the credit and collection department is brought into definite contact with the condition of the accounts. The management obtains a more precise picture of their condition and probable collectibility. Like the "percentage of receivable balances" method, it does not necessarily charge the bad debt loss to the period of the sale.

Reserves Based upon Arbitrary Amounts.-When an "arbitrary" 

method is adopted, the company, through experience, simply adjusts its reserve for bad debts to a desired total figure. There is no special attempt to allocate expense to the sales period and no attempt to keep the amount of the reserve in any uniform relationship to the balance of the receivables. Too frequently this method is used to "juggle' profit figures from one accounting period to another.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Reserves for Bad Debts Separated as to Years.-It is possible to maintain reserves for bad debts on a yearly basis. This necessitates carrying several reserves on the books. When an account proves to be uncollectible, it is charged to the reserve created at the end of the year in which the sale was made. For example, in 1943 an account of 

1941 proves to be uncollectible; it is charged to the Reserve for Bad 

Debts, 1941. After all accounts for any one year are collected, any balance remaining in the reserve for that year would be closed to Earned Surplus or to an extraneous profit and loss account. If the reserve for bad debts for any one year is depleted before all accounts are collected, the reserve for the year in question is increased by a charge to Earned Surplus or to an extraneous profit and loss account for an amount sufficient to cover the additional losses. The plan of carrying a reserve by years is not widely used, because of the work involved. 

Debit Balances in Reserves.-Occasionally, reserves are depleted because bad debt losses for accounts arising in preceding periods exceed the anticipated amounts and because sales of the current year may be written off before end-of-the-year adjustments are made to build up the reserve. When a debit balance is created in the Reserve for Bad 

Debts account, it should not be permitted to remain. The reserve should be restored to at least a zero balance by a debit to Earned Surplus if the accounts are from preceding years or by a debit to Bad Debts Expense if the accounts are from the current year. An alternate procedure for handling bad debt losses on current sales is to charge the Bad Debts Expense account and credit the Accounts 

Receivable account directly. 

Recoveries of Accounts Written Off as Uncollectible.-Upon reaching the definite conclusion that an account receivable is uncollectible, it is written off by a charge to the Reserve for Bad Debts and a credit to Accounts Receivable, both the controlling account and the subsidiary account. If the reserve method is not used, the charge is directly to Bad Debts Expense. 

When an account receivable, previously written off to the reserve as being uncollectible, is collected, the entries are: 

Accounts Receivable Reserve for Bad Debts.. 

Cash

Accounts Receivable 

XX XX

The first entry is made either (1) for the amount collected, or (2) for the entire amount of the account. It is desirable to make this entry reopening the account in order to re-establish the credit standing of the customer, and to show in the account the fact of collection. 

The credit to the Reserve for Bad Debts account is correct, as that account was charged when the account was written off in error. However, for income tax purposes, the collection of an account previously written off must be included in taxable income. Frequently excessive allowances for bad debt losses build up an excessive balance in the Reserve account. When this condition arises, one of two procedures may be adopted: (1) close the excessive amount of the Reserve to 

Earned Surplus, or (2) preferably, credit a non-operating income account, or (3) wait until the end of the next accounting period and reduce the Bad Debts Expense debit, thereby adjusting the Reserve to the desired amount.

Suspense Accounts Receivable.-When accounts receivable become past due, they may be removed from the current file and placed in a separate file called the Suspense Accounts Receivable Ledger. The accounts transferred to the suspense ledger are definitely earmarked as being past due, and more critical attention is devoted to their collection. 

When the transfer is made, the entry is: 

Suspense Accounts Receivable. 

Accounts Receivable 

XX XX If desired, the Accounts Receivable controlling account in the general ledger may control both the current and the suspense ledgers, in which case no journal entry is made.

Credit Balances in Accounts Receivable.-Subsidiary accounts receivable accounts occasionally have credit balances. The credit balance may be caused by (1) overpayment by a customer, (2) duplicate payment by a customer, (3) buying, paying for, and then returning all or a part of the purchase, (4) buying and paying for a purchase, and then obtaining an allowance or a discount. When credit balances occur, the balance of the controlling account is equal to the total of the debit balances minus the total of the credit balances. However, for balance sheet purposes, the debit balances should be shown gross in the current asset section, and the credit balances should be shown gross in the current liability section, under a title "Credit Balances of Accounts Receivable." If the principle of offset is followed the assets

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

and liabilities are incorrectly shown. Credit balances of accounts receivable may be liquidated (1) by cash payment, or (2) by subsequent sales to the customer. When credit balances exist in accounts receivable, the reserve for bad debts should be based upon the gross debit balances.

Reserve for Discounts.-Some accountants advise the creation of a reserve for sales discounts at the end of the accounting period. If such a reserve is created, it is based upon the estimated cash discounts that customers will take when they pay the balance of their accounts. 

The reserve is computed upon the uncollected balance of sales made during, say, the last ten days of the current period. This reserve has the effect of charging all discounts to the period in which the sale was made. If such a reserve is set up the entry is: 

Sales Discounts 

Reserve for Sales Discounts.

XX XX When a customer later remits, say, $98.00 in payment of a $100.00 account subject to a 2 per cent discount: Cash 

Reserve for Sales Discounts.

Accounts Receivable 

98.00 2.00 100.00 

Any unconsumed balance in the reserve will be returned to Earned Surplus, or preferably, to a non-operating income account. 

The creation and operation of such a reserve, while theoretically correct, is not used much in practice, although it is easily and accurately computed. From the standpoint of income determination it is not very important, where the sales discount expense is approximately equal from period to period. From the standpoint of the balance sheet, however, the value of the accounts receivable item is constantly overstated by the amount of the cash discounts yet to be taken. 

Reserve for Returns and Allowances.-If reserves for sales returns and sales allowances which are a part of the closing balance of accounts receivable are created, the procedure is the same as when a reserve for discounts is created. Such reserves are seldom used, but are necessary for some concerns at the end of certain months if large returns are anticipated from sales made in former months. 

Reserve for Freight.-Frequently, goods are shipped with the understanding that the freight thereon is to be paid by the buyer, but

that he is to deduct the freight from the face of the invoice and remit the net amount to the seller. In the valuation of the accounts receivable of the seller, the amount of the freight to be deducted by the customers should be charged to Freight-Out Expense and credited to a Reserve for Freight account. This reserve should be shown as a deduction from the face of the accounts receivable on the balance sheet. 

Accounts Receivable Assigned.-Frequently working capital may be secured from finance or discount companies by assigning or selling receivables; for the advance of funds secured by these receivables the finance company makes two charges: (1) a discount fee or commission based upon the amount of the assigned accounts, and (2) an interest charge based upon the amount of the assigned accounts and the time involved. The finance company will advance usually not more than 

75 or 80 per cent of the value of the assigned accounts; the remaining 

20 or 25 per cent acts as a factor of safety to secure the advance. The assigning company, when collections are made on the assigned accounts, remits to the finance company. In many cases, however, remittances are made directly to the finance company. Most contracts call for the immediate replacement of a bad account with a good account. 

When accounts receivable are assigned, the assigning company has a contingent liability which should be shown as such in the ledger and which must be shown on the balance sheet. The contingent liability must not be ignored, because if the customers do not remit, the assigning company is liable to the finance company. Consignment Accounts.-When merchandise is consigned, no receivable is due from the consignee until he has sold some or all of the consigned merchandise. The consignor shows the goods out on consignment as a part of his total inventory, separated in an account titled Consignments-Out.
