NOTES AND ACCEPTANCES RECEIVABLE 

Classification.

-Notes and acceptances receivable are classified as follows: 

Notes Receivable Trade Notes Receivable, Not Due (Current asset) Trade Notes Receivable, Past Due (Current asset) Nontrade Notes Receivable (indicate if past due) (Current asset) 

Officers' Notes Receivable (preferably not a current asset) Stockholders', Directors', etc., Notes Receivable (preferably not a current asset) (Notes receivable discounted must be shown in order to set forth the contingent liability.)

Trade Acceptances Trade Acceptances Receivable Bill of Exchange Receivable General Discussion and Definitions.-The Uniform Negotiable 

Instruments Law defines a promissory note as "an unconditional promise in writing made by one person to another, signed by the maker, engaging to pay on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time a sum certain in money to order or to bearer." 

The same law defines a bill of exchange as "an unconditional order in writing addressed by one person to another, signed by the person giving it, requiring the person to whom it is addressed to pay on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time a sum certain in money to order or to bearer." Bills of exchange are (1) demand, (2) sight, or (3) time bills of exchange, depending on when they are payable. Bills of exchange are also classified as (1) inland, or (2) foreign, depending on their place of payment.

The Federal Reserve Board defines a trade acceptance as a "bill of exchange drawn by the seller on the purchaser of goods sold and accepted by such purchaser."

The principal difference between an ordinary draft or bill of exchange and a trade acceptance is the statement on the face of the trade

acceptance to the effect that it has arisen out of the purchase of goods by the acceptor. A trade acceptance is a time draft drawn by the seller of merchandise on the buyer. The buyer "accepts" the obligation by writing his signature across the face of the instrument, thus accepting the provisions of the draft; then it is payable at the designated place on the specified date. In order to be negotiable, trade acceptances are usually made payable to a definite company or person. A trade acceptance is frequently used instead of sales on open account. An advantage of the trade acceptance is that it affords the seller the opportunity to finance himself by discounting the trade acceptance at a lower cost than by assignment of accounts receivable. Trade acceptances are eligible for rediscount at federal reserve banks. Another advantage of the trade acceptance from the standpoint of the merchant is that he has obtained a written promise of payment as opposed to an open account sale. Trade acceptances are also preferable to promissory notes from the standpoint of the bank, because the acceptance bears two signatures, (1) that of the acceptor who is the primary obliger, and (2) that of the drawer who is the secondary obliger. Another advantage from the point of view of the banker is that the acceptance usually arises from the sale of merchandise, and therefore should be self-liquidating to a far greater extent than if the borrowing took place unsupported by a sale. 

To be negotiable, an instrument must: 

1. Be in writing and be signed by the maker or drawer 

2. Contain an unconditional promise or order to pay a certain sum in money 3. Be payable on demand or at a fixed or determinable date 

4. Be payable to order or to the bearer 

5. If addressed to a drawee, he must be named or indicated with reasonable certainty In the balance sheet, trade notes and acceptances receivable may be carried in the same account. The better practice, however, is to separate them, particularly if the proportion of trade acceptances is large; this indicates a more liquid condition than do notes receivable which may have arisen because of the failure to pay an account receivable when it was due.

Notes Receivable Discounted.-Notes, drafts, and acceptances are commonly discounted at the bank as a method of borrowing money. 

The payee (the person discounting) indorses the note and thereby be-

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

comes secondarily liable; that is, if the original maker does not pay the note at maturity, the indorser (payee) must make restitution to the bank; thus a contingent liability is created. If the indorser adds "without recourse" to his indorsement, the indorsement is known as a qualified indorsement, made for the purpose of avoiding the liability ordinarily attaching to a general indorsement. Qualified indorsements are not common on notes and acceptances, as the negotiability of the instrument is thereby greatly restricted. The qualified indorsement simply assigns all interest in the note to the indorsee. 

When notes, drafts, or acceptances are discounted, the contingent liability must be shown as such. Assume that the Reck Company has $100,000.00 of notes receivable. It discounts $20,000.00, non-interest bearing notes for 60 days, at 6 per cent at the bank:

Provisions for Bad Notes, Drafts, and Acceptances.—The reserve for bad debts should be large enough to take care of losses on uncollectible notes. If the reserve for bad debts is set up on this basis, all losses on notes should be charged to the reserve. Also, on the balance sheet, the reserve should be subtracted from the sum of the accounts and notes receivable. If the reserve for bad debts is created for accounts receivable only, losses on notes should be charged to an expense account, titled "Losses on Notes." If this procedure is followed, on the balance sheet the reserve for bad debts should be subtracted from the accounts receivable alone.

Chapter XIII INVENTORIES The Classification and Nature of Inventories.—All goods ordi narily purchased or produced for immediate or future resale constitute inventory. The inventories may be resold in exactly the same condition in which they were purchased, or they may undergo many physical changes as to form and content, involving extensive processing, before they are offered for sale. In both the mercantile and the manufacturing concern, profits are realized or losses are incurred upon the sale of the inventory. Inventories are of vital importance in the consideration of the profit possibilities and the current financial condition of any business, because (a) the inventories usually comprise a large portion of the current assets and a considerable portion of the total assets and (b) the proper costing of the goods sold is one of the most important elements in correct profit determination. 

Inventories fall into many classes, and each class may be subject to its own individual base for valuation purposes. For purposes of general discussion, inventories may be classified as (1) those of mercantile or wholesale companies and (2) those of manufacturing companies. The mercantile or wholesale company normally has but one class of inventory, commonly known as merchandise inventory. The manufacturing company normally has at least three inventories: raw material, work-in-process, and finished goods; in addition, supplies, finished parts, and goods for jobbing purposes may be carried. 

Raw materials inventories consist of materials upon which no manufacturing has been performed at the inventory date. In many cases, the raw material.inventory of a manufacturer has been the finished goods inventory of one or more prior owners. Work-in-process inventories consist of goods which are only partially manufactured; the cost of the work-in-process inventories consists of the raw material placed in the manufacturing process, plus the direct labor and manufacturing overhead incurred prior to the date of the inventory of work-in-process. 

Finished goods consist of completely manufactured items, which are 245

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

ready to be sold. Finished parts are either classified separately or as raw materials.

Goods To Be Included in Inventory.-Under this title is consid ered (1) the items to be included in inventory and (2) the locale of the items and the legal title to ownership of the items which should be included.

Items. Items which enter the inventory without question are merchandise, raw material, work-in-process, finished goods, and finished parts.

Expense supplies, such as stationery, stamps, carbon paper, typewriter ribbons, wrapping paper, janitor supplies, and so on, none of which will become a part of the final finished product or the merchandise inventory, should not be classified as inventory in the current asset section of the balance sheet, but should be shown as prepaid supplies and expenses in the deferred charges section. 

Factory supplies, or more accurately, manufacturing supplies, may consist of items used directly in the manufacture of the products, or they may consist of items of a general service nature which do not enter into the products being manufactured. Manufacturing supplies used directly in the manufacture of the product, but in such quantities that it is impractical to attempt to allocate their cost to the product, may be classed either as raw materials among the current assets or as deferred charges. Manufacturing supplies which do enter the manufactured product but only service the general manufacturing operations, such as fuel or lubricants, preferably should be classified as deferred charges. 

Practice is not uniform with respect to the classification of expense supplies and manufacturing supplies, and there is much disagreement on the subject. All possibilities have been mentioned here and the preferences of the author have been indicated. 

Locale and Title.-Regardless of where it is situated, all inventory owned should be included as such. Goods out on consignment and unsold by the consignee must be included in the inventory of the consignor; conversely, goods on consignment in the hands of the consignee must be excluded from his inventory. Goods awaiting return to the seller should be excluded from the inventory of the buyer returning them. Goods in the hands of agents, salesmen, and at branches must be included.

With respect to title of ownership, as a general rule goods should be included in the inventories of the one who holds the legal title.

INVENTORIES 

247 Thus, if a seller has a sales contract with a buyer, the seller should include in his inventory all goods not actually applied to shipment on the contract; even though the seller may have gone so far as to segregate the goods for the contract, if he has not yet made delivery he owns the goods and must include them in his inventory until delivery. 

Order cancellations before delivery are rather common, and profits should not be recorded as such until a bona-fide sale is made, at which time the inventories are reduced. Orders for future delivery may be shown as a balance sheet footnote, if desired. 

If title to goods has passed to the purchaser, he should include the goods as inventory if he has knowledge that title has passed. If purchase invoices are received at the close of an accounting period and if the goods have not arrived, the situation should be shown by a charge to Goods in Transit and a credit to Accounts Payable; the Goods in 

Transit account shows that the purchase is included in the inventory, and that the corresponding liability is recognized. All goods shipped f.o.b. point of shipment become the property of the purchaser at the time of loading at the point of shipment. All goods shipped f.o.b. point of destination are the property of the seller until accepted by the buyer at the destination.

With respect to purchase commitments, the goods contracted for but not received should not be included in the inventory of the purchaser. An account, Goods on Order, may be charged and another account, Purchase Commitments, credited; both accounts are merely memorandum accounts, for no asset is as yet owned and consequently no liability exists. If it is desired not to reflect the purchase commitments in the balance sheet proper, a footnote describing the situation may be appended. If the purchase commitments are not in excess of normal, and if a price decline is not anticipated, the item need not be shown in the balance sheet, either by item or by a footnote. 

The Problem of Inventory Valuation. The problem of inventory valuation is two-fold. First, there is the problem of what goods to include in the inventories; this has been discussed in the preceding section. The second part of the problem deals with the valuation of the inventory for balance sheet purposes and for profit determination on the statement of profit and loss. The proper valuation of the inventory determines the periodic cost of goods sold, which in turn determines the profits. It must be emphasized at this point that inventories are of primary importance in the determination of income because profit

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

or a loss is incurred upon the disposition of the inventories. Inventory prices generally are subject to constant fluctuation and therefore the valuation of the inventories and the resulting effect upon the cost of goods sold vitally affects profits and losses. These phases are discussed in the subsequent sections of this chapter. The disagreement respecting the inclusion and exclusion of certain items in the inventory is much less severe than the varied opinions regarding the proper valuation of the inventory.

Methods of Inventory Valuation. Many methods are available for the valuation of inventories. The more widely used valuation methods may be classified as follows: 

1. Valuation at cost 

2. Valuation at market 

3. Valuation at cost or market, whichever is the lower 

4. Values based on selling prices 

5. Valuation under the gross profits method 

6. Valuation under the retail inventory method 

When inventories are valued at cost, the valuation may be at: a) Actual or historical cost b) Computed or derived cost (1) First-in, first-out method (2) Last-in, first-out method (3) Unweighted average method (4) Weighted average method (5) Moving average method (6) Base, minimum stock, or normal stock, method (7) Standard cost method

The Meaning of Cost.-At first glance, the term "cost" appears to be quite simple, but in many cases the determination of cost may be quite an involved and complicated process. Cost may be defined as the total outlay necessary to procure an inventory. The first element of this cost, then, is the invoiced purchase price of the goods bought. To this invoice price must be added freight, express, drayage, storage, and any import duties; all of these items increase the cost above the invoiced price. If the goods purchased in any one invoice are all identical, the computation of the unit cost is simply a matter of adding together the invoice price, the freight, the express, the drayage, the storage, and the duty charges and dividing by the number of items. However, if the invoice covers many different items it may be rather difficult to prorate the various costs among the items purchased. In most cases

INVENTORIES 

249 the freight, drayage, express, and storage can be prorated with only approximate accuracy, thus resulting in only an approximately accurate cost. For example, if a freight bill covered one full car of ten different items, the freight bill might be prorated on the basis of (a) the total weight of each of the items, (b) the total space occupied by each of the items, or (c) the total cost of each of the items. Each method would result in different amounts for the cost of the various items purchased.

When raw materials are purchased for factory fabrication, to the cost of the raw materials must be added the direct factory labor applied in the productive process and all indirect manufacturing overhead costs incurred. The cost of work-in-process at any stage of completion and the total cost of the finished product can be accurately determined only by the use of a good system of cost accounting. Even with a good cost system in operation, it is entirely possible to arrive at varying costs for identical products manufactured. The student must realize that the greater the number of items involved in any cost determination, the greater are the possibilities for inaccurate costing. 

Another item affecting cost is purchase discount. First, purchase discounts may be handled by showing all potential discounts as a deduction from purchases, and showing purchase discounts not taken as a financial expense; this is the best method. Second, purchase discounts taken may be shown as financial income; in practice this method is almost universal. Third, purchase discounts taken may be shown as a reduction of the price of the goods purchased; this is the most unsatisfactory method. If the entire possible discount is deducted from purchases, and the discount not taken shown as a financial expense, a clear picture is presented of income lost which might have been earned by better financial management and the goods purchased are valued at their net cash price. If discounts taken are treated as a financial income, the goods purchased are costed at their gross price. If discounts taken are treated as a reduction in the price of the goods, and if these discounts appear in the statement of profit and loss as a deduction from inventory, the goods are costed at a hybrid figure which is affected by financial policy. If the entire discounts possible are treated as purchase reductions and if the discount not taken is presented as a discount lost, the effect is a decrease in the value of the inventories and an increase in the gross profit; net profit is reduced by the amount of the discount lost. Treating purchase discounts as financial income has

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

the effect of increasing the value of the inventories and of decreasing gross profit; treating the discounts actually taken as a reduction of the cost of the purchases has the effect of decreasing the value of the inventory and of increasing gross profit. The Meaning of Market.-The term "market" has been defined for taxation purposes by the United States Treasury Department as follows: "Under ordinary circumstances 'market' means the current bid price prevailing at the date of the inventory for the particular merchandise in the volume in which usually purchased by the taxpayer." The inclusion of the word "volume" (that is, quantity) is of great importance, because some concerns buy in large quantities and others in smaller quantities, with price differentials existing because of the variation in quantity. The cost of Item X may be $.11 to the buyer of 100 units and $.09 to the buyer of 100,000 units. In valuing an inventory at market price, then, the quantity normally purchased must be considered; otherwise, incorrect market values will result. Freight and other incidental costs should be added to the bid price in order to make market costs comparable with cost.

Valuation at Cost or Market, Whichever Is Lower.-While there are many methods and rules for the valuation of inventories, perhaps the most universally accepted rule is to value the inventory at cost or market, whichever is lower, at the balance sheet date. To correctly value an inventory at the lower of cost or market, each item in the inventory must be listed and valued at cost, at market, and extended at the lower of the two figures. The foregoing statement considers the "lower" to be by items of inventory. Some accountants are of the opinion that the lower of cost or market should be applied to the inventory in total; others believe that it should be applied to groups. 

Different results are obtained by the three methods. 

In the following illustration, each item is extended at the lower of cost or market, on the basis that in any valuation each item entering a total should be individually considered. ITEM COST

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

When inventories are valued at the lower of cost or market, all losses are provided for and no profits are anticipated. This results in a most conservative valuation of the inventory for balance sheet purposes. The rule is based on the theory that if market prices decline, selling prices probably will decline; therefore losses are provided for before the sale by writing down the value of the inventory to market when it is below cost. The rule is also based on the theory that without a sale there can be no profit; if market value were above cost, and if the inventory were written up to market, a profit would be brought into the records by the increased value of the inventory. Accountants are well agreed that no profit should be brought into the records before the profit is realized, and by permitting the inventory to remain at cost when the market has risen, the profit is not taken up. Those accountants who disapprove inventory valuation at the lower of cost or market do so on the basis that the writedown of an inventory from cost to a new lower market price throws the loss into the period of price decline and not into the period in which a sale is made; this is quite true, but most accountants, bankers, and business men believe in writing off any loss as soon as it is discovered. Others disapprove of this method because of the large amount of work involved in ascertaining market prices at the date of the inventory, and because of the work involved in adjusting the inventory accounts, both control and subsidiary, and the factory cost records. 

The reader must understand that when inventories are valued at the lower of cost or market, the valuation takes place at the end of the accounting period; it does not take place every time a change in price Occurs.

Consideration is now given to certain pitfalls which must be avoided when inventories are valued at the lower of cost or market. The valuation of an inventory affects both the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss. For purposes of the balance sheet the inventory should be stated at the lower of cost or market. For the purpose of the statement of profit and loss, the closing inventory should be stated at cost, and the loss due to value decline shown in the nonoperating section of the statement; this avoids an incorrect statement of the cost of goods sold. To illustrate the correct procedure, assume that a company purchased $300,000.00 of goods during an accounting period; $200,000.00 of the goods were sold for $275,000.00; the ending inventory at cost, therefore, is $100,000.00; the market value

Reserve for Inventory Decline.-As indicated in the preceding section, losses in inventory caused by a decline in the market as compared with original cost may be (1) credited directly to the Inventory account or (2) credited to an account titled Reserve for Decline in Inventory. The account, Reserve for Decline in Inventory, is an asset valuation reserve account and should be shown on the balance sheet as a deduction from the inventory at cost. If perpetual subsidiary inventory records are not maintained, the use of a reserve is not recommended, as the Inventory account can be credited directly with a minimum of work. If perpetual subsidiary inventory records are maintained, and if the subsidiary records are each adjusted to market, when that figure is below cost, the reserve is likewise not necessary. If

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

perpetual subsidiary records are maintained, and if the work of adjusting each account to market is excessive, the reserve must be used; if it were not used, the controlling Inventory account would be out of agreement with the sum of the perpetual subsidiary accounts. 

When a reserve for inventory decline is used, there arises the question of its ultimate disposal. Theoretically, each time inventory (the market price of which was below cost as of the last balance sheet date) is sold, the reserve should be charged and the inventory credited for the amount of the decline as of the statement date; thus, the charge to cost of sales would be at market. Practically, such procedure is not reasonable when considered from the standpoint of the work necessary to obtain the results. The best procedure is probably somewhat as follows: At each subsequent closing date, adjust the reserve to its new required amount. The following table indicates the rule. If a larger reserve is required at the end of the second year than was necessary at the end of the first year, Loss on Decline in Inventory is charged and Reserve for Decline in Inventory is credited for the amount necessary to adjust the reserve to the new requirements. If the reserve at the end of the second year is to be smaller than the reserve established at the end of the first year (indicating market recovery), the reserve is charged and Loss on Decline in Inventory credited. In the latter case, the account title should be changed to Gain on Market

Reserves for Anticipated Future Inventory Losses. In addition to the declines below cost which have taken place before or at the balance sheet date, additional price decline may be anticipated for the

255 next accounting period. The declines which have taken place before or at the balance sheet date are provided for by the charge to Loss on Decline in Inventory and the credit to Inventory or to Reserve for Decline in Inventory. The anticipated future declines in the inventory will cause losses if the declines take place before the inventory is sold. 

The current period should not be charged with losses expected in the future. Consequently, anticipated future losses should be provided for by creating a Reserve for Anticipated Future Losses out of Surplus: 

Surplus Reserve for Anticipated Future Inventory Losses. 

XXXX XXXX This reserve is a surplus reserve created at the close of an accounting period, and is shown on the balance sheet as a part of the net worth. 

At the close of the next accounting period, the reserve is closed back to Surplus if no declines are anticipated at that time. If it is expected that the market will continue to decline, the reserve may be continued, or adjusted upward or downward. In any case, this reserve will finally be closed to Surplus. The recognition of a loss caused by a decline in the market value of the inventory should be charged to the Profit and Loss account, Loss on Decline in Inventory, and should never be charged to the Surplus Reserve. Valuation at Market.-Inventories are sometimes valued at market, regardless of whether market value at the balance sheet date is higher or lower than cost. Those who advocate this method of inventory valuation do so on the basis that they believe the balance sheet should show replacement costs. Naturally the method is not conservative, and if market prices have risen above cost prices, unrealized profits may be taken up through the increased values before the profit is realized through sale. To avoid overstating profits, if market is in excess of cost, the excess of market över cost may be treated as follows. Inventory 

Reserve for Market Increase.. 

To increase the inventory from cost to current market and to set up a net worth reserve for the amount of the increase. XX XX If, in the succeeding period, the inventory is sold, the reserve may be (1) closed to Profit-and-Loss, or (2) closed to Earned Surplus. The 

United States Treasury Department permits the use of market value for inventories of dealers in securities.

Valuation at Cost.-Although the most widely accepted method of valuing inventories is the lower of cost or market, valuation at cost is used almost as extensively. Valuation at cost is less conservative than valuation at the lower of cost or market only in those cases where inventory values have declined below cost at the balance sheet date. 

If inventory market values are above cost at the balance sheet date, then valuation at cost yields the same results as valuation at the lower of cost or market.

When cost is used for inventory valuation purposes, unrealized losses and unrealized profits are automatically eliminated from the profit and loss accounts; a profit is realized or a loss is incurred only in the period in which a sale is made. Consequently, though the profitand-loss statement will show only profits or losses actually realized or incurred, the balance sheet will show inventory values above market if market values have declined below cost.

INVENTORIES 

257 Certain businesses cannot readily value their inventories at the lower of cost or market because the inventories are not purchased in organized markets and market price at the balance sheet date may be almost impossible of determination. Also, in certain instances, the quantity of inventory on hand at the balance sheet date may be far above or below the quantity normally purchased, and if current market prices in terms of certain volumes were applied to a different volume on hand, the resulting inventory values might be quite incorrect. In other instances inventory prices are fairly stable, resulting in only slight variations between cost and market. In still other instances the rate of inventory turnover is so rapid that market and cost practically coincide.

Computed or Derived Costs.—Consideration is now given to the valuation of inventories under computed or derived costs. Computed or derived costing implies the use of a method of arriving at the cost other than an actual pricing of each individual item in the inventory. 

When inventories are valued under computed or derived costs, normally the number of units is large, purchases frequent, and the prices fluctuating, with the result that a derived costing method is applied to the inventory rather than individually pricing each item in the inventory array at its own specific cost.

The First-In, First-Out Method.-Perpetual inventory records should be maintained in the employment of the first-in, first-out method of accounting for inventory. A separate perpetual inventory record is maintained for each item of inventory. These records are designed to show for each item the receipts, withdrawals, and balances, in terms of quantities, unit cost, and total cost. When inventories are issued from stock, they are priced at the unit cost of the oldest items in stock; when the oldest lot is completely issued, further issues are priced at the unit cost of the next purchase until that lot is, exhausted. The balance on hand at the balance sheet date is priced at the unit cost applying to the purchases for which inventory is still on hand. In other words, as the inventories are requisitioned for sale or use, the inventories purchased first are credited to the inventory accounts and charged to operations before more recent purchases. The following illustration demonstrates the first-in, first-out method of costing inventories.

The Last-In, First-Out Method. This method is the reverse of the first-in, first-out method. The Federal Revenue Act has approved this method for all industries where it is appropriate. The inventory issued during the period is priced at the end of the period. Issues during the period cannot be priced until the end of the period because the last price is not ascertainable until the close of the period. Using the purchases and requisitions assumed in the preceding illustration, the value of the inventory at the end of the period is determined as follows:

In many businesses, sales prices are immediately affected by changes in cost prices. In equally as many other businesses, sales price changes lag somewhat behind changes in cost by a long or a short interval of

INVENTORIES 

259 time. In those businesses where sales prices fluctuate directly (or approximately) with costs, the use of the last-in, first-out method of costing inventory results in a closer correlation of current costs and sales price than does the first-in, first-out method. 

Inventories are requisitioned and charged to cost of sales at prices representing the most recent cost, thus reflecting current prices in the cost of sales and thereby determining income on a current cost basis. The reflection of income based upon current prices is the most important advantage of the use of the last-in, first-out method. It should be noted that an entirely different result is secured by the use of the first-in, first-out method which charges sales with the costs of the first oldest items on hand and costs remaining inventories at their most recent values; this results in currently accurate balance sheet figures, but the income is determined on the basis of the cost of the most remote purchases.

Consider the following illustration: A machine tool manufacturer, engaged in the construction of heavy machinery has an inventory of one machine which cost $8,500.00 and which is priced for sale at $10,000.00. Before the machine is sold, costs move upward to the point where the machine, if built under the new price level, would cost $9,350.00. The manufacturer therefore immediately raises the sales price of the first machine to $11,000.00. He builds a second machine identical to the first, at a cost of $9,350.00, and priced it at $11,000.00. 

Upon the completion of the second machine, the first machine is sold for $11,000.00. What is the profit?

The advocate of the last-in, first-out method bases his profit on the belief that current income should be determined in the light of current costs. The advocate of the first-in, first-out method wishes to include as profit the additional $850.00 which is tied up in the higher cost of the second machine, which is unsold.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

In considering either the first-in, first-out or the last-in, first-out method of accounting for inventory, it must be remembered that the methods deal only with monetary value and not with physical quantities. For example, the first-in, first-out method may be in use, but the physical quantities may be completely intermingled with no physical distinction as to which units were received first or last, or the last inventories received may be issued first because they are on top of a pile or bin. The methods deal only with costing. 

One disadvantage of the last-in, first-out method is that it is necessary to wait until the close of the accounting period to cost the inventories which have become a part of cost of sales. This is not a disadvantage, however, for computing the value of the final inventory. 

The first-in, first-out method permits immediate valuation for purposes of cost of sales.

The Unweighted or Simple Average Method.-Inventories may be computed by the use of averages, either unweighted, weighted, or moving averages. Under the unweighted, or simple arithmetical average method, the sum of all of the unit prices is divided by the number of purchases made (the beginning inventory at its unit price considered as one purchase) in order to arrive at the unweighted average unit price. This figure is multiplied by the number of units in the ending inventory to determine the inventory value; it is multiplied by the number of units issued to determine the cost of sales; as a result of the two computations, an adjustment to Cost of Goods Sold probably will be necessary in order to account for total values. Any method that forces the computation of inventory at the closing date is disadvantageous, for the pricing of cost of sales is delayed long past the date of issuing the inventory from stock; furthermore, the peak load of work at the end of the period is increased. 

Under the weighted average method, all issues are at a uniform price in any one accounting period.

The Base Stock, Minimum Stock, or Normal Stock Method.-This method of valuation, while not new, had been growing in importance until partially superseded by the last-in, first-out method. The method has been slow in gaining acceptance because opinions differ and confusion results as a failure to understand the operation of the method. 

The general operation of the method is similar to the last-in, first-out method, but different inventory valuations result from the two methods. 

The last-in, first-out has the advantage of being acceptable for incometax purposes.

The base stock method operates on the assumption, which is quite logical for the majority of businesses, that a certain minimum inventory is required at all times, regardless of business activity. The minimum is not the average inventory, but a basic quantity. This minimum inventory is viewed as a permanent capital investment rather than as a temporary investment; although the items in the inventories are sold and replaced, or turned over, periodically, the capital invested in the minimum stock is never released until the business is liquidated. 

Usually the best results are obtained if the inventory is consistently large. The rate of inventory turnover is immaterial to the operation of the base stock method. The method also assumes that the minimum inventory should be valued at a constant unit price, just as any fixed investment is normally valued. If, at the balance sheet date, the actual physical inventory is above the base stock, to this constant base stock is added the excess of the physical inventory over the base, at the current unit price; if the actual inventory at the balance sheet date is below the base, the deficiency multiplied by the current unit price is subtracted from the basic amount for valuation purposes. The effect of this method is to price issues more nearly at the current market price and to value the basic inventory at a normal price. The outstanding advantage of the method is that it reflects a long-range point of view with respect to profit and loss and eliminates short-run gains and losses due to inventory fluctuations.

INVENTORIES 

263 The computation of the inventory under the base stock method may be summarized as follows: 

Base unit stock X normal price + excess units over base X current market (or minus the units below normal X current market) the value of the inventory.

The Standard Cost Method.-Many manufacturing concerns set up predetermined or estimated costs of manufacturing a product; the predetermined costs are classified into material costs, labor costs, and overhead costs. The estimated cost of each element then becomes the standard cost, which remains fixed until the standards are changed as a result of changing price levels or changes in other cost factors. 

The standard cost established normally is the average cost for a long period of time tempered by expectancies for the forthcoming accounting

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

period. All purchases of inventories are recorded at the actual price paid, and all issues to work-in-process are recorded at the standard price. The balance of the inventory at the closing date is computed at standard, and any variation is written off to cost of sales (or cost of sales, work-in-process, and finished goods, in the ratio of each to the total). To illustrate valuation under the standard cost method assume:

Since the standard price has been increased $.02 (from $.80 to $.82) during the current period, then $20.00 of the adjustment (initial inventory of 1,000 units X $.02) should be credited to surplus and $300.00 should be charged to cost of sales, or divided between cost of sales, work-in-process, and finished goods. 

A review of the preceding methods of computing inventories shows that different results are obtained under the various methods. The effect upon the cost of goods sold and upon the net profit is different under each method. Each method has its own advocates and adherents. 

Regardless of the method employed, the proper determination of income and the correctness of the values of the ending inventories are the primary objectives.

Valuation Based on Selling Prices.—In certain industries it is vir tually impossible to ascertain correctly the costs of units, because each purchase may be broken into several parts after acquisition. For example, in the packing industry and in certain extractive industries the cost of one whole unit cannot be prorated accurately to the various products ultimately to be realized. In these industries, inventories are computed (1) by valuing the inventory items at sales price less estimated expenses; the resultant figure is an inventory valuation at the net amount of cash to be realized upon disposition, or (2) by prorating the entire cost over each unit part on the basis of the cost of the whole to the sales price of the whole in relation to the sales price of the part. The latter method is commonly known as the joint-cost method. Assume that the total cost of buying and processing a steer is 77745

INVENTORIES 

265 $150.00; it is estimated that the entire sales price to be realized from the sale of all parts of the steer will be $195.00. One certain section of the steer will sell for $16.00. The cost of that unit, after processing, is computed as follows: 150 195 of $16.00 $12.31 = computed joint cost of the part. 

With the exception of those cases wherein costs are difficult or impossible of determination, selling prices do not furnish a very satisfactory basis for valuing inventory. 

The Valuation of Work-in-Process and Finished Goods.-Early in this chapter, the three classes of inventory common to a manufacturing concern were stated to be raw material, work-in-process, and finished goods. In the subsequent discussion of valuation practice, certain distinctions between these three classes were not considered. 

It is advisable at this point to clarify valuation procedure for all three classes of inventory. Up to this point the discussion has been particularly applicable to raw materials and to goods bought for resale without processing.

Work-in-process should be valued at the lower of cost or market. 

If the raw materials put into process have declined in market or replacement value compared with cost, the material in process should be valued at market; if the direct labor and manufacturing overhead added to the material in process have increased above or fallen below cost, each of the elements should be valued at the lower of the two figures, cost or market. The proper valuation of work in process at the lower of cost or market is dependent upon the adequacy of the cost system; if a complete and satisfactory cost system is in operation, correct costs are not difficult to determine; if the cost system is incomplete and unsatisfactory, correct costs cannot be determined. Consequently, adequate comparisons cannot be made between costs and market values, and valuations of inventory are less accurate. 

The valuation of finished goods follows the same procedure as the valuation applicable to work-in-process. Each of the three elements of cost-raw materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overheadmust be separately valued at the lower of cost or market. Frequently, however, market prices for all of the elements of cost are difficult to determine; furthermore, the problem of recomputation of all costs in terms of current costs may be prohibitive. For these reasons inven-

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

tories of work-in-process and finished goods are frequently valued at cost.

The Gross Profits Method.-The gross profits method is used when it is decided to verify a previously calculated inventory value, or when it is impossible to obtain physical count of the inventory. The method is very useful to auditors as a check on the figures of the client; it is useful if a company desires to produce financial statements each month and at the same time does not maintain perpetual inventory records and does not wish to take a physical inventory each month; it is also useful in determining inventory in the event of a fire if perpetual inventory records are not maintained. of The gross profits method is based on the assumption that the rate gross profit is approximately the same in each successive accounting period, and the method is satisfactory only if the rate from period to period is approximately the same. The amount of gross profit has no bearing on the determination of the income; the rate only must be about the same for each period.

To illustrate the gross profits method of valuing the inventory, assume that the Bagg Company has maintained a gross profit rate of 30 per cent for several years. From the following data, determine the approximate value of the inventory on December 31, 1942.

The Retail Inventory Method. The retail inventory method is based upon the theory that current selling prices can be accurately established at the time of purchase. The basis of operation of the

INVENTORIES 

267 method is the estimated rate of mark-up (gross profit) for the current period, whereas the basis of operation of the gross profits method is the rate of gross profit for past periods. The method is widely used by retail stores of the departmental and other types and by jobbers, but it is not adaptable to manufacturers. 

The method was devised particularly for those businesses in which the number of commodities is large, and in which perpetual inventories may be maintained if at all, only in terms of selling prices. 

Primarily, the retail method of inventory valuation serves as a medium of merchandise control, and as a means of arriving at the value of an ending inventory without taking a physical inventory. Or physical inventories may be taken, priced at selling prices, and then valued by the retail method. 

Before proceeding with the demonstrations of the operation of the retail inventory method, the reader must become familiar with certain terminology: 

Initial Mark-Up (Mark-On, Gross Profit) is the difference between cost price and the originally established sales (retail) price. 

Additional Mark-Up (Mark-Up, Revaluation, Additional Gross Profit) is any addition to the sales price which raises it above the originally established sales (retail) price. For example: The original sales price is $5.00; later the price is raised to $5.25; $.25 is additional mark-up.

Markdowns are price reductions which reduce the sales (retail) price below the originally established sales price. For example: The original sales price is $5.00; later the price is reduced to $4.75; $.25 is markdown.

Additional Mark-Up Cancellations (Mark-Up Cancellations) are price reductions that do not reduce the sales (retail) price below the originally established sales price, but simply cancel some or all of the additional mark-up. For example: The original sales price is $5.00; an additional mark-up of $.25 is added making the new sales price $5.25; later the price is reduced to $5.10; $.15 is an additional mark-up cancellation.

Markdowns Cancellations are additions that do not increase the sales (retail) price above the originally established sales price. For example: The original sales price is $5.00; later the price is reduced (marked down) to $4.75; later the price is raised to $4.90; $.15 is a markdown cancellation.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Accumulated Mark-Up (Mark-On) is the difference between cost price and the originally established sales (retail) price plus net additional mark-ups.

Net Mark-Ups are additional mark-ups minus additional mark-up cancellations. 

Net Markdowns are markdowns minus markdown cancellations. 

Maintained Mark-Up is the initial mark-up plus additional markups, minus additional mark-up cancellations, minus markdowns, plus markdown cancellations.

Consider the following illustration: An article costing $500.00 is initially marked up to sell for $800.00. Later the price is increased to $900.00; therefore, the additional mark-up is $100.00. Later, the price is reduced to $875.00. The additional mark-up cancellation is $25.00. Later the price is reduced to $700.00; there is an additional mark-up cancellation of $75.00 and a markdown of $100.00. Later the price is raised to $725.00; there is a markdown cancellation of $25.00. 

The maintained mark-up is: $300.00 $100.00-$25.00-$75.00 — $100.00 $25.00 $225.00. 

With the retail method of inventory valuation in use, records of the opening inventory and all purchases made during a period must be kept at both cost price and at sales (retail) price. At the close of the period the inventory is computed at sales (retail) price; the inventory at retail price is then "valued" by the application of the mark-up percentage figure for the current period. If additional mark-ups are made, it is entirely possible that market prices have increased; therefore, the inventory should be valued at a lower figure which will not include the increase in market prices; including additional mark-ups and excluding markdowns accomplishes this objective.

If markdowns have been made, it is entirely possible that market prices have declined; market would then be lower than original cost; including additional mark-ups and excluding markdowns again accomplishes the purpose of valuing the inventory at a more conservative figure. Furthermore, if the marked-down goods have been sold, the per cent of mark-up to be deducted from the remaining inventory priced at the regular prices should not be reduced by including markdowns.

Departmentalization. The preceding illustrations make no distinction between departments and a store as an entirety. In most stores different ratios of cost to retail will exist for different departments. As a result, it is necessary to maintain the retail inventory records on a departmental basis so that cost ratios and percentages of mark-up may be distinguished for each department; only by such departmentalization can the inventory of each department, and consequently of the store as a whole, be properly valued. If different ratios

INVENTORIES 

271 of cost to sales exist for each department, and if records are not departmentalized, the application of an average percentage of mark-up for the store as a whole will result in overvaluations of inventory for some departments and undervaluations of inventory for other departments. 

Many retail stores break their control of inventory by units of stock, divided into individual prices, styles, sizes, etc., or divided into classifications within a department. The system is known as unit control, which amounts to departmentalization on an item basis rather than on the basis of a section of the store. Unit control is extremely effective if the variety of merchandise items is not too great; if the number of items is too great, the expense of operating a system of control over each classification or each item is prohibitive. 

Frequency of Inventory Computation.-Normally, percentages of mark-up on merchandise sold will vary from season to season; for example, a store dealing in men's clothing will mark its merchandise to sell at a higher price in October and April than in February and August. Consequently, the valuations of merchandise inventory under the retail inventory method should be made frequently, preferably once a month, rather than at longer intervals; a full fiscal year is too long under any circumstances, unless the same rate of total mark-up prevails for all months of the year.

Form for Retail Inventory Computations.-The form presented on the following page has been approved by the Controller's Congress of the National Retail Dry Goods Association. 

Advantages and Disadvantages of the Retail Method. As seen from the discussion of the retail inventory method, one advantage of the method is that it is readily discernible that no questions arise concerning depreciation of inventory. Inventory depreciation is taken care of by marking-down merchandise which does not move rapidly. 

The markdowns are reflected as cost reductions and consequently no entries for depreciation are required.

Inventory is charged and credited to the inventory accounts at retail, thus placing the accounting on an equality basis, in a manner similar to accounting for cash.

Under the retail method, a reduction is made in the time of taking physical inventories; this task may be done on a rotary basis, or at almost any time, thus reducing the amount of work at the close of a fiscal period. In addition, statements may be prepared immediately after the close of a period, as it is not necessary to wait upon physical inventories.

At retail, the closing inventory is twice the beginning inventory, at cost, the closing inventory is not twice the beginning inventory. The derived cost of the closing inventory figure is such that the company will have a mark-up of 40 per cent at the beginning of the next period. 

A last advantage is that price tags need be marked with sales price only; codes need not be used for cost. 

A disadvantage of the method is that it is based on averages. This may be overcome by proper departmentalization. Another disadvantage of the method is that if the ending inventory contains more low-cost goods with high mark-ups than the average inventory contains, the inventory is somewhat overvalued; the reverse is true for high-cost goods with low mark-ups. However, if the percentage of error is constant, the effect is of no significance. Also, undervaluations in one department are offset to some extent by overvaluations in another department. Proper departmentalization results in the elimination of undervaluation and overvaluation.

The method is disadvantageous if there is no established price policy, if trade-ins and repossessions are high, and if sliding-scale discounts exist.

Cash Discounts, Freight-In, Purchases, and Sales Returns.--Under the retail inventory method, the treatment of purchase discounts and sales discounts should follow the same procedure as that followed in the preparation of the company statements. If purchase discounts are treated as financial incomes, they should not be taken into consideration for retail inventory computations. If sales discounts are treated as financial expenses in the company statements, they should be ignored for retail inventory computations. If purchase discounts are deducted from purchases, they should be deducted in the purchase figures for computation in the retail inventory method. However, if company policy is to deduct sales discounts from sales, the discounts should not be deducted from the sales figure in the retail inventory computations, for no corresponding deduction can be made from the amount of mark-up.

Freight-in, if added to purchases on the books, should be added to the cost of the purchases in making the retail inventory calculations. 

Purchase returns and sales returns should be deducted from purchases and sales, respectively, both at cost and at retail. To illustrate:

Perpetual Inventory Records.-By perpetual inventory is meant the maintenance of the inventory records so that they show currently the correct quantity of inventory on hand. When perpetual inventories are maintained, stores ledgers or subsidiary records are kept for each item of raw material and finished goods inventory, showing the quantities and prices, or quantities only if deserved. Normally, the only

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

perpetual inventory records kept for work-in-process are the cost sheets for each order which serve as the record for quantity and value for work-in-process. Modern accounting demands the adoption of adequate perpetual inventory records, if costs of operations are to be determined, and if inventory valuations are to be correct for balance sheet purposes. 

The care of, and accounting for, inventory should be on a basis as rigid as the care of, and accounting, for cash. If inventories are not properly controlled, shortages and mistakes occur. Valuations are. incorrect if quantities are not correct, even if unit prices are correctly computed. 

The perpetual inventory records are controlled on the general ledger by the Raw Material, Finished Goods, and Merchandise Inventory accounts. Perpetual inventory records take a variety of forms, ranging from a simple subsidiary book record up to accounting machine cards. 

The perpetual records may be kept in terms of quantity only, or both quantity and price may be included on the record. When price is included, the pricing may be done under any method desired. 

One example of a perpetual inventory record is illustrated, using the moving average method.

275 Inventory Turnover.-Merchandise turnover is an important measure of the profitableness of operations of any business organization. 

Important to the valuation of inventory is the number of times the inventory figures are averaged in the computation. For example, in a seasonal business, if only opening and closing inventories are averaged together, a vastly different rate of inventory turnover is derived than if the inventories are averaged for each of the twelve months of the year. In the computation of any average, the greater the number of items in the array, the greater is the accuracy of the result. Mechanical computations for inventory are discussed in chapters XXV and 

XXVI, on Analysis of Statements. 

Trade Discounts.-Trade discounts are deductions from list prices granted to purchasers. Fundamentally, the amount of the discount depends upon the size of the purchase, although bargaining ability has played a large part in determining the size of a trade discount. One of the purposes of the Robinson-Patman act is to eliminate price discrimination between purchasers of the same volume of product from any one seller.

It must be distinctly understood that a trade discount is not a discount granted for the prompt payment of a bill, and therefore is definitely not a cash or purchase discount; the purchase discount is an additioral discount, over and above the trade discount. Normally, so-called cash discounts in excess of 2 per cent are viewed as trade discounts. Trade discounts are known as chain discounts when they are stated in terms of a chain or series, such, for example, as discounts of 30 per cent, 15 per cent, 10 per cent, 10 per cent, 5 per cent, 5 per cent, 3 per cent.

To illustrate the operation and computation of trade discounts, assume that a salesman informs a customer that the price of an article is $10.00, less discounts of 30 per cent, 20 per cent, 10 per cent and 

10 per cent. What is the price to the customer, The price to the customer is $4.54, computed as follows: $10.00-30% $ 7.00 

$7.00 

20% = 5.60 $ 5.60-10% $ 5.04-10% = 5.04 

4.54 

It is seen that the price is not the list price less the sum of the discounts multiplied by the list price, but is a running reduction of the

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

1 prices established by applying the successive discounts to the price after the application of the preceding discount in the chain. Discounts of 

30, 20, 10, 10 are the same as discounts of 10, 10, 20, 30, or any other rotation of the same numbers. The purchaser charges Purchases for $4.54 and credits Accounts Payable or Cash for $4.54. If a purchase. discount is also granted, it is treated in the customary manner of handling purchase discounts. Trade discounts are not recorded in the accounts, but are merely devices for price determination. 

The single equivalent of a chain of discounts may be computed as follows: Take the complements of the discounts, multiply them together and subtract the result from 100 per cent. The result is the discount; the complements multiplied together equal the cost percentage. Using the illustration above: Discounts

Uncompleted Contracts. It is a well-recognized principle that profits should not be taken up on work-in-process. The work must be completed and sold before the profit is realized. However, in the construction contracting business, the completion of a contract may extend over more than one accounting period. Consequently, if costs are incurred in one accounting period and if all income from the contract is received in a subsequent period, the accounting records for any one period would not be correlated for costs and income. The accounting for long-term contracts requires special treatment, deviating from the general rule of recording no profits until realization. 

If a long-term contract is taken at a flat price, it is somewhat dangerous to take up partial profits at the close of an accounting period while the construction is still in progress, because when the job is finally completed, a loss may result instead of a profit. On the other hand, if profits on the uncompleted contract are not taken up, retiring stockholders and retiring partners may not receive full value for the sale of their interests and non-cumulative preferred stockholders may receive smaller dividends than they should rightfully receive. Of course any understatement of profit will be offset later by an overstatement of profit; thus the income figures of two accounting periods are misleading.

If the contract is taken on a cost-plus basis, no reason exists for

INVENTORIES 

277 7 deferring the recording of the profit until completion, and the profit at the close of any accounting period can be determined by computing the costs and adding the profit. Even on flat price contracts it is considered proper to take up profits on uncompleted contracts for construction projects, because of the long periods involved. Furthermore the contractor must take into consideration the provisions of the federal income tax laws; his income will be forced into higher surtax or corporate tax brackets if he waits until a construction job is completed and reports the whole profit in one tax year. 

To illustrate the computation of profits on uncompleted construction work, assume that a contract is taken for $200,000.00, that the work finished on the contract at the end of an accounting period has cost $80,000.00, and that the estimated cost to complete the job is $90,000.00.

Merchandise in Foreign Branches.-When a domestic company has merchandise in foreign branches at a balance sheet date, there arises the question of the conversion of the value of the inventory from foreign currency to domestic currency. In general, merchandise in foreign branches should be converted to domestic currency at the rate of exchange prevailing at the balance sheet date. If rates of exchange on a foreign country are stable, a standard rate of exchange may be adopted. Any domestic company must follow a consistent method of valuing its inventory when merchandise is in branches in more than one foreign country. Gains or losses on the conversion should be credited or charged to a Profit-and-Loss on Foreign Exchange Fluctuation account.

Frequently, foreign goods are imported at a date close to the end of the accounting period, to be paid for in the next accounting period by drawing a bill of exchange against a letter of credit previously opened at a bank. The goods, received in one period, will be paid for in another period, and, in all probability the rate of exchange at the

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

time of payment will differ from the rate at the time of purchase. The correct cost of the goods purchased is computed on the basis of the exchange rate existing at the date the bank accepts the bill of exchange. 

The valuation of the goods at the balance sheet date may then be the lower or cost of market.

Valuation of Scrap Material.-The valuation of scrap is difficult. 

No consistent rules are universally applicable to the valuation of scrap material, and care and good judgment must prevail in all cases. In some instances, the allocation of a correct cost figure to scrap material is more expensive than to ignore the valuation. In any problem involving the valuation of scrap, care must be exercised to avoid including the scrap in the cost of the principal or original product and also setting up its value as scrap. In other words, if a value is placed on scrap material, the same amount must be deducted from the materials cost of the original product; otherwise, both inventory values and profits would be overstated. 

Scrap may be the result of (1) spoilage or (2) waste material thrown off from the manufacture of a main product. Scrap may be (1) of no value, (2) salable as scrap, (3) reprocessed because of spoilage or defects, or (4) used in the manufacture of a side-line or by-product.

If the scrap is valueless, no value should be assigned to it and no deduction should be made from the cost of the main product because of the mere existence of the scrap. If deductions are made for valueless scrap, the cost of the main product is understated. 

If the scrap is saleable as such, the sales value of the scrap may be (1) treated as income or (2) deducted from the cost of manufacturing the principal product. The latter treatment is the better as it results in a more correct costing of the principal products. 

If the scrap is reprocessed for use in the manufacture of the principal product no value is assigned to it, as the cost of the material originally was charged to work in process. The additional processing results in a higher unit cost of manufacturing than if spoilage had not taken place.

If the scrap is used in the manufacture of a "side-line” and if a correct value can be assigned to the scrap, this amount should be deducted from the cost of the original product and added to the material cost of the side-line. If at least an approximate value cannot be assigned to the scrap, no deduction should be made from the cost of

INVENTORIES 

279 the original product and no addition for material cost should be made to the cost of the side-line. 

Much more could be written concerning scrap material but that is reserved for texts dealing with cost accounting. For purposes of inventory valuation, the important points to remember are that scrap should be assigned no value if it has no market, that the allocation of a cost figure to the scrap must be equalized by a credit to another product cost, and that the allocation of the cost must be accurate and well founded. If the allocation is not accurate, the costs of the principal products are not accurate. As a result, selling prices may not be properly set; if they are set too high, volume will decrease, and if they are set too low, unwarranted expansion may take place. In either case losses will occur which can be traced to inaccurate accounting for scrap. 

Repossessed Merchandise.-Installment sales and the repossession of goods partially paid for are treated in chapter XIV, Consignments; 

Installment Selling. For purposes of inventory valuation, repossessed merchandise should be valued at either (1) the estimated resale value less the estimated sales expense, or (2) cost less an adequate allowance for price reduction because of damage.

Hypothecated Inventories. Inventories may be pledged as security for a loan under a chattel mortgage. The merchandise pledged as security is free for use, with the understanding that other goods will replace those used or that the loan shall be liquidated as the goods are sold. In the balance sheet, the fact that the merchandise is pledged be shown (1) by a footnote to the balance sheet or (2) by indicating the fact of hypothecation in parentheses both by the inventory item and the secured liability. The latter practice is the better as it shows the actual condition in the balance sheet proper. may

Chapter XIV CONSIGNMENTS. 

INSTALLMENT SELLING- LONG TERM CONTRACTS CONSIGNMENTS 

Terminology.-A consignment is a shipment of merchandise from the owner to another party who is employed to sell it for the owner on a commission basis. The owner is the consignor, and the person to whom the goods are shipped is the consignee. The consignee acts as the agent of the consignor. The consignment is a bailment of merchandise, and the entire operation of the accounting structure for consignments is based upon the laws governing agencies and bailments. 

Title. In a sale, title passes from the seller to the buyer; in a consignment, title to goods unsold by the consignee, remains with the consignor. As a consignment is not a sale, profits do not arise from mere consignment, but are realized only when the goods are sold by the consignee.

Consignment-In-Merchandise received on consignment is a consignment-in. As agent, the consignee has no title to the goods so received; he is merely holding them for sale for the account of the consignor. The consignment-in is not inventory of the consignee, and must be excluded from his inventory, both physically and for accounting purposes.

Consignment-Out.-Merchandise sent on consignment is a consignment-out. The consignor retains title until the consignee sells the goods. 

Consignments-out remain as inventory of the consignor until sold by the consignee.

Account Sales.-Periodically, or after each sale, the consignee renders to the consignor a statement known as the account sales. This statement contains information concerning the number of units sold, the sales price, consignee commissions, deductible expenses, prior advances to the consignor, and the balance of the cash remitted. 282

CONSIGNMENTS 

283 Consignment Contract.-The consignor has title; the consignee has the merchandise. The consignment contract should be carefully drawn and should include: 

1. Specific designation as to whether the consignor or the consignee will pay transportation charges. Usually the consignor pays these charges. 

2. Specific designation as to whether the consignor or the consignee will pay for storage and insurance on merchandise in the hands of the consignee. Usually the consignee pays these charges and recovers them from the consignor at the time of the first sale. 

3. The rights of the consignor to ask for advances from the consignee, before sale. 

4. The rate of the consignee's commission. 

5. The granting of credit to customers. If the consignee grants credit to customers, he usually assumes the risk of bad debt losses.

Under these conditions the consignee is known as a del credere agent, and the customer is released from action by the consignor. 

6. The time and method of preparing the account sales. 

7. The methods of terminating the consignment contract. 

Consignment Expenses. Consignment expenses paid by the consignor and applicable to unsold merchandise may be treated as deferred charges at the time of preparing statements applicable to future income. 

Reasons for Consignments.-The consignor may prefer consignments instead of sales because (a) he prefers that title remain with him so that he can control the price of the goods, (b) he may have access to wider channels of distribution because the consignee does not have to make an outright purchase, (c) in the event of the insolvency of the consignee, he (the consignor) can recover his own merchandise. 

The consignee may prefer consignments instead of outright purchases because (a) if the goods are unsaleable, his capital is not invested and the goods may be returned to the consignor, (b) if market prices decline the consignee suffers no loss.

INSTALLMENT SELLING 

Selling on the Installment Plan. When selling on the installment plan, the seller is interested in protecting his title to the goods sold until the purchaser has liquidated the entire sales price. If title is thus vested in the seller, he can, in the event the purchaser fails to meet his payments, repossess the goods sold. At the time of the sale, the seller may (a) transfer title to the purchaser, and take back a chattel mortgage to secure the unpaid balance, (b) convey title to a trustee pending the payment of the final installment, (c) retain title and lease the property to the purchaser until the final installment is paid, (d) retain title outright until the final installment is paid. 

Throughout the past several years, installment selling has spread from a few restricted fields into almost every phase of modern merchandising. When sales are made on the installment plan, the seller usually charges interest in the form of a "carrying charge." 

The major accounting problems in connection with installment sales are: (1) the determination of the method of recording profits, because of the fact that payments may extend over more than one accounting period; (2) the determination of the proper accounting period in which to take up profits; (3) the proper valuation of the installment sales receivables; (4) the proper valuation of inventories of repossessed merchandise; (5) the determination of the profit or loss on the sale of repossessed merchandise. 

Methods of Recording Profits.-The following methods are avail able for recording profits when installment sales are made: 

1. Record the entire profit as such in the period in which the installment sale is made, regardless of the length of the payment period. This method may lead to grossly overstated profits in those periods when sales are large, and grossly understated profits in later periods if defaults are large. In this method there is no correlation between collections and income. If this method is adopted, reserves for bad debts and reserves for collection expense should be large enough to take care of all possible contingencies. 

2. Record the profits on the basis of collections by considering the

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

first collections as gross profit and later collections as a return of the cost of the goods sold. If repossessed goods have depreciated in value, this method causes large losses in the periods of default. 

3. Record the profits on the basis of collections by considering the first collections as a return of the cost of the goods sold and later collections as gross profit. This method is probably too conservative. 

4. Record the profits on the basis of collections by considering each collection to be in part a return of cost and in part a realization of profit. The return of cost and the gross profit earned are recorded in the proportion of each in the sales price. For example: 

Sales price 

Cost price 

Gross profit

A collection of $20.00 is made on the installment account: 

Gross profit realized. 

Cost recovered 

Total accounted for 

40% of $20.00. 

60% of $20.00. 100%. $100.00 60.00 100.00% 60.00% $ 40.00 40.00% .$ 8.00 12.00 $20.00

This method is by far the most popular. It is approved by the internal revenue code. It is the method followed in the illustrative problems in the remainder of this chapter. This method is commonly known as the "installment basis."

Operations by Departments and by Products.-Modern business must know its profits by departments and, in many cases, by products within a department. The question then arises: Shall installment accounts be maintained to show realized gross profits by departments and by products in those cases where sales are made on the installment plan? On the basis that the sales divisions should not be responsible for the granting of credit and subsequent collection, but that the credit department should be responsible for these functions, it is not necessary to maintain installment accounts to show realized gross profits by products and by departments. After the sale is made the sales division ceases to function. The foregoing statements must not be interpreted to mean that profits should not be computed by departments and by products; it refers only to the maintenance of realized profits arising through collections.

If departmental or product gross profits rates are used, rather than the rate applicable to total sales (see page 295), it will be necessary to analyze collections per department and per product; the department or product gross profit rate will then be applied to the departmental or product collections in order to arrive at the realized profit for department or product.

Defaults without Repossession.-When a customer defaults in his payments, and when the items sold cannot be recovered or have no value, the customer's account balance and the unrealized gross profit applicable to the unrecovered installments should be written off the books. The unrecovered cost portion of the customer's account is a loss.

Defaults with Repossessions.-When a customer defaults in payments, usually the dealer repossesses the merchandise. The repossession of the merchandise thus reduces the loss caused by the default, and if the value of the repossessed merchandise exceeds the unrecovered cost, a profit may result.

Two problems arise through the repossession of merchandise sold on the installment plan: (1) the proper valuation of the repossessed goods, (2) the correct accounting entries. Repossessed merchandise should be valued conservatively, at its depreciated value; this may be difficult of accomplishment, but an experienced dealer normally can arrive at a fairly accurate appraisal. The correct accounting entries depend, to some extent, upon the laws of the state in which the sale was made; certain states require that the dealer remit to the defaulting purchaser the excess of the amount received upon resale over the amount of the unpaid balance. Other states require no refund to the defaulting customer.

Installment Expenses.-Because the profit element in uncollected installment balances is deferred until the period of collection, at first glance it might appear that the expenses of the period in which an installment sale is negotiated likewise should be deferred until the period of collection so that periodic income and expense could be correlated. Examination proves that the expenses should be recognized as such as they are incurred; the income has not been earned, but is contingent upon future collections, not upon future sales; the expenses have been incurred. Furthermore, substantial additional expense may be incurred in the process of collection. Although perfect correlation cannot be attained, practice follows the custom of recognizing expenses and deferring profits. 

Bad Debts on Installment Sales.—Although incurred expenses are not deferred, estimates of future bad debt losses are set up in the period of sale by reductions of the unrealized gross profit figure appearing in the balance sheet. This is logical on the basis that if the uncollected income is deferred, losses in collecting it should appear as a charge against that income. Assume that at December 31, 1941, the 

1941 Unrealized Gross Profits account contains a balance of $75,000.00. 

If, on the basis of past experience, an estimate can be made of the bad debts (future loss on defaults) involved in the $75,000.00 balance, the estimated bad debts should be set up by subtracting the desired

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

amount from the unrealized gross profits figure and by showing that amount as a deduction from the 1941 installment accounts receivable figure in the balance sheet. No journal entry is made for the creation of the reserve; the unrealized profit is merely apportioned for balance sheet purposes.

Likewise, if reserves for the expense of collecting the installment receivables are set up, they are reductions of the unrealized gross profit and are set up for balance sheet purposes only. The reserve for collections should be shown in the balance sheet as a subtraction from the installment accounts receivable, in the same manner as the reserve for bad debts is shown.

The reduction of the unrealized gross profit by the creation of reserves for bad debts and reserves for future collection expense has the effect of splitting the unrealized gross profits into three sections, as follows: 

Unrealized gross profits.
