The method of showing the unrealized gross profits on the balance sheet usually depends upon the preference of the accountant. Four opinions exist with respect to the method of displaying this item; these opinions suggest that the item may be shown (1) as a subtraction from receivables, (2) as a part of net worth, (3) as a deferred credit to income, (4) as a distinct item in the liabilities section. 

If the unrealized gross profit is treated as a valuation account, subtracted from the receivables, the value of the receivables is reduced to the unrecovered cost of the goods sold. The objection to the method is that unless the reader of the balance sheet is thoroughly familiar with installment contracts, he is likely to undervalue gross receivables and possible future income.

If unrealized gross profit is treated as a net worth item, it is viewed as earned and merely awaiting collection. In installment selling, collection is the important phase, and income is dependent upon collection. 

This method is not recommended, and if it is used, balance sheet footnotes should be fully explanatory. 

If unrealized gross profit is shown among the liabilities as a deferred credit to income, the situation is clarified because credit for the income actually is deferred. Some object to this method on the basis that a deferred credit is income received and not earned, and the amount of the deferred gross profit has not been received. However, if a deferred credit is viewed as a deferral of the collections, and the contract as the receipt, then the deferred credit classification appears logical. 

If the accountant disapproves of the three foregoing methods, the only alternative is to set the unrealized gross profit forth as a special credit in the balance sheet, separate from all ordinary classifications. 

The author favors displaying the item as a deferred credit to income, as this treatment most nearly fits the situation.

LONG-TERM CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS 

Frequently profits on short-term contracts are not taken into the financial records until the contracts are completed. If a construction period extends over more than one full fiscal period, and if costs and profits can be estimated with a reasonable degree of accuracy, profits on partially completed work should be recognized in the accounts. If profits were not accrued on partially completed work, and if, for example, two full fiscal periods are required to complete a contract and payment is made upon completion early in the third fiscal period, the first two periods would show expense only, while the third period would show income. Obviously, this would not truly represent the situation, as income has been earned as construction progressed. The profits of the owners of the construction company would be understated during construction periods, and would be greatly overstated in the third period.

To illustrate the computation of the profits to be taken up by the construction company at the close of the fiscal period, assume that a construction company contracts to build a bridge for $2,000,000.00. 

At the close of the first year, actual accumulated costs amount to $1,200,000.00; it is estimated that an additional $600,000.00 will complete the bridge. The estimated profit for the first year is computed

Chapter XV INVESTMENTS 

Classification of Investments.-Investments are securities of other companies, or assets not used directly in productive operations, and are classified as (1) temporary, or current, investments; (2) permanent, or long-time, investments. 

Temporary Investments.-Temporary investments represent the investment of an excess of cash over and above the current needs of the business. When the cash is needed for normal operating purposes, the investments are sold. A company may be engaged in a seasonal business, and if money is not extensively borrowed during the busy season, excess cash is on hand during the season of inactivity; this money may be temporarily invested until again needed in the active season.

The purposes of a temporary investment are to obtain a greater income than could be realized by permitting the surplus cash to remain in a bank account, or to build up a fund for emergency purposes in the near future.

The temporary investment may take the form of stocks, bonds, mortgages, or notes, but in all instances the nature of the temporary investment must be such as to make it liquid, readily marketable, and safe of principal. Speculative securities should be avoided and, if held, should not be classed as temporary investments as the requisites of safety of principal and liquidity are missing.

Thus we ascertain that there are two fundamental tests of a temporary investment: (1) it must represent the temporary investment of surplus cash, with the intention of reconversion when the cash is needed, (2) it must be liquid, readily marketable, and offer safety of principal.

Temporary investments are classed as current assets on a balance sheet, because they represent temporary conversions of cash. When buying, the intention is to sell them later, if necessary. 

Permanent Investments.-Permanent investments are investments in 314

INVESTMENTS 

315 other companies. The purposes of permanent investments are: (1) to exercise control of a subsidiary company (partially or fully owned), (2) to yield a permanent income, (3) to create specific funds, (4) to establish friendly business relationships. 

The permanent investments may take the form of: 

1. Stock of other companies. The stocks may be preferred or common. 

2. Bonds of other companies. The bonds may be first or subsequent mortgage bonds; collateral bonds; equipment trust bonds; debenture bonds; income bonds, or any other type of bond. 

3. Mortgages, either chattel or real estate mortgages. 

4. Notes. 

5. Funds. The funds may be sinking, stock redemption, endowment, pension, building, insurance, or other funds. 

6. Fixed tangible or intangible assets not connected with the usual operation of the business. 

7. Life insurance on officers with the company as the beneficiary. 

8. Loans to subsidiary or other companies. 

9. Investments in partnerships. 

10. Investments in treasury stock.

The permanent investment may or may not be readily marketable, but marketability is not a prerequisite for a permanent investment. 

Merely because an investment is marketable does not mean that the investment should be placed in the current asset section of a balance sheet. For example, a permanent stock investment might be made in a company whose stock has a ready market, but the intention of the investment might be to augment or stabilize the income of the company buying the securities; if this permanent investment were shifted to the current assets, both the working capital ratio and the amount of the working capital would be exaggerated. 

The purpose for which the investment originally is made must be considered in determining whether it is temporary or permanent. Of course, what is originally a temporary investment may become permanent if the cash is not needed when normally expected and the investment is retained; in this case the intention and purpose have changed. 

While temporary investments are classed as current assets, permanent investments are classed separately as "Investments"; because the permanent investments are fixed in nature, some accountants classify them with the "Fixed Assets."

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Valuation of Temporary Investments. As stated above, temporary investments are shown among the current assets in the balance sheet. Because temporary investments in stocks and bonds are current assets, they should be valued in accordance with the principles of valuation followed by the accountant for valuing current assets. This means, then, that temporary investments normally are valued at the lower of cost or market.

There are some advocates of valuation at market at all times for temporary investments; those who adhere to the theory of valuing temporary investments in stocks and bonds at market do so on the basis that the story told by the balance sheet is more accurate if current market prices are used. The Securities and Exchange Commission apparently approves valuation of temporary investments at market. 

If the accountant follows valuation at market, he should show the investments in the balance sheet thus: 

Marketable Securities, at Market (Cost $100.000)... .$104,000.00

The use of the market theory does not follow conservative principles for balance sheet valuation and income determination if market at the balance sheet date is in excess of cost; unearned profits are brought into the statement of profit and loss. For income tax purposes, securities must be valued at cost; no profit or loss is recognized prior to sale.

When temporary securities are purchased, they should be entered in the records at cost plus brokers' commission and taxes. Thus: 

Marketable Securities 

Cash 3,428.21

To record the purchase of 200 shares of the common stock of the Ocean Company, at $17; tax $2.00; brokerage $26.00. 3,428.21

Profit or Loss from Sale of Temporary Investments.-When temporary securities are sold, any profit or loss should be credited or charged to a Profit-and-Loss on the Disposition of Marketable Securities account. This is a non-operating profit-and-loss account. Profits and losses on sales are based upon cost. Purchases of temporary investments should be segregated in the event of more than one purchase of the same stock at different prices, so that a profit or loss upon disposition may be properly determined. Average costs should not be used as a matter of good accounting practice, and average costs are not permitted for the determination of profit or loss under the federal

INVESTMENTS 

317 income tax laws. Each block of stock must be identified. To illustrate, 100 shares of the stock of the Garm Company are purchased at $50.00 per share; later an additional 100 shares are purchased at $60.00 per share; later 50 shares are sold at $55.00 per share. What is the profit or loss? If the shares sold were from the first purchase, a profit of $5.00 per share resulted. If the shares sold were from the second purchase, a loss of $5.00 per share was incurred. If the seller cannot distinguish between his purchases, the Treasury Department invokes the first-in, first-out rule, based upon purchase price. 

Reserve for Fluctuation in Temporary Investments.-As pointed out in the opening paragraph of this section, the commonly accepted rule for the valuation of temporary investments is at cost or market, whichever is the lower. When market price has fallen below cost at the balance sheet date, a Reserve for Decline in Temporary Investments account should be created. For example: temporary securities costing $178,000.00, March 1, 1942, have a value of $170,000.00 on

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING Valuation of Securities for Security Dealers.-Dealers in securities may value their securities owned at (1) the lower of cost or market, (2) cost, or (3) market. Dealers are permitted, by the Federal Revenue Act, to value their inventories of securities at market for purposes of income taxation. Their method of valuation must be consistent from one year to the next. Security dealers keep a record of each stock or bond purchased and compute their profits or losses upon disposition on the basis of original cost, or upon an adjusted basis if at a prior period the securities have been written up or down to market. When a security dealer purchases bonds, he must also maintain an Interest account to which he will debit accrued bond interest at the time of purchase, and to which he will credit bond interest received at interest dates and bond interest accrued at the time the bonds are sold to a customer. Other investors in bonds should maintain a similar account with accrued interest.

Valuation of Permanent Investments.-The underlying basis for the valuation of permanent investments is cost. This underlying basis may of necessity be adjusted from time to time particularly if price declines are large and apparently permanent. In such a case an adjusted cost figure represents the valuation. Accounting problems which arise because of the necessity of adjustments to the original cost of the permanent investment are considered in the following sections of this chapter.

Valuation of Permanent Investments in Stocks.-Permanent in vestments in corporate capital stock should be recorded at cost upon acquisition. The permanent investment in corporate capital may represent (1) a non-controlling or minority interest in the stock, or (2) a controlling or majority interest.

If the block of stock is not sufficiently large to enable the owner to exercise control over the company whose stock is purchased, the entries for the purchase of the stock and for dividends are as follows: 

Investment in Stock of X Company. Cash 

To record the purchase of 1,000 shares of the stock of the X Company, par $100; total shares issued 10,000. Cash

Dividend Income 

To record the receipt of a dividend of $3.00 per share, paid by the X Company. .240,000.00 240,000.00 3,000.00 3,000.00

INVESTMENTS 

319 The Dividend Income account is closed to Profit-and-Loss, and is shown as a non-operating income on the profit-and-loss statement. 

If severe declines take place in the market value of the investment stock owned and the loss is not recognized by a charge to a loss account, a reserve for the decline may be created out of surplus. If a surplus reserve is not created to take care of such major declines, the balance sheet should set forth, as a notation, the current market prices of the non-controlling stocks which are carried at cost as permanent investments.

If the stock owned represents a controlling or majority interest, a parent-subsidiary relationship exists. The ramifications and differences of opinion concerning the valuation of stocks in controlled companies are treated in volume II. One method of accounting for controlling stocks is shown in the following illustration. 

Assume that the X Company purchases a controlling interest in the stock of the Y Company; the X Company pays $95,000.00 for 900 shares of a total of 1,000 shares. 

Investment in Stock of Y Company.. Cash.... .95,000.00 95,000.00

The investment is recorded at cost. The Y Company is now a subsidiary of the X Company, it is 90 per cent owned by Company X. 

At the end of the next period of its operations, the Y Company reports a profit of $20,000.00. Company X is entitled to $18,000.00 or 90 per cent of the profit. The book value of the investment has been increased because the subsidiary, Y, earned a profit. As a result of the increased book value of the controlling investment, Company X may adjust its books as follows: 

Investment in Stock of Y Company. 

Income from Subsidiary Y. 18,000.00 18,000.00

Thus, Company X takes up its share of Company Y's profits. This proportionate part of the profits of Company Y belongs to Company X. 

When the subsidiary pays a dividend, the value of the investment in the subsidiary is reduced because of the reduction of the net worth of the subsidiary. Assume that the Y Company pays a $10,000.00 dividend; the entry on the books of the X Company, for the receipt of 

90 per cent of the dividend is:

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Cash 

Investment in Stock of Y Company.. 9,000.00 9,000.00

Thus the value of the investment is reduced. 

When the subsidiary reports a loss, the book value of the investment is also reduced. Assume that in the second year, the Y Company suffers a loss of $5,000.00. The X Company takes up its proportionate share (90 per cent in this case) of the loss, as follows: 

Loss from Subsidiary Y.... 

Investment in Stock of Y Company. 4,500.00 4,500.00

To summarize the accounting treatment for controlling stocks: (1) Charge the Investment account for the parent company's proportion of the profit of the subsidiary company. (2) Credit the Investment account for the parent company's proportion of the loss of the subsidiary company. (3) Credit the Investment account for the parent company's proportion of dividends paid by the subsidiary company. 

Many accountants do not agree with the foregoing treatment for investments in controlled companies, believing that the accounting treatment should be such that the investment is constantly carried at cost, less reserves for severe declines. Opinion is about equally divided on the subject. If the cost theory is followed, the accounting is the same as for non-controlled stocks. 

Stock Dividends.-Stock dividends may be issued in the same class of stock owned or in a class of stock differing from the shares owned. 

A stock dividend in the same class of stock results in no additional wealth to the stockholder, because the company paying the stock dividend merely decreases one capital account, Surplus, and increases another capital account, Capital Stock, for the amount of stock issued; the issuing corporation does not distribute its assets, as it does in the case of a cash dividend. Consequently the recipient of such a dividend has his former proportionate ownership represented by a larger number of shares, with a consequent smaller value per share, and the same total value as before.

When a stock dividend is received in the same class of shares as those originally held, no value entries are involved; only the number of shares is changed. The unit cost per share is averaged downward to an amount determined by dividing the original number of shares plus the number received as a stock dividend into the total original cost. 

When a stock dividend is received in a class of shares different

INVESTMENTS 

321 from those originally held, alternative methods of handling the situation are possible, as shown by the following illustration. Assume that the Derringer Company owns 100 shares, par $100.00, of the common stock of the Pauly Company; the stock has a market value of $120.00 per share. The Derringer Company paid par at the time of purchase. 

The Pauly Company declares and pays a stock dividend, payable at the rate of one share of preferred stock, par $50.00 for each 10 shares of common stock owned; the preferred stock has a market value of $55.00 per share immediately upon its issuance. 

The first method is to treat the preferred stock dividend as an income at its market value at the time of receipt:

Dividend Income 

550.00 550.00 

This method is based upon the theory that, if the stock received is of a class differing from that originally held, it is equivalent to receiving any asset. This method apparently conforms to Treasury Department regulations for income tax purposes. 

The second method is to apportion the cost of the original shares over the original shares and the dividend shares on the basis of the market value of the shares after the dividend is paid. Thus for the

The Investment in Stock of Pauly Company, Common Stock account is credited for $314.20 ($31.42 × 10), and a new account, Investment in Stock of Pauly Company, Preferred Stock, is charged for $314.20.

Stock Rights. A stock right is a privilege accorded stockholders to purchase additional unsubscribed shares or new shares of stock in proportion to their present holdings, at prices below the market price.

This privilege to purchase additional shares has a value which may be realized by buying the additional shares at the advantageous price, or by selling the rights to some other party. When the rights are an-

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

nounced, the corporation states the date upon which the stockholders' ledger will be closed, and to the stockholders of record as of that date the corporation will send the rights, known as certificates or warrants. 

After the announcement of the rights and before the closing of the stockholders' ledger, the stock is dealt in "rights-on"; that is, the price of the share includes the value of the warrants to be received later; this necessary because the warrant has not been issued and consequently is still a part of the share. After the date of closing the stock ledger, the warrants are sent to the stockholders. From that date on, the stock and the rights are separately purchased and sold, and the stock is dealt in "ex-rights"; that is, the warrant is no longer a part of the share, but is a separate unit of value. is The investor does not receive a benefit from a stock right, any more than he receives a benefit from a stock dividend. On the date at which the stock begins to sell ex-rights, the stock declines in price by an amount equal to the value of the right. Upon the completion of the process, the market value of the investor's securities is the same as the value before the process began, plus the amount of cash paid for the new stock or less the amount of cash received if he sold his rights. 

Stock rights may (1) be sold, or (2) be used toward the purchase of additional shares. While the stock is dealt in "rights-on" no accounting problems arise, because the rights have not actually made their appearance. After the warrants are issued (1) profits or losses must be computed if the rights are sold, and (2) proper values must be assigned to all shares if the rights are exercised and additional shares purchased.

Rights may be issued in any proportion to the outstanding issue. As examples, a corporation may issue one right for each share held, stipulating that one new share, par $100.00, may be purchased at par, for each 10 shares held; thus 10 rights are necessary to obtain one new share at $100.00. If desired, a corporation might issue one right for each 10 shares held, and stipulate that one right plus the necessary cash would purchase one new share.

The following illustration demonstrates the computation of the profit or loss on the sale of stock rights and the revised values of the shares held. Assume that in 1939 an investor purchased 500 shares of stock at $125.00 per share. In 1942, the investor receives 500 warrants entitling him to purchase 100 additional shares at $100.00 per share. 

The stock, ex-rights, has a market value of $120.00 per share and the

INVESTMENTS 

323 rights have a market value of $4.00 each. Instead of subscribing to the additional shares, the investor sold the rights at $5.00 each. What is the profit on the sale of the rights? What is the revised cost of each share of stock? The original cost must be apportioned on the basis of the market value of the stock ex-rights and the market value of the warrants at the date of issuing the warrants. Thus: 

500 shares @ $125.00 

500 shares @ $120.00 $62,500.00, cost of the old stock $60,000.00, market value of the old stock 

500 rights @ $ 4.00 $2,000.00, market value of the rights 60,000 62,000 2,000 62,000 of $62,500.00 = $60,483.87, cost of old stock apportioned to such stock of $62,500.00 $ 2,016.13, cost of old stock apportioned to the rights 

If the 500 rights are sold at $5.00 each, the profit is: $2,500.00 - $2,016.13 = $483.87.

The journal entry to record the sale of the rights is as follows: Cash Investments

If additional shares of the old stock are subsequently sold, the basis for computing gain or loss is the adjusted cost of the shares, that is $60,483.87500, or $120.97 per share.

If the 500 rights are exercised and 100 shares are purchased at $100.00 per share, the entry is: Investments Cash. 10,000.00 10,000.00

The total investment is now made up of two parts, the 500 shares originally purchased and the 100 shares acquired through exercise of the rights, thus:

New, 100 shares ($10,000 + $2,016.13), $12,016.13; per share, $120.16 

The basis for the determination of gain or loss on the disposition of the old shares is $120.97 per share; the basis for the determination of gain or loss on the disposition of the new shares is $120.16 per share. 

Treasury Stock.—Some accountants are of the opinion that treasury stock, either donated or purchased, may be shown as an asset if the stock is to be held for a short time for some specific purpose, such as

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

the sale of it to an officer or an employee. If the treasury stock is shown as an asset, it should be shown in a category separate from either temporary investments or permanent investments. The best manner of handling treasury stock is to show it as (1) a deduction at cost from the total net worth or (2) as a deduction at par from the proper capital stock account. Showing treasury stock as an asset merely inflates the assets and inflates the capital stock; the treasury stock must be deducted from a capital stock account to arrive at the net capital value. All of the phases of accounting for treasury stock are treated in chapter VII. 

Unissued Stock.-Unissued capital stock should never be shown as an investment, temporary or permanent; neither should it ever be shown as an asset of any classification. Unissued stock merely represents an amount of potential capitalization, the conversion into an asset resting with the decision of the management. If unissued stock is shown as an asset, total asset values are overstated, and capital also is overstated.

Valuation of Permanent Investments in Bonds.-Temporary in vestments in bonds usually are valued at the lower of cost or market; the amortization of premiums and discounts is ignored. Permanent investments in bonds are valued at cost adjusted for the periodic amortization of premiums and discounts. If a permanent bond investment is purchased at the par of the bond, adjustments are eliminated, and the bonds are valued at par, which is cost. 

When a bond is purchased, (1) it is recorded in the Bond Investment account at its cost price, regardless of premium or discount, or (2) it is recorded at the par of the bond and separate accounts are used for premiums or discounts. The majority of accountants prefer the first method for entering bond investments. Bonds payable usually are recorded in the liability accounts at par, with separate accounts for premiums and discounts. We are here concerned with investments only, and not with bonds as liabilities. If a bond is bought at a premium, the premium is written off, that is, amortized over the life of the bond, by periodic credits to the Bond Investment account which reduce that account to par at the maturity date of the bond; the corresponding debit is to Bond Interest Income. If a bond is bought at a discount, the discount is amortized by periodic charges to the Bond Investment account, which increases that account to par at maturity; the corresponding credit is to Bond Interest Income. Thus we see that if a bond

INVESTMENTS 

325 is purchased at a premium, its value decreases to par at maturity, and if a bond is purchased at a discount, its value increases to par at maturity. These increases and decreases in value must be reflected in the balance sheet, and in the corresponding adjustments made to bond interest income.

In explanation of the foregoing procedure it must be understood that the price of a bond is closely allied to its interest rate and to the rate of interest prevailing in the market. If a bond bearing 4 per cent interest is offered for sale when the market rate of interest is 3 per cent, the bond will sell at a price at which the rate of return earned on the investment approximates 3 per cent. Therefore, it will sell above par, or at a premium. If a 3 per cent bond is offered for sale in a 4 per cent market, the bond will sell at a discount, so that the rate of return approximates the market rate of 4 per cent. If a 4 per cent bond is offered in a 4 per cent market, it sells for par. Entering into the price of a bond, in addition to the current market rate of interest, is the credit rating of the issuing company. Corporations with high credit ratings are able to sell their bonds at a more advantageous figure than are corporations with low credit ratings. 

Nominal and Effective Rates.-The nominal rate of interest is the rate stated in the bond itself. The effective rate is the compound interest rate earned on the principal sum of money invested, which may be the par of the bond, a price above par, or a price below par. 

If a bond sells at a discount, a rate of return greater than the nominal rate is earned; that is, the effective rate is greater than the nominal rate. If a bond sells at a premium, a rate of return smaller than the nominal rate is earned, that is, the effective rate is less than the nominal rate. If a bond sells at par, the nominal and the effective rates coincide. 

The Amortization of Premiums and Discounts.-When a bond is bought at a discount, the discount must be equitably distributed, that is, amortized, or written off, over the life of the bond so that the Bond Investment account stands at par at maturity. There are two methods of amortizing bond premiums and discounts, the straight-line method and the exact (or compound interest) method. 

The Straight-Line Method of Amortization.-The straight-line method of amortization prorates the premium or discount over the life of the bond in equal periodic amounts. To find the amount of the periodic amortization, the total premium or discount is divided by the number of bond interest periods from the date of purchase of the.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

bond to the maturity date of the bond. To illustrate: Assume that a $1,000.00 par value bond, due in three years, dated January 1, 1941, bearing interest at the rate of 4 per cent per year (or 2 per cent each six months), payable July 1 and January 1, is purchased at a cost of $972.46. The journal entry to record the purchase is: 

Bond Investments Cash. .972.46 972.46 

The discount of $27.54 must be amortized over the six interest periods: $27.546 $4.59 discount to be amortized each period. Bond interest of $20.00 is received in cash each six months (4 per cent on par for six months), but more than 4 per cent is earned because less than par is invested. The difference between the amount of interest received periodically at the effective rate (5 per cent in this case) and the amount at the nominal rate (4 per cent) is the amount of discount to be amortized. At each interest date the investor makes the following journal entry: Cash 

Bond Investment 

Bond Interest Income. .20.00 4.59 24.59

This entry is repeated at each successive interest date, and the discount is completely amortized by the maturity date of the bond, January 1, 1944. The following schedule shows the entries and the carrying value of the bond.

From the illustrations, this method prorates an equal amount of premium or discount to each interest period. It results in an equal amount of income on the investment each interest period. These are important points to remember at this point. 

The reader must also remember that when a bond is purchased at a discount, the discount is income in addition to the stated amount of interest. The rate of return is greater than the cash received each interest period because less than par is invested. When a bond is purchased at a premium, the premium is a deduction from the income, for the premium will not be recovered when the bond is redeemed at maturity. The rate of return is less than the cash received each interest period because more than par is invested. 

The Exact Method of Amortization.-As pointed out under the straight-line method of amortization, the amount of income is the same each interest period. Because the carrying value of the bond changes each interest period (the carrying value increases each period, if the bond is purchased at a discount, and decreases each period if the bond is purchased at a premium) the rate of return earned on the carrying value of the bond changes each interest period. For example, in the schedule of amortization presented on page 326 for a 4 per cent bond bought to yield 5 per cent, $24.59 is earned the first six months on an investment account balance of $972.46, whereas $24.59 is earned the last six months on an investment account balance of $995.41; thus, though the amounts are the same, the rate of return in the final period is less than the rate of return in the first period, because the carrying value is smaller in the first period. 

The purpose in buying a bond is to realize a uniform rate of return on an invested sum of money. For example, if an investor desires 3 per cent on the money he intends investing, he wants 3 per cent uniformly, and not less than 3 per cent for certain periods and more

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

or less than 3 per cent for other periods. The straight-line method does not produce a uniform rate; it produces a uniform amount at varying rates. 

The exact method of amortization maintains à constant periodic rate of return on the varying sum invested. The amount of the return. will vary periodically. To illustrate the operation of the exact method of amortization study the following application of this method to the same illustration used above: A three-year, 4 per cent, $1,000.00 par bond, interest payable semi-annually, bought for $972.46, the discount being $27.54.

329 In this illustration the constant rate of return is 11/2 per cent of the carrying value of the bond; that is, the amount of the interest income is 11/2 per cent of the periodic carrying value.

Of the two methods, the straight-line method is used almost exclusively, although the exact method produced the more scientifically accurate results.

For federal income tax purposes, the amortization of premiums and discounts must be ignored; the taxable gain or loss on the sale of a bond investment is the difference between the cost price and the sales price, and not the difference between cost, plus amortized discounts or minus amortized premiums, and the sales price. Debtor companies issuing bonds may, for income tax purposes, bring amortized premiums and discounts into the tax return.

If a trustee or other fiduciary fails to amortize bond premiums, the estate may be injured; if the trustee pays the full amount of interest to a beneficiary entitled only to the income, he is reserving nothing to protect the premium paid for the bonds. For example, if a trustee paid $110,000.00 for $100,000.00 of bonds at par, the $10,000.00 will not be recovered at maturity, and the estate will shrink to $100,000.00 when the bonds are redeemed. Had the trustee paid the beneficiary as income interest at the effective rate instead of at the nominal rate, he would have reserved a sufficient sum over the life of the investment ($10,000.00 in this case) to maintain the estate at $110,000.00. Courts have held that it is the duty of a fiduciary to reserve and withhold periodically from a beneficiary entitled only to income, the amount necessary to amortize the total premiums paid. 

The Price of a Bond.-When a bond is purchased, the buyer obtains an investment entitling him to two privileges: (1) the right to receive a definite future sum, the principal, and (2) the right to receive an annuity, the periódic interest payments.

An annuity is a series of equal payments, due periodically. The period interval may be of any length, such as a month, semi-annually, or annually. The majority of bonds pay interest semi-annually. 

The present value of a given annuity is the amount of money which invested now at compound interest would provide the stipulated number of equal annuity payments. Bonds start paying interest at the end of the first interest period, and an annuity whose payments start at the end of the first period is known as an ordinary annuity. 

The amount of an annuity is the total of the invested annuities

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

together with the compound interest which will accumulate on all of them, up to the date of the last payment. 

The present value of $1.00 receivable at a future date is the value today of an investment necessary to produce $1.00 at the given future date, including interest compounded at a stated rate and at stated intervals. 

The compound discount of $1.00 is $1.00 less the present value of $1.00. It follows that the compound discount multiplied by the efective rate of interest equals the present value of an annuity of one. 

The foregoing concepts are of primary importance to an understanding of the pricing of a bond. 

In calculating the price of a bond, the present value of the principal amount (par) and the present value of the interest (annuity) payments must both be computed. If bond tables are used to ascertain the price of a bond, all calculations are predetermined, and the price to be paid appears in the tables. 

The Price by the Use of a Bond Table.-Bond tables, also known as rate books or basis books, are prepared for different denominations, such as for a $100.00 bond, a $1,000.00 bond, a $10,000.00 bond, a $100,000.00 bond, and a $1,000.000.00 bond. The only difference lies in the number of decimal places; obviously a $1,000,000.00 bond table could be used to determine accurately the price or yield of a $100.00 bond, but a $100.00 bond table would be almost useless to an investor whose investments are in the larger denominations. Regardless of denomination every set of bond tables must provide in its computations for (1) different interest rates for each bond value, for example, from 1/8 of 1 per cent up to 10 per cent, (2) for maturities ranging from one month to 50 years, (3) for bonds with interest payable quarterly, semi-annually, and annually. 

Bond tables are arranged by years (usually one-half years) because the price of a bond depends upon its interest rate and its life. The longer the life of a bond with a nominal rate in excess of the effective rate, the greater the premium at which it sells; the longer the life of a bond with a nominal rate lower than the effective rate the greater the discount at which it sells. The bond gradually approaches par as it nears maturity.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

The use of the bond table may be explained as follows: 

1. Given the nominal rate of interest, the price of the bond, and its unexpired life, to find the effective rate: find the price under the proper "years" column and read to the left to the "Net Income" column to determine the effective rate of interest. For example, the price of a $1,000.00, 4 per cent, three-year bond, interest payable semiannually is, assume, $972.46. What is the effective rate? On the 4 per cent page, find the price in the three-years column, read to the "Net Income" column and 5 per cent appears as the effective rate. 

2. Given the life of the bond, the nominal rate and the effective rate of interest, to determine the price: refer to the proper nominal rate percentage page, find the effective rate in the "Net Income" column, read to the right to the proper "years" column to determine the price. For example, a $1,000.00, 4 per cent, three-year bond is sold to yield 5 per cent. What is the price? On the 4 per cent page, find the effective rate in the "Net Income" column, read to the threeyears column, and the price is shown as $972.46. 

When bonds are offered for sale as "4 per cent bonds to yield 5 per cent," they are priced "on a basis" of 5 per cent, the effective rate. 

The Price by Computation.-Under certain circumstances bond tables may not be available or the bond table may be one of too small denomination, or it may not include the proper number of years, or it may not carry its nominal and effective rates to the desired low or high range of rates. In such cases, the price is computed by using annuity tables and interest tables. It must be remembered that bond tables are the result of such price computations. The entire bond problem cannot be fully understood without a knowledge of the computations necessary to determine the price of a bond. 

There are two available methods of computing the price of a bond: 

Method 1. The Present Value of Par Method.-This method is based upon computing the present value of the par of the bond and the present values of the interest payments (annuity) and adding together the two present values. 

Method 2. Addition of Premium and Subtraction of Discount 

Method. In this method to the par of the bond there is added the present value of the additional annuities (interest payments if the bonds sell at a premium), or from the par of the bond there is subtracted the lost annuities (interest payments if the bonds sell at a discount).

The Purchase of Bonds between Interest Dates.-When a bond is bought "flat," either the accrued interest is included in the price, or the bond is purchased exactly on an interest date when there is no accrued interest. When a bond is purchased "plus interest," the price paid is exclusive of the accrued interest which is added to the purchase

INVESTMENTS 

337 price. When bonds are purchased between interest dates, as most bonds are purchased, the purchaser buys the accrued interest from the last interest date up to the time of his purchase. The purchase of the accrued interest is not a part of the cost of the investment, and the accrued interest purchased should not be charged to the Bond Investment account, but to an interest account. At the next succeeding interest date, the purchaser is reimbursed for his purchase of the accrued interest, for when he collects the interest for a full interest period, the interest accrued at the purchase date is included. In all preceding illustrations in this chapter, the assumption was made that the bond was purchased on an interest date. Optional Redemption of Bonds.-Many bond issues grant the issuing company the privilege of redeeming the bonds at a date preceding maturity. If a bond purchaser buys a bond with an optional redemption clause, and if he is buying it on a definite yield basis, the bond, in effect, has one of two maturity dates: (1) the optional redemption date, or (2) the maturity date. Consequently, the price must be computed on two bases: (a) on the assumption that the bond will be redeemed at the optional redemption date, and (b) on the assumption that the bond will remain outstanding until maturity. The purchaser pays the lower of the two prices; in effect, he is comparing two separate bonds, and the life of a bond affects its price. If a bond has a nominal rate in excess of the effective rate and therefore sells at a discount the longer the time to maturity the greater will be the discount, because the present value of a certain future sum is smaller far from maturity than it is closer to maturity. If a bond has a nominal rate lower than the effective rate and therefore sells at a premium, the longer the life of the bond the greater is the premium.

341 Funds. The subject of funds is treated in chapter XXII, Funds and 

Reserves. It might be well to point out at this time that in a balance sheet funds for mercantile and manufacturing concerns should be limited to money allocated to specific purposes. The fund money normally is invested in income-producing securities. The purpose of creating a fund may be to pay off a bond issue at maturity, to establish a stock redemption fund, to establish an endowment fund, or a building fund, a pension fund, an insurance fund. If funds are created for such purposes as working capital funds, petty cash funds, payroll funds, dividend funds, they are current, and not permanent, investments. 

The valuation of permanent investment funds must be considered from different angles: (1) if the funds are invested in the securities of other companies, (2) if the funds are invested in the securities of the company establishing the fund.

When funds are represented by the securities of other companies, the securities should be valued at cost, or at cost plus the amortization of the discount or minus the amortization of the premium, if the securities are bonds or mortgages. Reserves may be established for drastic declines in market values and the resulting loss shown as a non-operating loss. Thus, the valuation of long-term or permanent funds follows the same procedure as that used for any other permanent investment.

Sinking funds and stock redemption funds are normally invested in the corporation's own securities. In the case of a sinking fund, the bond indenture may state that the sinking fund trustee may, at his discretion, buy the bonds of the issuing company. The bonds purchased by the sinking fund trustee may be held for income (the interest paid to the trustee by the issuing company) or the bonds purchased may be cancelled. If the bonds are held for income, they should be valued at cost and the premium or discount amortized, just as though the bonds of another company were purchased as an investment. In the balance sheet, a notation should appear pointing out the fact that the bonds are those of the issuing company. If the bonds are cancelled, they should be retired at par, and the balance sheet should show the bond issue liability gross, with the par value of the retired bonds subtracted therefrom, showing the net amount of the remaining liability as an extension. Chapter XVI  The Nature and Classification of Fixed Assets. For accounting purposes, fixed assets are classified as (1) fixed tangible assets and (2) fixed intangible assets. Both fixed tangible and fixed intangible assets are relatively permanent and are acquired with the intention of immediately using them in business operations and of retaining them for their useful economic life; the normal intention is not to offer them for sale.

Fixed tangible assets are possessed of physical properties and are clearly perceptible; however, all assets possessing physical properties are not fixed tangible assets. For example, inventories possess physical properties, but are classed as current assets because of the intention of selling them within a short period of time; factory supplies, while possessing physical properties, are not fixed assets, because they will be charged to operations within a short time. Factory buildings, owned and used, are classed as fixed tangible assets because they are relatively permanent, are acquired with the intention of using them in business operations, and are to be retained for their useful economic life. A factory building owned, but rented to another, would not rank as a fixed tangible asset, but as an investment because it is not used in the normal business operations. Equipment discarded because of inadequacy or obsolescence, but not disposed of, should be removed from the fixed tangible asset classification, because it is no longer used in operations. If expansion of plant facilities is contemplated, and land is purchased for that purpose, but not immediately used therefor, it should not be included in fixed tangible assets; the land is most permanent but it is not used in operations. In a mining company, the mine properties are fixed tangible assets; if the company owned housing facilities for the miners, the facilities would not be fixed tangible assets. 

Fixed intangible assets, while possessing no physical properties, confer certain business advantages, or certain monopolistic privileges or rights upon the owner. Examples of fixed intangible assets are good- 345

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

will, patents, copyrights, trade-marks, franchises, and leasehold improvements; they possess value because of their ability to earn profits for their owners. Fixed intangible assets are considered in detail in chapter XX. 

Before proceeding further with a discussion of fixed tangible assets, the reader should become familiar with certain concepts applicable to fixed assets.

Depreciation is a decline in economic value caused by wear and tear, inadequacy, obsolescence, the passage of time, and the action of the elements; the result of depreciation is the physical deterioration of the asset; consequently depreciation applies to tangible assets. 

Depletion is a decline in the value of natural resources caused by the physical diminution of the available quantity; depletion applies to assets such as mines, oil wells, and timber tracts. 

Amortization is a decline in value caused by the expiration of time and it applies to the fixed intangible assets. 

Additions to, betterments of, and improvements to fixed tangible assets result in asset values which are greater than the original value of the asset so improved, bettered, or added to, when it was acquired. 

Because greater asset values result, additions, betterments, and improvements to fixed tangible assets are capitalized in the asset account concerned, by charging the asset.

Major repairs and replacements have the effect of cancelling or eliminating accrued depreciation and therefore prolong the life of the fixed tangible asset beyond the life originally estimated, but the asset value is not enhanced above its value when originally acquired new. 

Major repairs and part replacements are therefore charged to the reserve for depreciation, thereby restoring to the book value of the asset the amount of depreciation eliminated by the replacement. 

Ordinary repairs and part replacements merely tend to maintain a fixed asset in useful and efficient condition; they do not add value to the asset over and above original values and they do not prolong the life of the asset beyond the originally estimated life. Consequently, ordinary repairs and part replacements are charged to operating expense, or to a reserve for repairs if one has been created by charges to expense.

These concepts will be fully developed and illustrated as the study of fixed assets progresses. 

The accounting for and the valuation of fixed tangible assets com-

prises one of the major activities of the accountant, and it also constitutes one of the most complicated phases of modern accounting. 

Because of the relatively costly nature of fixed assets and because they are acquired infrequently rather than regularly, such acquisition is given serious consideration before expenditures are made. Although scrupulous attention is devoted to the acquisition of a fixed asset, it may be grossly neglected from both a physical and an accounting angle once it is acquired. 

The accounting control of fixed tangible assets is concerned with the separation of fixed asset expenditures from other expenditures; the correct accounting for depreciation and obsolescence; the accounting for ordinary and major repairs and part replacements, and for additions and betterments; the comparison of original cost with reproduction costs and the subsequent decisions to be made with respect to future valuation. Federal income tax regulations are extremely strict with respect to the proper accounting for fixed assets. If fixed asset expenditures are erroneously charged to an expense, profits are understated; if expenditures on fixed assets are erroneously charged to an asset, profits are overstated. With the exception of land and good-will, all fixed tangible and intangible assets decline in value and eventually must be replaced. The capital invested in fixed assets must be recovered by the sale of the products which result from the use and consumption of the fixed assets subject to depreciation, depletion, and amortization. 

Because most fixed assets are used up in the productive process, and their expired values charged to expense, they are in effect longterm deferred charges to operations; consequently it is of vital importance that the accounting for fixed assets be so designed that proper charges are made to periodic expense for the expired values of the assets.

The Valuation of Fixed Assets. In earlier chapters, the theory was developed that current assets were valued at the lower of cost or market. The valuation of the fixed assets of a going concern is on an entirely different basis, because there is no intention of converting fixed assets to immediate cash; the original value of the asset must be spread over its entire life in the form of depreciation or amortization charges. 

In the majority of cases, the valuation of fixed assets at the lower of cost or market would result in a figure closely allied to a forced liquidation figure, which would be out of line with all reasonable longtime fixed asset values.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Fixed assets are valued at: a) Cost of acquisition (if the asset does not depreciate; for example, land). b) Cost of acquisition minus accumulated depreciation, depletion, or amortization. c) Appraisal values (treated in chapter XIX). 

The cost of acquisition may be easy or difficult of determination, depending upon the ease or difficulty of valuing the property given in exchange for the fixed asset. Our first step in the valuation of fixed assets will be to determine the cost of the assets under various methods of acquisition, such as the following: 

1. Assets purchased for cash 

2. Assets acquired by exchange 

3. Assets acquired by giving securities 

4. Assets acquired by giving capital stock or bonds 

5. Assets acquired by donation 

6. Assets constructed for own use 

7. Assets acquired by discovery 

8. Assets acquired under conditional sales contracts 

Assets Purchased for Cash.-When a fixed asset is purchased for cash, the cost includes the invoice price, or the contract price, plus insurance during transit, transportation costs, title examination fees, and installation costs. In general, it can be stated that the cost of a fixed asset includes its invoice price plus all costs necessary to place the asset in useable condition in the hands of the purchaser. The valuation of the cash given in exchange is definite; hence it is not difficult to determine the cost of fixed assets purchased for cash. 

Assets Acquired by Exchange.-Frequently, an old fixed asset is traded-in, that is, given in partial payment toward the purchase of a new asset.

Among accountants, there is difference of opinion concerning the proper treatment of such situations. Some favor the theory that the new asset be recorded in the accounts at its regular cash list price. Others are of the belief that the newly acquired asset be recorded in the accounts at the sum of the remaining book value of the asset given in exchange plus the cash "to boot." Today these problems arise particularly in connection with automobile and machinery purchases. The entire question of the exchange of fixed assets is complicated by federal

income tax regulations. Full illustrations of assets acquired by exchange are presented in chapter XIX. 

Assets Acquired by Giving Securities.—If stocks and bonds, held as investments, probably temporary in nature, are given in exchange for fixed assets, the assets acquired should be valued at the current market price of the securities given. Assume that a company held as a temporary investment, some stock which cost $10,000.00, at which figure the stock was carried on the books. A machine, list price $12,000.00, was acquired in exchange for the stock, at which time the stock had a market value of $11,000.00. The entry upon acquisition of the asset should be:

Machine 

Investments, Temporary. 

Profit on Disposition of Investments .11,000.00 10,000.00 1,000.00

In the foregoing case, the machine evidently has a value of only $11,000.00, or the seller would be unwilling to dispose of it for securities which had a market value of only that amount. 

Assets Acquired by the Issuance of Capital Stock or Bonds.- 

When corporate capital stock is issued in payment of fixed assets, several difficult problems of valuation are involved. The reasons for the difficulties may be summarized as follows: a) In many cases it is erroneously assumed that the par value of the stock issued establishes the value for the asset acquired, when it may be that the value of the asset should establish the value to be attributed to the stock. b) In many instances, it is impossible to value correctly the asset acquired, particularly if the asset has no market value; examples of such cases are the exchange of capital stock for untested patents, unexplored oil or mine deposits, uncruised timber tracts, and manufacturing privileges. c) The mere compliance with state legal requirements as set forth in acts of incorporation when assets are acquired by exchanges for capital stock at the time a corporation is organized does not necessarily impart to the assets acquired a value equal to some "nominal" value placed on the stock issued. This is particularly true when the entire issue of stock is exchanged for assets. 

If the market price of the stock given can be established, and it normally can be in the case of a going concern, the proper cost of the prop-

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

erty is the market price of the stock given in exchange. This basis of valuation has been approved by the Bureau of Internal Revenue. 

If a market price for the stock is not available, the value of the assets should first be established at their cash cost figure if one is available. This procedure assigns indirectly a value to the stock so issued. 

If the par value of the stock so given exceeds the cash cost basis, the difference between the par value of the stock and the cash value of the assets should be charged to discount on capital stock, because, in effect, the stock is being issued at a discount. 

If a cash cost figure is not available for the asset, an appraisal of the assets may result in a reasonable valuation figure. In the past, corporate directors, in the absence of fraud, have enjoyed almost unlimited freedom in establishing values for assets acquired in exchange for capital stock; as a result, assets so acquired have frequently been overvalued in order to prevent the showing of a discount on the capital stock. The use of no-par value stock has eliminated this excuse for asset overvaluation, but it has not eliminated the practice, because the no-par stock account likewise is often inflated. At the present time, twothirds of the states prohibit the issuance of par value stock at a discount, except under specific circumstances. The present tendency among regulatory bodies, state and federal, is in the direction of requiring proof of the asset values established. 

In all those cases where asset values and capital stock values cannot be reasonably established, good judgment and honesty must be exercised in order to arrive at fair valuations.

When assets are acquired in exchange for an entire issue of stock, the stock has never been accorded a cash value. In the absence of the rulings of regulatory bodies, the possibility exists for gross overvaluation of the assets. Subsequently, creditors who have extended credit on the basis of overvalued assets and have therefore suffered losses may attempt to hold the stockholders liable for a discount, if the stock is of par value, or they may attempt to prove fraud if the stock was of no-par value.

When bonds are issued in exchange for assets, the same procedure should be followed as in the case of the issuance of capital stock. The problem normally is not so complicated, because there is no objection to showing discount on bonds as a deferred charge to operations. Discount and interest on bonds during a construction period will be treated under "assets constructed for own use." 1

Assets Acquired by Donations.-Occasionally, assets are donated to corporations or other business entities, either by stockholders or by municipalities. Donations by municipalities usually take the form of land sites, or, rarely, buildings. If assets so acquired were valued at cost to the recipient, the values of the assets would be grossly understated, because the only costs involved are the minor ones incidental to acquisition, plus the costs of placing the assets in condition for use. In any case, asset values should be fairly expressed, neither overstated nor understated. Consequently, the principle of valuation at cost cannot be followed for donated assets.

Donations of assets may be conditional or unconditional; when stockholders donate assets, the gift usually is unconditional, that is, the transaction is complete upon acceptance by the corporation. When a municipality donates assets, the gift may be subject to certain conditions, such as some specific performance on the part of the recipient company; for example, City X may offer to donate a land site to Company Z if the latter erects a building on the site and employs five hundred men continuously for five years. Final free title to the land is contingent upon fulfillment of these conditions.

If the gift is unconditional, it should be charged to the proper asset account at its fairly appraised value; if the donor acquired the gift by purchase, close to the time of giving it to the beneficiary corporation, the price paid by the donor should serve as a fair valuation figure. 

Assume, for example, that the City of A paid $10,000.00 for some land and immediately and unconditionally donated it to Corporation M. 

The entry on the books of Corporation M would be: 

Land (or Donated Land).. 

Donated (or Capital) Surplus. 

. 10,000.00 10,000.00

The credit portion of the entry will depend, in great measure, upon individual preferences among accountants. To the author it seems that 

Donated Surplus is most accurate; if the corporation does not desire such an account, then Capital Surplus is the next choice; it is not desirable to credit Earned Surplus, as the amount was not earned in the usual sense of the word, and, generally, earned surplus is construed as being free and available for dividends; if cash dividends were declared from a donated surplus, capital would thereby be impaired. 

Let us now assume that the beneficiary corporation paid $1,000.00 for grading the land. Should the cost be charged to Land or to Donated

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Surplus? Since additional outlays would not be made unless they resulted in enhanced asset values, it is reasonable to charge the outlay to the donated asset account.

If the gift is conditional, that is, contingent upon the fulfillment of some obligation, both the asset and the increase in capital should be held in suspense pending the performance of the contract. Assume that 

City B offers a land site to Company P on the condition that the latter continuously employ five hundred men for five years. At the time the company takes possession, the entry should be:

Land, Contingent Asset.. 

. 10,000.00

Contingent Surplus, Land Donation.. 

10,000.00

All outlays made for the conditioning of the asset may be treated in the same manner as for unconditional donations, with full notes appended to the balance sheet in order to clarify the difference between the balances of the contingent land and the contingent surplus. 

If the P Company, above, failed to maintain a minimum of five hundred employees at any time, the City of B is free to reclaim the property on the basis of forfeiture. If the company fulfilled the contract, title would pass at the end of the fifth year, and the account Land, Contingent Asset, would be closed to Land or Donated Land, and the 

Contingent Surplus account closed to Donated Surplus or Capital Surplus. 

When assets which are subject to depreciation are conditionally donated, the question of depreciation on the books of the donee, during the contingent period, sometimes arises. If depreciation on contingent assets is ignored until the contingency is removed, operating costs during those periods are understated; during the periods following the removal of the contingency, operating costs would be overstated by the amount of the depreciation not absorbed during the period of contingency. The better procedure is to recognize depreciation during the contingency period by the following entries:

Depreciation Expense 

Reserve for Depreciation

Contingent Surplus 

Earned Surplus

XX XX XX XX The balance of the Contingent Surplus account is in accord with the balance of the asset account less the reserve for depreciation at the time

title passes. This topic is discussed fully in chapter XIX, in connection with appraisals.

Assets Constructed for Own Use.-When a company constructs fixed assets for its own use, there arises the question of the costs to be included in the total cost of the asset constructed. 

The cost of all materials used, including such incidental costs as transportation, storage, and inspection of the materials, should be included; likewise wages paid to regular employees engaged on the construction and to workers hired specifically for construction purposes. 

Special charges, such as licenses, architect's or designer's fees, interest on money borrowed for construction, liability insurance premiums, and injury damages - all the result of the construction - should be capitalized as part of the cost of the fixed asset. These items are in the nature of directly applicable overhead charges. 

Interest expense, during a construction period and bond discount amortized during a construction period may properly be charged to the cost of the construction, on the basis that income is not available preceding completion, and consequently all costs and expenses are related exclusively to construction. Theoretically, the practice of capitalizing interest, even on owned capital used during construction, can be defended. Practically, however, interest and discount are capitalized only when the funds are borrowed.

The only remaining element of cost is the general factory overhead. 

There is some disagreement among accountants as to whether any portion of the general factory overhead should be capitalized as a part of the cost of the fixed asset constructed. Some contend that no portion of the overhead should be capitalized, while others are of the opinion that some portion should be capitalized. The entire problem is completely interwoven with the correct determination of profits. The correct analysis of such a situation appears to be along the following lines:

If a portion of the regularly incurred overhead were charged to the fixed asset, the cost of the goods manufactured for sale would be relieved of part of their usual costs; therefore, the cost of the goods manufactured would be understated and the net profit for the period would be overstated. This overstatement of profits could result in the payment of excessive dividends. In any event, surplus would not be reduced to its correct amount until the constructed fixed asset were completely depreciated by periodic charges to depreciation expense.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Therefore, if the production of the fixed asset does not increase the factory overhead to be consumed normally by the products manufactured for sale, no portion of the regularly incurred overhead should be charged to the fixed assets. 

If the production of the fixed asset does increase the factory overhead, and if the increase were absorbed by the regularly manufactured inventory, its cost would be overstated and profits for the construction period would be understated. Therefore, the increased overhead logically should be added to the cost of the fixed assets, because such construction was responsible for the increase. 

In the application of increased factory overhead to the cost of manufactured fixed assets, reason and judgment must be used. In certain instances it may be virtually impossible to determine a slight increase in overhead. In no event should the cost of idle personnel time or the cost of idle capacity be capitalized in the constructed asset; the cost of idle time and idle capacity is a charge against profits.

Accountants are also in disagreement upon the proper procedure to follow when a constructed fixed asset has a cost in excess of the market price of a similar asset. Assume that a machine tool manufacturing company could purchase a milling machine for $6,000.00, but thought that it could construct the same machine for $5,500.00, it proceeded with the construction, and, when completed, the actual cost was $7,000.00, that is, $1,000.00 in excess of the market. Some accountants advocate placing the machine on the books at $6,000.00, charging the $1,000.00 to Profit-and-Loss as a non-operating expense. To do so, places the fixed asset on the books at the lower of cost or market, which is not an accepted practice for fixed asset valuation. If this reasoning were followed, why not reduce all fixed assets to market value? 

To the author, it appears as though the asset should be recorded at its cost of $7,000.00, to be depreciated on the estimated life, just as though the asset were purchased in a high-priced market for $7,000.00. If the actual cost to construct was but $5,500.00, it should be capitalized at that figure; upon that point there appears to be no disagreement among accountants, as they all agree that there can be no profit upon construction.

Assets Acquired by Discovery.-When assets are acquired by discovery, their values should be ascertained by appraisal, and the same accounting treatment accorded them as in the case of unconditionally donated assets. In many instances, assets acquired by discovery cannot

be properly valued for many years following discovery; this statement applies particularly to wasting assets, that is, assets commonly found in the extractive industries, such as coal mines, oil wells, gas wells, minerals in general, and timber stands. Because of the uncertainty of value at the time of discovery, occasional readjustments of the asset values may be necessary as development proceeds. The assets to which discovery value applies are subject to depletion rather than to depreciation or amortization. The subject of depletion of wasting assets is treated in chapter XVIII. 

Assets Acquired under Conditional Sales Contracts.-There are several types of conditional sales contracts; one of them, the hirepurchase plan, is used when equipment is rented by the vendee, the rental payments to apply on the purchase price in the event of sale. 

The vendor may repossess the equipment if the vendee fails in his payments. After a stipulated number of payments have been made by the vendee, title passes to him, but he still is liable for the remaining payments.

If the vendee has no intention of finally purchasing the asset, rental payments should be charged to expense. If the intention of the vendee is to purchase the equipment, he must set up his accounts during this rental period so that the entire situation is shown. The effect is the same as though an asset were purchased on the installment plan. 

The transactions should be shown as follows: Assume that an accounting machine, priced at $1,800.00 is purchased under a conditional sales contract, stipulating rentals of $100.00 per month, in advance. At the time of acquisition, the entry is: 

Equipment Purchased on Contract. 

Contracts Payable. 

Cash.

As the payments are made each month: 

Contracts Payable 

Cash... 1,800.00 1,700.00 100.00 100.00 100.00

Because the intention is the ultimate purchase of the asset, depreciation should be recorded periodically. 

Discounts on Fixed Assets Purchased. Two schools of thought exist with respect to the treatment of discounts granted on the purchase of fixed assets. Some accountants are of the belief that if discounts on inventory purchases are treated as financial income, it is but logical to

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

treat discounts on fixed assets purchased as financial income. In like manner, this same group believes that if discounts on inventory purchases are considered a reduction of cost, discounts on fixed assets should be similarly treated. 

There is but one correct manner in which to handle purchase discounts and that is to show them as deductions from cost whether or not the discount is taken. The fact that this principle has been quite generally disregarded in practice with respect to inventory purchases has nothing to do with fixed assets purchases where the correct principle has been followed.

Chapter XVII  Concluded 

General. The preceding chapter began the general development of the cost and valuation of fixed assets and the related expense and cost problems. This chapter and the three following will continue that development by reference to specific assets, methods, and procedure. 

Separation of Accounts.-Separate accounts should be maintained. 

for each asset. For example, an account entitled Buildings and Machinery is meaningless because no information is presented as to the value of the buildings or of the machinery. Furthermore, the probability is that the rate of depreciation applicable to the buildings is different from the rate applicable to the machinery; if one rate were applied to machinery with an estimated life of ten years and to buildings with an estimated life of fifty years, it would be wholly accidental if the accumulated depreciation represented the correct figure for both classes of assets. Furthermore, if more than one building is owned, separate accounts should be maintained for each one; otherwise the cost of any one unit would be hidden in the accounts, and if depreciation rates varied between buildings, the expired values could not be properly measured.

In order to relieve the general ledger of burdensome detail, the controlling account principle should be applied to accounting for fixed assets. For example, in the general ledger an account called Machinery-Plant 1 may be set up, with a subsidiary plant ledger carrying an account for each individual machine. The Reserve for Depreciation of 

Machinery, Plant 1, also a general ledger account, is the controlling account for the accumulated depreciation of all machinery in the plant, while the subsidiary plant ledger cards for the various machines serve as the individual subsidiary records for the accumulated depreciation on those machines. On these subsidiary ledger cards is recorded the annual depreciation expense, thus serving, too, as a subsidiary record of the Depreciation on Machinery Expense account on the general ledger. In addition, the subsidiary ledger card for each machine carries 358

a full history of the asset, including all repairs, replacements, betterments made, rearrangement costs, and other information, as shown in the illustrations on pages 360 and 361. 

The remarks with respect to subsidiary asset records for machinery apply with equal force to each fixed asset. The need for a detailed record of each fixed asset has always existed in every manufacturing, mercantile, and financial institution, but the now famous Treasury Decision 4422 with respect to depreciation, has forced the use of detailed records. According to this decision, the sale of a fixed asset for which no detailed record is kept furnishes no basis for a loss or gain upon disposition; the difference between disposition price and book value must be charged or credited to the reserve for depreciation. Only if detailed records are kept which supply proof can losses or gains be claimed. 

Plant Ledger Illustrated.—Subsidiary plant ledgers, or individual asset records, may take any desired form. Two different forms are shown on pages 360 and 361. The dollar detail for cost, installation, freight, repairs, replacements, additions, depreciation, disposal, etc., and the historical data for location, vendor, insurance, use, method of payment, and life should be thoroughly studied. 

To summarize the effectiveness of the individual asset record: 

1. It identifies, locates, shows the origin and value of the asset. 

2. It shows the treatment accorded transportation and installation charges. 

3. For constructed assets, it shows the elements of cost. 

4. Maintenance costs are recorded. 

5. Depreciation charges are shown separately. 

6. Transfers of equipment from one location to another are noted. 

7. A complete inventory is available for insurance purposes. 

8. Retirements are clearly set forth. 

9. Federal income tax data is available. 

10. Personal property tax base figures can be supplied. 

11. Figures are available for detailed cost analyses. 

12. The effectiveness of similar assets may be measured. 

13. A basis exists for the issuance of appropriation orders for additional equipment. 

14. Budget preparation is facilitated. 

15. Public utilities may establish better cases for rate changes.
