When land used for business purposes and land held for speculation or future plant expansion or abandoned plant site land are owned, only the land used for business purposes should appear as a fixed asset; 1 1

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

the remaining lands should appear as other assets or permanent investments. 

Land Cost.-The cost of land used in a business should include the contract purchase price, cost of options, broker's commissions (if paid by the purchaser), attorney's fees, the cost of title search and guaranty, fees for recording the transfer, back taxes assumed, costs of clearing the site, the net cost of demolishing old structures on the land, liens assumed when title was acquired, local assessments for such items as sidewalks, street paving (not repairing) sewer lines, water mains, may be added to the cost of the land or carried separately as Land 

Improvements. 

Among the foregoing items to be capitalized as a part of the cost of business land, the net cost of demolishing old structures merits fuller discussion. If a land site with a building on it is purchased for $10,000.00, and if the old structure is to be removed to clear the site for the new building, the real objective of the purchase is the land; therefore, the entire cost is land cost. If it costs $1,000.00 to wreck the old structure, this cost is added to the $10,000.00 purchase price, resulting in a total cost of $11,000.00 for the land. Had the wrecking process produced net proceeds of $800.00, the land cost would be reduced to $9,200.00.

If land is purchased for speculation or for future expansion, its cost is the same as the cost of land purchased for business purposes. 

Furthermore, according to sound theory, if land held for future use is currently non-productive, taxes and interest charges on mortgages may be added to the cost of such land or carried forward in some other asset account to be written off against the income to be realized from this property sometime in the future. The more conservative practice dictates that all carrying charges on this type of land be charged to current expense, for the future income may never materialize; this practice is approved by the Bureau of Internal Revenue. 

If the land is used in business, taxes and carrying charges should be capitalized only during the construction period preceding business operations and the production of revenue. 

The Valuation of Land.-Normally, land is valued at its complete cost, the elements of which were set forth in the preceding section. 

Occasionally, deviations from cost are permitted on the basis of sound appraisal; for example, assume that fifty years ago a company acquired land in a section of a city which today has grown to be the center of

It the industrial or mercantile activity of the community, with resultant sizeable increases in land values; in such a case it appears proper (1) to cite the fact of increased land value as a footnote to the balance sheet, or (2) to increase the amount of the Land account with a credit to a Reappraisal Surplus account. The latter practice would be particularly justified if statements were being prepared for credit purposes. must be remembered that these remarks apply to long-time trends in value, and not to current market fluctuations which should be ignored because business land is not inventory for sale. Similarly, if land values have declined over long periods, the better practice is to write the land down to its current value. 

Land other than agricultural land and extractive industries land is not subject to physical exhaustion; consequently depreciation is not recognized. Farm land and extractive industries land is subject to exhaustion caused by cropping, erosion, and extraction; in those cases the expired economic value should be charged off; these topics are treated under "Wasting Assets."

In the section "Land Costs," the statement was made that local assessments could be carried in the Land account or shown separately as Land Improvements; the preferable treatment is to show such charges separately because of their depreciable nature. Assume that an airport corporation acquired a tract of land near a river; the cost of runways, landing lights, and dikes for the river floodwaters, none of which are a part of any structure but are an integral part of the land, may be separately set up in a Land Improvements account or accounts.

BUILDINGS 

Buildings are subject to depreciation, while site land is not; the rates of depreciation depend upon the type of construction, and the severity of the use of the buildings. Buildings may be acquired by any of the methods described in chapter XVI. 

Building Cost.-When a building is purchased, its cost includes the contract purchase price, the cost of altering and remodeling the building for the purposes of the new owner, unpaid taxes assumed by the purchaser, accrued interest assumed, and legal costs. When land and buildings thereon are purchased for one lump sum, the independent value of the land and the buildings should be established by competent appraisal and recorded in separate accounts.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

When a building is constructed instead of purchased, the cost is not so easily determined; the cost of construction includes: architect's fees for plans and supervision; the salaries of officers engaged in supervising construction; permit and license costs; the cost of materials; the cost of construction labor; the cost of construction shacks; premiums on workmen's compensation insurance; damages paid to injured workmen; all insurance for the construction period, such as fire, tornado, public liability, and property damages; interest costs during the construction period; bond discount to be amortized during the construction period; the cost of easements; strike costs. In addition to the foregoing costs, certain other items of cost are frequently incurred which deserve special discussion.

When land and an old building are purchased as a unit, the old building to be razed, the entire cost should be charged to Land; furthermore, as pointed out earlier in this chapter, the cost of demolition is added to the cost of the land, or the net proceeds of wrecking credited to Land. The cost of the new building is in no way affected by old building costs, because the old building was acquired merely as a means to acquiring the desired land. However, if a new building replaces one formerly used by the company, the undepreciated cost of the old building (plus wrecking costs, less salvage received) should not be charged to the new building, but to non-operating profit and loss. The fact that an old asset must be retired to make way for a new one does not increase the value of the new one. 1 If a building and land are purchased, and if the building tenants are paid certain amounts to induce them to vacate their leases so that the building may be demolished, the bonus should be charged to the Land account. However, if the building thus vacated is to be occupied by the new owner, the bonus should be charged to the Building account as a part of the cost of acquisition. 

After a building is in readiness for occupancy, additional costs such as taxes and interest on notes or mortgages should not be capitalized as a part of the structural cost. Occasionally, a building may be erected and then remain unoccupied for a considerable period of time; certain costs nevertheless occur regularly, such as taxes, interest, heat, and maintenance. If this period of vacancy was contemplated when the building was planned, the costs may be established as deferred charges to future operations; otherwise they must be charged to expense even though there is no revenue or surplus and a deficit is thereby created.

Valuation of Buildings.-The valuation of buildings follows the same valuation principles applicable to all fixed assets; that is, the most commonly accepted valuation is at cost less accumulated depreciation. However, as a result of relatively permanent changes in market values and in reproduction values, buildings may be appraised and the resultant changes in value recorded; fixed asset appraisals are treated in chapter XIX. 

Ordinary repairs and minor replacements of a maintenance nature should be charged to expense accounts; major repairs and replacements which do not increase the value of the building over its originally booked value but which cancel past depreciation and thereby lengthen its life in excess of the original estimate, should be charged to the  Additions to the building or improvements or betterments which result in a value in excess of that at acquisition should be capitalized. If, for example, a company paid $100,000.00 for a building with an estimated life of fifty years, and after ten years constructed a wing to the building at a cost of $25,000.00, the cost should be charged to the Building account. If it is estimated that the wing and the building proper will be retired at the same time, the $25,000.00 should be depreciated over the remaining forty years of the life of the building.

Let us now consider the following case: A tin roof on a building is to be replaced with a slate roof; a new tin roof would cost $1,200.00 and a new slate roof $2,000.00; of the entire reserve for depreciation against the building, $300.00 is applicable to the old roof. The entry to record the transaction is as follows: 

Reserve for Depreciation of Building.

Building 

Repairs 

Cash .300.00 .800.00 .900.00 2,000.00

Thus, only the added value is capitalized. The added value of $800.00 should be depreciated over the estimated remaining life of the entire unit. 

Leaseholds are classified as intangibles; therefore improvements to leased buildings are treated in chapter XX, Fixed Intangible Assets. 

Construction in Process at the Balance Sheet Date.-When build ings or other fixed assets are under construction at a balance sheet date, the total accumulated costs should be shown in the balance sheet as Construction in Process; liabilities incurred for construction should be

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

shown among the current liabilities. If a company is under contract with an architect or a builder, and if periodic payments are made as construction progresses, the amounts certified by the architect should be taken up in the Construction in Process account. The balance sheet should contain full disclosure of all parts, as follows: 

Construction in Process, Building, Contract Price.. 

Less Cost to Complete.... 

Construction in Process, Cost to Date.

Building Equipment.-Building equipment includes all wiring, piping, heating, and ventilating equipment, signal systems, drinking fountains, sprinkler systems, partitions and lighting fixtures, and other items of such a nature that they cannot be removed without affecting the building. Building equipment therefore is a part of the building, and the cost of such equipment is a part of the total cost of the structure. The subsidiary plant ledger should contain detailed information. concerning the equipment, because the equipment may carry rates of depreciation differing from that applicable to the building proper, and also may require frequent replacements. 

MACHINERY 

Land and buildings are considered as real property while the term machinery refers to personal property ordinarily used in and around factories, such as milling machines, grinders, broaching machines, lathes, drill presses, punch presses, sewing machines, mixers, pumps, blowers, construction equipment, railroad equipment, calculators, agricultural equipment, and power transmission equipment. 

The use of a plant ledger, described earlier in this chapter, is of particular importance for machinery, because machines constantly are being repaired, rehabilitated, and replaced. The use of adequate records for machinery cannot be overemphasized. It is upon the basis of efficient machinery, efficiently used, that profits partially depend. 

In addition to plant ledger records for each machine, many companies prepare detailed factory maps setting forth the location of each unit, so that each individual item may be studied in its relationship to the entire plant; this plan is particularly helpful when general plant rearrangement is contemplated. 

The individual machine record provides useful information in the establishment of insurance claim losses. It also permits the proper com-

putation of gains or losses on the sale of used machinery. In addition, it aids in properly depreciating any individual item. For example, assume a general ledger Machinery account balance of $100,000.00, a depreciation rate of 10 per cent, and a credit balance of $50,000.00 in the Reserve for Depreciation of Machinery account. It is apparent that the machinery as a whole is 50 per cent depreciated. Now assume that one machine originally costing $1,000.00 is 12 years old; in effect, it is overdepreciated to the extent of $200.00. If subsidiary plant records were used, the situation would be clarified, and depreciation on the one machine would have stopped at the end of ten years or the reserve would have been adjusted. Again, a composite rate of 10 per cent may be used on the total machinery account but the rate applicable to specific machines may vary from 5 to 20 per cent; the individual accounts in a plant ledger would provide information for the analyses of any particular case. The record also serves as the basis for ascertaining values for the purpose of borrowing money. 

Machinery Cost.-The cost of machinery purchases includes the invoice price, duty, freight, and insurance in transit, and installation costs-in other words, all costs necessary to place the machinery in condition for use. Auxiliary equipment which is an integral part of the machine, such as a chuck for a lathe, should be added to the cost of the machine. When a machine is constructed for a company's own use, its cost includes material, labor, and factory overhead under the conditions set forth in chapter XVI. 

Valuation of Machinery. The simple statement may be made that machinery should ordinarily be valued at cost less accumulated depreciation; however, practical operations highly complicate the valuation of machinery. General guides for the proper valuation of machinery follow.

Ordinary or minor repairs and part replacements, that is, regularly recurring costs such as sharpening, cleaning, aligning, simply tend to maintain an asset in efficient condition for useful productivity; they do not prolong the originally estimated life, nor do they result in asset values which are enhanced over original acquisition price. Such costs should be charged currently to Machinery Maintenance Expense, or to a Reserve for Maintenance if one has been created by periodic charges to expense.

Extraordinary or major repairs of a general overhauling character and major part replacements present a difficult problem; they do not

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

1 increase the value of an asset over its original cost when new, but in effect they cancel accrued depreciation and thereby prolong the life of the asset over its originally estimated life; such expenditures should be charged to the  For example, assume that a machine, new, cost $2,000.00, with an estimated life of ten years; at the end of six years, the condition was: Machine 

Reserve for Depreciation.. .$2,000.00 1,200.00 

At that time, it was estimated that by spending $200.00 for major overhauling and part replacements, the machine will last an additional five years, or a total of fifteen. The recording of the cost of the general rehabilitation is as follows: 

Reserve for Depreciation..

Cash .200.00 200.00 

The reserve balance is reduced to $1,000.00; the net value of the machine is $1,000.00; the undepreciated balance of $1,000.00 will be spread over nine years, or, if desired, the reserve may be adjusted to a fifteen-year basis from the date of acquisition. 

If a used machine is acquired, operated for a time, then rehabilitated, the asset value may be increased over the value when acquired. 

In no case should the rehabilitated value exceed the cost new. 

In certain cases a machine may be acquired new, and later a major part replaced at a cost in excess of the cost of the same part upon original acquisition. The Machinery account should be increased to the extent of the difference in cost at the two dates; for example, part 

A originally cost $100.00; it was replaced by a new part A at a cost of $150.00; $50.00 should be capitalized.

The line of demarcation between minor and major repairs and part replacements is difficult to determine. Usually, decisions are based on individual judgment and analysis, tempered by the sometimes arbitrary policy of the particular company. This topic is discussed at greater length in chapter XVI. 

Additions and improvements to machines resulting in asset values in excess of the original value when new should be capitalized to the machinery account involved.

The retirement and disposition of machinery is treated in chapter XIX.

Machinery Rearrangement.-Occasionally, machinery is rearranged within a plant in order to improve the efficiency of production. The treatment of the cost of rearranging the machinery raises difficult questions. The original cost of installation has already been capitalized, and the capitalization of a reinstallation would be incorrect because the asset is not increased in capital value, even though it may be of greater productivity. Machinery rearrangement costs may (1) be charged to expense if the expense is not an unwarranted burden on the current period, or (2) set up as a deferred charge to operations, to be amortized over a period not in excess of the period to be benefited. At the present time, many corporations show as deferred charges huge amounts of rearrangement expenses caused by plant rearrangements necessitated by production for defense purposes. 

Leased Machinery.-Certain manufacturers of machinery lease rather than sell their products. The lessee pays for the use of the machinery either on a time basis or on the basis of units produced by the machine. On the books of the lessee, only memorandum notations of the existence of the machinery should be kept. The lessor should treat the machinery leased as an investment, and should depreciate it. 

Depending upon the lease agreement, either the lessor or the lessee will be responsible for maintenance, which should be charged to expense.

TOOLS Tools include hand tools and those used on machinery. If the tool is an integral part of a machine, and if its life is approximately the same as that of the machine, it may be capitalized as machinery. Most tools are loose, and wear out more rapidly than machines, and are broken or disappear more readily.

Valuation of Tools.-The cost of tools is their purchase price, or the cost to make them. Because of the relatively rapid depreciation, obsolescence, and disappearance of tools, one of three methods is used in writing them off into expense. 

The first method is to use a depreciation rate and a reserve for depreciation, operated in the same manner as any other reserve for depreciation. Usually, the method is not very satisfactory, because of the rapid turnover.

The second method is to value the tools by inspection; at the end of each period the tools are inventoried, and an estimate made of their

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

remaining dollar value. For example, at the balance sheet date, the 

Tools account, to which all tools are charged at cost, shows a balance of $10,000.00; by inventory and appraisal it is estimated that their remaining value is $7,000.00; $3,000.00 represents the expense for the period, to be set up as follows:

Tools Expense (or Depreciation of Tools). 

Tools. .3,000.00 3,000.00

Under this method, a reserve is not used, and the tools would be shown in the balance sheet at $7,000.00. 

The third method is to place a value on the tools when they are first acquired and this value remains constant. As additional tools are purchased, they are charged to Tools Expense. Depreciation is not taken on the permanently capitalized value. At infrequent intervals, the asset value may be changed to conform with long-time increases or decreases in the amount of the tools required. 

PATTERNS, MOLDS, MAPS, DRAWINGS, DIES, LASTS, MODELS, ETC. 

Miscellaneous items of this nature usually depreciate rapidly, due principally to obsolescence. The chief point in accounting for these assets is to depreciate them rapidly enough. Unless there is absolute certainty that the item will be used for more than one job, its entire cost should be written off against the first run of products produced therefrom. If the item is not too much subject to style changes and there is a reasonable certainty that the item will be used for more than one order its cost may be prorated over a reasonable period. 

DELIVERY EQUIPMENT 

Delivery equipment includes all assets used in the physical distribution of goods. Distribution costs have assumed a role of increasing importance in the determination of the final net profit on each item sold and on each department's operations, profit by territories, salesmen, customers, etc. Consequently, detailed cost records for delivery equipment are of importance. 

Delivery Equipment Cost.-The cost of delivery equipment includes all costs necessary to place the equipment in condition for use. 

When a chassis is purchased with a special body made to order, the complete cost including original painting and decoration should be

capitalized. License fees for new equipment are considered as expenses chargeable to the period to which they apply. The same principles and procedure followed for machinery are applicable to delivery equipment. 

Valuation of Delivery Equipment.-The valuation of delivery equipment follows the same principles and procedure as that applicable to machinery. The trading of used delivery equipment for new equipment constitutes a major problem, but discussion of it is deferred to chapter XIX. 

FURNITURE AND FIXTURES 

Furniture may be defined as all movable factory, store, and office equipment such as desks, chairs, filing cabinets, bookcases, typewriters, calculators, accounting machines, and the like. Distinction should be made between store furniture and office furniture, because depreciation and expense on store furniture may be charged as a selling expense, and on office furniture the costs of maintenance may be considered as administrative expenses.

Fixtures may include the more immovable items such as shelving, partitions, heating equipment, light fixtures, shafting, show windows, and the like. In most organizations, distinction between furniture and fixtures is not maintained in the general ledger; such distinction should be maintained by means of an equipment record. Between organizations, uniformity of practice does not exist with respect to distinction between buildings or building equipment on the one hand and between building equipment and fixtures on the other. For example, one company may consider a built-in safe as building, another as building equipment, and a third may treat it as furniture or fixtures. 

The cost and valuation of furniture and fixtures follows the same pattern as that applicable to machinery. Small items of furniture may be depreciated under either of the three methods suggested for tools. 

RETURNABLE CONTAINERS 

Returnable containers include bottles, boxes, caddies, tanks, drums, casks, kegs, barrels, and reels. The present tendency in merchandising is to eliminate returnable containers wherever possible. When the container is not returnable, as in the case of an ice cream package, the container cost is an expense and any amounts on hand are treated as supplies-deferred charges to operations.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

When returnable containers are delivered to customers, the vendor will follow one of three policies: first, the customer is requested to return the container but no charge is recorded against his account; second, the customer may be charged or may be required to pay a cash deposit, and, upon the return of the container, is given credit or a cash refund; third, the vendor may include in the invoice price of his product a charge for the container and upon its return either credit the customer with the amount included in the invoice price or give him a cash refund.

Containers, like tools, should be valued at cost less accumulated depreciation or by periodic revaluation, or they should be set up as an asset and all subsequent purchases charged to expense. If the latter method is followed, and if replacements are quite regular, care should be exercised by means of frequent inventories to insure that the asset value is not inflated.

If no charge is made against the customer for the container, the rate of depreciation on the containers should be high because losses probably will be large. 

If a charge is made to the customer or cash is received as a container deposit, the method of accounting will depend upon whether the container is charged at cost or at cost plus a profit. For example if the container is charged at its cost of $0.50, the entries are:

If the container deposit has been charged to Trade Accounts Receivable, the amount of the container deposits therein should be separated for balance sheet purposes, and the charges to the customers for containers shown as "Containers in the Hands of Customers." The balance of the Containers-Out account represents a liability of the company to the customer for deposits on the containers. The two foregoing items should be about equal in amount. 

When cash deposits are taken for containers, which is an almost universal practice in the sale of returnable container merchandise to householders, the cash deposit received may be segregated in a separate fund or be carried with the general cash of the company. 

WASTING ASSETS 

Wasting assets are stores of natural resources, such as deposits of gold, silver, lead, slate, stone, gravel, coal, oil, gas, and timber stands.

They are subject to depletion, which is caused by the lessening of the physical quantity due to extraction or other removal. Fixed assets subject to depreciation wear out, become obsolete or inadequate, and thereby diminish in value, whereas in the case of fixed assets subject to depletion the actual physical quantities are exhausted. 

The Cost of Wasting Assets.-The cost of a wasting asset is the amount paid for it or paid for the rights to operate it, plus the cost of physical equipment such as tipples, separators, wells, mills, shafts, and the like, plus all costs of exploitation and development. The costs of development and exploitation should be segregated between the total amount subject to depreciation and the total amount subject to depletion. Developmental costs on projects which do not produce

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

should be charged to expense or loss; an example would be an amount spent to strip overburden from potential coal land, only to discover that the project is not commercially profitable. 

The cost of protecting natural resources prior to active production should be capitalized. In the case of timber stands, the cost of fire prevention and underbrush elimination is frequently capitalized, even during active operations, because these costs apply to uncut stands.

At this point it may be well to call attention to one peculiarity of accounting for wasting assets. Depreciation and depletion charges are expenses; the soundness of recognizing depreciation before dividends to stockholders is well established. On the other hand, the treatment of depletion sometimes constitutes a general departure from the requirement that capital shall not be returned to stockholders in the form of dividends; in the case of wasting assets it is considered quite proper to include a portion of the capital along with the dividends from profits; that is, depletion need not be deducted in determining surplus available for dividends. This is on the basis that the asset ordinarily is not replaced once it is depleted. In the event that capital invested in depletable assets is to be reinvested in another project, the dividends to the stockholders should not include a return of capital. In any case, dividends before provision for depletion should be labeled as dividends out of capital rather than profits. 

Valuation of Wasting Assets.-Wasting assets are valued at cost of acquisition plus the cost of development and exploitation, less depletion; frequently, however, because of the fact that many wasting assets are discovered after the payment of only a nominal sum for the land involved, they may be assigned a discovery value, in which case they are valued at the discovery value plus the cost of development and exploitation, less depletion. 

As natural resources are worked, additional discoveries may be made which require adequate appraisal and valuation; on the other hand, it may be learned that the original cost or discovery values were overstated. From an income tax point of view, the fair value appraisal of depletable assets is recognized by permitting a depletion deduction based on the fair market value at the date of discovery or within thirty days thereafter. The valuation depends upon the units available, tempered by quality, location, accessibility, and shipping conditions. Depletion of wasting assets is treated in chapter XVIII.

Chapter XVIII  

General Concepts of Depreciation.-As pointed out in chapter 

XVI, depreciation is a decline in economic value caused by wear, tear, the action of the elements, the passage of time, obsolescence, and inadequacy. Practically all problems surrounding the valuation of fixed assets are inextricably interwoven with depreciation. Because depreciation is a lessening in value, it is the function of accounting to record correctly the loss in value as those values are absorbed in business operations. If losses in value did not occur with their resultant requirements for repairs, replacements, and renewals, each expenditure on a fixed asset would enhance asset values. As assets give forth their services, depreciation expense is incurred. It is a non-cash expense; the depreciation is added to the cost to manufacture, distribute, and administer, and in this manner is passed along to the customer. When the customer remits, an amount is received which, under normal conditions, is sufficiently large to cover all costs, including depreciation expense, and a profit. If the amounts so received are properly conserved in the form of assets, the general asset position is maintained without an impairment of capital.

The importance of accounting for depreciation has been re-emphasized in the past few years by the constantly increasing and more drastic requirements of the Bureau of Internal Revenue. For many businesses, mercantile, industrial, and public utility, depreciation is one of the largest expenses, and because of the difficulty frequently encountered in measuring it correctly, one of the most perplexing problems of modern business. Preceding the date of the enactment of our federal income tax law, business men did not adopt regularized depreciation policies, but frequently took small depreciation in years of low profits and large depreciation charges in years of high profits, both circumstances being without regard to the depreciation incurred in relation to the expired usefulness of the asset. After the adoption of the federal income tax law, all business organizations have admitted the legitimacy of depre- 379

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

ciation as an expense. In the past several years, since the adoption of 

Treasury Decision 4422, depreciation allowances for federal income tax purposes have been increasingly regulated, with the burden of proof for the reasonableness of the depreciation deduction placed upon the taxpayer.

Because of the stringency of the regulations surrounding depreciation, the plant ledger for each asset, one form of which is illustrated in chapter XVII, has come into almost universal use. 

Physical, Functional, and Contingent Depreciation.-The physical causes of depreciation are: wear, tear, the action of the elements, and the passage of time. The functional causes are: obsolescence and inadequacy. The contingent causes are: accidents and contingency losses.

In estimating the depreciation based upon the anticipated life of the asset, all causes should be considered, because an asset declines in value from all causes. If functional and contingent causes are unpredictable, the loss in value from those causes should be recognized upon the disposition of the asset.

Physical depreciation is the result of wear, tear, the action of the elements, and the passage of time; these include the deterioration promoted by ordinary usage, friction, decrepitude, negligence, vibration, electrolysis, oxidation, and other natural causes. Ordinary wear and tear is the primary basis upon which depreciation is calculated. A fixed asset may become valueless simply because it is standing; the natural ravages of deterioration caused by elapsed time cause a loss in useful life. The efficiency of an asset may be partially maintained by repairs, for a long period of time, but in the end physical factors will cause the asset to be of no useful value.

Functional depreciation interferes with and retards proper functioning, viewed from the standpoint of efficient operations. Inadequacy or obsolescence causes less efficient operation when compared with more modern assets. Inadequacy exists when an asset is no longer capable of fulfilling the demands made upon it; it may be a perfectly sound asset but for the sake of economical operation a new asset, adequate for the purposes, must be obtained. The inadequacy may be caused by growth and expansion, engineering economies, and unpredictable events.

Obsolescence refers to that condition which exists when new and better assets exist to perform the duties now performed by the old assets, and when current fashion replaces old styles. Horse cars and

wooden rails were made obsolete by electricity and steel rails, carriages by the automobile. As an example of obsolescence caused by style vagaries, the dies for the past year's automobile fender are obsolete because of the new shape of those of the current year. Obsolescence is dependent upon utility value at the present date compared with the utility value at the date of acquisition. 

Complete and Incomplete Depreciation.-Occasionally, deprecia tion is referred to as complete or incomplete. When the service life of an asset terminates, depreciation is complete. Incomplete depreciation is the total amount of accrued or accumulated depreciation on an asset which is in service. On the basis of complete depreciation, reasonable estimates may be made for the depreciation provisions for new assets of the same general class. 

Unit and Average Depreciation.-Unit depreciation is the total amount of the value decline for one individual asset, such as one machine. Average depreciation is the amount of the value decline for all assets of one group, such as all machines in a factory. All of the machinery in a factory may have an average depreciation of 30 per cent, whereas some individual machines may be new and others old, with unit depreciation varying from zero to 100 per cent. Individual asset records are of importance in segregating unit depreciation in order to facilitate the determination of loss or gain on disposals. 

Deferred Maintenance and Accrued Depreciation.-Deferred maintenance refers to repairs and part replacements which are necessary to keep an asset in good operating condition, but which have not been made. The reasons for deferring the maintenance are either a lack of time, a lack of money, a contemplation of complete replacement, or satisfaction with the results obtained without the maintenance. 

Accrued depreciation represents the depreciation which has taken place between the date of acquisition and the present date. Depreciation is continuous, but it is customary to record it only at the close of each fiscal period and upon the disposition of an asset. 

Depreciation and Maintenance.-In determining the estimated life of an asset, based upon normal usage, the most important factor entering into consideration is the general maintenance policy of the owner. If an asset is kept in constant repair by granting attention to small repairs and part replacements, it will enjoy a longer life than one which is constantly neglected. In addition, more efficient produc-

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

tion and satisfaction are attained by a liberal and far-sighted maintenance policy. It must be remembered, however, that regardless of the liberal nature of the maintenance policy, any depreciable asset will in time become of no economic value. 

Depreciation Allowed and Allowable.-These terms are used in connection with depreciation in a federal income tax return. Depreciation "allowed" is the amount actually taken as an expense in a past return. Depreciation "allowable" is the amount the taxpayer could have taken had he taken full advantage of the law. The amount allowed cannot exceed the amount allowable. The failure in any one year, to take a full allowance for depreciation cannot be recovered during future years by higher depreciation deductions in those future years. If this were permissible, depreciation deductions might show a tendency to fluctuate with profits. The failure to take depreciation to its fully allowable amount in any one year alters the gain or loss on disposition of the asset. From a tax angle, when property is disposed of, the loss or gain is the cost or other basis minus the total depreciation allowed or allowable, whichever is the greater. 

Bases of Depreciation. Several possible bases exist for the computation of depreciation. The bases are: 

1. Cost 

2. Cost adjusted 

3. Reproduction cost new 

4. Present sound value 

5. Income tax base

These bases will receive consideration in the following chapter. 

They are placed here so that the reader will realize that more than one base exists. At this point it might be well to mention that the almost universally accepted base for general accounting purposes is cost, because it is the cost of the asset in use which should be recovered through depreciation expense charges. Depreciation based upon reproduction cost new is growing in favor and will be fully discussed in chapter XIX. 

By cost recovery through depreciation charges, the net cost, that is, the cost minus the estimated salvage value, is the value to be recovered. 

When an asset is acquired new or used, it is virtually impossible to determine accurately its salvage value many years hence. Theoretically, salvage value on an estimated basis should be determined in arriving at the periodic depreciation charge; practically, it is impossible to assign

reasonable salvage value in advance. Originally incorrect life estimates, changes in price levels, and temporary market fluctuations all conspire to change actual final salvage from the original estimate. 

Factors of Depreciation.-Three factors must be taken into consideration in estimating periodic depreciation; they are: 

1. Cost. Cost includes all costs to make ready for use, as set forth in chapters XVI and XVII. 

2. Salvage. Salvage, scrap, or residual value is the estimated amount recoverable upon the retirement of the asset. If a discarded machine were sold for $1,000.00 and if it cost the seller $200.00 to dismantle and move it, the salvage was $800.00 net. 

3. Estimated life. The estimated life may be expressed in terms of: (a) years, (b) months, (c) units of output produced, (d) working hours.

Methods of Depreciation. There are many methods of computing depreciation. The more important methods, demonstrated in the following pages, are: 

1. Proportional method: (a) straight line method, (b) working hours method, (c) unit production method, (d) composite life method. 

2. Reducing charge methods: (a) Fixed percentage on diminishing. book value method, (b) Diminishing rates on cost-method, (c) Sum of the life-periods method. 

3. Interest methods: (a) Annuity method, (b) Sinking fund method. 

4. Appraisal method.

Proportional Methods.-The proportional methods charge off the depreciation on a fixed base, and the depreciation is in proportion to time or production.

The Straight-Line Method.―This is the method most commonly used to record the periodic depreciation of an asset. Depreciation charges are spread equally over all life periods; the passage of time is predominant in this method; wear may or may not be proportional to time elapsed.

The Composite Life Method.-In this method, depreciation is calculated on a diversity of assets, rather than on each individual asset. 

By the use of this method, the mean average life is calculated. After calculating the mean average life, any method of depreciation (straight line, unit production, fixed percentage of diminishing value, etc., may be employed). The objectionable feature of the method is the failure

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

to set forth depreciation on any one asset; therefore no loss or gain may be taken on the disposal of an asset. The method is advantageous as a check on total depreciation computed on individual assets. It is a good method to use when an asset is composed of varying parts, as, for example, a hotel. Reducing Charge Methods.-Reducing charge methods are based on the theory that depreciation is large in the early years of the life of an asset, and that as a result high depreciation charges should be made early in the life of the asset, with the charges gradually decreasing as the asset grows older. Advocates of the methods contend that as an asset grows older, repair costs increase, and if depreciation decreases, the total cost of maintenance including depreciation is more nearly stabilized.

Under reducing charge methods, the percentage of depreciation per period may remain fixed but be applied to a constantly decreasing carrying value, as in the first two methods illustrated. 

Fixed Percentage on Diminishing Book Value.-As indicated, the rate of depreciation remains constant, but is applied to the diminishing carrying value of the asset.

Sum of the Life-Periods Method. The sum of the life-periods method accomplishes the same general result as the fixed percentage on diminishing value method: The Base remains constant and the periodic rates decline. The rate is a fraction, having a denominator made up of the sum of the life periods; for example, an asset with an estimated life of five years: 

The denominator: 1+2+3+4+5=15.

The numerator of the fraction is the remaining estimated life as of the beginning of the current period; therefore the depreciation for the first year is 5/15 of the total amount to be depreciated; the remaining estimated life at the beginning of the second year is four years; therefore the depreciation for the second year is 4/15 of the total amount to be depreciated.

To illustrate, assume the five-year asset, cost $10,000.00, estimated scrap value $1,000.00, used in preceding illustrations.

Interest Methods.-These methods employ the principle of compound interest in order to determine the periodic depreciation. The two compound interest methods illustrated here are the annuity method and the sinking fund method. As will be shown, the two methods violate to some extent accepted accounting principles; but the utilities commissions of certain states occasionally require the use of one of these methods in order to determine more adequately current income deductions to provide for equipment replacements and to provide bases for the calculation of utility rates. Also, in those cases where interest on investment should be included as a cost of operation, the annuity method is preferred because it does provide for the interest on investment.

If an asset has a short life, these methods, when compared with the straight-line method, are less effective than when an asset has a relatively long life, because interest does not compound rapidly over short periods. The methods never did enjoy wide application and today they are used less than ever before. Distinctions between the annuity method and the sinking fund method are noted in the following two sections; at this stage, it must be remembered that while both are compound interest methods, they are two separate and distinct methods, both in procedure and in application. 

The Annuity Method. The theory underlying this method is that interest on the investment in the depreciable fixed asset should be included in the cost of production. In turn, this reasoning is based on the assumption that the corporation is paying interest for the capital invested in fixed assets or is using its own capital which otherwise could be invested and thereby earn an interest income. Using this method, the periodic entries for depreciation are as follows: 

Depreciation Expense 

Interest Income

. 

.XX XX XX Thus the constant depreciation charge includes two factors: (1) the assumed interest cost and (2) the value decline of the asset. The reserve accumulates to its proper amount at the end of the life of the asset.

Each period the carrying value of the asset is reduced by the amount of the decline in value and interest for the next period is computed on that reduced figure; therefore the interest credit is successively smaller

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

each period and the credit to the reserve for depreciation increases each period by a corresponding amount. The sum of the credits to interest income and to the depreciation reserve makes up the total charge to depreciation and is a constant amount. 

When this method is adopted, the rate of interest on invested capital must be arbitrarily assumed, because interest actually is not being earned on loaned funds at any specific rate. The method is demonstrated below.

The Sinking Fund Method. In the use of the sinking fund method of computing depreciation, a fund may or may not be established. In practice, it is most unusual to find a fund. When the sinking fund method is used, with or without a fund, the depreciation is at an increasing amount per period. The increase per period is the actual interest earned on the fund if one is used, or the computed interest if a fund is not created. Normally, the later periods of the life of an asset do not consume more of the asset than the early periods; consequently the method is not sound from this viewpoint. 

If a fund is created, the income earned on the fund is added to the fund, thus compounding, and constantly increasing the interest credit. 

As the carrying value of the asset decreases, the fund increases, and in this manner the capital is maintained and at the same time is segregated for its specific purpose.

The Appraisal Method.-When the appraisal method of depreciation is used, the value of the asset at the end of the period is estimated or appraised, and the difference between the value at the beginning of the period and at the end of the period is charged off as depreciation expense. Decidedly fluctuating amounts of depreciation frequently are the results of the method. Its best application is to small tools or containers, where breakage and loss are high and where replacements are rapid; beyond that use, the method does not possess much merit. Care must be exercised by the appraiser to remember that he is dealing with physical deterioration and not with fluctuations in market value.

Comparison of Methods. No one method of depreciation will ever satisfy all persons, and no one method exists or will be designed which will apply equitably to all of the diverse kinds of fixed assets. 

An appraisal of methods frequently develops into an argument in which personal preferences are emphasized. Practical operating conditions in any one plant should be the primary force in arriving at a decision concerning the correct method to adopt under those given circumstances.

The straight-line method, based upon the expiration of time, is simple to calculate and easy to apply. Time expiration being its basis, fluctuations in operating conditions do not receive consideration. As a result, in those cases where depreciation is controlled primarily by inadequacy and obsolescence, action of the elements, and any other time factor, and where severity of usage is fairly constant, the straightline method should produce satisfactory results. Furthermore, of major importance is the fact that this method is used almost universally and that it is the method approved by most governmental regulatory bodies. 

As an asset increases in age, repair costs normally increase; the sum of the depreciation expense charge and the repair costs equals the total cost to maintain an asset; the total maintenance cost for any one asset thus increases under the straight-line method. In practical operations, the total asset value for any one plant consists of a great many assets of varying characteristics, ages, and conditions; after a period of time, a somewhat regular repair cost is established for the plant as an entirety, thus tending to equalize from period to period the sum of the repair and depreciation charges. The foregoing statement is made because it is a fact, and is not made in defense of a method of depreciation; in accounting, it is important that each asset be properly

394, ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

handled, and if average conditions in a plant as a whole are permitted to conceal specific asset and expense conditions which are above and below the average, no justification can be accorded the procedure. 

Some persons object to the straight-line method because the rate of return on depreciable assets increases as the value of the assets decline; increasing repair and maintenance costs usually offset the tendency to increase total profits.

If it is desired to regularize expense charges for repair costs, a reserve for repairs or a reserve for maintenance may be established by regular periodic charges to expense and credits to a reserve, as follows: 

Repair (or Maintenance) Expense.... 

Reserve for Repairs (or Maintenance) 

XX XX When the repairs actually are incurred, the reserve is charged, and cash, payroll, or some other account credited.

The working-hours method, distributing depreciation on the basis of the hours of operation, prorates the cost of an asset to the product in much more equitable fashion than does the straight-line method. If the mere passage of time, obsolescence, and inadequacy were not vital factors of depreciation, the method would be practically perfect for the cost accountant of a factory. It must be noted, however, that when an asset is acquired, a working-hour estimate of its life must be made on the basis of a normal eight-hour day; if the asset is suddenly operated twenty-four hours a day, the increased load without opportunity for a normal maintenance policy may materially shorten its total workinghour life; incorrect depreciation charges will result if revisions in the estimated life are not prepared.

The discussion of the working-hours method applies with equal force to the unit production method. However, if one machine performs more than one operation, with a variance in the severity of the operations, the method is impracticable of adoption. As in the workinghours method, the question of normal, above-normal, and belownormal production arises in the unit production method. If one is of the belief that depreciation should be proportionate to the units manufactured, the vital factors of depreciation must be considered to be wear and tear, and not inadequacy, obsolescence, and the of passage time. Also, advocates of this method are of the opinion that a straightline charge causes unit costs to vary, depending upon production, whereas unit costs may be stabilized by charging depreciation to each

unit on a unit basis. An argument against the use of the method is that all depreciation is not dependent upon wear and tear. Under "Depletion," later in this chapter, we shall see that the unit production method is particularly adaptable to assets used in the extractive industries. 

As stated earlier in the chapter, the composite-life method is not recommended for purposes other than a check upon the general adequacy of the depreciation provided under the straight line or any other method in use.

The theoretical argument in favor of any reducing-charges method · is the equalization of depreciation and maintenance over the life of the asset. One practical argument against the method is the assumption of the expiration of large economic values early in the life of the asset, which condition normally does not exist for a going concern, unless the obsolescence factor is great; if this factor is important, the method is good, and prevents heavy losses upon premature disposition of the asset. Reducing-charge methods do not enjoy wide adaptation, because of certain practical objections and because of the mathematical computation involved.

The almost universal discontinuance of the compound-interest methods has been cited. The methods were predicated upon the belief that interest on investment in fixed assets should be considered as a cost of production. If the life of an asset is short, and if interest rates are low, the compound interest feature loses its inherently intriguing nature, and variations from the straight-line method will not be great. 

The best theoretical argument in favor of the methods is their precise mathematical calculation; practically, however, the labor involved in these calculations is a strong argument against their use; furthermore, there is no evidence that depreciation expense increases precisely in any such mathematical progression. And finally, the inclusion of interest as a depreciation charge cannot be justified, because there is no relationship between the two items. 

Reserves for Depreciation.-A reserve for depreciation represents the total past amounts of depreciation charged to operations in preceding periods, and the balance of a reserve represents the expired economic value of an asset. The reserve is a valuation reserve; the asset acquisition figure originally booked or subsequently adjusted, minus the reserve for depreciation represents the carrying value of the asset. 

For certain specific assets, particularly intangibles expiring on a pure

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

time basis, reserves are not used, and the asset account receives the direct credit for the expired values. For depreciable tangible fixed assets, it is preferable to carry a reserve, because (1) the original cost, the total charged off, and the carrying values are shown, (2) because depreciation is an estimate and may be incorrect. The handling of reserves upon the disposition of assets is treated in chapter XIX. 

It may not be amiss to repeat again the non-fund nature of a reserve for depreciation. Courts, as well as others, still imagine that a reserve contains money. To quote from a well-known case, "The depreciation charge permitted as a deduction from the gross income represents the reduction of capital assets through wear and tear of the plant used. 

The amount of the allowance for depreciation is the sum which should be set aside for the taxable year, in order that, at the end of the useful life of the plant in the business, the aggregate of the sums set aside will (with the salvage value) suffice to provide an amount equal to the original cost. . . . . The words used by the court cannot but mislead the uninitiated into the belief that a "sum" (of money) is available; nothing could be farther from the truth. Courts are not clear in their thinking and in their decisions concerning the purpose of recording depreciation; in defense of the courts it must be said that most depreciation cases have dealt with situations involving rate-making for public utilities; with the controversial views of the utility, the regulatory commission, and the accountant, confusion has resulted. 99 

Depreciation, Dividends, Stockholders.-Depreciation is now universally recognized as an expense. Courts rightly hold that depreciation must be deducted before dividend distributions may be made to stockholders without impairing capital. Of course, if depreciation policies are too liberal, secret reserves may be created, earnings understated, and the interests of stockholders thereby impaired when considered in terms of the market value of the stock. Today, however, excessively liberal depreciation charges may not pass the Bureau of Internal Revenue. If depreciation charges are too low, the interests of the stockholder can be adversely affected by the overstatement of earnings and the resultant inflation of asset values. Today, the business earning a profit is anxious to deduct all depreciation allowed by the Bureau of Internal Revenue, in order to reduce income taxes. 

Depreciation Rate Revisions.-Frequently, after an asset has been used for several periods, discovery may be made that depreciation provisions have been excessive or deficient. These situations usually arise

because of the inability to estimate correctly the life of an asset when it is first acquired. If depreciation provisions have been excessive, the proper correcting entry is:

Earned Surplus.. 

XX XX Earned surplus is credited because past profits have been understated to the extent of the excess depreciation, and past profits have been closed to the Earned Surplus account. The reserve is charged with an amount sufficient to reduce it to the balance which would now be in this account if past depreciation charges had been correct. After the reserve has been adjusted, the rate of depreciation applicable to future periods must be corrected so that depreciation charges will not continue to be excessive.

If depreciation charges have been too low in the past, a reversal of the foregoing procedure is followed. 

Depreciation During Construction.-Depreciation is assumed to begin upon the completion of a constructed asset; the deterioration occurring during construction exerts no impairment to the value of an asset as an entity, unless the construction period is unnecessarily prolonged. If an apartment building were constructed and occupied in sections, each finished section should be depreciated from the time it is completed and put into service. On the other hand, if a stretch of railroad were finished and used as a means of hauling material and men for continued construction on other sections of the same road, depreciation on the finished portion need not be considered until the entire unit is completed. 

Depletion. Depletion is a loss in value caused by a diminution in quantity brought about by physical extraction and removal. Assets subject to depletion diminish and thus lose their value whereas assets subject to depreciation wear out and thus lose their value. 

The method of depletion should be such that the total cost or other value, as set forth in chapters XVI and XVII, is written off or allocated to the total production. Consequently, if the total cost of the wasting asset is divided by the estimated number of units to be extracted, a depletion charge per unit results. 

The requirements of the federal income tax law have done much to complicate depletion charges, with the result that several methods are in operation; a few of these are demonstrated below. For federal

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

income tax purposes, the cost of a depletable asset is either its acquisition price or its value March 1, 1913, whichever is the larger; if the asset was acquired after March 1, 1913, the basis for calculating depletion is cost, or discovery value; by discovery value is meant the appraised value within 30 days following discovery. If a person bought a farm and then discovered that it contained valuable ore deposits, the cost of the farm would not be in keeping with its real value, and if a higher value could not be assigned to the property, an obvious injustice would result from the inability to deduct reasonable depletion charges. 

The unit method of computing depletion is as follows: Cost or discovery value of a mine, $1,000,000.00; estimated total tonnage, 5,000,000.

Unit depletion charge = cost total tonnage $1,000,000.00 5,000,000 = $.20 per ton.

In 1942, 60,000 tons were sold: 60,000 X $.20 $18,000.00 deple-. tion, 1942. It must be remembered that for federal income tax purposes, the depletion deduction is on the basis of the units sold, not mined.

For natural gas wells, a geologist's estimate of the change in pressure is required, and depletion charges may not necessarily be on the basis of production. 

An alternate method is known as the percentage of income method. 

It is arrived at by deducting from the value of the property a percentage of the gross income. Under the federal income tax law, the amount deducted cannot be in excess of 50 per cent of the net income from the property, computed without the allowance for depletion. The law designates the percentages for various deposits. In the case of timber stands, the percentage of income method is not permitted. 

Depreciation on buildings, equipment, machinery, etc., located on wasting assets must be provided. If the life of the depreciable properties is greater than the life of the wasting asset, and if the depreciable properties will have only scrap value at the termination of the wasting asset, the properties should be depreciated over the life of the wasting asset. The cost of the depreciable properties therefore is charged into cost in proportion to depletion; consequently, the unit-production method of depreciation is employed. If buildings, etc., costing $500,- 

000.00 with no salvage value were erected on the mine properties illustrated above, the depreciation charges in 1942 would be:

Cost of fixed assets X units sold total units 60,000 $500,000.00 X or $6,000.00. 5,000,000

In the event of a temporary cessation of operations, depreciation of properties should be charged off by using the straight-line method if the passage of time is an important factor in their depreciation. 

Both depletion and depreciation are expenses of operations which must be deducted in arriving at net profits. However, in the payment of dividends to stockholders in wasting asset corporations, it is permissible to return the depletion charge to the stockholder if the venture is to be terminated at the exhaustion of the supply. If the stockholder's dividends included profits only, the corporation would be holding the entire original capital until the final depletion, at which time each stockholder's entire share of invested capital would be returned. If an extractive industry's corporation intends to reinvest in other properties, the capital should not be returned. In any case dividends paid out of capital (before depletion) should be so labelled.

Chapter XIX  DISPOSALS OF FIXED ASSETS 

Methods of Disposition. Fixed assets may be disposed of by (1) sale, (2) retirement without sale, (3) exchange. Within any business, fixed depreciable assets are constantly being retired from service and new assets are being acquired. Exactness of accounting procedure is essential not only from the point of view of good accounting but also because of the requirements of the federal income tax law and the personal property tax laws of many states. 

Practice has not been uniform in accruing depreciation from the end of the last accounting period to the date of the disposition of the fixed asset, nor has it been uniform in depreciating the newly acquired asset from its date of. acquisition to the end of the first accounting period. Variations between companies may be illustrated as follows: a) Depreciation is computed from the exact date of acquisition to the exact date of disposition. This method, of course, is precise. b) Depreciation at the annual rate is computed on the period-opening balance of the account, and acquisitions and dispositions are not considered. c) Depreciation at the annual rate is computed on the periodclosing balance of the account, and acquisitions and dispositions are not considered. d) Depreciation at the annual rate is computed on the periodopening balance of the account, plus or minus one-half of the annual depreciation on net acquisitions or dispositions during the year. e) Depreciation at the annual rate is computed to the nearest end of the month on assets disposed or acquired. 

Sales of Fixed Assets. When fixed assets are sold, the asset account and all accounts related to the asset should be eliminated. If depreciation has been accurately provided, the difference between the net carrying value of the asset and the amount realized from its sale 402

represents a loss or gain upon disposition. The determination of the accuracy of the past depreciation provisions sometimes is very difficult; if it is known with reasonable certainty that past depreciation provisions have been incorrect, precise theoretical accounting would demand that past periods be corrected before recording the disposition. 

The practical difficulty here is that a gain or a loss on the sale of a fixed asset is reportable for federal income tax purposes, and if the income of past periods is corrected (through surplus) for former incorrect depreciation deductions, either too much or too little tax would result in the period of sale. Of course the income tax return need not show precisely the same figure for taxable income that appears as net profit on the statement of profit and loss, but differences should be avoided wherever possible.

To illustrate the disposition of a fixed asset by sale, assume that a machine cost $10,000.00. Depreciation has been at the rate of 10 per cent per year. At the end of seven and one-half years the machine is sold for $3,100.00 cash, and $200.00 is spent in moving the machine to its new owner. The entries for the disposition are as follows: Cash 

 Machine... 

Profit on Sale of Fixed Assets 

Profit on Sale of Fixed Assets. Cash..... .3,100.00 .7,500.00 10,000.00 600.00 200.00 200.00

Thus the net profit on the sale was $400.00, which would be treated as a non-operating income in the statement of profit and loss. 

Next assume the same condition, but the asset was sold for $2,000.00. The entries are as follows: Cash 

Reserve for Depreciation... 

Loss on Sale of Fixed Assets. Machine... 

Loss on Sale of Fixed Assets. Cash..... .2,000.00 .7,500.00 500.00 10,000.00 200.00 200.00

Thus the net loss on the sale was $700.00, to be treated as a nonoperating expense in the statement of profit and loss. 

At this point it may be advisable to mention that occasionally when a fixed asset is sold, Cash is charged and the asset is credited; this is incorrect, because the cost of the asset is not removed from the asset

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

account at its total acquisition price, the corresponding depreciation reserve is not eliminated, the gain or loss on sale is not shown, and the carrying values of remaining assets is incorrect. Where such situations exist, adjusting entries must be made in accordance with the foregoing illustrations. Today, errors of this nature are not as prevalent as they were before the exacting requirements of the federal income tax law. 

Assets Retired without Sale.-The majority of people visualize a . retirement as synonymous with the physical disposition of the asset, but an asset may be retired from productive service without junking it, disposing of it, or removing it from its customary location. When a fixed asset has ceased to function and when the probabilities are that the asset never will be used again for productive purposes, preferably the asset should be removed from the fixed asset category. Whether or not the asset is physically removed or demolished has no bearing on the problem of the proper record in the fixed asset accounts. It must bè understood that this accounting retirement is effective only in the face of functional cessation; a business depression, for example, furnishes no basis for retiring fixed assets which are temporarily idle but which will be used again when there is general improvement in business conditions.

When an asset is retired without sale, the asset may or may not possess a net salvage value. If the asset has a salvage value it should be recognized in the accounts. If an asset which cost $4,000.00 and which carries a reserve of $3,500.00, is retired from service, but not sold, and has an estimated salvage of $100.00, the preferred entry is as follows: 

Retired Assets (or Other Assets) 

.

Loss on Retirement of Fixed Assets. 

Fixed Asset.. 

100.00 .3,500.00 400.00 4,000.00

The account, Retired Assets, is not to be considered as a fixed asset account in the customary sense of fixed assets used in operations. A treatment less desirable than the foregoing is to permit the retired asset to remain in its former account at salvage value. 

Under either method, when the retired asset is sold at a price differing from its retirement carrying value, a gain or loss is involved; if the asset in the foregoing illustration were sold for $150.00, a gain of $50.00 must be recognized in the period of sale. If this gain was caused by the incorrect estimate of the salvage value at the time of

retirement, the profit properly belongs to the period of retirement; however, a profit or loss cannot be denied upon occurrence, and consequently the proper synchronization of profits and losses of this nature cannot be attained from any other than a theoretical angle. 

If the retired asset possesses no salvage value, the retirement loss is the difference between the balance of the asset account and its reserve for depreciation.

In many instances fixed asset disposals by sale or retirement are of an unusual nature and are unusually large. Good accounting demands that a loss be shown when it is incurred. With respect to abnormally large disposals and retirements of fixed assets at a loss, two additional schools of thought exist. The first of these is to the effect that unusual losses caused by inadequacy and obsolescence should be set up as deferred charges to future operations, and be written off to expense in future years. This stand is taken on the basis that the future will benefit by the new and more modern assets acquired to replace those removed. 

It must be remembered, however, that the future periods are benefited by the new assets, and not because of the retirement of the old or the failure to depreciate the old assets at a rate rapid enough to recover their costs during their life. The question of deferring disposal losses must not be confused with the question of deferring equipment rearrangement costs, wherein the future is benefited directly by additional expenditures on the same equipment.

If management prefers not to show an entire disposal or retirement loss as a charge against current profits, a better treatment is to show a portion of the loss as a current income charge and a portion as a charge against past periods (surplus), because the income of those past periods was inadequately charged for depreciation. If the loss is deductible for federal income tax purposes, management is more willing to charge it in entirety to income. 

The second school of thought is to the effect that abnormal retirement and disposal losses should be capitalized as a part of the cost of the newly acquired assets. The effect is the same as setting up the losses as deferred charges, but it is difficult to visualize how a new asset can be of greater value because past losses are added to its cost. The unrecovered cost of the retired asset is buried in the new asset account; it is not shown separately. Depreciation charges would include not only depreciation on the new asset but also that on an asset no longer in existence. This entire question of capitalization of unrecovered costs

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

is closely allied with exchanges and the resultant income tax problems, both of which are treated in the following section. 

Exchange of Fixed Assets.-The problem of accounting for assets acquired in exchange was discussed briefly in chapter XVI. If an asset is traded in toward the purchase of another similar asset, the Bureau of Internal Revenue will not permit the recognition of a gain or loss on the asset traded in if the past depreciation policy has been acceptable. 

The unrecovered cost of the asset traded in plus the net expenditure for the new asset are held to constitute the basis for future depreciation of the new asset. This ruling of the Bureau is in general conformity with the thoughts expressed in the preceding paragraph, and the proper accounting for assets exchanged is thereby discouraged. 

Two illustrations are presented, one assuming proper accounting and one in accordance with federal income tax regulations. 

1. If the new asset is recorded at its full cash market price. Assume that the Fairfax Company originally paid $2,000.00 for a delivery truck; it carried a reserve for depreciation of $1,500.00 at the time it was traded in for a new truck which had an established market price of $2,500.00; the old truck plus $2,200.00 cash were given in exchange for the new truck. cash. The entries to dispose of Truck No. 1 and to acquire Truck No. 2 

would be as follows: b) Cash

2. Procedure for exchanges under the federal income tax law. As pointed out, for federal income tax purposes the Bureau of Internal Revenue does not recognize gains or losses arising from the exchange of similarly productive equipment; the basis of the newly acquired

asset is taken to be the sum of the net book value of the retired asset, plus the expenditure for the new asset. Assuming the same conditions as those illustrated in the foregoing exchange, the entry would be as:

Truck No. 2, to the extent of $2,700.00 ($2,500.00+ $200.00) will be depreciated over its life. Over the total life of both Trucks No. 1 and No. 2, the expense deduction will be the same under both methods illustrated, but its periodic incidence will be different. It should be noted that if the old asset is not traded in but is sold for cash and the new asset bought, in two independent transactions, any loss or gain on the disposal of the old asset is recognized for income tax purposes. 

Therefore, even for tax purposes, the accounting entries may be those illustrated in 1 (b) above.

FIXED ASSET APPRAISALS 

Appraisals.-The traditional method of valuing fixed assets is at cost less the accumulated depreciation. In special cases, the use of historical costs may be entirely inadequate as a means of showing fair valuations. An appraisal results in a revaluation of an asset or assets. 

Arbitrary write-ups and write-downs of asset figures most definitely are not appraisals; often they have no basis other than the desire of management to reflect a specific predetermined financial condition, whether true or not.

Normally, the accountant does not make the appraisal, for that is the function of the engineer and the appraisal company; the latter have become increasingly prominent in recent years. The accountant, however, is faced with the responsibility of certifying to statements involving reappraisals, and he is also responsible for the correct preparation of tax returns. The accountant is traditionally a conservative individual, and this tendency has been strengthened by the reports of certain cases of gross overvaluations resulting from appraisals; therefore many accountants still abhor appraisals. However, the well-founded appraisal is here to stay, and perhaps justifiably so. If price levels rise over a long period of time, assets acquired under conditions of low cost may cause an improper portrayal of condition in the accounting statements..

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Frequently assets are acquired from a company in forced liquidation at a "bargain"; consequently, if an appraisal is made and reflected in the records, a more accurate statement of condition may result. It is to be emphasized that minor changes in value and even large changes caused by conditions of a strictly temporary nature are not to be considered as affecting plant values from the point of view of recording appraisals.

Appreciation is the excess of the appraised value over the book value of an asset. It represents an increase in value caused by higher replacement costs and upward changes in market value.

Devaluation or declination is the excess of the book value over the appraised value. It represents a decrease in value caused by lower replacement costs and downward changes in market value. The opposite of appreciation is not depreciation.

Sound value is the present replacement cost or appraisal value of an asset minus depreciation computed on the basis of replacement cost or appraised value, accumulated from the date of acquisition to the present date; stated in another manner, it is appraised reproduction cost new minus depreciation computed on appraised reproduction cost new, accumulated over the past life of the asset. 

Condition per cent is the percentage of sound value to appraised value. If the appraised value new is $100,000.00, and if depreciation on appraised value amounts to $35,000.00, the asset has a condition per cent of 65.

The foregoing concepts are illustrated in the following table:
