ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

The statement of the appraised values in parenthetical fashion does not lend as much weight to the validity of the higher appraisal value as does the reflection of the appraisal in the money columns of the statement.

Insurance Coverage. - Recoveries under insurance contracts are based upon present sound value and not upon book values. Consequently, many appraisals are made for the purpose of determining correct amounts of insurance. If the reasonable present sound value of insured assets is unknown at the time of loss, negotiation is the basis of settlement with the insurance companies. Naturally, an asset cannot be appraised accurately after it is destroyed or materially damaged. In connection with appraisals for purposes of insurance coverage, the question occasionally arises as to the desirability of placing appraised values upon the books. If the appraisal is a true reflection of changed values, there seems to be no good reason for failure to adjust the books; however, if one is not in favor of reflecting appraised values on the books, at least an appraisal schedule should be prepared and retained. 

Sale of Assets. If a portion or all of the assets of a business are to be sold, an appraisal may result in figures widely divergent from those carried in the accounts. No one denies that the appraisal values furnish a better basis for the determination of the sales price. 

Tax Valuations.-Frequently, business organizations desire adjustments of valuations for real and personal property tax purposes. Appraisal reports serve as material in support of the claim. Rarely are these reports reflected on the books. 

Reorganization, Refinancing, Merger, and Consolidation. - When businesses are reorganized with or without a restatement of the capital, appraisals are desirable for the more accurate portrayal of asset values. 

In mergers and consolidations, the book value of the assets of the various companies entering the combination may be on widely varying bases, for the assets may have been acquired under highly different conditions of purchase and at different levels of the business cycle. So that all assets of the participating companies may be reduced to a common basis appraisals are necessary; if appraisals were not made, inequitable distribution of the new stock to the shareholders of the former companies would result. These conclusions are not intended to imply that asset values furnish the only or even the principal basis for the division of stock among the stockholders of the former companies. The earning power of the various companies is always impor tant in such a division; frequently it is the dominant factor.

The Recording of Appraisals.-In accounting for appraisals, it must be remembered that when assets are appraised upward, (1) the increase in value must not be credited to Earned, Capital, Paid-In, or Donated Surplus, (2) no income is realized from the appraisal, (3) future depreciation must be correctly computed and recorded. 

There are two variations of one method in use for the recording of an appraisal.

In many instances, appraisals are made to verify the propriety of depreciation accumulation. In the preceding illustrations, estimates of changes in the life of the asset were accompanied by changes in the value of the assets. If asset acquisition values are not altered by the appraisal, but if the life-estimate is altered, the only adjustments are to the depreciation reserve and to Earned Surplus for past periods' incorrect depreciation. If the purpose of the appraisal is to estimate the actual depreciation to the date of the appraisal, it may not be necessary to adjust the reserve, because the reserve is created on an accounting basis rather than on an actual basis, and actual and accounting depreciation seldom coincide except at the termination of the life of the asset.

Depreciation after Appraisal.-After depreciable fixed assets have been appraised, subsequent charges for depreciation expense must be based on either (1) the original cost of the asset, or (2) the gross appraised value of the asset.

The purpose of recording depreciation as an expense is to charge operations with the cost of the expired portion of an asset, just as operations are charged for wages, materials used, taxes, and other expenses. 

In the sale of a product, business desires to recover the cost of manufacturing, of administration, and the cost of selling plus a reasonable profit. Depreciation does not provide a fund for the purchase of new assets; rather, it simply recovers expenditures already incurred. Consequently, if depreciation is charged on figures which are in excess of the cost of the asset, actual expenses are overstated. On the basis of the purposes of depreciation and the cost recovery theory, it appears logical to compute depreciation on cost. Now let us consider this question in connection with the depreciation of property revalued at reproduction new appraisal figures.

If depreciation is based on appraisal figures, the depreciation will reflect current cost conditions. If Company A entered its field under

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

low cost under cons, and if Company B entered the same field later under conditions of high costs, Company B is at a cost disadvantage as compared with Company A. Theoretically, Company A could charge less for its products but its prices will almost certainly reflect the higher current costs, particularly if it charges depreciation on the higher present costs of equipment. Practically, Company A will enjoy a higher rate of return for dollars of capital invested, but unless costs are com puted on a current basis, the higher profits may be paid out as dividends and capital will not be conserved for the replacement of new assets at the higher price levels. If trade associations, or member companies of a contemplated merger, desired comparative operating statistics, and if the different members of the association or merger acquired their fixed assets under varying cost conditions, comparative figures would not be possible unless depreciation is computed on appraised values for all assets.

Basing depreciation on original cost and basing it on reproduction cost each has its advantages and disadvantages. In public utility accounting the problem is vital because in that industry cost determines the selling price--the rates charged for service. Today, more accountants than ever before prefer replacement value as a base.

Illustrations are now presented, basing depreciation on original cost and also basing it on reproduction cost. Assume that the accounts, after appraisal at December 31, 1942, were as follows:

At the end of the life of the asset, the Reserve for Depreciation, based on cost, will contain a balance of $250,000.00; the Reserve for 

Depreciation, based on the appraisal increase, will contain a balance of $50,000.00; the sum of the two reserves will be $300,000.00, which equals the cost of the building, $250,000.00, plus the appraisal of $50,000.00. There will be no balance in Surplus Arising from Appraisal of Fixed Assets at the end of the life of the asset. 

It is necessary that the appraisal surplus be reduced annually, so that, when the asset is exhausted, all accounts connected with the asset are eliminated from the books. The annual charge of $2,500.00 (1/15 of $37,500.00) accomplishes the elimination of the appraisal surplus at the termination of the life of the asset; at the end of the life of the asset, there is no remaining unearned appraisal surplus, because there is no asset upon which such an increment can be created if life expectancy is correct and the asset exhausted and retired.

If the foregoing entry was the only annual entry, at the end of twenty years the account, Surplus Arising from Appraisal of Fixed Assets would still contain a balance of $37,500.00; thus, with an asset of $300,000.00 and depreciation reserves of $300,000.00, it would appear quite peculiar if a reappraisal surplus of $37,500.00 was in existence. Therefore, the following annual entry should be made:

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING Surplus Arising from Appraisal of Fixed Assets.. 

Earned Surplus 

To transfer 1/15 of $37,500.00 from reappraisal sur plus to earned surplus. 2,500.00 2,500.00

Thus, if depreciation is based on gross appraisal, depreciation expense is $2,500.00 greater than if it is based on cost; net profit is $2,500.00 less; the $2,500.00 additional depreciation is considered realized because it was charged to operating expense; the net effect on 

Earned Surplus is zero, because Earned Surplus was lowered by the additional depreciation and restored by the Earned Surplus credit. The costs of the products manufactured include the current costs of the fixed assets being used. The depreciation on appreciation separates the profit due to the increased prices of fixed assets from the normal trading profit.

Federal income tax provisions for the allowable deduction for depreciation are on a cost basis; that is, only cost may be recovered through depreciation charges; depreciation on appreciation is not deductible. Consequently, meticulous care must be exercised to distinguish between depreciation on original cost and depreciation on replacement value.

Appraisal of Fixed Assets is not retained on the books. A capital stock dividend, legal in nearly all states, may be declared and paid in amount equal to the value of the appraisal surplus. Most state laws prohibit the payment of a cash dividend from appraisal surplus. If such action is taken, the appraisal surplus disappears and a capital stock is increased. 

When a company is refinanced with an accompanying appraisal of assets, or when a merger is effected with accompanying appraisal of assets, capital stock almost always is issued to the full value of the appraisal figures; consequently, an Appraisal Surplus account does not appear. Since there is no appraisal surplus, it cannot be amortized over the remaining life of the asset. In order to prevent the impairment of the value of the capital stock resulting from appreciation in book figures where appraisals may be none too accurate, care must be exercised to maintain adequate depreciation reserves and to prevent an overstatement of earned surplus. One of two plans may be followed. a) Depreciation may be charged to expense on the basis of appraisal figures, thus effecting a reduction in profits and in earned surplus. Using the illustration presented on page 415 (Illustration 2), the annual entry for depreciation would be as follows:

Depreciation Expense on Building.. 

Reserve for Depreciation of Building (on cost)...

Reserve for Depreciation of Building, Appreciation per Appraisal 15,000.00 12,500.00 2,500.00 b) Depreciation may be charged to expense on the basis of original cost, and earned surplus periodically reduced in order to conserve the integrity of the capital. The annual entries would be as follows: 

Depreciation Expense on Building.. 

12,500.00 

Reserve for Depreciation of Building (on cost) 12,500.00 

Earned Surplus 2,500.00 2,500.00

Reserve for Depreciation of Building, Appreciation per Appraisal Declinations, or Decreases Resulting from Appraisals. The preceding discussion and illustrations have assumed that appraisals resulted in increases in value; just as frequently, appraisals result in decreases in values. It may happen that original capital values were excessively high, or it may happen that prices were high at the time of asset acquisition; later, asset values may severely decline, probably accompanied by a decrease in business volume and in profits. The result

of the generally less attractive condition is a desire to reduce fixed asset figures so that depreciation charges will be lower in the operating statements.

The valuation downward may or may not be accompanied by changes in the capital stock structure of a corporation. In periods of business depression, the chances are always favorable for a value reduction of the capital stock because of a poor condition of the surplus accounts. There is no real justification for reflecting reductions of asset values in capital stock accounts, unless the admission is made that the stock was watered when the assets were acquired. Likewise, there is no justification for charging arbitrary value reductions to Surplus, as this merely buries future operating charges in Capital; however, actual reductions in asset values must be charged to Earned Surplus. In any case future expenses are thereby reduced in the statements prepared by the company.

Chapter XX  

Sources and General Nature. The general sources of intangible assets are as follows: (1) favorable differentials in profits arising from the skill and ability of owners and managers, advantageous locations, customer satisfaction, and other public relations factors; (2) monopolistic privileges granted by governmental authority; (3) monopolistic privileges obtained through private initiative. All must result in favorable profit differentials in order to gain proper recognition in the accounts.

From the first source arises good-will in all its forms; patents, copyrights, franchises, and trade-marks arise from the second source; secret processes, formulas, and leaseholds arise from the third source. These sources of intangibles may be interlocking and dependent upon each other; for example, good-will may be the result of a patent or a secret process.

All intangible assets are non-physical, but not all non-physical assets are classified as intangible; for example, accounts receivable and securities are intangible, but they are not classified with the intangible assets of a business; a leasehold is intangible, but the item leased may be tangible. 

Many intangible assets cannot be independently and separately transferred; for example, it is impossible to sell good-will without selling all or a part of the physical assets of a business. The majority of the intangible assets are inextricably interwoven with the general operations of the business as a whole, and are closely related to the earning capacity of the business. A company may own patents or trade-marks, but if these assets fail to produce income, they are of not much value. A tangible asset, such as a building, would not necessarily lose a large amount of its value if the occupants failed to earn profits, because the building might be sold to be used for another and more profitable purpose.

Because of the close relationship of intangible assets and their 423

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

income-producing ability, the entire problem of the proper valuation of the intangibles is closely connected with the valuation of the business as a whole. Consequently, as we shall see, the customary cost approach applied to the valuation of intangible assets may produce unsatisfactory and inequitable results, thereby making necessary other approaches to the valuation of this group of assets. Proper valuation of intangibles is one of the most difficult phases of valuation, because of the relationship to the earning power of the business; and because the earning power of a business is subject to wide fluctuations intangible valuation is further complicated. For purposes of valuation, an intangible asset may be compared with a tangible asset which is so highly specialized that it is of value only to its immediate owner. For any intangible to have value, there must be profitable operations, and usually the operations must be more profitable than normally experienced among competitors in the industry. A differential advantage must exist before value can be attributed to an intangible. 

Good-Will.-Good-will is a profit value advantage represented by a favorable profit differential. Stated in another manner, it is the capitalized value of the profits which are in excess of the normal rate of return on the invested capital (excluding good-will) for the industry as a whole. The advantage leading to the good-will may result from name, renown, reputation, personality, merchandise quality, price policy, location, labor relations with employees, the ability to hold present and gain new customers, the approval of investors, the approval of creditors, service, and all other attributes in favor of a business. 

Thus good-will is defined as a profit value advantage or the capitalized value of the profits which are in excess of the normal rate of return on the invested capital. To illustrate, assume that companies 

A and B are each capitalized at $1,000,000.00. Company A has an average net profit of $100,000.00 per year, while Company B has an average net profit of $175,000.00 per year. Assume, also, that the average rate of return for the industry as a whole is 10 per cent per year on the invested capital. Company B enjoys an additional profit of $75,000.00 per year; this differential profit may be attributed to goodwill; the value of the good-will may be determined by capitalizing the excess profits at an interest rate that measures the degree of risk involved. At the rate of 10 per cent the value of the good-will is determined to be $750,000.00; at 15 per cent the value is $500,000.00.

The Recognition of Good-will.-Generally, accountants prefer that

good-will be recognized in the accounts only to the extent of its actual cost to the purchaser of a business. It is true that good-will may exist in cases where a business does not change hands, but the peculiarly intangible nature of the item often makes it difficult to value accurately, and therefore it is considered best not to create such an elusive asset on the books. Those persons who favor the recognition of good-will even if it is not actually purchased point out that it is inconsistent to show donated and discovered assets as such and not be willing to admit good-will to the accounts even though the determination of its value be difficult. This is true, but the donated or discovered assets possess value even when divorced from their present owners, whereas the value of good-will represents a value inseparable from the business as an entity. In addition, the cost of a tangible asset is influential in the determination of operating expenses and in the establishment of administrative policies. The earning power of a business is measured in terms of the capital assets, at cost or cost adjusted, and to create good-will values which were not purchased simply tends to hide the existence of excess profits. It is the function of accounting to record determinable values, principally cost; as the estimates of future profits vary, the value of good-will varies, and the determination of an assignable value without a sale would be well-nigh impossible. When nonpurchased good-will is recognized in the accounts, it reflects an attempt to segregate an advantageous position into one element, good-will, when actually the advantageous position might be caused by factors other than true good-will. From the foregoing, it is evident that as a general rule good-will should be recognized in the accounts only upon its purchase.

One permissible divergence from this attitude is in connection with reorganizations. There the necessary restatement of capital structures often results in intangible values which may be recognized in the accounts. Care should be exercised to be certain that intangible values actually exist and are not the result of a shuffling of corporate capital structures designed to reflect a better position than actually exists. 

In a partnership, a retiring partner often is paid for his good-will. 

No question exists as to the validity of setting up good-will for the amount paid. In such a case, however, the question may arise as to the desirability of using the price paid to the retiring partner as a basis for estimating the entire good-will of the business and of entering this amount on the books with offsetting entries to all of the partners'

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

accounts. If good-will is to be recognized only upon purchase, only the amount of the payment to the retiring partner should be so recognized. 

In the event of a merger involving several companies of varying earning capacities, the stockholders of the high-profit companies are entitled to receive larger payments for their holdings than are the stockholders of the lower-profit units entering the merger; the highprofit companies enjoy a differential advantage and the payment for this differential advantage represents a purchase of good-will which should be recognized in the accounts. 

The position adopted, that good-will should be recognized in the accounts only upon its purchase, means that the amount of the goodwill is the price paid in excess of the fair value of other assets acquired, regardless of how the excess is determined; it does not mean that certain costs of other items should be viewed as a cost of good-will. 

Several of the items which should not be considered as good-will are discussed in the following paragraphs. 

Large expenditures for advertising made for the purpose of creating a future demand may result in good-will, but the result is no justification for charging advertising expense to the Good-will account. If advertising is in excess of normal and is made for the purpose of creating long-time demand, the best method of handling the expenditure is to charge the entire amount to expense, because the increased business may not develop; the next best method is to charge the current period with its normal portion of the advertising cost and set the remainder up as a deferred charge to future operations. 

Frequently, the Good-will account is charged with organization expenses. Organization expenses may be charged to Surplus immediately, but more usually they are set up as a deferred charge to future surplus; until written off to Surplus-perhaps within a period of three to five years the amount of these charges should be carried in the Organization Expense account; this is an intangible account and the unamortized balance should appear in the intangible asset section of the balance sheet. The costs of effecting a business organization definitely are not chargeable to good-will.

Occasionally the losses of early years are charged to good-will on the assumption that such losses are inevitable and only by incurring them can the business ever reach a period of profitable operation. Since the validity of this assumption is doubtful, such practices understate losses and overstate surplus and are to be condemned.

In many instances the ownership of a patent results in an advantageous position, conferring large profits upon the owner. Even after the legal expiration of the life of the patent, the past advantageous position may enable the owner to continue indefinitely to earn higher than normal profits. Thus the patent ultimately results in good-will; however, the advantage gained during the life of the patent should not be capitalized as good-will even upon the expiration of the patent, because the advantageous position may be lost, and also because goodwill was not purchased. If it is proper to write off the patent into expense over a period not to exceed its life, it is likewise proper to refrain from capitalizing good-will emerging from the patent. 

In the past, the discount on capital stock issues frequently was charged to the Good-will account. But good-will is the result of profits in excess of normal and is in no way related to capital transactions; fortunately this practice has been almost completely discontinued. 

A variation of capital stock discounts may arise when the assets of a corporation or a partnership are sold to another corporation, and payment is received in the form of capital stock of the vendee corporation with a total par value in excess of a fair value of the assets transferred. If the par value of this stock reflects its market value then it is true that a payment was made for the excess value, and consequently the establishment of a Good-will account is proper; however, if the market value of the stock is less than its par value, to this extent the charge should be to Discount on Capital Stock rather than to Good-will. 

In other cases of corporate financing and operation, a portion of capital stock issue may be sold for cash at a premium and a portion of it may be exchanged for tangible assets. Evidently the value of the stock is the total cash received, that is, par plus the premium. Should the difference between established cash price of the stock and the value of tangible assets be charged to good-will, or as a part of the cost of the asset? If the tangible assets acquired were transferred from an organized and operating company, it appears as though good-will may have been purchased; if the assets were acquired to be put in operation for the first time, good-will was not purchased, and evidently the total value of the stock should be assigned to the tangible assets acquired. 

Finally, there have been many cases where a Good-will account has been set up arbitrarily without regard as to whether good-will exists or not. Even if an organization actually does possess good-will, as reflected in excess profits, there is little justification for the arbitrary

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

recognition of intangible earning power as an asset, even if the credit is made properly to a reappraisal surplus reserve. It should be noted, however, that such a write-up does little harm, for (a) it is obvious to the reader of the balance sheet, and (b) it has no effect on the income or expense of any accounting period. 

The Valuation of Good-Will.-In arriving at the capitalized value of good-will for purposes of the purchase and sale of a business or a portion of it, one of several methods of valuation may be followed; the exact method selected will depend upon, and will vary with, the conditions and circumstances surrounding each individual case. If an entire business organization is sold at a round price arrived at by bargaining between buyer and seller, no attempt may be made by the seller to segregate good-will values; the difference between the values of all the tangible assets and sales price may be considered as profit on the sale due to good-will. Of course the buyer must either set up the assets at the price paid for them rather than at their previous book values, or he must set up the difference as good-will or another intangible asset. 

Although bargaining between the buyer and the seller is the method frequently employed to arrive at good-will values, more accurate methods may be employed. Even in the case where a seller asked $1,000,000.00 for a business, assigning $800,000.00 to the tangible assets and $200,000.00 to the good-will, and finally sells for $900,- 

000.00, it does not necessarily follow that the reduction of $100,000.00 represented a reduction in good-will; it may have represented a general price reduction or a reduction in other specific assets. 

When establishing a value for good-will, several factors must be taken into consideration: 

1. When a purchaser buys a business and pays for good-will, he is buying the probable excess profits of the future and not the known excess profits of the past. In many phases of business activity, however, the past is the primary basis for measuring future action; this holds true for the valuation of good-will to a considerable extent, although any certain or even probable future variation from trend would assuredly be given consideration. 

2. When the past is used as the basis of future good-will computation, the period considered should not be so long that the distant past exercises too much influence in a current situation; nor should the period be so short that one or two unusual years are given un weight. A five-year period normally indicates current trends. due

3. When past profits are used as the basis of computation, net operating profits should be used and not net profits, because nonoperating incomes and expenses vary and are not directly related to operations. 

4. The profits should be submitted to thorough audit. They should be corrected for unusual items, such as abnormally high or subnormally low salaries or other expenses. 

5. Recognition must be given to the improbability of the maintenance of the present excess earning capacity. 

6. If possible, the effect of any contemplated change in personnel, should be measured. 

7. Variations in profits between years should be analyzed and scientifically corrected for major fluctuations, so that the normal rate and normal earnings are ascertained.

If the profits have fluctuated widely over a period of five years, with losses in one or more of the five years, the instability of the profits would indicate a high risk and the necessity for a high capitalization rate in measuring good-will. Predictions for the future would be very uncertain. For example:

YEAR 1940 1941  

PROFITS $ 40,000.00 60,000.00 

10,000.00 loss 25,000.00 85,000.00 $200,000.00 ÷ 5 = $40,000.00 average

If profits have decreased steadily over a five-year period, the indication is that the average profits for future years will be lower, other factors being equal. For example:

YEAR 1940 1941 1942 1943 1944 

PROFITS .$ 80,000.00 60,000.00 40,000.00 15,000.00 5,000.00 $200,000.00 ÷ 5 = $40,000.00 average

If the profits have remained fairly stable, but showed a slight tendency to increase, it is probable that the average of future profits will

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

be higher, other factors remaining constant. Furthermore, the stability of profits justifies a relatively low capitalization rate in measuring goodwill. For example:

YEAR 

1940 1941  

PROFITS 

.$ 37,000.00 38,000.00 39,000.00 41,000.00 45,000.00 $200,000.005 $40,000.00 average

If the profits have steadily increased, other factors being equal, the chances are that future profits will be much higher. In such a case the good-will is entitled to a higher valuation than in the preceding illustration because of the probability that profits will increase more rapidly. For example: YEAR 1940 1941 1942 1943 1944 PROFITS 30,000.00 35,000.00 40,000.00 45,000.00

50,000.00 $200,000.00 ÷ 5 = $40,000.00 average

In each of the preceding illustrations, the average annual profits are the same, $40,000.00; however, a study of the stability and the trend of the profits in each case indicates wide ranges in the estimates of future profits and in the rate of capitalization to be used in measuring good-will, even though other factors are assumed to be equal. 

There are several methods available for the computation of the value of the good-will, some of which will be illustrated. As the basis of the illustrations, assume:

Agreed value of the net tangible fixed assets plus net current assets (net worth)....

Method 1.-Capitalization of the past average annual excess profits. 

Average annual profit for the company. 

Normal return on capital... 

Average annual excess profit. 

Capitalization of the average annual excess profit at the normal rate of return ($15,000.00.10) results in good-will of..... .$ 45,000.00 30,000.00 .$ 15,000.00 . $150,000.00

Thus the value of the good-will is viewed as a perpetuity; if the average annual profit in future years is $45,000.00, the rate of return earned on the new capitalization is 10 per cent. If this company continues to earn 10 per cent on its increased capitalization and if that rate continues to be normal for the industry, there are no more excess profits for this company. 

Method 2.-Capitalization of the past average annual excess profits projected for a given number of years. If it is thought that the excess profits will continue for a given number of future years, the valuation of the good-will would be the present value of an annuity for the given number of years. Using the same figures as in the foregoing illustration the value of the good-will would be the present value of an annuity of $15,000.00 at 10 per cent for the given number of years. 

In any business, the probabilities are remote for the indefinite continuation of excess profits; competition, changing capital requirements, and many other factors tend to level the profits of existing enterprises. Consequently, it may be agreed between buyer and seller to view the value of the good-will as an annuity for a specific number of years rather than as a perpetuity.

Method 3.-Capitalization of the average annual excess profit at an agreed rate of interest higher than the normal rate of return, still using the same figures, the average annual excess profit capitalized at an agreed rate of 20 per cent would give a good-will value of $75,000.00 ($15,000.00 ÷ 20%). The reason for the rate of interest higher than the normal rate is the uncertainty of the continuance of profits in excess of a fair return on tangible value, and therefore the uncertainty as to the permanence of good-will.

This method is incorrect in that it assumes that all profits are the result of good-will, whereas only the excess profits are the result of good-will.

The Amortization of Good-Will.-Accountants, businessmen, and laymen all are in disagreement concerning the amortization of goodwill acquired by purchase and properly capitalized. 

At this point it should be repeated that good-will should not appear unless acquired by purchase for cash or created by proper treatment during the course of a merger or reorganization. If good-will, resulting in a differential profit advantage, is created by management, labor, the product, or the customer, such good-will should not be set up on the books nor appear on the balance sheet. Unfortunately this general principle is not always followed. If good-will is viewed as a perpetuity, it seems that it should not be amortized. However, if one follows the theory that long-time permanent declines in the values of fixed assets should be provided for by direct write-off or by the creation of surplus reserves, then it would appear proper to write off good-will if it declines in value. The practical trouble is that if the good-will has declined in value, Earned Surplus, against which a write-down of good-will must be charged, is probably already in a rather depleted condition; this causes management to refrain from writing down good-will because there is no other account to absorb the devaluation. 

If excess profits continue it would seem to be improper to write good-will, the income-producing asset, off the books. Conservatism cannot well be advanced as an excuse for writing off good-will properly acquired. The federal income tax law does not permit the amortiza-

tion of good-will as an allowable deduction in an income tax return. 

If published accounting statements were required to state the source of good-will as an asset, perhaps the good-will item would be eliminated except in those cases where it was actually purchased. The problem of the amortization of good-will is one which is individual and peculiar to each situation. 

If good-will is amortized, it should not be shown as an income deduction but as a charge to Surplus; the Good-will account may be credited directly or a valuation reserve may be created. 

Patents. A patent is a monopolistic privilege granted by the government, giving the owner of the patent the exclusive right to manufacture or sell or otherwise benefit from the patent. The value of a patent emanates from its ability to earn income and not from the mere fact that it is a patent. Protection under a patent begins at the time of application for the patent and extends for seventeen years from the time it is finally granted; therefore, the period of protection may exceed seventeen years.

Patents may be acquired with the other assets of a going concern, or they may be acquired independently. They may be acquired by purchase from an owner or they may be acquired by development and grant of an original patent. 

If a patent is acquired by purchase, the purchase price constitutes its cost. If it is acquired by development, its cost is made up of the cost of experimentation and development, the cost of drawings and models, filing fees, and legal fees. Many companies maintain experimental departments whose sole function is to develop products or processes which may be patented. The costs incurred by the experimental department and which produce patents should be capitalized as a cost of the patents; costs incurred which do not result in a useful patent should be charged to expense. Frequently all costs incurred by an experimental or research division are charged as a cost of the successful patents developed. This procedure is satisfactory so long as these costs do not exceed the value of the patents developed. 

In many instances patents are purchased for the sole purpose of stopping a competitor from obtaining them; these patents are then "buried," that is, they are not used and there is no intention to use them. In such cases, the cost of the patent should be charged to expense because the patent is non-productive. 

A patent may cover a product or a process; in general, process

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

patents are of greater income productivity than are product patents, because of the opportunities to earn royalties. Today there are in existence large corporations whose sole function is the holding and leasing of patents.

When a patent is acquired by purchase or by development, its cost should be charged to the Patent account. The value of a patent is always questionable until the patent has been successfully defended in an infringement suit. If an infringement suit is won, the cost of the suit may be added to the cost of the patent, as an additional cost of final acquisition. If an infringement suit is lost, the cost of the suit and all capitalized costs of the patent should be charged off to expense and that particular patent removed from the Patent account. 

The cost of a patent should be amortized over seventeen years or the estimated useful life of the patent, whichever is the shorter; in no event should the amortization period exceed seventeen years. If a patent covers strictly style merchandise, it is advisable to charge off the cost of the patent in the first period or two of production. In no case should an obsolete patent appear as an asset. If a patent decreases in productivity, its amortization should be accelerated. In amortizing the cost of a patent, a reserve for patent amortization may be created or the patent account may be credited directly. The latter is the more usual practice. 

Subsidiary ledger accounts should be maintained for each patent. 

However, if several patents are acquired for a lump sum, it may be impossible to assign separate costs to each patent; in such cases the group should be treated as a unit in the computation of the annual amortization. For example: 

Cost of 20 patents of varying ages.

Leaseholds.-A leasehold represents the right to use and operate real property for the period of the contract; it differs from outright ownership in that the period of enjoyment is limited to the period of the lease and the privilege to dispose of the leased property does not exist as it does in the case of ownership in fee simple.

If the owner of the lease was a party to the original contract and the lease calls for periodic rental payments, it is not usually treated as an asset; the periodic rentals should be charged to expense. If an original lessee subleases property at a substantial profit, it may be proper to set up the asset value of the income-producing ability of the lease; this will be treated later in this chapter. If a lease requires an advance payment covering the life of the lease, the advance payments may be set up as an asset, Leaseholds, and amortized over the life of the lease.

When leases are executed covering a period of years and payment is made in advance, the advance payment is the present value of an annuity. A rental of $10,000.00 per year for ten years is obviously not the same thing as $100,000.00 for ten years to be paid as a single advance payment. On a contract calling for $10,000.00 per year for ten years the lessee might be willing to pay single advance payment equal to the present value of the series of $10,000.00 annual rentals computed at a proper rate of interest. To illustrate the computation, assume the foregoing figures, with the $10,000.00 annual rental payable at the beginning of each year. Improvements to Leased Property.-When a lessee improves leased properties, the improvements revert to the owner of the property at the expiration of the lease. For example, a lessee of land may erect a building thereon; the building becomes the property of the owner of the land at the expiration of the lease. As another example, a building may be leased; alterations, additions and improvements made by the lessee revert to the lessor at the termination of the lease. 

Improvements made by the lessee to leased property should be charged to an account entitled Leasehold Improvements. The Leasehold Improvements account should be depreciated over the life of the improvement or over the life of the lease, whichever is the shorter. 

As an example, assume that a loft building is leased for 25 years; the lessee makes improvements at a cost of $50,000.00 which are estimated to last 40 years; the $50,000.00 of improvements should be depreciated over the twenty-five-year period. If the lease was for fifty years and the improvements were estimated to last forty years, they should be depreciated over the forty-year period. 

Assume that a building was leased for twenty-five years with the privilege of renewal for an additional twenty-five years, and that upon occupancy the lessee made improvements to the extent of $50,000.00 which will last fifty years. Should the $50,000.00 improvements be

depreciated over twenty-five or fifty years? The depreciation should be on a twenty-five-year basis, because it is not known until close to the end of the first twenty-five-year period whether or not the renewal privilege will be exercised. If the lease is renewed, past depreciation should be corrected by proper adjustment of the Reserve for Depreciation and the Surplus accounts and depreciation at the reduced rate (2 per cent in this case) continued through the second twenty-five-year period.

Leasehold Appraisals. In certain cases, leaseholds become valuable because of increased rentals over a long period of time. For example, if a fifty-year lease were executed in 1940 at an annual rental of $25,000.00, and if property values increased in that particular neighborhood, it might be possible, by 1955, to sublease at an annual rental of $75,000.00. The possession of the lease, at a differential profit of $50,000.00 per year for the remaining thirty-five years, represents a valuable asset. If the asset is taken up on the books of the lessee, it should be valued at the present value of an annuity of $50,000.00 for 35 years at (assume) 3 per cent, or $1,074,361.00. If the leasehold is set up as an asset, because of increased rental values, it should be treated as any tangible asset subject to appraisal and the credit should be to Appraisal Surplus. If the party holding the lease prefers to follow a more conservative practice, the value of the lease can be shown as a footnote to the balance sheet. 

When a lease is executed, and the lessee intends to sublease the property, he will continue to be liable to the owner whether or not subleases are executed and whether or not sub-tenants pay their rent. 

In such cases, the lessee should provide for his possible loss by setting up a contingent liability which can be extinguished when the liability is terminated.

Copyrights. Copyrights, like patents, confer a monopolistic privilege upon the owner, affording protection to writings, drawings, and literary productions. Copyrights are granted for twenty-eight years,

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

with a privilege of renewal for an additional twenty-eight years if a new application is made before the expiration of the twenty-seventh year. A large portion of copyrighted materials does not enjoy a publication period of twenty-eight years; consequently, copyrights normally should be amortized over a period of less than twenty-eight years. The period of amortization must be judged in the light of past actual sales and potential future sales.

If a copyright is secured by a publisher directly from the government the cost is negligible, not exceeding a few dollars in any instance. 

If a copyright is purchased from a grantee, any amount, commensurate with its value, large or small, may be paid for it. When copyrights are obtained from the government, it is advisable to charge their nominal cost against the cost of the first reproduction. If a copyright is purchased for a considerable sum, it should be amortized over a period assumed to be reasonable in view of anticipated sales. 

Franchises.-A franchise is a contract between a governmental subdivision and a private company, usually a utility, granting the latter certain privileges, for the benefit of the public. A franchise may be perpetual or it may be of limited life; it also may be revocable by the granting body or it may be irrevocable; also, it may be granted gratis, for a lump-sum fee, or for a recurring fee. Where a franchise is revocable, the contract usually stipulates that the governing body shall buy the properties upon revocation.

If a franchise is secured gratis, no value should be assigned to this privilege, although without it the grantee could not operate. It has value, but its value is similar to that of non-purchased good-will, and is closely related to the entire profit operation of the organization. 

If a perpetual, irrevocable franchise is purchased for a substantial amount, the full cost of obtaining it should be capitalized in the Franchise account. There is no necessity for amortization. If the same franchise were revocable, it should be amortized over a few years. If a franchise is of limited life, its cost should be amortized over its life. 

In amortizing franchises, the straight-line method is almost universally adopted. A Reserve for Franchise Amortization may be credited, or the charge-off may be directly to the asset. 

The public utility or service commissions of most states specify the items which may be charged to the Franchise account, and also specify the method of amortization of the account. 

Trade-Marks.-Trade-marks are symbols, designs, brand names,

and any other accepted indication of ready recognition attached to a company's products. Trade-marks are valid under common law, but they may be and should be registered. If a company has the ability to build up a valuable trade by the use of a trade-mark, it possesses a valuable asset which should be protected. Trade-marks do not expire, and ownership is determined by priority and continuous use. Because they do not expire, their costs need not be amortized unless the trademark loses its value or unless it is discontinued. 

Trade-marks should be valued at cost including both the cost to develop and the cost of legal protection. If a trade-mark, like goodwill, results in high profits, the practice of writing up the value of the trade-marks is not recommended; indeed, the valuation problem is similar in all respects to that of good-will.

Chapter XXI  FIXED LIABILITIES 

Forms of Fixed Liabilities.-Fixed liabilities, also known as the long-term debt or the funded debt, include long-term notes payable, chattel mortgages, real property mortgages, permanent advances from affiliated companies, and bonds payable. A liability maturing after one year from the date of the balance sheet generally is regarded as a fixed liability. Frequently, fixed liabilities have maturities up to one hundred years; long-term debts of this nature almost always are in the form of bond issues.

Fixed liabilities in general are incurred to finance additional plant, to raise working capital, to purchase additional equipment, to purchase another business, to fund a current (floating) debt, or to refund another fixed liability. The liquidation of a fixed liability involves special problems, such as the creation of a sinking fund, so that sudden drains will not be made upon current assets. The cost of borrowing fixed liabilities should be less than the revenues derived through the use of the assets acquired by them, thereby providing for the periodic interest and for an accumulation toward the repayment of the principal when it is due. 

Except for the issue of capital stock, the sale of bonds is the most common method of raising capital to be used for long periods of time. 

Bonds commonly are issued by (a) governments, such as federal, state, and municipal; (b) by industrial concerns, either mercantile or manufacturing; (c) by public utilities, such as electric power companies, railroads, and street railways; (d) by real estate organizations, such as hotels, office buildings, and apartment buildings. 

Corporations may use bonds advantageously because the purchasers of the bonds realize the continuous nature of the corporation. When a corporation requires additional long-term capital, a decision must be made as to whether stocks or bonds shall be issued. Bonds are advantageous if additional capital is required for a fairly long period, but 447

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

not permanently. They are also advantageous if it is desired to restrict voting power and the sharing of profits to the present group of owners. 

Viewed from the point of view of the present owners, the issuance of participating preferred stock rather than bonds might mean the sharing of extra dividends with the new stockholders; if non-participating preferred stock were issued, the dividend rate would almost certainly be above the rate at which a bond issue could be sold. Assuming that dividends will be paid regularly on capital stock issues, it generally is cheaper to borrow on long-term loans as opposed to the flotation of additional stock. Furthermore, interest is deductible from taxable income and dividends are not. Of course, interest on borrowed money constitutes a fixed charge against operations, and it must be paid when due whether or not it is earned, or foreclosure proceedings may follow, with their damaging effects upon the equities of the stockholders. Corporations also use bonds in order to appeal to certain classes of investors not interested in stock.

Normally bonds are issued when relatively large sums of money are required, and they are usually issued for long periods of time. One credit source could not supply the entire sum required or would not care to take the risk of lending such a large sum to one borrower. In order to appeal to a wide market and to spread the risk of lending, bonds are issued in various denominations; the majority of bonds other than governmental issues have a par of $1,000.00, although recently more industrials and utilities have tried to reach the small investor by issuing smaller denominations. Governments frequently issue bonds with a par value as low as $25.00 in order to appeal to a wider market. 

The bond is an instrument under seal, promising to pay a specific sum at a determinable future date, together with interest at stated dates. 

Behind every secured bond issue is a mortgage, known as a deed of trust, which is held by the bond trustee who acts as the fiduciary representative of the bondholders. The mortgage conditionally transfers title in the pledged property to the trustee. On the basis of the mortgage, bonds of equal denomination and rank are sold to the investors. 

When the bonds are repaid by the issuing corporation, the trustee executes a release and the mortgage is cancelled. In a small real estate mortgage there are but two parties, the borrower and the lender; in the case of a bond mortgage there is interposed a third party, the trustee, to act for the lenders; because of their proportionately small holdings and their wide geographical distribution, bondholders could not easily

act individually. The bond trustee is usually a bank or a trust company. 

When a bond issue is sold, it is usually sold to an underwriting syndicate, or to one investment dealer. The underwriter then sells the bonds to the investing public. Corporations seldom market their securities directly to the investor, because they do not have the proper marketing machinery to do so. Not infrequently, however, the whole issue is sold directly to one or a very few large institutional buyers such as insurance companies. The bond issue may be sold outright to the underwriters, or the underwriter may contract to sell the bonds at a price plus a commission; in the latter case the underwriter may or may not agree to purchase all bonds still unsold at a certain date. 

Authority for the Bond Issue. The authority for the issuance of bonds need not be provided for in the corporate charter. Subject to the laws of the state of incorporation, either the board of directors or a stipulated percentage of the preferred stockholders or of the voting stockholders may authorize a bond issue. The by-laws of the corporation should state the procedure to be followed in issuing bonds. 

Types of Bonds.-There are many specialized types of bonds other than the more ordinary kinds considered here. Books on corporation finance should be consulted for additional material. Features of the more ordinary types of bonds are discussed below. 

First Mortgage Bonds.-A mortgage is a conditional transfer of title. It does not convey title absolutely to the lender, but it does create a lien on the property to secure the payment of the debt at maturity. 

First mortgage bonds are secured by real property, specifically named, and constitute a prior lien on the pledged assets. If interest or principal is not paid when due, and if foreclosure follows, the amounts realized from the sale of the mortgaged property must be paid to the first mortgage bondholders to the full extent of their claims before any residual amounts may be applied to second or subsequent mortgage bonds, or to unsecured liabilities. First mortgage bonds are underlying or senior liens; other bonds of less rank are junior liens. 

Investors must read the bond contract or indenture to be sure that they are buying first mortgage bonds; simply because the word "first" is used in the bond description does not necessarily mean that they are first liens; for example, if two companies merged and if each had a first mortgage on its property, and, after the merger, the new organization issued a "first consolidated" mortgage bond issue, in effect it is really a second mortgage.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING Second (and Subsequent) Mortgage Bonds.-Second and subse quent mortgage bonds are secondary liens upon the same property pledged under a first mortgage bond issue. Assume that a plant, valued at $1,000,000.00, were mortgaged for $600,000.00 under a first mortgage bond issue. The remaining equity or margin of safety would be $400,000.00. If a second mortgage bond issue of $200,000.00 were sold, there would remain an equity of but $200,000.00. If interest or principal were not paid when due and the property were sold, the $600,000.00 claims of the first mortgage bondholders would be satisfied first, and any remaining amounts would be available for the satisfaction. of the second mortgage bondholders or other creditors. Example:

FIRST MORTGAGE HOLDERS

$500,000.00. $500,000.00 600,000.00. 600,000.00 700,000.00. 600,000.00 $100,000.00 800,000.00. 600,000.00 900,000.00. 600,000.00 200,000.00 200,000.00 $100,000.00

If a first, second, and third mortgage on the same property are in existence, and if the first and second are paid off, the third mortgage would thereby become a first mortgage. 

Equipment Trust Bonds.-Equipment trust bonds are secured by property other than land and buildings; railroads frequently issue equipment trust bonds, pledging the rolling stock as security. Because of the necessity of frequent replacement of equipment, the security behind this type of bond usually is fairly well maintained. 

Collateral Trust Bonds.-Collateral trust bonds are secured by the stocks and bonds of other companies, pledged with the bond trustee. 

Upon the retirement of the issue, the collateral is returned, or it may be partially returned as parts of the issue are retired. The trust indenture normally specifies the minimum amount which the market value of the total pledged securities must equal at all times. Collateral trust bonds frequently are issued by holding companies, secured by the pledged securities of their subsidiaries. 

Debenture Bonds.-Debenture bonds are not secured by property or collateral, but are issued against the general credit of the corporation. The bond constitutes a lien on all free and unpledged assets. In

the event of the non-payment of interest, the holders may take action in conformity with the deed of trust. Normally, foreclosure may be effected if interest is not paid when due. 

Income Bonds.-Like debentures, income bonds are unsecured by the pledge of specific assets. They rest on the general credit of the corporation. The payment of interest is contingent upon its being earned. If interest is not earned and therefore not paid, the bondholder has no recourse. Income bonds may be cumulative or non-cumulative, usually the latter. 

Registered and Coupon Bonds.-Any bond may be (1) registered, (2) coupon. Registered bonds may be: (a) registered as to principal only, (b) registered as to principal and interest. 

If a bond is registered as to principal only, it is recorded in the name of the owner on the books of the corporation, or on the records of the fiscal agent of the corporation, that is, the trustee. The bond will pass only by indorsement, assignment, and registration, thus protecting the owner against loss. To bonds registered as to principal only, coupons are attached, which are payable to bearer and which may be clipped and cashed at each interest date. Thus the issuing corporation need not prepare interest checks.

If a bond is registered as to principal and interest, interest is paid by check to the registered owner. The bond will pass only by indorsement, assignment, and registration. It is evident that when a bond is registered as to interest, the work of the corporation in handling interest payments is increased. 

If a bond is not registered, interest is paid by cashing the coupons. 

Such bonds pass by delivery, no indorsement being necessary. Unregistered coupon bonds increase the risk of loss to the owner, but reduce the work of the issuing corporation. Subsidiary records must be kept for registered bonds; no subsidiary records are maintained for unregistered coupon bonds.

Convertible Bonds.-Bonds may be convertible, at the option of the bondholders, into some other security, usually a security of lower rank, such as preferred or common stock. The trust indenture states the conditions of conversion, which may be par for par, par for the bond, and par plus a premium for the stock or at a stated ratio such as two shares of stock for each $100.00 par of bonds; there are various other possibilities. Conversion features frequently are placed in the bond issue of a new company; if the company is successful the bondholder may

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

become a stockholder and thus increase his income; if the company is not successful the bondholder has prior claim to earnings or to assets. 

Almost any type of bond may carry conversion features. 

Participating Bonds.-A participating bond entitles its owner to share in the profits along with the stockholders. The participation may be limited or pro rata, just as in the case of participating preferred stock. Participating bonds are rarely issued in this country. 

Accounting for Bond Issues.-Corporations frequently do not issue, upon original offer, the entire authorized bond issue; rather, they wait until additional funds are required, and issue the additional authorized bonds in accordance with their needs. For example assume that $1,000,000.00 of bonds is authorized when only $700,000.00 is currently required; $300,000.00 may be raised later under the same issue, thereby eliminating the necessity for a second mortgage. 

Bonds may be sold originally at a discount, whereas, in most states, original issues of capital stock must be issued at a minimum of par. 

To illustrate the accounting procedure for the issuance of bonds, assume that a corporation is to issue first mortgage bonds to the extent of $1,000,000.00 in total. Of the authorization, $600,000.00 of the bonds are sold, as follows: $200,000.00 at par

The balance sheet should show the amount of bonds authorized, even if all bonds are not issued. If the interest is paid by the corporation, the entries are as follows, assuming that the bonds were issued at par:

Bond Interest Coupons Payable..

Cash XX XX XX XX Any unpaid amount remains as a liability of the trustee. The coupons are collected and retained for audit, after which they should be retained for a reasonable length of time and then destroyed. 

If the bonds are registered as to interest, either the corporation or the trustee will remit the interest by check. If the corporation remits to the trustee, the corporation charges Bond Interest and credits Cash; the trustee charges Cash and credits Bond Interest Payable; then as he sends out the interest checks he charges Bond Interest Payable and credits Cash.

The question of issuing bonds for fixed assets was discussed in chapter XVI. There it was pointed out that both the interest and the

discount on bonds, during the construction period, may be charged to the cost of the fixed assets. 

The Amortization of Bond Premium and Discount.-The amorti zation of bond premium and discount was fully discussed in chapter XV, Investments. The same procedure is followed for the amortization of premiums and discounts on bonds payable; when bonds are a liability the bonds are carried at par, and separate Discount or Premium accounts are used, whereas for bonds held as investments, the bonds are carried in their investment account at par plus unamortized premium, or at par minus unamortized discount. 

Either the straight-line method of amortization or the scientific method of amortization may be adopted. If the straight-line method is used, the total interest charge is not as accurate as when the scientific method is used. The scientific method is more accurate but it is more complicated in operation; it does produce an exact interest cost, based upon the proceeds received from the sale of the bond issue. The scientific method of amortization is based on the theory that, if the bonds are issued at a discount, the borrowing corporation incurs interest cost at a constant rate on the par of the bonds less the remaining unamortized discount; if the bonds are issued at a premium, interest is computed on the par plus the unamortized premium. The rate of interest remains constant at all times. 

The following schedules show the amortization of bond premiums and bond discounts, for a five-year, 4 per cent, $1,000,000.00 issue, sold, first, to net 3 per cent, and sold, second, to net 5 per cent. Interest is payable semi-annually.

Bonds Issued without Periodic Interest Payment.-The majority of corporation bonds bear interest as an annuity; governments frequently issue bonds without the interest annuity. Such bonds are worth the present value of their maturity par, at a given rate of interest. At any date preceding maturity, the actual liability is the present value of maturity par.

Assume that a corporation decided to issue bonds similar to United States Savings Bonds, and sold a $1,000.00 par value bond, due in ten years, for $750.00; interest is at the rate of 2.9 per cent compounded semi-annually. The entry to record the bond issue would be as follows: Cash 750.00

Serial Bonds.-If fixed amounts of a bond issue mature and are redeemed periodically, the bonds are known as serial bonds. Serial bonds frequently are issued in order to avoid the accumulation of a large sinking fund. Also, if the rate of bond interest is larger than the net earnings of a sinking fund, it would be wise to retire the bond issue serially, rather than accumulate a fund. 

When bonds are issued to be retired serially, there arises the question of the proper amortization of premiums or discounts. Because the early periods of the life of the bond issue enjoy the use of a greater sum of money, and because more bonds are outstanding in the early periods, these early periods should bear a relatively larger portion of the amortization of the premium or discount. If serial bonds are issued at par, this problem does not arise.

Premiums and discounts on serial bonds commonly are amortized by a straight-line method, proportionate to the bonds which are outstanding in each period. The method is known as the bonds-outstanding method, and may be illustrated as follows.

Assume that a $6,000,000.00 serial bond issue is sold. The bonds bear a nominal rate of 3 per cent and are sold to cost (yield) 31½ per cent. They are five-year bonds, interest payable semi-annually, and they are to be retired as follows: $1,000,000.00 at the end of two and onehalf years and $1,000,000.00 at the end of each interest period thereafter.

The entire issue is really made up of six separate items of $1,000,- 000.00 each, maturing $1,000,000.00 at the end of two and one-half, three, three and one-half, four, four and one-half, and five years. By the use of bond tables, or by the use of methods shown in chapter XV, the price of the issue is as follows: 

3%, $1,000,000.00 bond, to cost 32%, due in 2.5 years. 

3%, $1,000,000.00 bond, to cost 32%, due in 3.0 years. 

3%, $1,000.000.00 bond, to cost 32%, due in 3.5 years. 

3%, $1,000,000.00 bond, to cost 32%, due in 4.0 years. 

3%, $1,000,000.00 bond, to cost 312%, due in 4.5 years.

One of the straight-line methods, usually the bonds-outstanding method, is used more frequently than the scientific method. The results of the scientific method are more accurate, but the method involves additional work. If the cost (yield) rate is unknown, the scientific method is particularly cumbersome, because, as pointed out in chapter XV, the effective rate can be determined only approximately. 

Annuity Bonds.—If a bond is issued so that equal periodic payments include both interest and principal, thereby gradually reducing the principal, the bond is known as an annuity bond. The problem is the same as that discussed in chapter XV, under the section titled "The Valuation of Mortgages," wherein the periodic payments of equal amount included principal and interest. The same illustration used at that point is presented below, reversed for a bond payable. Assume

The $10,000.00 of bonds represents the present value of an annuity of ten equal installments. Bond Conversion.-When a bond carries the privilege of conversion into another security, the entries at the time of conversion must accurately reflect the entire situation. Bond conversion is at the option of the owner, and it may be that he will never exercise that privilege; therefore, the original amortization schedules for the entire life of the bonds should be followed until conversion takes place. If the bonds were originally issued at a premium or at a discount, the unamortized portion of that premium or discount must be eliminated at the time of conversion. Both the bonds and the stock may be given conversion prices or a conversion ratio must be stated; usually, differences due to the inability to match the amount of bonds and stock in the conversion ratio are settled by cash transfers, or by the issuance of fractional shares of stock. Accrued interest must be accounted for if conversion is at a date other than a bond interest date; most conversions are specifically stated to be at an interest date, thereby eliminating accrued interest. In addition, dividends may be accumulated on preferred stock given in the conversion.

In order to illustrate several conversion possibilities, assume that $10,000.00 of ten-year bonds were issued at 90, six years ago; the amortization has been on the straight-line basis; therefore, today the bonds are carried at $9,600.00 net. Accrued interest on the bonds today, which is the conversion date, amounts to $100.00. The bonds are convertible into preferred stock which has a par of $100.00 per share. The conversion ratio is ten shares of stock for one $1,000.00 bond. Accrued dividends on the stock amount to $3.00 per share. All differences are to be settled in cash. 

In order to clarify the transactions, a temporary account, Bond Conversion, is set up. The entries for the conversion would be as follows:

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Frequently, when a corporation has available cash it will purchase for retirement some of its outstanding bonds in the open market, especially if the bonds are selling below par; of course, if these purchases are extensive, the market price of the bonds will tend to rise. Assume that $500,000.00 of bonds payable, carrying unamortized premium of $7,000.00, were purchased at 90 by the issuing corporation. 

Bonds Payable Unamortized Premium 

Profit on Redemption. Cash 500,000.00 7,000.00 57,000.00 450,000.00

Frequently, one bond issue is retired by marketing a new bond issue; this procedure is followed extensively in the field of public utilities and railroads. Refunding prior to maturity usually is effected when interest rates decline, enabling the refunding corporation to reduce fixed charges. When an old issue is replaced by the new issue, there arises the question of the treatment of unamortized premium or discount and other costs incident to the retirement of the old issue. 

There are three different views concerning the treatment of such items; they are: (1) write off all unamortized premium or discount and other costs applicable to the original issue to Profit-and-Loss or to Surplus, at the time of refunding; (2) defer the unamortized premium or discount and other costs applicable to the original issue and write them off over the life of the new bond issue; (3) to defer the unamortized premium or discount and other costs applicable to the original issue and write them off over the remaining life of the original issue just as though refunding had not occurred. Although, today, deferment of the unamortized amounts over the life of the original bond issue is widely advocated, sound practice dictates that all unamortized balances be written off at the time of refunding, because the original contract is a closed transaction.

When a bond issue is refunded, not only the lower interest rate, but all costs of retiring the old issue and marketing the new issue, must be taken into consideration in order to determine the net saving on the refinancing.

Treasury Bonds.-Treasury bonds differ from treasury stock, in that all bonds unissued, and issued and repurchased, are treasury bonds, unless they are purchased and retired. Treasury bonds are never an asset of the issuing corporation, although they may be pledged as security to other loans. If a Treasury Bond account is used to record

treasury bond acquisitions, it should be adjusted to par at each balance sheet; otherwise, if the acquisition cost differed from par, a true liability balance would not be shown; the premiums and discounts also must be adjusted.

To illustrate, assume that bonds of a par value of $100,000.00 are purchased as treasury bonds, at a cost of $110,000.00.

Bonds on the Balance Sheet.-On the balance sheet, bonds payable should be carried at par. Treasury bonds and unissued bonds should be deducted from the total authorized issue, at par, and the net par liability extended. The unamortized premium balance should be carried as a deferred credit and the unamortized discount as a deferred charge to bond interest cost; unamortized discount should never be captioned "prepaid interest." If a bond issue, or one series of a total serial issue, is payable within one year, and no special fund is available for their payment the amount currently due should be moved from the fixed liability to the current liability classification. If a special fund is available for the repayment of the amounts currently due, this fund becomes a current asset at the same time the amounts due become current liabilities. Probably both the fund and the liability should be left in the "fixed" sections of the balance sheet, for by their removal to the current section, the current ratio is temporarily disturbed. If these amounts are permitted to remain in the fixed asset and the fixed liability sections, the amounts should be separately set forth, as follows: 

BALANCE SHEET AT DECEMBER 31, 1942 Fixed Assets: 

Bond Sinking Fund: 

For Series A, due July 1, 1943. 

For Remaining Series, due after one year. .$100,000.00

XXX,XXX.XX Fixed Liabilities: 

First Mortgage Bonds Payable, Series A, due July 1, 1943.... $100,000.00 

First Mortgage Bonds Payable, Remaining Series, due after one year 900,000.00

Costs of Issuing Bonds.-The costs of issuing bonds, such as the cost of printing, advertising, underwriters' fees, and so on, may be amortized along with the discount, or, if the bonds are issued at a premium, the incidental costs may be deducted from the premium, and the net premium amortized. Or these items may be separately stated and not mixed with premiums and discount. 

CURRENT LIABILITIES 

General. The proper valuation of current liabilities does not present major difficulties. Liabilities are seldom subject to debatable

valuation, as are current assets. The major problems for the current liabilities are those of inclusion and classification. Normally a liability is a fact and not a matter of opinion; there are a few exceptions to this general statement--notably certain accrued liabilities. 

The one-year dividing line between current and fixed liabilities is rather arbitrary, but it is based on the theory that current liabilities are paid for by the sales conversion of the product into cash; normally this conversion period is not more than one year; consequently, the amounts received are available for the liquidation of the currently due liabilities. 

At a balance sheet date, all liabilities should be included in the statement. Care must be exercised to determine that the liability for goods purchased or expenses incurred shortly before the end of the period are included as liabilities.

Liabilities should never be cancelled against assets and only the net amounts shown. In only very rare cases should an asset be shown as a deduction from a liability; currently an exception is made for the 

United States Treasury Tax Notes. Because they are purchased and held for use in payment of federal income taxes, they may be shown as a deduction from the accrued tax liability. Even debit balances in accounts payable should be shown as such on the asset side of a balance sheet, because the gross liability, shown as such, is the amount which must be paid. If the principle of offset were invoked, an understatement of both assets and liabilities would result. 

Likewise, if a concern maintains accounts in two or more banks, and if one account shows an overdraft, the available cash should be listed as an asset, and the overdraft as a liability, even though the net balance of all accounts is a debit. 

Current Liability Classification.—On a balance sheet current liabili ties should be so separated that there can be no question concerning them. Each should be fully described, setting forth any peculiarities. 

The following classification is typical:

Notes Payable, X bank (Secured by Marketable Securities): 

Notes Payable, X Bank, Unsecured

Trade Notes Payable. 

Non-Trade Notes Payable, Officers.. 

Non-Trade Notes Payable, Fixed Asset Purchases.

Accounts Payable, Trade, Past Due.
