XOX XX XX XX XX XX XX Short-time deferred credits to income may be shown in the current liability classification, or they may be shown in a separate classification. 

Long-time deferred credits such as unamortized bond premium, should be shown separately or in the fixed liability section; they should never be classed with the short-time (current) deferred credits. 

Notes payable and accounts payable should be broken down so that the source of the indebtedness is clearly shown. Overdue notes and overdue accounts payable should be so indicated; if items are in dispute and are overdue for that reason exclusively, it is not necessary to indicate the fact that the amount is past due. 

Certain liabilities are not liquidated in cash. An amount received on a contract to be completed is an example of this type. If the Z 

Company received an advance of $10,000.00 for products to be manufactured and delivered by it, the Z Company is liable for $10,000.00 worth of merchandise, or possibly, the return of the $10,000.00 in cash if the contract is broken. When the $10,000.00 is received, cash is charged, and a liability account, Deposits Received on Contracts is credited. Upon completion of the contract, or portions of it, Deposits 

Received on Contracts is charged and an income account credited. 

Thus, whether a liability is to be liquidated in cash or goods has no effect upon its amount or classification. 

CONTINGENT LIABILITIES 

General. A contingent liability is a possible future debt which is the result of a past act or a possible future event. It may be expressed as an "if" liability; that is, if an event occurs, a liability may result. 

There are two general classes of contingent liabilities: 

1. Possible direct obligations, unsettled as to certainty and amount, usually pending the result of litigation; after final judgment has been rendered, the liability, if any, becomes real, and not contingent. 

2. Secondary obligations, wherein there is no liability unless the primary obligor fails to act.

1 Frequently, the determination of contingent liabilities is a difficult matter, because of the uncertainty of future developments. The accountant must examine carefully the minutes of the meetings of the board of directors, and must depend for much of his information upon conversation, legal documents, and general correspondence. Even after the decision is reached that a contingent liability does exist, its valuation in many instances may be almost impossible of determination. 

On the balance sheet, contingent liabilities may be expressed in one of several different ways: a) A separate balance sheet heading, Contingent Liabilities, may be used, the contingent liabilities listed thereunder, but the amounts not extended and added into the total liabilities. b) The contingent liability may be deducted from a corresponding asset, and the difference between the two extended; in these cases, the assets are listed gross. c) The contingent liability may be indicated in a balance sheet footnote; in such cases, the corresponding asset values, if any, are expressed net. Several contingent liabilities are discussed briefly below: 

Discounted Notes, Drafts, and Other Commercial Paper.—When commercial paper is indorsed and discounted, the indorser, that is, the secondary obligor, must reimburse the bank at which the paper was discounted, if the original maker fails to liquidate his obligation at maturity. To this secondary obligor, the commercial paper receivable is at the same time a contingent asset, and a contingent liability of the same amount.

Assigned Accounts.-When accounts receivable are assigned, the assignor is contingently liable to the assignee, and is fully liable when a customer fails to pay his account. The treatment of assigned accounts is similar to the treatment of discounted commercial paper. The accounting entries for these items are treated in chapter XII. 

Federal Income Tax Additional Assessments.-If litigation develops over the amount of federal income tax assessments, the taxpayer is contingently liable for assessments for which he has not provided. The contingent liability, in this case, should be provided by an earned surplus segregation. If adverse judgment is rendered, the contingent liability becomes a reality. 

Goods Sold Under Guaranty.-If goods are sold under a guaranty which provides for repairs or part replacements, the seller is contingently liable until the warranty period has elapsed. Past experience is

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

the best guide as to the amount of the contingent liability, and, if such experience has shown a regularized service cost, it is proper to remove the liability from the contingent to the current classification. Where a fairly good estimate of this item can be made, a profit-and-loss account should be charged and an accrued liability or a liability reserve account should be created. However, if the liability is only contingent, the charge should be to Surplus.

Cumulative Preferred Stock Dividends in Arrears.-Arrearages in cumulative preferred stock dividends make it impossible to pay current dividends on other classes of stock. If dividends in arrears become too large, corporate reorganization probably will follow. These amounts in arrears are best expressed as a balance sheet footnote: frequently, however, they are shown as appropriations of Surplus. 

Accommodation Indorsement.-Indorsements of an accommodation nature render such indorser contingently liable until the instrument is paid. If an accommodation indorser is held liable he proceeds first against the maker, and if that fails, then usually against the last preceding indorser. Before non-payment by the maker, the contingent liability perhaps is best expressed as a balance sheet footnote; after non-payment by the maker, it becomes necessary to include what is now an actual liability in the current liability section of the balance sheet. 

Purchase Commitments.-Possible losses arising from purchase commitments in a declining market should be charged to a profit-and-loss account and credited to an account entitled Reserve for Loss on Purchase Commitments. This reserve should be carried until future commitments are received, at which time it is used to absorb the excess of cost over market price at the time of receipt. Any balance may be closed to Earned Surplus. If purchase commitments for future delivery are made and if the market is rising at the balance sheet date, no reserve is necessary; the situation the situation may be ignored, or at most, a balance sheet footnote would be adequate. 

Lawsuits.-Lawsuits may be in process or contemplated. A contingent liability should be created by a surplus reservation. Adverse judgment charges the contingent liability into a true liability. Normally, the actual loss will be charged to a profit-and-loss account and credited to an actual liability account; at the same time, the reserve for the contingent liability is restored to Surplus. 

Lease Breakage.-Possible loss arising from the breaking of a lease may be provided for by surplus reservations.

Surety Bonds.—If one person acts as surety for another, he is contingently liable; he may become actually liable if the assured person breaks the surety bond. This fact should be reflected in some manner on the balance sheet if the possible amount involved is substantial.

Chapter XXII  FUNDS 

Funds are assets. They may be held by the company owning them, or by another acting as trustee. A fund may be composed of cash or securities, or both. In mercantile, industrial, and financial institution accounting, a fund is established by a charge to a Fund account and a credit to another asset, usually cash. 

Purposes of Funds. Funds may be provided for: a) The retirement of a bond issue b) The creation of a stock redemption fund c) The construction of a building d) The payment of pensions e) The replacement of assets destroyed by fire or other casualtiesfrequently called an insurance fund f) Petty cash operations g) Payroll purposes h) Dividend payments

Of the foregoing, (f), (g), and (b) represent current assets; the remainder represent non-current assets. 

Stated in another manner, a fund may be established for the payment of a definite or contingent liability, for the retirement of capital stock, for the acquisition of an asset, and for the purpose of facilitating current operations.

Funds may be invested in (a) cash, or (b) the securities of other. companies, or (c) in the corporation's own securities; the latter practice predominates when the fund is to be used for retirement of securities. Funds should be valued at cost, or at cost plus or minus amortized discounts or premiums on bonds in the fund; if the market value of fund securities declines permanently, a surplus reserve should be established for the general protection of the fund. 473

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Funds may be voluntary or obligatory. If the fund is voluntary, it should be established by action of the board of directors. If the fund is obligatory, it is the result of a contract. 

Funds may be created so that they are intact as to principal, and so that only the fund income is used; an example of this type is a cemetery care fund. Or a fund may be established whereby the interest is added to the principal of the fund, and after the fund has reached its desired size, both principal and interest will be used; an example of this type is the sinking fund for the retirement of a bond issue. 

The following pattern is typical of the operation of a fund: (a) establish the fund by a charge to the Fund account and a credit to Cash; (b) invest the fund cash in securities; (c) collect the income earned on the fund, and debit the Fund and credit a Fund Income account; (d) amortize the premium or discount on bonds in the fund; (e) pay the expenses of conducting the fund by a charge to expense and a credit to the Fund account; (f) apply the fund to the purpose for which it was created. Examples of the foregoing routine are presented on page 476. 

Sinking Funds.-A sinking fund is established for the payment of a liability at maturity; it usually is employed in connection with bonds payable. When the sinking fund plan is used in connection with the retirement of capital stock, the fund is known as a stock redemption fund.

The periodic contributions to a sinking fund for the retirement of bonds are stipulated in the deed of trust under which the bonds are issued. Periodic contributions to the fund may be: a) A percentage of periodic profits. This method is common for the establishment of stock redemption funds, but it is uncommon for funds for the payment of liabilities. The method is inadvisable for bond retirement sinking funds, because, if there are no profits, the failure to increase the fund is detrimental to the bondholders. b) A uniform amount of money per unit of product sold. This method is common for the creation of sinking funds in the extractive industries. The sinking fund increases in size as the raw material is depleted. If this method is employed, it is best to state a minimum amount, in order to be certain of a contribution in the event that no sales are made. c) An equal number of dollars each year, the amount determined by dividing the total of the desired fund by the number of years

involved. For example, if a fund of $100,000.00 is required in ten years, the annual contribution to the fund would be $10,000.00. If this method is used, the interest earned on the fund should not be added to the fund, but returned to the company establishing the fund; if the interest were added to the fund, an amount in excess of the desired principal would be accumulated at maturity. d) An amount arrived at by the use of a compound interest method, known as the sinking-fund method. This method was illustrated in chapter XV, Investments, and in chapter XVIII, Depreciation and 

Depletion. In the sinking-fund method, the rate of interest to be earned on the fund must be anticipated. The periodic contribution to the sinking fund is the total fund divided by the amount of an annuity of $1.00 at the given rate of interest for the number of periods involved, or 

Sinking fund contribution S. F.

A. 

As an illustration of this method, assume that a fund of $10,000.00 is desired at the end of five years. The fund is estimated to earn 3 per cent per year. The annual contribution is to be made at the end of each year. The amount of an ordinary annuity of $1.00 for five years at 3 per cent is $5.30913581. $10,000.00 ÷ 5.30913581 $1,883.54, the annual contribution.

The sinking fund trustee records the daily fund transactions on his books; periodically he reports the sinking fund transactions to the issuing corporation; the corporation then takes up the sinking fund transactions on its books. The expenses and incomes in connection with the operation of the sinking fund are shown in the non-operating section of the statement of profit and loss of the issuing corporation.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Bonds of the Issuing Company in the Fund.-A trust indenture usually permits the sinking fund trustee to purchase the bonds of the issuing company. Therefore, if the bonds of the issuing company can be purchased at a price below net carrying value, a saving is effected. 

One of two alternatives exist when the bonds of the issuing company are purchased: (a) the bonds may be retired, or (b) they may be kept alive in the fund.

If the funds are retired when purchased, the entries on the books of the issuing company are as follows: 

Bonds Payable (par). 

Unamortized Premium Unamortized Discount Sinking Fund Cash 

Profit (debit, if a loss) Upon Retirement. .XX XX XX XX XX If the bonds are retired upon acquisition, the fund actually is a redemption fund; the total of the fund is never accumulated, for interest payments from the corporation to the fund cease when the bonds are cancelled before maturity. If the bonds to be retired are bought at or above the actuarial balance of the fund available for those bonds, the issuing company must add to the fund an amount necessary to make up the actuarial balance. 

If the bonds purchased are held alive in the fund, the trustee continues to collect interest from the issuing company; if the interest were not paid to the trustee, the sinking fund would not accumulate on the predetermined actuarial basis. When kept alive in the fund, the bonds may be resold by the trustee. The liability on the books of the issuing company remains at par. 

When the bonds of the issuing company are purchased by the sinking fund trustee at a premium or at a discount, and are to be kept alive in the fund, two alternative procedures are available for the treatment of the entire situation. The first plan is to record the bonds at the price paid to acquire them. The original amortization schedule of the bonds is in no way disturbed. Using this method, the entries on the books of the trustee would be as follows:

When the bonds are purchased for the fund, at an interest date: 

Sinking Fund Securities Sinking Fund Cash.. 

To purchase 10 bonds of the issuing company, par $10,000.00; purchase price $9,600.00. .9,600.00 9,600.00

At each interest date:

Sinking Fund Cash... 

Sinking Fund Securities. 

Sinking Fund Income. 

To record the receipt of interest on the bonds purchased for the fund, and to amortize the $400.00 discount over the remaining life of the bonds (assume 8 years). 200.00 50.00 250.00

Thus the entries on the books of the sinking fund trustee are the same as though the bonds of a company other than the issuing company had been purchased.

The issuing company continues to pay full interest on its entire issue originally sold, and premium or discount on original sale is amortized on the same basis as though the sinking fund trustee had not purchased the company's bonds.

The second available method follows the plan of recording at par the bonds purchased; at the date of the purchase, the unamortized premium or discount is charged off; the difference between the unamortized discount or premium at the time of original sale and the discount or premium at the date of purchase will be a non-operating profit or loss. To illustrate, assume the same figures used to illustrate the first method: $10,000.00 par value bonds were purchased at an interest date, for $9,600.00; the remaining life is eight years; the bonds originally were twenty-year bonds, issued at 98; amortization has been by the straight-line method. The entries follow: 

Sinking Fund Securities (par) 

Cash

Unamortized Bond Discount. 

Profit on Purchase. 

Original discount 

Amortized, 12 years. $200.00 120.00 

Unamortized at purchase.. $ 80.00 . 10,000.00 9,600.00 80.00 320.00 

At each succeeding interest period, the discount on the bonds not purchased for the fund would be amortized in the regular manner. 

Of the two methods, the first is the better, because it follows the same procedure as though the bonds of any outside company were purchased.

The majority of sinking funds for the retirement of bonds are obligatory. Voluntary funds, established by board action, usually are for such purposes as a building fund, a pension fund, an advertising fund, a cemetery care fund, and so on; voluntary funds are occasionally encountered for the payment of liabilities. The establishment and accumulation of voluntary funds usually is productive of a systematic saving plan. After the fund assets have been spent in accordance with the purpose for which the fund was established, remaining amounts in the fund are restored to cash.

If a voluntary fund is established for the retirement of a capital stock issue, the entries would be as follows:

Funds may be established for any conceivable purpose. In practice, the majority of business funds are for liability retirement and for capital stock redemption. Also, the majority of funds are obligatory. 

Funds on the Balance Sheet.-Funds are assets and should be shown as such on the balance sheet. The caption, Investments in Funds, should be set up, preferably between the current and the fixed asset classifications. The following is typical:

A fund should never be deducted from the liability for which it is being created.

RESERVES 

A reserve is never an asset. In accordance with their sources of establishment, reserves are of two classes: a) Profit and loss reserves; these are created by charges to profit and loss accounts. b) Surplus, or net worth, reserves; these are created by charges. to the Surplus account. A discussion of surplus reserves is presented in chapter VIII. 

When a reserve is established, the action should be in accordance with proper authorization by the board of directors, and a reserve should be created for some specific objective. A reserve should never be created in order to arbitrarily reduce a proper presentation of free and unappropriated surplus, and neither a reserve nor a fund should be created in order to segregate otherwise productive assets. 

To the layman, a reserve frequently is thought of as an asset; this misconception is natural, and, in great measure is the fault of the accountant in his use of such terms as "reserve fund," "general reserve fund," and others. If possible, the terminology should be specific and fully descriptive; if a fund exists, it is advisable to change account titles so that the word "reserve" does not appear; if an item is a reserve, the attempt should be made to delete reference to a fund in the account title.

Purposes of Reserves.-Reserves, in accordance with their sources, are established for the following purposes:

Profit-and-loss reserves are established by charges to a profit-and-loss account, and they represent: (a) asset valuation, or deduction, reserves; (b) actual liability reserves. 

Surplus, or net worth, reserves represent segregations of the Surplus account, and they are established for the following purposes: 

1. Reserves created from earned surplus: a) Sinking fund reserve for bond retirement b) Reserve for capital stock redemption 

Reserve for contingencies d) Reserve for plant extension 

Reserve for possible lawsuits

· ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

f) Reserve for fire loss g) Reserve for flood loss b) Reserve for future anticipated declines in inventories 

Reserve for strike loss 

2. Surplus reserves resulting from asset appraisals: a) Reserves for appraisal of land, buildings, etc. 

Net worth reserves are either created voluntarily or are obligatory by contract. Sinking fund reserves for bond retirement and reserves for capital stock redemption are the two reserves normally of the obligatory type; most of the other net worth reserves are usually created voluntarily.

Asset Valuation Reserves.-Examples of asset valuation reserves are: reserve for bad debts, reserve for depreciation, reserve for depletion, reserve for patent amortization, reserve for amortization of leaseholds, reserve for cash discounts, reserve for freight. Each of these reserves is set up by a charge to the proper expense account and a credit to the reserve. On the balance sheet, each is shown as a deduction from the asset which is thereby reduced from a gross to a net book value.

Actual Liability Reserves.-These are the results of accruals of amounts not exactly determined, such as accrued taxes or a reserve for maintenance. If the amount is exactly determinable and is accrued, a direct liability and not a liability reserve should be set up. Liability reserves should be shown in the liability section of the balance sheet, usually in the current liability section. 

Certain items of deferred income are commonly called "reserves." 

For example, the following items frequently are seen: "Reserve for 

Outstanding Tickets," "Reserve for Unearned Subscriptions," or "Reserve for Premiums." Usually, these items are not reserves, but are liabilities or deferred credits to income, and should be so shown. 

Net Worth Reserves.-Net worth reserves may be created voluntarily or they may be obligatory by contract. If the reserve is voluntary, it must be for a specific purpose, for otherwise information is being withheld from the stockholders, and their free and available equity is understated.

Reserve for Sinking Fund.-The accumulation of a reserve for sinking fund protects the bondholders against the possibility of the

unwarranted dissipation of the corporate surplus through the payment of excessive dividends to stockholders. If surplus were dissipated in profitable years, it might be insufficient to absorb the losses of unprofit able years; if a deficit existed, the position of the bondholders might be somewhat insecure.

The reserve for sinking fund may be created at the theoretical rate used for the accumulation of the sinking fund. If bond retirements are made for the sinking fund, the accompanying reserve may or may not be reduced; if it is not reduced, the result is a greater protection for the remaining bondholders. If both a sinking fund and a sinking fund reserve are established, the bondholder receives additional protection. In this manner, working capital need not be used for excessive dividends, because of the retention of funds by the limitations placed upon the surplus by the creation of the sinking fund reserve. The amounts retained in the business by the creation of the sinking fund reserve may be used to build up the sinking fund without encroachment on the other assets needed for the operation of the business. 

When a reserve for sinking fund is established, Earned Surplus is charged. The deed of trust usually stipulates the provisions necessary for the reserve. On the balance sheet, the reserve for sinking fund is shown among the net worth items. If the reserve for sinking fund is deficient, full explanation of the deficiency should be made in a footnote to the balance sheet. If the sinking fund is proper, and if bond retirements have been made from the fund, and if the reserve for sinking fund has not been reduced, the difference between the fund and the reserve should be fully explained. When a bond issue has been retired, the reserve for sinking fund is returned to surplus, usually Earned Surplus. The reserve for sinking fund may be retired to 

Capital Surplus or may be used in payment of a stock dividend. 

Reserve for Contingencies.—A reserve for contingencies should be established only when a specific contingency is in view. If a board of directors established a reserve for contingencies merely in order to reduce the size of the Earned Surplus account, such action might be held to constitute fraud toward the stockholders. A reserve for contingencies normally is created by the appropriation of a single amount rather than by the periodic segregation of a regular portion of the surplus. Upon the occurrence or the passing of the contingency for which the reserve was provided, the reserve is returned to Earned Surplus. Any loss or cost resulting from the occurrence of the contin-

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

1 gency for which the reserve was provided is charged to the proper expense account and credited to an asset or a liability account. 

Reserve for Fire Loss.-When a reserve for fire loss is set up out of surplus, it is best to accumulate the reserve on an actuarial basis. 

When a fire occurs, a profit-and-loss account should be charged and the account for the burned asset credited; if this method is followed, fire loss costs are recognized in the period of the fire. If a fire occurs, the event for which the reserve was created, the reserve may be permitted to remain or it may be reduced to be followed by periodic additions from surplus in subsequent periods. If, at the time of a fire, the amount of the loss suffered is restored to earned surplus from the reserve, there is no reduction of earned surplus caused by charging the fire loss to an expense; while the fire loss reduces surplus, the reduced surplus is restored by transfer from the reserve. 

In establishing a reserve for fire loss, some companies charge expense and credit reserve; in this case the reserve is a liability profitand-loss reserve. For fire loss reserves, this procedure may be better, because fire insurance premiums are profit-and-loss charges. In addition, a fund may be built up to replace the destroyed assets, although this is not a common practice. Thus periodically, two entries would appear as follows:

Insurance Expense (for premiums otherwise payable). 

Reserve for Fire Loss..

Fire Loss Fund. 

Cash

XX XX XX XX Income earned on the fund should be added to the fund. The objection to the creation of a fire loss fund is that the segregation of assets in the fund reduces the working capital available for use by the company. 

Reserve for Flood Loss.-A reserve for flood loss is established by a charge to Earned Surplus and a credit to the reserve. Net worth is thus maintained at a larger amount. When a flood occurs, the flood loss is charged to expense and the assets damaged are credited. The reserve is then returned to Surplus, unless additional floods are anticipated. 

Reserve for Lawsuits.-When set up out of surplus, a reserve for lawsuits does not designate a liability; it maintains a larger net worth to absorb any loss that might arise from a lawsuit now contemplated. 

If an adverse judgment is rendered, a liability reserve should be established by a charge to a profit-and-loss account. The reserve for

lawsuits is set up in anticipation of a possible loss resulting from the suit. After the suit is settled, the protective reserve is closed to Earned 

Surplus. 

Reserve for Plant Extension. The purpose of a reserve for plant extension is to reduce dividend distribution and thereby retain assets in the business for the building of additional facilities. When the additional facilities are required, cash or a liability is credited; having fulfilled its purpose, the reserve is then returned to Earned Surplus, or to Capital Surplus, or is distributed as a stock dividend. 

Reductions of Reserves.-The reduction of reserves has been partially exemplified in preceding sections of the chapter. The general statement can be made that when the event occurs for which the reserve was created, the reserve may be reduced or eliminated. 

If the reserve is a profit-and-loss reserve, it is charged as it fulfills its purpose; generally, an asset is credited. For example, if a reserve for bad debts is set up, it is reduced by charges which are offset by credits to Accounts Receivable or Notes Receivable when such items prove to be collectable. If a reserve for state taxes, that is, a liability reserve, is set up by an expense charge, the reserve is charged and Cash is credited upon the payment of the item. A profit-and-loss account was charged when the reserve was established; hence it should not be charged again.

If the reserve is a net worth reserve set up as a protective device, a profit-and-loss account (or Surplus) is charged upon the occurrence of the event, and the reserve is returned to Earned or to Capital Surplus. 

Where a reserve for sinking fund is established, upon the retirement of the liability the reserve is charged and Earned Surplus credited. If a reserve for future possible declines in the value of inventory is established out of surplus, and if the value of the inventory does decline, a non-operating expense account should be charged for the loss and the asset should be credited. If no further declines are anticipated, the reserve may be restored to surplus. The same procedure applies to flood losses, fire losses, damages, lawsuits, and to any other event for which a surplus reserve was created. If such losses were charged directly to the surplus reserve, the loss would be buried and would not be shown as a non-operating profit-and-loss item. 

Relationship Between Funds and Reserves.-If a fund exists, should a related reserve exist? If a réserve is set up, should a related fund be established? If both a reserve and a fund are established,

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

should they be of equal amount? The statement can be made that no specific relationship need exist between a fund and a related reserve, unless the relationship is obligatory. 

Funds and No Reserve.—A fund may be established without a corresponding reserve. If a fund is established for the purchase of an asset, or for the payment of a current or contingent liability, a reserve is not necessary. For bonds payable, representing long-term debt, a sinking fund may be accumulated; a reserve may or may not be required; in many cases the reserve is obligatory in order to afford long-term protection. If a fund is accumulated for the retirement of capital stock, a reserve is not necessary because outside parties do not exist.

If the assets for the fund must come out of profits, either a reserve must be set up or surplus be allowed to increase. If assets for the fund are available from other sources such as depreciation charges in excess of replacements, or the sale of assets, or reduced working capital-then no reserve is necessary. 

Reserve and No Funds.-With the exception of sinking fund reserves for the retirement of bonds payable, it is uncommon to find related funds. If bonds payable have been retired from a sinking fund, a reserve for sinking fund may remain until all bonds are retired. In connection with a reserve for fire losses, funds are sometimes set up out of which losses are met. Other surplus reserves normally do not require funds. In connection with a reserve for depreciation, a fund seldom exists; if there is a fund, it represents an asset replacement fund. 

When liability reserves are established, funds are seldom used, the general cash position of the organization being depended upon for the liquidation of the liability. Thus generally the cash account is a fund for all purposes. If a contemplated expenditure is to be or may be so large that the Cash account cannot cover it (and if other sources of cash are not dependable) then a fund is desirable. 

Funds and Reserves.-Where it is desirable, funds and related reserves may both exist; funds and related reserves must both exist if they are contractual. In the extractive industries, funds and reserves are advisable, in order to assure the proper return of capital, or the proper retention of amounts for reinvestment in other extractive projects.

When both funds and related reserves are established, several conditions exist: the fund may be voluntary and the reserve obligatory;

the fund may be obligatory and the reserve voluntary; both the fund and the reserve may be voluntary; both the fund and the reserve may be obligatory. If the fund and its related reserve are voluntary, no necessary relationship need exist between the size of the two items; the reserve may exceed the fund, or the fund may exceed the reserve. 

If the fund and its related reserve are obligatory, they may differ in size because of expenditures made from the fund; they may differ because the reserve accumulates on an actuarial basis and the actual accumulation of the fund varies from its theoretical actuarial accumulation; they may differ because of gains or losses incurred upon the disposition of fund securities. 

If the fund is obligatory, and the reserve is voluntary, the fund is created by contract, and the reserve is created by good accounting procedure. For example, assume that a building is leased for ten years at an annual rental of $1,000.00 per year. The lease requires that if it is not renewed at the end of the first ten years for an additional ten years, the lessee shall pay the lessor the sum of $4,000.00 cash; a fund for this possible payment for non-renewal must be provided and retained by annual contributions of $400.00 placed on deposit in an approved bank. The annual entries on the books of the lessor might be as follows: 

Lease expense

Surplus Lease Payment Fund. 

1,000,00 400.00 400.00 1,400.00 Cash 

Reserve for Lease Payment. 

400.00 

In this manner the periodic profits and the surplus are protected by the establishment of the reserve for lease payment; this conforms to sound accounting procedure.

As another illustration involving an obligatory fund and a voluntary reserve created as a matter of good accounting procedure, assume that the Spring Lawn Memorial is a newly organized cemetery. In the sales contract of each lot, the provision is made that "of the sales price, $75.00 shall be deposited with the Ever Trust Company as a perpetual care fund; after the fund has reached a total of $450,000.00, contributions shall cease, as this sum, when invested, shall provide annually a sum sufficient for perpetual care." The cemetery grounds contain 9,000 lots. At a deposit of $75.00 per lot sold, 6,000 lots must be sold before the fund reaches $450,000.00. Therefore, no fund contribution is made

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

from the sale of the final 3,000 lots. However, the cost of the perpetual care should be spread over 9,000 lots, or $450,000.00 ÷ 9,000 or $50.00 per lot. The entries would be as follows, upon the sale of each of the first 6,000 lots.

Perpetual Care Fund.. 

Cash in Bank..

In accordance with sales contract. 

Perpetual Care Expense. 

Reserve for Perpetual Care. 

To provide a reserve for perpetual care on the basis of $450,000.00 

9,000 lots. .75.00 75.00 50.00 50.00

Upon the sale of the 6,000 lots, contributions to the fund cease. 

The condition at that time would be: 

Perpetual Care Fund (6,000 × 75.00).. 

Reserve for Perpetual Care (6,000 × $50.00). .$450,000.00 300,000.00

Upon the sale of each lot from 6,001 through number 9,000, a debit to perpetual care expense and a credit to the reserve will be made. 

This procedure will conform to good accounting, because the expense will be equalized over all lots and because it would be logical to create a reserve equal to the perpetual fund, Secret Reserves.-Secret reserves exist when the true net worth is understated. Net worth may be understated by: a) Understating assets. Assets may be understated by charging capital expenditures to expense; by recording excessive depreciation, depletion, bad debts, or amortization; by writing assets off directly to surplus. b) Overstating liabilities. The overstatement of liabilities may be accomplished by too large accruals of taxes and other expenses, but this is not a common method of creating secrc icserves. 

Of course, secret reserves do not appear as such; what is really meant by the term "secret reserves" is an understated net worth position. The understatement may be intentional or unintentional. If the understated stockholders' equity is unintentional, the understatement may be the result of ultra-conservatism. Such a secret reserve is no more justified than is the overstatement of asset values. Accuracy should be the objective of every financial statement and values should be neither understated nor overstated.

If secret reserves exist as a result of intentional understatement of

net worth, fraud is being practiced against the stockholders;

the hidden values are taxable, fraud may also be exercised against tax authorities.

26. The Digdeep Mining Corporation of Collins, Kentucky, sold, at par, $1,000,000.00 of stock and $500,000.00 of 4 per cent bonds. With the 44444

proceeds it purchased a mine for cash, $700,000.00. Geological surveys indicated 3,500,000 tons of minable and salable coal. 

The bond deed of trust provided for a sinking fund and a sinking fund reserve, at the rate of $.20 per ton of coal mined each year, until the fund equals the par of the bonds. 

The corporation officers, fearing that the estimate of 3,500,000 tons might be rather high, decided to create a non-profit reserve at the rate of $.06 per ton mined.

During the first year, 400,000 tons were mined. 

At the close of the first year of operations, the Profit-and-Loss account showed a profit of $200,000.00. Investigation proved that depreciation on mining equipment had been provided before showing the $200,000.00 profit. Other than that, none of the necessary reserves had been created; $60,000.00 had been turned over to the sinking fund trustee. 

Prepare all necessary journal entries. Close the Profit-and-Loss account to Surplus. What surplus balance is legally available for dividends?

Chapter XXIII COMPARATIVE STATEMENTS 

General. After accounting statements are prepared, it is necessary to analyze and interpret them. For proper study of the financial data of a business organization, it is necessary to have certain tools of analysis, which in general comprise the balance sheet, the statement of profit and loss, the statement of cost of goods manufactured and sold, and a statement of surplus-all preferably arranged in comparative form for as many periods as are to be covered in the analysis. This and the following three chapters present material for the analysis and interpretation of financial statements. 

The Accounting Period.-Regardless of its length, the accounting period has certain limitations as a basis for study of the trends existing in a business either over long periods of time or within the current period.

The analysis of trends over long periods of time may be facilitated by means of comparative statements. Trends within the current period are not so easily ascertained, except where the accounting period can be subdivided into shorter periods, as the year into months, the month into weeks, the week into days. The calendar month is not completely satisfactory for comparative purposes, because it varies in length from twenty-eight to thirty-one days. The adoption of the natural business year of thirteen equal months would materially remedy this defect. 

There are no objections to the adoption of a natural business year as such, but the division of the year into thirteen equal months, while laudable, is subject to several objections; for example, the quarterly social security reports are based upon a calendar quarter; and the adoption of a thirteen-month year would necessitate end-of-the-quarter adjustments.

In this chapter, the year or month will be regarded as the suitable time-unit of comparison. The number of months or years to employ in a comparison depends upon and varies with the requirements of the 494

COMPARATIVE STATEMENTS 

495 comparative analysis. Some companies, in their annual statements, present balance sheets and statements of operations in comparative form for several years.

The Expression of Comparisons.-Where values are involved, comparisons may be expressed in the following ways: 

1. As absolute sums, showing increases and decreases in amounts 

2. As percentages, showing increases and decreases in amounts 

3. As ratios

If the gross sales of a concern are $100,000.00 in 1941 and $150,- 

000.00 in 1942, the three ways of expressing this comparison, mentioned above, are illustrated below.

Analysis Based on Comparison.-Comparative statements usually are made the means to an end, namely, analysis. This subject is treated fully in chapters XXV and XXVI, but it may be noted here that there are possibilities of analysis in the illustration presented above. It is possible.that: a) Cost price per unit has changed but the selling price per unit has remained the same. b) Cost price per unit has not changed but the selling price per unit has changed. c) Both cost price per unit and selling price per unit have changed; the amount of change in each case may be known or unknown. 

At this point only (a), above, is illustrated; further consideration is given to these problems in chapter XXVI. Since the selling price per unit is the same, the change in gross profit is accounted for as follows: 

Increase in gross profit to increase in sales (33.33% of $9,000.00)...

Decrease in gross profit due to increase in unit cost of sales .$3,000.00 2,000.00 (8.33% of $24,000.00)... 

Net increase in gròss profit.. $1,000.00

The Statements to Be Presented.-The extent to which statements should be expressed in comparative form depends upon circumstances, the comparisons desired, and the availability of the data. There exist certain physical limitations to the reproduction of data in comparative form. Those statements which most clearly indicate trends should therefore be selected. The following are typical: 

1. The balance sheet. 

2. The statement of profit and loss. 

3. The statement of cost of goods manufactured and sold. 

4. Schedules: a) Manufacturing expenses b) Selling expenses c) Administrative expenses d) Financial expenses and financial incomes 5. The statement of surplus.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING The Comparative Profit-and-Loss Statement.-Earlier in the chap ter the method of showing comparative sales, comparative cost of goods sold, and comparative gross profit was illustrated. The same plan may be applied to the complete statement of profit and loss for two or more periods. In the illustration on page 502, any one of the following columns could be eliminated: the "Percentage of Sales" column, the "Increase or Decrease in Amounts" column, or the "Percentage of 

Increase or Decrease" column. 

Comparative Statement of Cost of Goods Manufactured and 

Sold. The form for the comparative statement of cost of goods manufactured and sold is the same as for the comparative statement of profit and loss, of which it is merely a part; it is displayed separately to permit the presentation of the statement of profit and loss in condensed form. The form of comparative statement on page 503 shows percentages based on the cost of goods manufactured as 100 per cent. 

Comparative Expense Schedules. For any given company, comparative schedules of manufacturing expense, selling expense, administrative expense, and financial expense and income should be presented in the same form. Such procedure makes for uniformity and facilitates comparisons.

The Comparative Statement of Surplus.-Comparative statements of surplus are presented for the Exterior Company.

Reference Forward.-Extended illustrations of comparative state ment analyses are presented in chapters XXV and XXVI, for the Montana Company.

Chapter XXIV  Purpose of the Statement.-Comparative balance sheets show changes in each balance sheet item at one date as compared with another date. Statements of profit and loss show incomes, expenses, and resultant profit or loss. Neither of these statements answers the question: From what sources did the business obtain funds (net working capital) during the year, and what disposition was made of these funds (net working capital)? The statement of application of funds is designed to show the sources from which the funds were provided, and the uses to which the funds were applied. The basic data necessary for the preparation of the statement are comparative balance sheets and other data to be set forth later in the chapter. 

The ordinary sources of funds are: 

1. Net profit 

2. Sale of capital stock 

3. Sale of bonds, or other fixed liability 

4. The sale of fixed or investment or intangible assets 

The ordinary dispositions of funds are: 

1. The payment of dividends 

2. The retirement of fixed liabilities 

3. The retirement of capital stock 

4. The acquisition of fixed or investment or intangible assets 

5. To cover a net loss 

The difference between the sources and the dispositions of the working capital funds equals the increase or decrease in net working capital. 

Working Capital.-Net working capital is the excess of the current assets over the current liabilities. If the amount of net working capital increases or decreases, changes also have taken place in other sections of the balance sheet. A change in any one item of working capital may not necessarily alter the net amount of working capital; for example, if a current liability of $1,000.00 is paid, the amount of net working 508

Because of the nature of working capital, changes therein are summarized in a schedule separated from the statement of application of funds. Each source of money increases working capital and each disposition of money decreases working capital.

Adjustments: Case III. Surplus Dividends, Depreciation, Intangibles, Amortization, Bad Debts.-In Cases I and II, the increase or decrease in each item in 1942 compared with 1941 resulted in (a) a change in net working capital, or (b) a fund provided, or (c) a fund applied. 

In many instances the increase or decrease in an account does not represent a change affecting the statement of application of funds; such increases and decreases must be adjusted in the work sheet so that a true statement of application of funds may be obtained. 

In other instances, certain expenses do not represent a disbursement of cash, yet they do reduce net profit. Depreciation expense is an example of this type. If all incomes were received in cash, the funds provided thereby would exceed the funds applied by the net profit plus the depreciation and all other non-fund expenses. Consequently, for non-fund expenses, it is necessary to add such expenses to the net profits in order to determine the true funds provided by profits.' 

Before proceeding with the next illustration, certain necessary adjustments will be considered; these adjustments are then reflected in the illustration, Case III. Additional adjustments will be considered after Case 3.

Surplus

Net Loss Instead of Net Profit.-Up to this point, the illustrations have assumed a net profit for the period. If a net loss is incurred, funds have been applied to cover the loss; however, by adding back non-cash charges such as depreciation and bond discount amortized, the net loss debit may be changed to a credit. In such cases, funds are actually provided by operations exclusive of non-cash charges. To illustrate, assume a net loss of $11,000.00 after depreciation of $18,000.00 and bond discount amortization of $2,000.00; the statement of application of funds, for these items, would appear as follows: 

Funds Provided:

By Adding Back Non-Cash Charges: 

Depreciation

Bond Discount Amortized. 

Deduct Net Loss.. 

Funds Provided . $18,000.00 2,000.00 $20,000.00 11,000.00 $ 9,000.00

If the addition of the non-cash charges do not exceed the net loss, funds have been applied. The loss may be shown (1) in the funds provided section of the statement of application of funds as a deduction from total provisions, or (2) in the funds applied section. The better procedure probably is to show the situation in the funds applied section, even though non-cash charges, reducing the loss, are shown in the same section.

Chapter XXV  

The Meaning of Analysis.-The analysis of financial statements involves the preparation and interpretation of data supplied by those statements. The objective of financial statement analysis is to prepare financial and operating data which, when properly interpreted, will serve as guides for the proper managerial control and direction of a business. The analysis of financial statements involves three steps: the financial and operating data must be compiled, the data is then compared for certain significant facts to be set forth in this and the following chapter, and, finally, the comparisons of the data are analyzed in terms of the. specific conditions of the business for which the analysis is prepared.

Normally, analysis is the determination of a direct relationship between two items or groups of items and the comparison and interpretation of that relationship with the same relationship of other fiscal periods or dates; or its comparison with other relationships, or with other similar companies, or with the industry as a whole, or with the average for several preceding periods. 

Statement analyses may be made in terms of amounts, showing increases and decreases in amounts, by items, from one date to another date. Analyses may also be made in percentage figures with increases or decreases in the percentage figures shown between fiscal periods. 

By percentage analysis is meant the reduction of items to a percentage of another item or to a percentage of a total. For example, if net sales are $100,000.00 and if the net profit is $10,000.00, the percentage of net profit realized on sales is 10 per cent. 

By ratio analysis is meant the preparation of ratios so that analyses may be made by the interpretation of these ratios. Through the establishment of ratios, trends are ascertained, and the interrelationship of balance sheet items and profit-and-loss items in their movements and the effect of those movements on other balance sheet and profit-andloss items is shown. Control of the business is exercised by studying 529

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

these trends and using them to guide the business into sound financial channels.

Basic Data. The basic data of analysis are the statements and other financial data used in making comparisons and drawing conclusions. The possibilities of analysis are limited by the nature and accuracy of the basic data. Normally, the balance sheet and its supporting schedules, and the statement of profit and loss and its supporting schedules constitute the basic data for percentage and ratio analysis. 

Both the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss are necessary for complete analysis, as each statement is directly related to the other, and each complements the other. 

Financial statements must reflect correct classifications of assets, liabilities, incomes, and expenses to be of most value for purposes of analysis. Likewise the statements must be prepared on the same basis each period.

The analyses to be considered in this and the following chapter are based on data found in the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss, and on data which serve to amplify the information found in these two statements.

Analysis may be based on percentages, or ratios, or both, derived from single statements, or it may be based on percentages, or ratios, or figures, or all three, derived from comparative statements. Limitation of the analysis is immediately imposed when statements for a single period are used; as only one period is shown, dollar and percentage increases and decreases are not possible. The better practice is to use comparative statements for several periods, as a longer range picture and analysis is thereby made possible. 

Persons Interested in Analysis.-Three classes of persons are interested in financial statement analyses. The first of these is the management group. For them studies may be made which are useful in the proper guidance of the business and the adequacy or inadequacy of (a) profit trends and (b) the relationship of various phases of the business unit may be ascertained. Furthermore statistical studies may be made by which business data and trends may be compared with those of competitors and the industry as a whole; also, studies of a customer's business may be made prior to the extentsion of credit.

The second class is made up of present owners and prospective investors. The first group of this class is interested in analyses by

which they may adequately judge the business efficiency of the management and the safety of their investment. The second group of this class is interested because they may wish to determine the relative merits of investment in one company as opposed to some other company.

The third class consists of the banks and other grantors of credit. 

This group is interested in analyses that enable them to determine the advisability of extending credit to the business. 

The Ratios and Percentages Considered.-The ratio and percentage analyses presented in this and the following chapter are based upon the ratios and percentages indicated in the following outline. 

Those relationships considered to be of vital importance to the average business are indicated by capital letters, such as A, B, C, and so on; those relationships of less or even minor importance are indicated by sub-numerals to the important relationship, such as A,, S₂, and so on. 

If analysis is made of only those items indicated by capital letters, an adequate analysis will result in the majority of instances.

There are many additional ratios and percentage analyses. The limits of a book of this nature do not permit the inclusion of all, as analysis is a large and specialized phase of general accounting. 

Not all of the foregoing ratios and percentages will be of interest to all of the three classes of persons interested in ratio studies and interpretations.

Basis of the Analysis.-The following statements for the Montana 

Manufacturing Company are presented as the basis for the ratio and percentage studies and analyses. The analyst should not expect drastic changes from year to year. Business operations normally are conducted

over a smooth wave of increases and decreases. Some persons are disappointed when a ratio study does not show tremendous changes in items and in relationships from one year to another year.

BALANCE SHEET RELATIONSHIPS 

By balance sheet relationship is meant the direct comparison of two or more items of a balance sheet. From these relationships, interpretations may be made in order to determine the adequacy or inadequacy of the relationships; from the results of the relationships trends and comparisons may be established.

A. The Current Ratio. 

Current Ratio= Current Assets (net) Current Liabilities 

The net working capital of a company is the excess of the current assets over the current liabilities; expressed another way, if a company liquidated all of its current liabilities, the available current or working capital with which to buy and sell would be the remaining current assets.

The current ratio, also called the net working capital ratio, is obtained by dividing the current assets (net) by the current liabilities.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

It is the relationship of current assets to current liabilities, and, of all the ratios, the current ratio is best known and most universally employed. The ratio may be stated in dollars of current assets to one dollar of current liabilities; for example, if a company has $178.00 of current assets and $100.00 of current liabilities, the current ratio is expressed as 178 per cent, or it may be expressed as $1.78 of current assets to $1.00 of current liabilities.

In expressing any ratio, the reader must remember that the trend of the ratio from year to year is a vitally important factor. 

The current ratio is commonly employed as a measure of the ability to pay current debts as they fall due; it is also employed as a measure of the ability to pay current obligations under conditions of possible forced liquidation of the current assets. 

At one time, a current ratio of 2 to 1 or better was commonly accepted as a satisfactory condition. This is no longer necessarily true, as the current ratio depends upon the type of industry, methods of buying and selling, the methods of financing in general, the season of the year, and the period of the business cycle. 

When an analysis is made of business within an industry, the current ratios are large for some and small for others. In any event, a favorable current ratio is essential to the maintenance of a good credit position. 

The current ratio within reasonable limits may be of more importance than is the amount of net working capital, as shown by the following illustration:

Current Assets... 

Current Liabilities. 

Working Capital.. 

Current Ratio.. 

Company I $50,000.00 25,000.00 $25,000.00

Company II 

$625,000.00 600,000.00 $ 25,000.00 $2.00 to $1.00 $1,04 to $1.00

The net working capital is $25,000.00 in both cases, but the relationship is quite different for the two companies. 

The current ratio increases if current assets increase proportionately faster than current liabilities, or if current assets decrease less than proportionately to a decrease in current liabilities; if the reverse of these situations occur, the current ratio decreases.

A1. The Acid Test Ratio.- Acid Test Ratio = Cash + Net Receivables Current Liabilities 

This is the ratio of cash and net receivables (known as quick assets) to current liabilities. The acid test ratio is more critical than the current ratio, as inventories and marketable securities are eliminated from consideration. In a current ratio, there are always the questions of the speed of conversion of raw materials and the saleability of finished goods, and the marketability of the marketable securities at a reasonable price. Therefore, in order to determine the quick or near future ability to meet current obligations, only cash and good receivables are taken into consideration. An acid test ratio of $1.00 of quick assets to $1.00 of current liabilities is quite satisfactory, as each dollar of quick assets enables the payment of one dollar of current liabilities.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING B. How Capital Is Invested.—To show how the capital is invested is to determine the percentage of each classification of assets (net) to the total assets (net). The asset side of a balance sheet shows the investments in each asset and in each class of asset, such as current, fixed, and other groups. A harmonious relationship should exist among the various classifications and between each class and the total. A large increase in the percentage of fixed assets compared with the total assets, for example, with no appreciable increase in sales, might easily indicate undue plant expansion. A decrease in the percentages of inventories might indicate that inventories are being curtailed because of declining business, or it might indicate that insufficient inventory is being carried for current needs. The investment of capital, as represented in the asset side of a balance sheet is directly related to the turnover of the assets; by proper distribution of the various asset classes, turnovers are better, meaning that more sales per dollar of capital are possible. The investment in each class of assets depends upon the industry and the business within that industry; there are no universally characteristic percentages. Usually, however, the business organizations within one particular industry tend to show common characteristics for invested capital.

The distribution of the investment of capital and the trend of the investment for the Montana Company is shown below.

C. The Sources of Capital.-The sources of financing a business are shown by computing the percentage of current liabilities, fixed liabilities, and net worth to the sum of the liabilities plus net worth. 

The liability and net worth sections of a balance sheet show the sources employed in obtaining capital. The methods of financing a business are: the sale of capital stock, the retention of profits, borrowing on short-term credit, and borrowing on long-term credit. If the percentage of each source of capital is shown, an indication is given of the various classes of equities in the company; if the yearly trends of the percentage sources are watched, an indication is given of the increasing or decreasing interests of insiders (the stockholders) and the increasing or decreasing interests of outsiders (the creditors).

The methods employed by a company in financing itself and the fortunes of a particular company will in great measure determine the sources of capital. Two companies, in a similar business, may show quite similar percentage distribution of assets among the various classes, but, at the same time, those two companies may show entirely different sources of capital, if one company is dependent upon stockholders' investments for the greater portion of its financing and if the other company borrows heavily.

Short-term borrowing is normally limited to about 50 per cent of the value of the current assets; long-term borrowing is limited to perhaps 50 per cent to 70 per cent of the value of the fixed assets and permanent income-producing investments. Most public utilities and railroads obtain a larger portion of their capital from long-term borrowings than do industrial corporations; the latter depend primarily upon the investment of stockholders, regardless of the fact that fixed assets normally constitute a large proportion of the total assets. 

The reader must not believe that the proportion of net worth to total liabilities and net worth need necessarily be large. If money can be borrowed at, say, 4 per cent, and if 8 per cent can be earned on

the borrowed capital, borrowing may prove advantageous, as the additional profits earned on the borrowing results in a greater return on the

D. The Ratio of Net Worth to Total Liabilities.-This ratio, Net Worth shows the relation of net worth to total liabilities, Total Liabilities, both current and fixed. As the interests of the stockholders increase, the size of the ratio increases. A 100 per cent ratio is attained when net worth equals total liabilities, that is, when one-half of the total capital is supplied by the stockholders. The ratio is closely connected with the percentages for the sources of capital. Again, an excessive ratio is not necessarily an indication of sound financing as profitable opportunities may be overlooked by the failure to borrow.

This ratio is of importance when considered in connection with the current ratio. The current ratio may be improved by funding a portion or all of the floating debt, but such a conversion does not alter the total liabilities; consequently the relationship of net worth to total liabilities is not bettered.

TURNOVERS 

Turnover means the number of times per period that the value of some balance sheet item or group of items is disposed of and replenished in terms of sales. Stated another way, turnover is the rate of sales to some balance sheet item or group of items. Turnovers measure the efficient employment of an asset, from the point of view of obtaining the maximum rate of return on the value of the investment in the asset. may be a definite indication of underinvestment or overinvestment in assets, in terms of sales. The trend of any turnover is of vital im- `portance, as is also a comparison of the turnovers of a given company with the average for the industry. It

E. Turnover of Total Assets.-The turnover of the total assets, Net Sales shows the relationship between the volume of 

Total Assets (net)' 

business and the total assets of the business. The greater the sales made per dollar of assets, the larger is the profit earned on each dollar of assets invested in the business. Therefore, this turnover is a measure of the efficient use of the capital employed. It also shows whether there is a tendency toward overinvestment in the assets. The turnover of total assets naturally includes all of the asset classifications, except incomeproducing investments of a permanent nature; therefore, it is a general measure of the efficient use of all assets employed in business operations. To determine the efficient use of any one class of assets, the total of that class divided into net sales will give the turnover of the class; for example, the total fixed tangible asset turnover will indicate the efficient use of those assets or the trend of efficient or inefficient use of those assets.

The greater the per year ratio of sales to total assets or the greater the turnover of total assets, the more efficiently employed is the asset

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

total. Conversely, too great a turnover may mean that insufficient capital is resulting in loss of sales, through failure to meet demand. 

In order to obtain an average asset turnover, the average of the assets, except permanent investments, for twelve months of the year should be used; in many instances this is impossible; consequently, the asset total (except permanent investments) at the end of the year is ordinarily used in the computation.

At this point, it may be advisable to remind the reader that certain businesses make annual sales equal to many times their total assets, while certain other businesses have annual sales of only a fractional part of their total asset investment. Consequently, there is no uniformity of the turnover of total assets between industries and between individual business concerns within an industry. 

The turnover of total assets may be stated in dollars of sales ($3.25) to one dollar of total assets, or it may be stated in turnover times per year (31/4 times) or in percentage (325 per cent). As a result of the computation of the turnover and after a study of the trend of the turnover, the management can determine policies and execute plans for the more efficient employment of capital; if the turnover is too slow, the remedy may be to scale capitalization downward or to attempt to secure more sales; if the turnover is too high and if at the same time it is known that sales possibilities are being lost because of insufficient capital, an attempt will probably be made to secure additional capital. The reader must remember that a better turnover of total assets may be achieved by increasing the turnover of any asset or class of assets, such as inventories or the total current assets, or any other asset or class. An improved turnover should always have one important result, namely, a higher profit on the invested capital. A comparison of the turnover of the total assets for any company with the average turnover for the industry as a whole gives a direct insight into the efficiency of that one company. The turnover of total assets (except permanent investments) for the Montana Company is presented.

E1. The Turnover of Net Working Capital.-The turnover of the net working capital is important because business profits are closely related to sales, because business activity is closely related to the availability of working capital, and because sales are closely related to inventory acquisition and disposition. Working capital is increased through the earning of profits and is reduced by losses; it is also decreased through the purchase of and payment for fixed or other assets which are not within the current classification. Therefore, if fixed and other assets are not acquired and if profits continue to increase as a result of the efficient use of working capital, the turnover of net working capital should continue to rise. In computing the turnover, an average net working capital figure for the year is preferable to the net working capital at the end of the year. The net working capital turnover for the Montana Company is presented.

F. Net Working Capital Represented by Inventory.-The net working capital represented by inventory is in answer to the question: what portion of the operating funds is tied up in inventories? Profits depend upon the conversion and sale of inventories at profitable prices. 

If the percentage of inventories to net working capital increases, the indication might be that money is tied up in inventories which may be slow of conversion into cash or receivables. In computing the percentage of net working capital involved in inventories, yearly averages of both net working capital and of inventories are more satisfactory than if the figures are taken as of the end of a period; at the end of a period, either working capital or inventories might be abnormally high or abnormally low, leading to distorted relationships. 

Changes in net working capital of a business take place but slowly; and in profitable years the working capital tends to rise. Consequently, with increased profits, an increase in this ratio is possible only by larger inventories at the end of the period. For the Montana Company:

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING

It is seen that the percentage of working capital represented by inventory increased from 1943 to 1944 by a faster rate than did working capital in total, but at the same time the increase in inventory was less than the percentage increase in sales, leading to the conclusion that the increase in inventory is justified by larger sales expectancies. 

In those cases when the percentage of inventory increases with a decreased sales figure, there is instant warning of an overstocking in inventory.

G. Turnover of Inventory.-The turnover of inventory is repre- 

Cost of Goods Sold sented by

Ending Inventory 

A substitute formula, Net Sales Ending Inventory is satisfactory only in those instances where cost of sales cannot be ascertained. The proper formula bases both the numerator and the denominator on a cost basis. In both formulas it is better practice to use the average annual inventory (averaged monthly), because end-of-the-year fluctuations from normal are thereby eliminated. When inventory turnovers are computed for an entire business, departmental turnover computations should also be made, as turnovers vary widely between departments. Also, for manufacturing concerns, turnovers should also be computed for each class of inventories, that is, raw materials, work-in-process, and finished goods. 

The rapidity with which inventories are sold and replenished is measured by the inventory turnover. The greater the number of times per period that an inventory can be bought and sold, the smaller will be the amount of capital necessary to accomplish a given amount of sales. Every time an inventory is sold a profit is made, and the greater number of times per period the inventory value can be sold, the greater will be the return on the investment, because a smaller investment in inventory is needed. The newspaper vendor turns his investment in inventory at least once a day; consequently, an extremely small capital is tied up in inventories, and the rate of profit on the investment is

large. On the other hand, a jeweler may turn his inventory only once in several years; consequently, a large capital is needed. The rate of profit on newspaper sales can naturally be smaller than the rate of profit on the sales of jewelry. Groceries also depend upon a fast turnover, low rate of profit per dollar of sales, total sales of many times the capital investment, as compared with the jeweler who depends upon a slow turnover, high rate of profit per dollar of sales, and total sales of only a fraction of the total capital investment. In any case, the higher rate of turnover offers less danger of the accumulation of obsolete merchandise; the highest possible turnover usually effects savings which are beneficial to the organization. Every business wishes to move its inventories as rapidly as possible. Naturally, prices are constantly rising and falling; consequently the businessman can more easily maintain his gross margin of profit by avoiding inventory accumulations in a falling market and by avoiding excessive speculation even in a rising market; such speculation, if carried on, will result in unduly large inventories, which may still remain on hand when prices fall. 

The function of a merchandising or manufacturing business is not price speculation; speculation in inventories means that more capital is necessary to carry the larger inventory; and anyway in many instances, the cost of borrowing to carry the larger inventories and the costs of handling and storage more than offset the speculative profits.

averaged monthly, should be used if this average can be obtained; the average is more representative than the balance as of any one date. If possible, only charge sales should be used..

The turnover of accounts receivable expresses the relationship between sales and the receivables; if the turnover increases, receivables are smaller in relation to sales; that is, the accounts are being collected more promptly than when the turnover decreases. Too large a volume of accounts receivable which are not rapidly collected often necessitate borrowing in order to pay off liabilities.

Turnovers of accounts receivable vary widely between industries and between individual businesses within an industry. The trend is of vital importance in any case, as a slower turnover will eventually mean greater bad debt losses and greater credit and collection expense. I. The Number of Days' Sales in Accounts Receivable.-This is not a turnover or a ratio. It is determined by taking the days in the year, say 365, and dividing by the turnover of accounts receivable. The result is the average days' sales represented by the balance of the accounts receivable. The number of days' sales in accounts receivable is the same as the turnover of accounts receivable, expressed in a different manner. To express the turnover in days' sales is probably the more effective, as a clearer picture of the rapidity of account collection is thereby presented. The desired trend is a constantly smaller number of days' sales represented by accounts receivable, as this is indicative of faster collection and subsequent smaller bad debt losses.

The fewer the days' sales represented in accounts receivable, the smaller the capital requirements of an organization, and the smaller may be a satisfactory rate of profit on sales. In order to demonstrate the advantage of rapid collection, the following example is submitted.

J. The Turnover of Property Investment.-The formula is Net Sales Net Plant and Equipment Units of Product Sold 

-; or 

Net Plant and Equipment 

Expenses of operation, particularly fixed charges such as depreciation, taxes, insurance, and maintenance, are closely related to the value of the capital invested in fixed tangible assets. The tendency to overinvest in fixed assets is directly measured by computing the turnover of those fixed assets. For each dollar placed among permanent assets, the greatest possible dollars of sales should be forthcoming. If fixed asset turnover declines, either sales are declining, or additional investments are being made in property assets which are not resulting in a proportionately increased sales volume. The operation of a plant at capacity usually results in the best ratio possible. When changes in sales prices occur, either upward or downward, the turnover is affected; this is one reason why it is better to use the units of product sold as a base. Chapter XXVI - Concluded 

Measures of Earnings.—If certain comparisons are made between the profits of a business and the sales, the cost of sales, and the capital employed, it is possible to measure the profits from the point of view of their adequacy or inadequacy based (1) on sales, and (2) capital employed. By comparing the profits with the sales and the capital employed, from period to period, it is possible to determine the trend of the profit over several periods. 

The measures of earnings, outlined in chapter XXV, are presented in this chapter.

K. Percentage of Net Operating Profit to Net Sales.--Net operat ing profit is the profit realized from normal buying, manufacturing and selling operations; and excludes financial and non-operating profits and losses. Profits vary from year to year because of variations in many factors, including the cost of the goods manufactured and sold, the sales price, the sales volume in units, and operating expenses. 

The rate of net operating profits to net sales is closely related to the rate of profit earned on the total capital employed in a business; the return on both must be satisfactory; in certain cases the rate of profit on sales may be satisfactory, but the rate of return on the capital employed may be far below normal, due to decreased sales volume. Also, with relatively small capital it may be possible to obtain a satisfactory rate of return on the invested capital, with a below-average rate of return on sales. Therefore, the rate of net operating profit on net sales and on the total capital employed are complementary to each other, and both must be analyzed in order to determine the adequacy and propriety of the net operating profit. 

When analyzing the rate of net operating profit on net sales, the computations should be made not only with respect to total sales but also by products, by departments, and by branches or divisions. This may be necessary to determine whether some products are sold at a net loss, and whether some of the departments operate at a net loss; the 351

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

discovery of such conditions often surprises the owners who never before have made that kind of an analysis of operations. Net sales should be used as a base, for sales returns and sales allowances decrease revenue.

There are no standard rates of net operating profits to net sales, for the rates vary widely between industries and between individual business concerns within an industry. In general, the greater the capital investment necessary for the efficient operation of a business, and the slower the normal rate of inventory turnover, the larger will be the rate of net operating profit on sales. Conversely, where inventory turnover is rapid, and where capital requirements are smaller, the rate of profit on sales normally is smaller. In either case, the rate of profit on employed capital might be the same; here, as elsewhere, managerial efficiency plays a large part toward the attainment of satisfactory results.

For the Montana Company, the percentage of net operating profits to net sales is as follows:

The rate of net operating profit to net sales is high, but the capitalization of the company is necessarily high, resulting in a satisfactory, but not too great a return on the invested capital. 

K₁. Under relatively stable operating conditions, the net profit figure may be subject to greater fluctuations than will the net operating profit figure, because of fluctuations in financial and non-operating items.
