L. The Percentage of Net Operating Profit to Total Assets at the End of the Year.-The net operating profit divided by the total assets shows the rate of operating profit earned on the income-producing capital employed in the business. Permanent investments in incomeproducing securities should be eliminated from the asset total, as those assets are not productively employed in earning operating profits. As pointed out in the discussion of the percentage of net operating profit to net sales, that relationship and the percentage of net operating profit to total assets are closely related and are complementary to each other. 

From a strictly managerial point of view, the percentage of operating profits earned on net assets is the true barometer of the adequacy of the financial return earned on an investment although from the stockholders' point of view, the return is measured on the net worth, and not on the total of the assets or capital employed. Effective turnovers increase the return on the asset investment-the capital. The efficient and satisfactory use and operation of the assets results in a satisfactory return on the investment in those assets. Thus, the present relationship is the true measure of the profitableness of the investment in assets, regardless of the sources of the capital employed. 

As in the percentage of net operating profits to net sales, the per- . centage of net operating profit to total assets should be analyzed by units, departments, or branches. 

By eliminating financial and non-operating incomes and financial and non-operating expenses, methods and costs of financing are eliminated from normal business transactions. the The percentage of net operating profits to total assets at the end of for the Montana Company is presented. year 1942 1943 1944

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING M. The Percentage of Net Operating Profit to Total Tangible 

Net Worth. The net operating profit divided by the net worth minus all intangible assets eliminates the intangible assets from consideration. 

Intangible assets may have intrinsic value, or they may be the result of appraisals which are not necessarily well founded. If they are eliminated from consideration, only assets which presumably represent sound cost values are taken into consideration. 

The percentage of net operating profit to total tangible net worth naturally takes into consideration the methods employed to finance a business, this is, whether stockholders or creditors, or both, supply the capital. If the rate of net operating profit to total tangible net worth is larger than the interest costs involved in borrowing, then greater financing through borrowings will result in a larger return on the stockholders' investment. For example, if a company earns 10 per cent net operating profit on its tangible net worth, and if it can borrow one-half the capital at 5 per cent interest, the return on the tangible net worth is increased to 15 per cent, because a net operating profit of 5 per cent is realized by borrowing. The profits made possible by borrowing should not lead to excessive borrowing, however, because risks are increased and in a depression period the large burden of interest costs might prove disastrous.

O. Net Profit After Federal Taxes per Share of Common Stock 

Outstanding. If all of the capital stock is common stock of one uniform class, the entire net profit belongs to the owners of the common stock. If both preferred stock and common stock are outstanding, the total corporate net worth is attributable to both preferred and common interests. Thus, when preferred stock is outstanding, some part of the profits are assigned to the preferred stock and the remainder is allocable to the common stock. In order to determine the rate of profit (or dollars earned per share) on the common stock outstanding, it is necessary to divide the net profits between the various classes of stock outstanding.

In order to divide the profits between preferred and common stock, the provisions of the features of the preferred stock must be followed; see chapters VI, VII, VIII, and IX. The preferred stock may be participating, in which case additional dividends over the stated rate may be payable to the preferred holders. 

Most preferred stock issues provide for preference over common stock for a specific limited dividend per share, with no participating rights beyond this amount. Thus all profits in excess of this preferred dividend are assignable to the common shareholders. In such cases it is only necessary to deduct preferred dividends from the profits for the period, and to divide by the number of shares of common stock outstanding, in order to arrive at the final net profit' per share of common stock.

P. Percentage of Net Profits Left in the Business. In order to conserve and to expand capital, it is imperative that a portion of the annual profits be retained in the business. This policy prevents excessive borrowing in times of capital increases and it also prevents stock issue flotations at times when there is no long-time necessity for such expansion. Some persons, some agencies, some stockholders, do not desire capital expansion through retention of part of the profits, believing that all profits should be distributed to stockholders. Such views apparently have no merit when considered from the point of view of permanent financial stability. It is true, of course, that isolated instances exist of the obvious failure of corporations to pay adequate dividends in the face of large earnings. However, no large, old, sound, honest company is in existence which has not followed the policy of some savings from profits. The retained profits accrue to the stockholders and in normal times are reflected through higher stock prices in the market. The percentage of net profits left in the business, for the 

Montana Company is as follows:

Apportionment of the Sales Dollar Over Costs and Profit.-By apportioning the sales dollar over costs and profit, comparative figures are obtained which show for each period the amount of the sales dollar required for the various elements of cost and expense incurred by the sales activity. If the cost per dollar of sales increases, the tendency is for the net operating profit per dollar of sales to decrease. A study of the changes in such figures is highly important in analyzing costs and expenses.

ACCOUNTING FOR PROFIT VARIATION 

The causes of changes in net profit may be outlined as follows: 

1. An increase or decrease in net sales volume 

2. An increase or decrease in sales price 

3. An increase or decrease in the cost of sales 

4. An increase or decrease in operating expenses 

5. An increase or decrease in non-operating expenses 

6. An increase or decrease in non-operating incomes 

Net sales may increase, decrease, or remain constant, and at the same time the unit selling price may or may not change. In some cases, however, unit costs and unit selling prices are not available; consequently, THE MONTANA MANUFACTURING COMPANY STATEMENT ACCOUNTING FOR PROFIT VARIATION

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

analysis must stop with a consideration of changes in total cost of sales and total net sales. 

Causes of the changes in profits brought about by changes in sales, costs, and expenses are now considered. 

Changes in sales may be the result of: 

Increased or decreased volume. 

Increased or decreased prices. 

Changes in costs and expenses may be the result of: 

Increased or decreased volume.

Increased or decreased unit costs and expenses, brought about by changes in price levels or changing economies of production. 

The foregoing statement accounting for profit variation is based upon the condensed Statement of Profit and Loss of the Montana Company, appearing on page 561, for the years 1943 and 1944 only. 

The statement of accounting for profit variation shows that net profit was increased by an increase in the gross profit and a decrease in the net financial expenses; it also shows that income was decreased by an increase in selling and administrative expenses, but the rate of increase in these expenses was at a slower rate than the rate of increase in sales. A sales increase of 33.18 per cent and an increase in the cost of goods sold of 32.47 per cent resulted in a 34.10 per cent increase in gross profit. Selling expenses increased only 7.67 per cent compared with an increase of 33.18 per cent in sales; administrative expenses increased 27.38 per cent compared with an increase of 33.18 per cent in sales. 

Changes in Cost Prices and in Sales Prices.-If changes in prices have been effected, the following statement may be prepared setting forth the extent to which gross profits were affected by changes in sales prices and changes in the margin of gross profit. 

Assume, for the Montana Company, that 1944 sales prices were increased 10 per cent over those of 1943. The net sales of 1944 of $2,777,200.00 at 1943 levels would be: $2,777,200.00 ÷ 110% $2,524,727.27. Cost of sales, 1943, was 56.50 per cent of sales; on the 1943 basis, the 1944 goods sold would have cost: 56.50 per cent of $2,524,727.27, or $1,426,470.91.

The changes in gross profit can now be accounted for as follows:

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

Gross Profit Changes.-From the information normally available in a statement of profit and loss, it is impossible to determine whether the rate of gross profit was caused by a change in cost or sales prices or volume, or some combination of these variables. Changes in total gross profit are caused by changes in sales, both as to price and volume, and by changing cost of goods sold figures. 

A few examples are presented showing comparative studies accounting for various changes.

In addition to the above mark-downs, the selling price of certain merchandise was reduced in connection. with a special store-wide sale held annually in October of each year. During the season the selling price of a special lot of imported gloves which proved to be unusually popular was increased from the original selling price of $6.00 per pair to $7.50 per pair. This additional mark-up applied to 500 dozen pair of gloves. Later in the season the additional mark-up of $1.50 was cancelled on 75 dozen pair of gloves of a certain color which were not moving as fast as the remainder of the line and the price reduced to the original price of $6.00 per pair.

A physical inventory taken at the close of business December 31, 1942, aggregated $94,500.00 at retail. The physical inventory at retail was found to be unusually close to the book inventory and did not show the normal expected shrinkage. Investigation revealed that a lot of 50 dozen pair of gloves received in the last few days of the year had not been included in the purchases recorded in the stock records because the invoice had not been received until after the close of the year. This lot of 50 dozen pair of gloves was purchased at a cost of $3.75 per pair and were marked to sell at $6.00 per pair. 

Some of the gloves included in this lot had been sold before the close of the year and were not included in the inventory.

625 computes its state income tax liability on the same basis that it takes up income, but pays its state income tax on the installment. sales basis, which is permissible under the law. Requirements: From the data presented below, prepare: (a) the entries to record the transactions on the books of the Polar Corporation. (b) Comprehensive summaries of these entries showing and explaining the following resulting balances at December 31,1941: 

1. Consignment. 

2. Repossessed refrigerators.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

3. Cash. 

4. AB Company. 

5. Profit realized.

On June 1 the Polar Corporation consigned 100 refrigerators to the AB Company, to be sold as follows: 

Cash price-$180.00 less 5 per cent discount.

Time-payment plan -$180.00 net, one-third cash on delivery, the balance in 24 monthly payments of $5.00. All credit sales are subject to the approval of the Polar Corporation as to credit risk.

Refrigerators will be repossessed when time-payment contracts are two months in default and will be returned to the manufacturer for reconditioning. 

The manufacturing cost of each refrigerator was $60.00 and $400.00 freight was prepaid on the shipment. The AB Company paid $200.00 truckage and deposited with the consignor $7,500.00 cash, thus advancing in all $7,700.00 to secure the consignment. 

This sum is to remain credited to the AB Company until all refrigerators are sold and fully paid or reposessed. However, on December 

31, 1941, and thereafter on the last day of each month, the consignor must refund to the AB Company the amount, if any, by which the original deposit exceeds the aggregate of (1) the full sales price of the unsold refrigerators and (2) the uncollected installments on time-payment contracts.

The AB Company will receive a commission of $30.00 on each refrigerator sold for cash or on approved time-payment contract. The AB 

Company will promptly remit all collections less commissions in full on all such sales. Commissions on defaulted contracts that have been approved by the Polar Corporation will not be recoverable from the AB Company.

On June 30, 1941, the AB Company reported that they had sold 60 refrigerators, 20 for cash and 40 on the time-payment plan. The latter sales had been duly approved by the Polar Corporation. The amounts collected had been remitted according to agreement. 

Installments on the 40 time-payment contracts were collected for July, August, and September and had likewise been remitted. 

In October and November, collections were made and remitted on only 30 of these contracts and the refrigerators sold on the 10 defaulting contracts were repossessed and returned to the Polar Corporation on November 30, 1941. The latter expects to sell these refrigerators at $100.00 each after spending $10.00 each for inward freight and cost of reconditioning. (Note: Repossessed goods are to be valued at the unrecovered manufacturing cost to the Polar Company). 

December collections on time-payment contracts were made in full and the AB Company reported cash sales of 20 refrigerators, and 20 remaining in stock. The Polar Corporation received these collections and the net proceeds from the sale on December 31, 1941. 

The Polar Corporation, in accounting for installment sales, follows the plan of recognizing income only in terms of amounts collected. (A. I. A.)

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 18-4. Purpose: 

The determination of the advisability to purchase new equipment.

Requirements: From the information presented below, (a) show all computations necessary to determine the recommendation or the rejection of the purchase of the new equipment; (b) if the new equipment was purchased, what entries would be made? 

The City Nut and Bolt Company has four automatic screw machines of a certain design. Each machine produces 400 units per day but has a higher operating speed capacity of 500 units. The cost was $10,000.00 each, with an estimated life of twelve years, and an estimated scrap value of $1,000.00 each. At present, the machines are seven years old. Maintenance costs are $200.00 per year per machine. 

Each machine requires one operator who receives $.80 per hour; the machines operate eight hours per day for 300 days per year. 

Two new multiple-head machines are being considered to replace the old machines. Each of the new machines has a capacity of 1,000 units per day. The cost is $25,000.00 each installed, with an estimated life of ten years, and a salvage value of $1,000.00 each. Maintenance per machine is estimated at $300.00 per year. Each machine requires one operator at $1.50 per hour.

For future periods, the capacity production of the new machines will be attained.

The vendor offers a trade-in allowance equal to twice the estimated salvage of the old machines.

The Corbin Mining Company owns coal deposits estimated at 20,000,000 tons; under the mining methods in operation, only 70 per cent of the coal can be extracted. The land cost $700,000.00. Machinery, buildings, tipples and railroad facilities cost $70,000.00, with no salvage value.

In 1942, 30,000 cars of 50 tons each were extracted and sold.

20-6. Purpose: The amortization of leaseholds and lease expenses 

Requirements: From the following information, prepare specimen initial and weekly entries to be set up on the books of the theatre company.

Electrical sound-producing equipment is leased to a theatre company under a ten-year agreement which provides for (a) the return of the equipment at the expiration of the lease, in good condition, allowing for reasonable wear and tear and for obsolescence; (b) an initial payment of $6,000.00 plus weekly payments of $ 300.00 for the first two years (104 weeks) and $75.00 per week during the remaining eight years.

The initial payment represents part of the license fee and the entire cost of installation of the equipment. 

Fifty per cent of the amounts payable weekly during the initial two-year period represent license fee and the other 50 per cent represents insurance and interest under the deferred payment plan. Payments during the last eight years represent service and inspection charges.

You may consider five years (260 weeks) as a conservative basis for the amortization of all costs, regardless of the longer life of the lease, in view of the frequent improvements in motion picture equipment. (A. I. A., Adapted) 

20-7. Purpose: A problem in royalties. 

Requirements: From the following information: (1) submit a summary of royalty liability account showing the following transactions and the final settlement; (2) submit the journal entry recording the adjustment of October 1, 1939 inventories; (3) submit the journal entry setting up the advance royalty at December 31, 1941, as a deferred charge.

ADVANCED ACCOUNTING 

On October 1, 1933, the Lee Publishing Company entered into a special royalty contract for the publication of a book on a religious subject, the royalty of $40.00 a hundred to be paid on or before October 1, 1939, on a minimum publication of 50,000 copies. It was stipulated that in the interval the payments were to be made from time to time as the books were bound and ready for sale. The publishing company proceeded to print the minimum number of sheets and included the royalty in the sheet cost, setting up the liability therefor. Up to 

October 1, 1939, the royalty had been paid as agreed on the basis of 13,500 copies bound, and the balance on the remaining 36,500 became dué.

However, owing to the slowness of the sale of the book, it was agreed on the latter date that the original contract was to be modified for the balance of the royalties and negotiations commenced to fix the new terms. The publishing company, having on hand 2,840 copies of bound stock, then also decided to write off against its surplus all the royalty included in its inventories. 

During the years 1940 and 1941 there were 1,300 additional copies sold and on December 31, 1941, there remained in the hands of the publishers 1,540 bound copies, but no further sheet stock had been bound. On that date a final agreement was made whereby the remaining royalty liability was settled and paid at fifty cents on the dollar. 

Thereupon the publishing company, in view of a revived demand for the publication, reinstated as a deferred charge the advance royalty actually paid on the stock on hand. (A. I. A.)
